topics.topic: Classroom safety, bullying, violence, and learner protection
topics.summary: Members raised bullying, school violence, online harms, learner-rights implementation, and the need for mental-health and counseling personnel. DepEd said more than 30000 of over 36000 schools had functioning Child Protection Committees, all schools had learner formation officers, and hiring for 10000 school counselor-associate positions was underway after more than 20000 applications. Members questioned the use and possible harms of active-shooter drills; DepEd said drills were funded through school MOOE, had been postponed and toned down after psychiatrists' concerns, and remained subject to revision. DepEd cited proposed additional funding of about 100 million dollars for mental-health capacity building and 8000000000 for security measures, while a later safety discussion stated 54000000000 pesos, with the precise component unclear. Members also secured commitments on immediate protection for severe bullying, verification of a Grade 1 material, noncoercive Pride Month activities, reports on learner protection and gender-and-development compliance, and counselor-allocation data. The issue landed with ongoing implementation and reporting commitments, rather than a fully resolved determination of funding adequacy.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DepEd would prevent and respond to bullying, school violence, and online harms; protect learners; and fund school security and mental-health measures. Members also asked whether counselor vacancies, Child Protection Committees, reporting systems, drills, and related policies were adequately staffed, implemented, and monitored.

topics.topic: Textbook, instructional-material, and furniture procurement backlogs
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar and other members questioned the reduction in textbook and instructional-material funding and pressed DepEd on whether procurement would translate into delivery, particularly in remote schools. Secretary Angara said DepEd had procured all 105 curriculum titles and was pursuing a one-textbook-per-learner goal, but acknowledged delivery delays, including delays of 1 year. Rep. Amato and civil-society questions highlighted classroom and repair backlogs, while DepEd cited a backlog of roughly 142000 classrooms, more than 350 LGU partners, and a request for 98000000000 in infrastructure funding. DepEd said early procurement, regional or decentralized procurement, and PPP and LGU participation would improve absorptive capacity and delivery. Rep. Catulpos separately cited a drop in textbook procurement from about 19 billion to 6 billion and questioned the FY 2027 classroom target. DepEd did not resolve the funding and delivery concerns, and it undertook to verify whether a questioned grade 1 material was officially authorized.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DepEd’s proposed FY 2027 procurement and infrastructure allocations would reduce backlogs in textbooks, instructional materials, classrooms, and related facilities, particularly in last-mile and poorer schools. Members also asked how DepEd would address delayed delivery, underutilization of funds, procurement decentralization, and the age appropriateness and authorization of learning materials.

topics.topic: Computerization, connectivity, and digital-transformation funding
topics.summary: The committee questioned DepEd's reduced Computerization Program, the funding for 50000 teacher laptops, undelivered computer packages, school connectivity, and the absence of a dedicated AI appropriation. Secretary Angara said prior computerization deliveries had been completed and that DepEd would improve tracking through early procurement and decentralization. He reported 99 percent internet coverage, 460 schools without internet, an aspiration for 100 Mbps minimum bandwidth, and a goal of reaching 10 to 12000 schools with AI tools from about 3000 schools. DepEd described AI applications for hazard mapping, teacher support, administrative work, and learner reading assessment, while warning that safeguards and teacher training were necessary. Angara said over 1000000 faculty and students had been trained and that 115000000 had been carved out in 20 26 for an AI research center, but there was no AI line item in the 20 27 budget. Members expressed support but left funding adequacy and the scale-up of digital services for the continuing budget process.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DepEd's proposed computerization, connectivity, and digital-transformation funding would address prior delivery and absorptive-capacity problems, expand meaningful school and learner access to computers and the internet, and support responsible use of AI. Members also asked what specific AI uses, training, bandwidth, monitoring, and funding were in place.

topics.topic: Inclusive and special-needs education funding
topics.summary: Representative Sandania questioned the apparent reduction of special-needs education funding from about 1 billion to 850 million and proposed restoring or increasing the allocation. DepEd said the comparison was affected by congressional insertions in the prior budget and appealed for an additional 541.5 million to support staffing, facilities, equipment, schools, and multidisciplinary-team capacity-building. The agency said 81.6 million would construct six Inclusive Learning Resource Centers, bringing the projected total to 38 against a target of 1,642, and reported 10.8 million for learner-support-center enhancement. Representative Caroline Agiau sought additional funding for disability assessments and assistive devices, but the transcript did not provide the requested counts of learners awaiting assessment or lacking devices. The committee later identified a shortfall of about 190 million to reach FY 2026 levels for the group of programs that included SNED and requested a reprioritized list. The matter therefore landed with DepEd commitments for further submissions and with funding augmentation left for committee consideration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 funding for special-needs and inclusive education was sufficient to implement the Inclusive Education Act. Members asked what additional funding would cover, how many Inclusive Learning Resource Centers could be built, and whether DepEd could provide adequate assessment, assistive-device, staffing, and learner-support services.

topics.topic: Indigenous Peoples Education and culturally responsive learning
topics.summary: Dadah Kiram Ismula questioned the proposed Indigenous People's Education allocation and whether it could meet the needs of IP communities and learners. DepEd described funding for delivery in additional schools, translanguaging training, curriculum localization, indigenous traditions, classrooms, integrated schools, and last-mile schools. The agency cited 560700 learners and 4400 schools and said 78000000 was needed to bring the program to the 20 26 level, while Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara said the IPED grant was 76000000 and that DepEd had appealed for an additional 78000000. Rep. Caroline Agyao separately urged a substantial increase and clearer treatment of IPED within inclusive education, including support for indigenous learners with special needs. DepEd acknowledged the appeal but did not secure a stated approval, leaving the adequacy and final amount unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed Indigenous Peoples Education allocation could address the needs of IP learners, including culturally responsive materials, indigenous-language instruction, staffing, school access, and learning spaces. Members also asked whether DepEd could substantially increase and separately identify funding for IPED within inclusive education.

topics.topic: Madrasa, Arabic-language, and Moro education programs
topics.summary: Representative Dada Ismula asked DepEd for the original request and adequacy of funding for the 2027 Madrasa Education Program, citing an allocation of about 504 million and receiving an agency figure of 2030000000 for the proposed DepEd budget. The agency said funding covered increased subsidies, additional assets, and compensation connected with Alive and Arabic-language classes, but several personnel and compensation figures were unclear. Ismula said Akbayan would push to increase the Madrasa budget because the system was integral to Muslim Filipinos. The discussion also covered Indigenous Peoples education, including a 2027 figure of about 76 million, support for 4471 more schools, and figures for learners and schools that were not fully explained. DepEd described curriculum localization, culturally responsive materials, access measures, and last-mile schools, but the subsequent question on Islamic studies and Arabic-language teachers in Sulu was left unanswered.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish DepEd's original request for the 2027 Madrasa Education Program, its proposed allocation, and whether the funding was adequate for Moro learners, Arabic-language classes, and related education programs. The member also sought details on Indigenous Peoples education funding and began asking about Islamic studies and Arabic-language teachers in Sulu.

topics.topic: School feeding, ECCD, and learner nutrition programs
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar flagged a 55 percent reduction in school-based feeding, and Secretary Angara said the proposed funding would support only 120 days rather than 180 days and would reduce coverage, including universal feeding for Grade 1. DepEd linked feeding to weight gain, attendance, and improved learning, and said ECCD responsibilities were shared with DILG, LGUs, DSWD, and the National Nutrition Council, with DepEd focused on curriculum and participation in the ECCD Council. Rep. Zubiri supported increasing ARAL funding from about 9 billion to 16 billion after DepEd reported that 6.7 million learners were covered and 4.5 million advanced reading levels. The committee chair questioned whether the 26 billion 2026 feeding allocation was being utilized, and DepEd reported 45.8 percent current utilization, with school-year carryover and higher historical rates. DepEd said it would submit a reprioritized list of priority programs, and the committee agreed to consider restoration or augmentation before the budget moved forward.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed reductions would affect school-based feeding, including the number of feeding days, learner coverage, and nutrition and learning outcomes. Members also asked how DepEd's ECCD responsibilities related to day-care feeding and malnutrition response, and whether funding for ARAL and other foundational-learning programs should be restored or augmented.

topics.topic: Voucher programs and senior-high-school beneficiary controls
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar questioned a reported 100 percent reduction in senior-high-school voucher assistance and sought clarification of the FY 2026 and FY 2027 amounts. Secretary Angara said the consolidated voucher program, including JDVP and ESC, was PHP 38000000000, about PHP 3000000000 below the prior year. Rep. Montes asked whether the allocation would cover unpaid obligations to private participating schools; DepEd said the backlog was less than 10000000 and that the FY 2027 voucher budget was 38000000000. A representative then raised ghost beneficiaries and fictitious claims. Secretary Angara described five validation layers, payment holds, post-audits, inspections, and end-of-year enrollment checks, and reported one conviction and four filed cases. The issue ended with members recognizing that the safeguards were expected to minimize, but not entirely eliminate, recurrence.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the FY 2027 funding level for senior-high-school voucher programs, including whether appropriations were adequate to cover obligations to participating private schools. It also examined whether DepEd had controls to prevent ghost beneficiaries, fictitious claims, and payments for learners who were not actually enrolled.

topics.topic: Teacher loans, APDS payroll deductions, and take-home pay
topics.summary: Rep. Adrian Amato raised teacher financial literacy, loan support, and the possibility of an annual allocation, while Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara said DepEd would examine the proposal and work with him. Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. then questioned the legal basis and welfare effects of allowing APDS loans for up to 7 years, including the number of teachers with multiple loans and their average and median take-home pay. Secretary Angara said the arrangement was voluntary, complied with the GAA protection for 5000 in net take-home pay, and could give teachers longer repayment periods and lower payments. Rep. Nazal cited a reported rate of 3.5 percent per month, roughly 42 percent per year, and asked about lender oversight. DepEd stated that accredited lenders were subject to a 9.6 percent per annum ceiling, while higher-rate lenders were probably not accredited and fell outside DepEd's police power. The requested loan and take-home-pay data and specific legal basis were not resolved during the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DepEd legally authorized APDS automatic payroll deductions for loans of up to 7 years, whether extended loan terms helped teachers or prolonged indebtedness, and what teachers' take-home pay was after deductions. Members also questioned the interest-rate ceiling and DepEd's ability to police nonaccredited lenders.

topics.topic: National Museum operating, exhibition, and new-museum funding
topics.summary: Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles asked whether a building in her district could support a component museum, and Jeremy Barnes said the National Museum was developing a regional museum in Koronadal City while exploring Lake Sebu, General Santos, and other culturally significant locations. Barnes agreed to coordinate with her team about the offered premises. Secretary Angara said DepEd encouraged museum visits and stronger arts and culture education, while Representative Benitez supported early and sustained exposure to creativity. Barnes reported that the National Museum had opened its 5th museum under the administration in the last 3 years and was preparing facilities in several locations for 2027. He said MOE needed an augmentation of 65000000 and that 79000000 was proposed for exhibitions. Representative Zubiri supported the requests, warned against opening unfurnished or understaffed museums, and asked that Bukidnon be considered; Secretary Angara committed to the request, but no funding was approved during the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the National Museum and DepEd could support new or component museums, including their staffing, operations, utilities, maintenance, and exhibitions. Members also asked whether proposed museum sites could be considered and whether the agency's operating and exhibition funding requests should be augmented.

topics.topic: AI, curriculum reform, and teacher capability development
topics.summary: Members questioned DepEd's readiness to use AI, train teachers, upgrade the curriculum, strengthen GMRC and Values Education, and prepare learners for future work. Secretary Angara said AI could support teachers and personalized learning but required safeguards, age-appropriate introduction, teacher training, and stronger connectivity. DepEd cited about 3 billion for teacher training, 150 million for its eCare AI research center, and 115 million in 2026 AI-center research funding, while acknowledging no dedicated AI line item in the 2027 budget. Officials described GMRC teacher training for grades 1 to 10, values integration across subjects, and curriculum additions involving life skills, AI, and future skills. Members manifested support for DepEd's budget, and the agency agreed to monitor AI's effects and share relevant GMRC survey results.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DepEd would fund and implement AI, curriculum reform, teacher capability development, GMRC and Values Education, and future-skills preparation. Members also asked how AI would be used without weakening critical thinking, creativity, or human-centered education.

topics.topic: Tourism infrastructure, access roads, and interagency project priorities
topics.summary: Members questioned whether priority and emerging tourism destinations had adequate roads, visitor facilities, and related infrastructure, and whether DOT's promotional work was matched by national investments. DOT said promotions and infrastructure required equal resources, but road construction generally remained with DPWH through TRIP, while DOT funded facilities and coordinated with DPWH, DOTR, TIEZA, and local governments. DOT disclosed that 28 Tier 2 projects worth approximately 6.02 billion were proposed, but continuing and new TRIP projects were not included in the FY2027 NEP. Members also discussed a proposed 1.64 billion augmentation, a Region 6 allocation of about 50.8 million, and roughly 5.2 billion for TIEZA multiyear projects. DOT committed to destination inventories, regional planning, and follow-up on unresolved environmental and infrastructure matters, while the committee requested a list of TIEZA's ongoing multiyear projects.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether priority tourism destinations had adequate roads, facilities, and basic services, and whether DOT, DPWH, DOTR, TIEZA, DBM, and local governments were coordinating their investments. Members also asked how projects would be funded, continued, and prioritized across emerging, high-potential, and regional destinations.

topics.topic: TIEZA funding, travel-tax resources, and multiyear infrastructure projects
topics.summary: DOT presented about 1.64 billion in additional requests for its attached agencies, including about 1.31 billion for TIEZA infrastructure projects, while warning that travel-tax abolition could create funding implications. TIEZA said around 300 personnel could be affected if the travel tax were abolished. DBM said no FY 2027 national government subsidy tied to the proposed abolition was included because the measures had not been enacted, but TIEZA could use available collections and other resources. A minority member sought a tourism-destination inventory and received the Secretary's commitment. Howard Gintu raised the Region 6 allocation, clarified at 50800000 pesos after conflicting figures, and questioned the continuity of TIEZA's multiyear projects. TIEZA said almost all projects were multiyear and cited around 5.2 billion pesos for 2027; Gintu requested a project list for possible committee support.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much additional funding DOT's attached agencies, particularly TIEZA, were requesting; how travel-tax abolition could affect TIEZA resources and personnel; and whether ongoing tourism infrastructure projects, including projects in Region 6, had secure multiyear financing. Members also sought destination inventories and a list of ongoing TIEZA projects to support possible appropriations.

topics.topic: FY 2027 DOT budget, OSEC funding, and proposed augmentation
topics.summary: Secretary Dita Angara Matai presented a total FY 2027 DOT budget of about 5.47 billion, including about 3.53 billion for DOT OSEC, and requested 82330000 in additional funding. She also asked the committee to restore the DOT's FY 2026 funding level, which was about 3.69 billion for OSEC. Representative Rufus Rodriguez supported the DOT budget and proposed augmentation, citing 82000000 for OSEC and 1600000000 for attached agencies; the transcript also contained an unclear rendering of the combined amount. Representative Javi Benitez asked about funding for Terra Madre Asia Pacific, and DOT officials said the 45000000 FY 2027 Tier 2 request had not been approved, despite a projected ROI of about 132 percent. The secretary committed to approach DBM, while another official said the DOT would seek other funding options and coordinate with the Tourism Promotions Board. The issue therefore landed with agency commitments but without a recorded final approval of the requested augmentations.
topics.question: What was the DOT's proposed FY 2027 budget, particularly for the DOT Office of the Secretary (OSEC), and what additional funding did the department seek? The committee also sought to determine whether members would support augmentation and whether specific unfunded tourism initiatives, including Terra Madre Asia Pacific, could be restored.

topics.topic: Tourism promotion, domestic and international marketing allocations
topics.summary: The DOT presented 1000000000 for its FY 2027 branding campaign and said the campaign would combine international visibility with conversion into travel and spending. Members supported additional funding but questioned competitiveness, private-sector counterparts, infrastructure needs, and whether promotion could be separated from broader tourism reforms. On domestic and international marketing, the DOT stated that 60 percent of the branding allocation would target international markets and 40 percent domestic travelers, serving 13 key markets. It cited 69 percent growth for China, around 29 percent for Vietnam, around 30 percent for India, and a 17 percent South Korea decline addressed through 50000000 in campaign funding. The DOT also cited a training allocation of 198752000, pesos, while a member referenced 230000000 for training. The discussion ended with support for the budget, but without final action on the augmentation or a definitive destination-investment road map.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOT would allocate limited tourism-promotion resources between domestic and international markets, and whether the allocations were tied to measurable returns. Members also asked how branding, celebrity or influencer campaigns, training, and destination investment would support tourism competitiveness.

topics.topic: Domestic travel affordability, airfares, and possible fuel subsidy
topics.summary: Rep. Perci Cendaña raised the affordability of domestic travel and asked how the DOT would respond to volatile fuel prices, limited aircraft capacity, and infrastructure gaps. The DOT said island routes were expensive because turbopropeller aircraft carried only about 70 to 80 seats and airport limitations restricted supply, while larger aircraft and runway improvements could lower costs. It said a fuel subsidy modeled on Vietnam's program could help but was still finalizing the proposal and gathering data. Cendaña requested the DOTR's airport-improvement commitments and the DOT's FY 2027 contingency plan, while another member cautioned that affordability claims required actual investment and reforms. Rep. Elmer Catulpos later asked whether Filipinos traveled abroad because neighboring countries were 20 to 30 percent cheaper; the DOT answered that domestic tourism remained the backbone of the industry and cited 80 percent of tourism income as domestic. The matter landed with agency follow-up commitments and remained open pending the requested documents and subsidy details.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why domestic airfares remained high, whether the DOT had a plan to make domestic travel more affordable—including a possible fuel subsidy—and how infrastructure, tourism promotion, and competitiveness measures would address the problem. Members also sought to clarify whether Filipinos were choosing foreign travel because neighboring destinations were cheaper and how the DOT balanced domestic and international marketing.

topics.topic: Tourism destination inventory and integrated development planning
topics.summary: Members supported DOT budget augmentation while citing existing road maps for Cagayan de Oro, Bukidnon, Mindanao historical sites, and other destinations. Rep. Sergio Dagooc sought a coordinated inventory of tourism destinations, and the DOT secretary committed to it. Rep. Salvador Pleyto asked how high-potential destinations and access-road needs were integrated into DPWH and DOTR spending; DOT described interagency coordination but acknowledged that infrastructure funding was not included in the FY 2027 NEP. Members also proposed an integrated classification of top, rising-star, and hidden-gem destinations and interprovince tourism plans. DOT reported training, disaster-assistance, and regional funding figures, although the Region 6 amount was stated inconsistently. TIEZA said almost all projects were multiyear and cited around 5200000000 pesos for FY 2027, while a list of ongoing projects was requested for further committee action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DOT and other agencies were identifying, prioritizing, and financing tourism destinations, particularly emerging and high-potential sites. Members also asked whether infrastructure plans were coordinated across agencies and provinces, and whether funding and multiyear projects would support those priorities.

topics.topic: Travel-tax abolition and its effect on DOT personnel and projects
topics.summary: The committee first asked about personnel consequences of abolishing the travel tax, and DOT said around 300 travel-tax personnel would be affected, with some terminated and others receiving separation incentives. A committee member also sought alternative financing for tourism, heritage and related projects. Representative Sergio Dagooc then asked DBM why TIEZA's requested subsidy and tourism-infrastructure funding were not augmented. DBM said the FY 2027 subsidy was not included because abolition bills remained under deliberation, but TIEZA could use available funds totaling about 2.355 billion, including the stated unobligated allotment and unreleased operations figures. DOT described its sustainable-tourism convergence program, which had conducted 13 trainings for 417 participants. The Secretary committed to the requested tourism-destination inventory, while no specific budget augmentation or deadline was resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the personnel consequences if the travel tax were abolished and how tourism infrastructure and related projects would be financed without that revenue. It also asked whether TIEZA could receive augmented funding and whether DOT would prepare an inventory of tourism destinations.

topics.topic: Tourism-worker training, certifications, and employment
topics.summary: A committee member asked the DOT about its FY 2027 tourism-worker training and certification program. Assistant Secretary Tina Aquino said the indicative core training activities would amount to 198752000, pesos. A member also cited 230000000 for training, 1000000000 for the branding campaign, and 230000000 for industry training, while referring to 7.7 tourism workers and four certificates; the precise context of those figures was unclear. Aquino said the programs would serve various affected stakeholders and include recognized certification programs. The member then proposed infrastructure road maps distinguishing top destinations, rising-star destinations, and hidden gems to guide investment. The member manifested support for the DOT budget, but no substantive agency answer on the infrastructure framework or quantified employment outcome appeared before the excerpt ended.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much the DOT proposed for FY 2027 tourism-worker training and certification, how broadly the effort would cover tourism stakeholders and workers, and whether it would improve employment outcomes. It also asked whether destination infrastructure planning would be organized around different categories of tourism destinations to guide investment.

topics.topic: Women and child safety, anti-trafficking, and tourism safeguards
topics.summary: Sarah Elago asked the DOT about regional focal persons, training, monitoring, and referral systems for women and child safety and anti-trafficking in tourism areas. The DOT reported 19 activities and 931 participants for 20 25, 16 hires, 1 responsible personnel in each regional office, and 40 trainings with 2001 participants from January to July 20 26. It said regional offices coordinated with police and with DOJ, DSWD, LGUs, ECPAT Philippines, the PNP, and IACAT. Elago also raised the 20 25 trafficking report and asked about access roads to declared tourism destinations. The DOT said those projects were not funded in the 20 27 NEP and committed to further coordination with DPWH and TIEZA on continuity and implementation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DOT had functional regional focal persons, training, monitoring, and referral systems to address trafficking, sexual exploitation, violence against women, and child safety in tourism areas. It also asked about continuity of access-road projects serving declared tourism destinations.

topics.topic: Dive, marine, and environmentally sustainable tourism
topics.summary: Secretary Dita Angara Matai presented dive tourism as a high-value sector generating about 1.3 billion in revenue, with 29 clusters and 956 dive sites identified nationwide. She said annual dive-tourism revenue could rise to about 100.5 billion by 2030 from about 73 billion in 20 23, and reported 3 30 certified dive professionals and individuals as of June 20 26. The committee cited 15200000 pesos for dive-destination development, promotion, and sustainability and asked how environmental safeguards were incorporated. The PCSSD executive director answered that the commission worked with the Marine Science Institute, Coral Beach Watch, and DENR-related officials, and that all programs included environmental standards. Representative Javi Benitez later questioned the balance between promotions, infrastructure, and cost, and raised dynamite fishing affecting marine sanctuaries. The DOT said promotions and infrastructure required equal effort, while an agency official said DENR generally led enforcement and undertook to revert with the missing data.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOT and its attached agencies would develop dive tourism while protecting marine ecosystems and ensuring environmental sustainability. Members also asked whether the DOT helped protect marine sanctuaries and how tourism promotion would be balanced with infrastructure and enforcement against threats such as dynamite fishing.

topics.topic: Terra Madre Asia Pacific event funding
topics.summary: Rep. Javi Benitez asked whether the DOT's FY 2027 proposal included funding for Terra Madre Asia Pacific, citing the event's participation by 25 countries, around 2500 delegates, and 75000 visitors. The DOT said the event was not specifically identified in the proposal and disclosed that its 45000000 pesos Tier 2 request to DBM had not been approved. Director Paulo Tugbangpo said the agency projected an ROI of about 132 percent. Benitez also cited reported sales of about 46.59 million and a combined return of almost 398 million, while the organizers' reported 1400000 earnings figure was unclear. The secretary undertook to seek approval for the second-tier request, and the undersecretary said the DOT would find funding options and coordinate with the Tourism Promotions Board. The matter was left committed but dependent on subsequent approval or funding action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DOT's FY 2027 proposed budget contained funding for Terra Madre Asia Pacific, scheduled for July next year, and whether the agency would pursue restoration of the requested amount. It also sought the event's projected tourism return and the basis for supporting the request.

topics.topic: Intramuros relocation and services for informal settler families
topics.summary: Rep. Elago asked about the Intramuros administration's relocation of informal settler families and the services available at the relocation sites. Attorney Joanne Padilla said 388 families had been relocated to Marong Resal out of 470 intended beneficiaries. She identified a perimeter fence, solar streetlights, a material recovery facility, and solid waste management as program provisions. Rep. Elago continued to question the adequacy of community support services, utilities, and transition assistance. The transcript did not contain a clear answer or commitment concerning the utilities problem or the transition period.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how many informal settler families had been relocated under the Intramuros administration program and whether the relocation sites provided the necessary support services, facilities, and utilities. It also raised concerns about the transition period and services for displaced families.

topics.topic: Disaster assistance for tourism establishments and workers
topics.summary: Representative Rufus Rodriguez asked whether the DOT had a dedicated program for tourism establishments and workers affected by disasters. He cited canceled bookings, damaged establishments, small resorts, homestays, guides, drivers, vendors, and other tourism workers. The DOT said its regional offices assessed affected workers, establishments, and infrastructure and that it endorsed workers to DSWD and LGUs for family food packs and emergency cash transfers. The agency referred to an amount transcribed as "2 5000000 pesos" for incorporation or carrying under the NDRRMC for fiscal year 2027. The discussion landed with an agency commitment, although the amount was unclear in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DOT had a dedicated program or budget to assist tourism establishments and workers affected by disasters, including small resorts, homestays, guides, drivers, vendors, and other tourism workers. It also sought to clarify how affected workers and businesses would be identified and supported.

topics.topic: Duty Free Philippines Fiesta Mall rightsizing and employee claims
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co asked Duty Free Philippines why it was rightsizing Fiesta Mall and whether the agency would remain an anchor tenant under a redevelopment by a private lessor. COO Joel Cinco said the lease had expired, the complex was underused, and rightsizing was intended to reduce rent and operating-cost pressures while using the appropriate space. He clarified that the current action concerned mall space, while the earlier restructuring had occurred in 20 22 20 23, and said employee claims were being addressed through notices, human-resources assistance, compensation facilitation, and earmarking of remaining obligations. Co also asked about partnerships with local and homegrown businesses; Cinco cited hotels, e-wallet companies, tourism organizations, and other government agencies. Duty Free committed to provide the requested rightsizing plan, employee-claims updates, and partnership information.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why Duty Free Philippines was rightsizing its Fiesta Mall operations, whether the arrangement involved a new lessor and continued occupancy, and whether there were broader rightsizing or asset-disposition plans. It also asked how employee claims would be addressed and how Duty Free partnered with local and regional businesses.

topics.topic: Outbound travel, foreign arrivals, and tourism competitiveness
topics.summary: Rep. Perci Cendaña raised the effects of fuel prices, airline capacity, and airport limitations on domestic travel costs and asked for DOTR commitments and a 2027 contingency plan. The DOT attributed high island-destination airfares to limited supply and infrastructure, and said it was finalizing a fuel-subsidy proposal while pursuing airport improvements, training, accreditation, branding, and private-sector partnerships. Rep. Elmer Catulpos then asked whether Filipinos were choosing neighboring countries because they were 20 to 30 percent cheaper, citing 7650000 outbound Filipinos and 5870000 foreign tourists; the DOT responded that domestic tourism remained the backbone, with 134000000 domestic tourists in 2024 and roughly 6000000 to 6480000 foreign arrivals in 2025. The DOT said 80 percent of tourism income came from domestic tourism and 20 percent from inbound tourism, while international marketing received 60 percent of the branding allocation and domestic marketing 40 percent. It identified 13 key markets, cited growth in China, Vietnam, and India, and said 50000000 was being used to address a 17 percent South Korean decline. The agency also discussed influencers and homegrown talents such as SB19 and cited a 230000000 pesos training budget for 2027; requested documents and the fuel-subsidy proposal were not shown as delivered.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why domestic travel remained costly and how the DOT would improve tourism competitiveness amid fuel-price pressures, infrastructure constraints, and a limited budget. Members also asked whether outbound Filipino travel and changes in foreign-tourist arrivals reflected cheaper competing destinations, and how the DOT was allocating and targeting its marketing resources.

topics.topic: PSA civil-registration funding and organizational capacity
topics.summary: The bill sponsor sought funding for a modernized civil registration system, including digitization, expanded access, and anti-fraud safeguards. The PSA supported the bill and said the existing civil-registration law dated to 1931, but requested a stronger civil registration office under Section 6. It said the PSA and local civil registrars lacked sufficient capacity to expand registration services and protect records from fraud. The DBM answered that any office creation or strengthening would require its usual evaluation and review under the government optimization program. It also recommended using "existing retirement laws" and clarified that the legal service in Section 61 referred to the PSA's existing legal service. The organizational and funding issues remained open.
topics.question: The committee was considering whether the substitute bill and its funding should provide for a stronger Philippine Civil Registry Office within the PSA, given the need to expand services and protect records from fraud. It also sought to establish how the proposed organizational changes would be evaluated by the DBM and how the bill's legal-service provision should be interpreted.

topics.topic: 10% PSA registration-income retention for immediate operations
topics.summary: Rep. Monique Lagdameo initially moved to delete the Section 78 provision concerning PSA-generated income. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez objected, arguing that PSA should retain 10% of registration income for immediate operations and modernization instead of waiting for congressional appropriations. DBM said it preferred the one-fund concept but deferred to the committee, warning that retention would reduce money entering the General Fund. The PSA-side author subsequently supported retaining the provision, while Rep. Romeo Momo cautioned that other earning agencies might seek similar treatment. The agency estimated the 10% at about 1.139 billion based on 2025 revenue. Lagdameo revised the motion to exclude the Section 78 deletion, and the chair approved it without objection.
topics.question: The committee sought to determine whether Section 78 should retain a provision allowing the PSA to use 10% of civil-registration income for immediate operations and modernization, rather than placing all such income in the General Fund. Members also asked how much the retained income would yield.

topics.topic: Infrastructure master plan council size and agency overlap
topics.summary: Romeo Momo Jr. sponsored a thirty-year infrastructure master plan and a presidentially chaired MIND Council. DEPDEV argued that the CIDMP and council substantially overlapped with functions already assigned to DEPDEV and related bodies under Republic Act number 12145, while DBM addressed staffing and appropriations language. Rep. Rodriguez questioned the proposed council of 28 members and suggested reducing it to about 11, with Rep. Pomerangay supporting agency participation only as needed. Romeo Momo Jr. said the broad membership was intended to prevent conflicts among infrastructure plans and agreed to review the membership issue. The committee ultimately adopted amendments requiring use of DEPDEV's existing staffing complement, DBM evaluation and approval of designations, and more general appropriations language, then approved the measure subject to those amendments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed master plan and MIND Council duplicated existing DEPDEV functions, and whether the council's proposed membership was workable. It also considered how the council secretariat would be staffed and whether DBM approval would be required.

topics.topic: Disaster risk financing, DREAM Funds, and insurance structure
topics.summary: Rep. Joseph Lara sponsored the DRFI framework, citing annual disaster-related asset losses of about 177 billion and an equivalent of about US3.5 billion dollars. OCD supported the measure but asked that its relationship with the existing DREAM Funds be clearly defined and protected against duplication. DOF supported prearranged financing, multilayered risk financing, and parametric insurance, while the Insurance Commission sought clearer boundaries over government assets, existing institutions, asset prioritization, and claims guidelines. Treasury objected to creating a special fund because of the regular budget process, trust-receipt treatment of insurance proceeds, and the one-fund policy. DBM recommended calling it a program funded through a GAA line item and requiring DBM review of positions. The committee adopted those amendments and approved the measure, although a member's parametric-insurance clarification received a garbled and unclear response.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish how the proposed disaster risk financing and insurance framework would complement existing DREAM Funds and government insurance arrangements, and whether the proposed financing mechanism should be a special fund or a program. It also sought to clarify the respective roles of the Insurance Commission, Department of Finance, Bureau of the Treasury, DBM, and the proposed DRFIB.

topics.topic: Community Driven Development appropriations and implementation safeguards
topics.summary: Rep. France Pomeran sponsored the substitute bill institutionalizing CDD and described its community-participation, transparency, accountability, and poverty-reduction objectives. DSWD supported the measure without objection, including the appropriations provision and the inclusion of amounts necessary for continued implementation in the annual General Appropriations Act. DBM requested flexible language referring to prevailing community-participation procurement guidelines and fiscal safeguards for agreements with LGUs. The committee adopted both amendments and approved the measure subject to them. No specific peso amount was stated; the appropriations commitment was described as current agency appropriations and amounts as may be necessary for continued implementation.
topics.question: The committee was determining whether to institutionalize Community Driven Development (CDD) as a national strategy, provide appropriations for its sustained implementation, and establish safeguards for participation, procurement, LGU agreements, accounting, and auditing. It also considered whether the proposed implementation provisions required technical amendments.

topics.topic: Medical education infrastructure and CHED funding
topics.summary: The bill sponsor and an author presented the proposed Philippine Medical Act as a modernization measure covering medical education, internship, postgraduate training, and physician regulation. PRC supported the bill and noted the proposed increase in PRB membership from six to seven and terms from three years to five years. PRC nevertheless questioned the creation and budget of the PGMEC and proposed adapting the existing CPSP program instead. CHED supported the bill but requested financial support for subsidiary bodies, an organic secretariat, data infrastructure, fee utilization, and state universities and colleges. PRC committed to submit its position, but the transcript recorded no final resolution on the funding or PGMEC issues.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish how the proposed Philippine Medical Act would affect medical education, postgraduate training, regulatory councils, and the budgets of PRC and CHED. It also sought the agencies' positions on the proposed postgraduate medical education committee and the financial and infrastructure requirements of the new functions.

topics.topic: Resident and fellow compensation and DBM salary review
topics.summary: The DOH supported improving resident and fellow compensation but requested further study and a budgetary impact analysis. It identified the current entry-level resident classification as salary grade 21 and the proposed classification as salary grade 22. DBM warned that a fixed salary grade 22 minimum could distort hospital employee salaries and proposed using the revised compensation and position classification system, subject to DBM review and applicable rules. The sponsors accepted the DBM recommendations, including safeguards for the medical councils and budgeting, accounting, and auditing provisions. The committee approved the amendments and then approved the measure subject to those amendments, while the requested budgetary impact study remained unaddressed as a separate action.
topics.question: The committee was determining how the proposed compensation increase for residents and fellows should be evaluated, including its budgetary impact and compatibility with the government compensation system. It also considered DBM safeguards for the creation of medical councils and provisions affecting foreign medical graduates.

topics.topic: Local-government performance incentives and SGLG funding
topics.summary: Rep. Albert Garcia sponsored a bill establishing a data-driven performance-measurement system for local governments and linking improvements to performance-based rewards. He cited a system covering about 42,000 barangayes, 1,400-plus local-government units, about 180 cities, and 82 provinces. DBM recommended removing national government agencies from the scope, requiring DBM approval for additional positions, coordinating with DILG on barangay bonuses, retaining the SGLG fund, and preserving the 2% operating-fund provision. Garcia accepted the DBM comments, and the committee adopted corresponding amendments, including retention of SGLG provisions and deletion of references to national government agencies. The committee approved the amendments and the measure, subject to style.
topics.question: The committee was determining how the proposed performance-measurement and meritocracy system would apply to local governments and barangays, including the treatment of national government agencies. It also examined whether the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) fund, barangay performance-based bonuses, DBM approval requirements, and the 2% operating-fund cap should be retained or amended.

topics.topic: DFA FY2027 budget request, allotment classes, and utilization
topics.summary: The DFA presented an FY2027 request of about 35 billion, while its stated net level for the department and attached agencies was 35,170,000,000, 17% above the 2026 net. Maintenance and other operating expenses accounted for 54% of the request, personnel services for 39%, and capital outlay for 7%; major items included next-generation passport funding, the International Commitments Fund, ATN and legal assistance, ICT, and the building fund. The agency reported an 80% 2025 BUR and close to 53% utilization in the first half of the current year, attributing lower performance to delayed retrofitting, transferred ATN functions, deferred building projects, and changing passport demand. Members requested detailed spending and program documents, particularly for the Security Council campaign, ATN Fund, ICT, and ePassport allocations. Rodriguez supported placing 250,000,000 for cybersecurity and restoring 300,000,000 to the building fund, while the Foreign Service Institute sought MXN 6,500,000 for HMO coverage. The committee left the additional funding requests for written submission and subsequent consideration, with a deadline set for the following Wednesday.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the DFA and attached agencies’ FY2027 funding requirement, the distribution of that request across allotment classes, the reasons for the increase, and the department’s utilization performance. Members also examined specific funding needs for passports, ICT and cybersecurity, buildings, consular operations, HMO, and permanent positions, and identified documents or augmentations to be submitted for further consideration.

topics.topic: Assistance to Nationals and Legal Assistance Funds for overseas Filipinos
topics.summary: The committee asked the DFA to clarify ATN and LAF coverage, appropriations, utilization, eligibility rules, and approval authority after the DMW assumed responsibility for more OFWs. The DFA said 1,000,000,000 was appropriated annually for the ATN Fund from 2022 to 2025 and reported 2,884 ATN beneficiaries from January to July 2026, including 387 repatriation beneficiaries. It also cited welfare assistance of dollars 559,000,000, medical assistance of 20,000,000, and shipment of remains of 40,000,000, although some wording and currency attribution were unclear. The DFA said it generally did not deny qualified requests and that its office handled recommendations below 20%, while the Secretary approved amounts above that threshold. Members requested the ATN guidelines and detailed ATN and LAF utilization records, including balances, expenditures, approvals, rejections, nonqualifications, and beneficiaries. The DFA also described ongoing coordination on distressed seafarers and safe passage through embassies, MWOs, DMW, the IMO, and bilateral channels.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Assistance to Nationals (ATN) Fund and Legal Assistance Fund (LAF) were allocated, utilized, and administered, including which overseas Filipinos remained covered after the creation of the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW). It also sought beneficiary, expenditure, approval, rejection, eligibility, and utilization data, as well as the DFA's continuing assistance to distressed OFWs and seafarers.

topics.topic: Consular-service expansion, satellite offices, and passport access
topics.summary: Rep. Niko Raul Daza supported the DFA budget and cited the funded forty third consular office in Katarman, Northern Samar as an example of service expansion. The DFA reported 42 consular offices, more than 1.5 million passports processed, and 35 passport on wheels activities as of 08/31/2026. Rep. Eulogio Rodriguez asked the DFA to account for distance, isolation, travel costs, and accessibility in underserved provinces and specifically raised a possible satellite office in Catanhuanes. The DFA said it was assessing existing and proposed offices under operational, fiscal, geographic, DBM, and Executive Order 45 criteria, while studying a satellite model and offering passport on wheels in the interim. Bukidnon and Virac-Catanhuanes requests, consular vehicles, and facility funding remained under review. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported an additional building-fund request of about 300 million and other DFA requests, subject to written submissions and further budget consideration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DFA was expanding access to consular services, particularly for provinces without a consular office, and whether new, satellite, or mobile facilities could address geographic isolation and travel costs. It also examined the funding and administrative requirements for proposed offices, vehicles, buildings, and related consular infrastructure.

topics.topic: ePassport budget of 5,500,000,000 and procurement breakdown
topics.summary: Assistant Secretary Emilio Fernandez presented passport funding as a major component of the DFA's proposed budget, including 2,800,000,000 for initial next-generation-passport funding and PHP 5,800,000,000 for passports overall. Representative Antonio Tinio then questioned the separate proposed ICT allocation of 956,610,000 and asked what the agency was actually purchasing. The ICT official described a shift toward large-scale capital assets, cited 511,000,000 in ICT projects, and identified the ePassport and passport appointment system among the covered systems. Tinio requested a year-by-year breakdown of ePassport services, providers, and procurement for 2025 through 2027. The DFA committed to provide the list and said the passport database was maintained by a third-party government printer at its facility in Lima, Batangas. The spending breakdown remained pending, so the issue landed as committed rather than fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the DFA proposed a large ePassport allocation separate from its ICT expenditures, and how the passport budget would be divided among services, providers, and related procurements. It also sought clarification on the location and security of the passport database.

topics.topic: ICT budget of about 956.6 million, cybersecurity, and data privacy
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the DFA's proposed ICT spending of about 956.6 million and sought utilization data and a detailed breakdown of the separate ePassport budget of about 5.5 billion. The DFA explained that ICT spending had shifted toward major capital assets and identified cybersecurity, data privacy, digital transformation and consular systems as priorities. It said current ICT projects totaled 511,000,000 and committed to submit a year-by-year and provider-by-provider breakdown. In response to questions about passport-data security, the DFA said the passport database was maintained on a server at the Apo production facility in Lima, Batangas, rather than in an external cloud. Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro and an ICT official sought cybersecurity funding, with the transcript containing an unclear initial reference to 10,000,000 followed by "Billion," while 250,000,000 was ultimately placed on the record as the minimum request. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez and the chair supported further consideration of the request, subject to a written, signed and endorsed wish list.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DFA's proposed ICT expenditures and ePassport budget were allocated, how much had been utilized, and why the proposed ICT amount had increased. It also sought assurances about cybersecurity, passport-data privacy and sovereignty, and considered additional funding requests for cybersecurity and related ICT capital outlay.

topics.topic: Passport data storage, sovereignty, and cloud-security arrangements
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the proposed ICT allocation of about 956.6 million and asked why it had increased, as well as what the capital spending would acquire. The DFA attributed the increase to cybersecurity, data protection, digital transformation, infrastructure resilience, and support for passport and other consular systems; it cited ICT projects of about 511 million. Tinio then contrasted the ICT allocation with the separate ePassport budget of about 5.5 billion and requested a 2025–2027 breakdown by services and providers. The DFA committed to submit the requested list. Tinio also asked where passport data was stored and how its privacy, security, and sovereignty were assured. The DFA said APO maintained the database and data center at the passport plant in Lima, Batangas, and confirmed that the database was in-country, although the exchange about cloud hosting remained unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the DFA proposed 956,610,000 for ICT expenditures, how that amount related to the separate 5,500,000,000 ePassport budget, and what the funds would acquire. It also sought to determine where Filipino passport data was stored and how the DFA could assure its privacy, security, and data sovereignty.

topics.topic: Foreign-service building fund, facilities, and office accommodation
topics.summary: Eulogio Rodriguez asked how the DFA would bring consular services closer to residents of underserved and geographically isolated provinces, and the DFA said it was assessing 42 offices and considering a smaller satellite-office model for Catanhuanes. The chair proposed passport-on-wheels services while the request and DBM guidelines were pending, and the DFA undertook to provide a written status update. Jay Vergara raised a 31,000-square-meter LGO-funded consular site and related regional concerns. Rufus Rodriguez then sought the DFA's broader facilities and funding priorities; the agency identified cybersecurity, a special leasing provision, and the building fund. The committee placed 250,000,000 for cybersecurity on the record and supported restoring 300,000,000 to the building fund. The requests were not finally appropriated in the exchange; the DFA was required to submit a signed additional wish list for further committee consideration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DFA would expand consular access in underserved and geographically isolated areas, including through a possible Catanhuanes satellite office and an LGO-funded site. It also examined the DFA's facility, building-fund, cybersecurity, vehicle, health-insurance, leasing, and permanent-position requirements, and what additional support or documents would be needed.

topics.topic: Foreign-service allowances, HMO, and permanent-position requirements
topics.summary: Assistant Secretary Emilio Fernandez reported that the DFA's foreign-service allowances accounted for about 9.9 billion and that about 345 million was set aside for terminal leave benefits. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez then asked for the DFA's priority wish list, which included a special lease provision, cybersecurity funding, building-fund augmentation, and consular vehicles. DFA officials identified 250 million as the reduced cybersecurity request and sought an additional 300 million for the building fund. The Foreign Service Institute requested HMO coverage amounting to MXN 6.5 million for almost 100 personnel, and the VFA Presidential Mission requested 13 permanent positions requiring a little less than 3 million in additional PS. Rodriguez supported the requests and undertook to work for them, while the chair required a signed and endorsed wish list by the following Wednesday. The permanent-position request and DBM-dependent funding actions were not finally resolved during the hearing.
topics.question: What recurring personnel and operating support did the DFA and its attached agencies need for foreign-service allowances, HMO coverage, cybersecurity, facilities, vehicles, and permanent positions? The committee also sought to determine which requests could be supported in the budget and what documents or further DBM action were required.

topics.topic: West Philippine Sea diplomatic protests and China provisional arrangement
topics.summary: Rep. Perci Cendaña asked the DFA to explain the written Philippines-China provisional arrangement for RORE missions, its negotiating authority, and whether it limited Philippine activities in the exclusive economic zone. Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said it was an exchange of notes limited to Ayungin Shoal, without prejudice to Philippine positions under UNCLOS and the 2016 arbitral award, and focused on information exchange for daily necessities. She committed to making the arrangement's details available, and reported 16 RORE missions without incident over two years. Rep. Brian Poe asked about diplomatic protests, and DFA officials reported 39 protests in 2026 and 296 from 2022 to 2026, while noting that diplomacy could take time to produce results. In the second round, Rep. Antonio Tinio challenged Chinese Embassy statements concerning construction materials and the arbitral award; the DFA denied that construction materials were covered by the arrangement and said it raised concerns through diplomatic channels. The complete text and the DFA's response to each public embassy statement were not fully resolved in the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the scope, legal character, operational effect, and disclosure status of the Philippines-China provisional arrangement for rotation and resupply missions in the West Philippine Sea. It also examined the DFA's diplomatic protests against China and its response to public statements by the Chinese Embassy in Manila.

topics.topic: Austerity measures and DFA official-event spending
topics.summary: Rep. Percy Cendaña asked whether the DFA had held Independence Day celebrations in five-star hotels despite austerity directives. The Secretary answered that most foreign service posts had practiced austerity, but some important posts had held more elaborate events for major anniversaries, including the eightieth anniversary of Philippine-U.S. relations in Washington, D.C. She said that additional funds could sometimes be sourced and that spending tied to an important celebration was not necessarily extravagant. Cendaña requested a post-by-post spending breakdown covering venues, catering, receptions, entertainment, transportation, and related costs for submission in time for plenary. No expenditure totals or breakdown were presented, so the issue remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DFA held Independence Day celebrations in five-star hotels despite directives to observe austerity measures. It also sought a post-by-post breakdown of the related spending, including venues, catering, receptions, entertainment, transportation, and other costs.

topics.topic: UN Security Council campaign expenditures and outcome
topics.summary: Representative Dada Kiram Ismula asked why the Philippines lost its bid for a nonpermanent UN Security Council seat and how much had been appropriated and spent on the campaign. The DFA secretary attributed the loss to geopolitical issues and said a detailed explanation could be provided in writing. The DFA fiscal management official reported that 70,000,000 pesos had been appropriated for 2025 and 2026, of which 52,500,000 was obligated, or 75% utilized. Ismula requested a breakdown covering diplomatic missions, travel, representation, promotional activities, and other campaign expenses, as well as the DFA’s accountability and post-campaign assessment. The DFA did not provide those details during the exchange, and Ismula reiterated the need to account for taxpayers’ money.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the Philippines lost its bid for a nonpermanent seat on the UN Security Council and how much was appropriated and actually spent on the campaign. It also sought a category-by-category expenditure breakdown and an account of the DFA’s post-campaign accountability and assessment.

topics.topic: Critical Minerals Agreement review and US-Philippines economic relations
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co asked the DFA to submit the Critical Minerals Agreement or MOU with the United States and clarify whether the DFA had reviewed it. The DFA said the DENR led the agreement, with DTI and BOI involved, and that the DFA did not possess the document. DFA officials said the DENR and DTI had assessed the economic aspects, so the Office of International Economic Relations did not conduct a separate economic review, although the DFA concurred with the agreement. The agency said the arrangement could support value-added processing of copper and nickel, technological know-how, investment protection, and participation in chip, artificial-intelligence, and electric-vehicle applications. Rep. Co emphasized that the agreement had implications beyond one bilateral relationship and that the DFA should consider consistency with related agreements. The secretary committed to requesting the MOU from the concerned agency, but the scope of the DFA's review role remained partly unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DFA had reviewed the Critical Minerals Agreement or MOU between the Philippines and the United States, what role it played in clearing or assessing the agreement, and whether it could provide the committee with a copy. It also sought clarification on the agreement's broader implications for US-Philippines economic, trade, and political relations.
