topics.topic: Visiting-forces exercises, fishing-community assistance, and commission staffing
topics.summary: Rep. Pinho asked about the Visiting Forces Commission's implemented and prospective agreements and requested the complete agreement texts. The commission said five agreements were currently implemented, with France awaiting ratification and concurrence and the United Kingdom in the negotiation pipeline. It said no funding was currently needed for the Canada and New Zealand agreements because no activities had been scheduled, but requested 13 permanent positions costing a little less than 3,000,000 in additional personnel services. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported the request and undertook to help advance it, subject to DBM processing and a signed written submission. Rep. Antonio Tinio asked about fishing bans and lost catch or income during exercises; the commission said the AFP, local governments, DSWD, and sometimes United States forces provided or coordinated assistance. The commission committed to seek actual assistance data, leaving that documentation unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status and funding needs of the Presidential Commission on the Visiting Forces, including whether new visiting-forces agreements required additional resources and whether contractual staff could be made permanent. It also asked what assistance was provided to fishing communities affected by visiting-forces exercises and which agencies were responsible.

topics.topic: Overseas voting administration and 2025 turnout
topics.summary: Antonio Tinio raised the very low turnout in the 2025 overseas elections and asked about the DFA's voter-awareness, education, and information efforts after the introduction of online voting and counting. A DFA official said turnout was affected by various factors and cautioned against comparing the 2025 results directly with the 2022 elections. The official cited registration without subsequent voting, technical and online-voting difficulties, regional differences, and challenges faced by elderly voters. The DFA said it had established a technical working group with COMELEC to improve awareness and participation. It also committed to provide a paper with more detailed reasons for the difficulties in overseas voting.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why turnout in the 2025 overseas elections was very low, particularly after the introduction of online voting and counting, and what the DFA had done to promote registration, voter awareness, and participation. It also sought an explanation of the operational difficulties affecting overseas voting.

topics.topic: OFW and seafarer safe passage and right to refuse dangerous sailing
topics.summary: Sarah Elago raised the need for DFA action on OFW and seafarer assistance, safe passage, and the right to refuse sailing through dangerous areas. The DFA said the DMW had primary jurisdiction, while the DFA coordinated through its migrant affairs offices, embassies, MWOs, manning agencies, and shipping companies. An agency official reported that 14 seafarers were on the same ship and said seafarers could refuse work in areas determined to be dangerous. The DFA secretary cited prior efforts to obtain safe passage for a Philippine-flag vessel in the Middle East and said the DFA was pursuing IMO and bilateral engagement, including with Panama, which was cited as having 180,000 seafarers. The secretary said a detailed report had been begun or submitted two days earlier, but the transcript did not clarify the reference to Nayari or establish a completed safe-passage guarantee.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DFA was assisting OFWs and seafarers exposed to unsafe conditions, including whether seafarers could refuse to sail into dangerous areas. It also sought an update on the DFA's coordination with the Department of Migrant Workers, the International Maritime Organization, foreign governments, manning agencies, and seafarers' unions to secure safe passage.

topics.topic: Repatriation of remains and overseas crisis assistance
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Poe asked how the DFA was assisting Filipinos affected by the Nepal crisis and sought an update on Sam De La Cruz’s remains. The DFA said it was working through the New Delhi embassy and an honorary consul in Kathmandu, with one Filipino missing amid reports of about 4,000 missing persons. On De La Cruz’s case, the DFA explained that his remains had been buried in Bosaso after his death in July 2018, and that pandemic, legal, logistical, and diplomatic obstacles had stalled exhumation. The DFA committed to renewing instructions to its Nairobi embassy to pursue the case with Somali authorities. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula then asked about ATN Fund use, and the DFA reported an annual appropriation of about 1 billion from 2022 to 2025, along with 2026 assistance figures including 387 repatriation beneficiaries and 2,884 total beneficiaries reported for the first six months. The member requested the ATN Fund guidelines, leaving the matter with a document submission and continued agency follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DFA was assisting Filipinos affected by the Nepal crisis and whether it could secure the repatriation of Sam De La Cruz’s remains from Somalia. It also examined the scale, beneficiaries, approval rules, and documentation governing the Assistance to Nationals (ATN) Fund.

topics.topic: FY2027 CHR budget reduction and restoration request
topics.summary: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato presented an original FY 2027 proposal of about 2.75 billion against a 2027 NEP allocation of about 1.27 billion, describing an almost 53% reduction and the elimination of capital outlay. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez sought restoration of the 74,000,000 Tier 1 reduction and asked the CHR to identify its highest-priority Tier 2 items; Palpalato identified preventive monitoring, mandatory expenses, productivity, capacity building, information systems, and international participation, with the exchange pointing to a package of roughly 200 million to 250 million. Another vice chairperson confirmed with Palpalato that capital outlay had been completely wiped out, while Vice Chair Sia Agyong supported reinstatement or a substantial increase. De Lima and Aris Montes separately supported restoration and received answers on the CHR’s monitoring and gender-ombud functions, while Salazar said the 592,000,000 trust fund remained with the Bureau of the Treasury and had not been released. In response to the NGO caucus, Palpalato reiterated the 2,749,000,000 proposal, the roughly 1.27 billion NEP amount, the 53% reduction, and a 34,000,000 MOOE cut, although some figures in that exchange were unclear. The committee required a consolidated, prioritized wishlist with the Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission by September 9, and the hearing was terminated without a final restoration decision.
topics.question: What was the extent and effect of the reduction in the CHR’s FY 2027 proposed budget, and which Tier 1 and Tier 2 items did the committee seek to restore or augment? The committee also sought to establish how the reduced funding would affect the CHR’s statutory and constitutional functions and requested a prioritized written wishlist.

topics.topic: Tier 2 priority requests and written funding list
topics.summary: CHR Richard Palpalato presented an original FY 2027 proposal of about 2.75 billion, including about 1.58 billion in Tier 2 requests, and identified productivity enhancement, preventive visitation and torture prevention, mandatory expenses, capacity building, information systems, infrastructure, and institutional roles as priorities. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez supported restoring the CHR’s reduction and asked for the first three Tier 2 priorities in writing. Palpalato identified a remaining preventive-mandate request of around 4,000,000, mandatory expenses of 59,000,505, productivity enhancement of 108,000,237, capacity building of 18,416,000, information-systems training of 10,000,000, and regional and global institutional activities of 1,900,000, while also stating a total priority figure of 227,000,000 whose breakdown was unclear. Rodriguez said he would seek an increase based on the CHR’s computation of 250,000,000, subject to fiscal space. In response to the NGO caucus, Palpalato said the CHR had no administrative or programmatic oversight over NTF-ELCAC or the Support to the Barangay Development Program, but needed resources for field monitoring, investigations, assistance, and human-rights education in vulnerable communities. The committee required a consolidated, prioritized CHR and Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission wishlist by September 9, and the CHR agreed to comply.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the CHR’s Tier 2 priorities, the amounts required for each, and which requests should be considered for possible restoration or augmentation. It also sought clarification on the CHR’s resource needs for monitoring the Support to the Barangay Development Program and requested a prioritized written wishlist.

topics.topic: Capital outlay reduced to zero
topics.summary: The CHR chairperson said the FY 2027 NEP was reduced mainly because it contained no capital outlay, affecting the commission’s proposed infrastructure, ICT, facilities, and vehicle requirements. The deputy minority leader asked how zero capital outlay would affect mandate delivery, and the chairperson answered that it would constrain ICT infrastructure, facilities, and regional-office workplaces. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez and Vice Chair Sia Agyong supported restoring or substantially increasing the CHR budget, with Rodriguez specifically identifying retrofitting, ICT, buildings, and vehicles. Rodriguez requested a written list of the CHR’s highest priorities, and the chairperson committed to submit it by the next day. Representative Reneko linked funding needs to jail visitation, torture prevention, rapid response to red-tagging, and digital evidence capabilities; the CHR provided a total protection-program figure of 323,278,000 but did not provide the exact jail-visitation allocation. In the later NGO-caucus exchange, the chairperson restated the proposal as 2,749,000,000 and the NEP as 1,272,000,000, and cited a capital-outlay amount transcribed unclearly as “ND152 million.” The issue was left for subsequent budget amendments rather than finally resolved during the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed zero allocation for capital outlay would affect the Commission on Human Rights’ infrastructure, ICT capabilities, regional offices, transportation, and delivery of its constitutional mandate. Members also sought the restoration of the capital outlay and clarification of the related Tier 1 and Tier 2 funding requests.

topics.topic: CHR personnel, job-order funding, and regional vacancies
topics.summary: The deputy minority leader questioned whether the CHR’s funding for 20 job-order workers in its central and regional offices was adequately provided and asked about the operational effect of a zero capital-outlay allocation. The CHR chairperson said job-order funding was under MOOE and that capital outlay was needed for ICT infrastructure, facilities, and regional-office workplaces. The deputy minority leader said he would move to restore the capital-outlay proposal. The Caucus of Development NGO Networks then sought vacancy, workload, staffing, and appropriation data for the regional offices. The CHR said insufficient manpower contributed to backlogs and slower investigations and identified Region 4 B, Region 7, and the Negros Island Region as areas of concern. The chairperson undertook to submit the actual personnel numbers by region.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CHR’s proposed budget adequately funded job-order personnel and capital outlay, and how staffing shortages and vacancies affected regional operations. It also asked which regional offices were below minimum staffing levels and what additional positions and FY 2027 funding were needed.

topics.topic: Case backlog and capacity to resolve investigations
topics.summary: Leila de Lima asked which CHR mandate faced the greatest resource constraints and whether the commission had case backlogs. CHR identified prevention as the most resource-constrained mandate and reported that it had resolved 95.8 percent of a historical backlog of about 28,000 cases, leaving roughly 1,200 pending. De Lima and Antonio Tinio separately pressed CHR on drug-war investigations; CHR cited 493 cases for reinvestigation, 289 cases investigated or concluded by the task force, and 140 cases for resolution, with delays attributed to lack of evidence, noncooperation, missing documents, and reprisal risks. CHR committed to prioritize the 140 cases within the year and submit a written update before plenary. An NGO caucus raised regional staffing and workload concerns, and CHR acknowledged that Regions 4-B, 7, and the Negros Island Region remained affected by manpower and geographic constraints. CHR agreed to submit regional personnel figures, but the additional staffing and FY 2027 appropriation required remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of CHR case backlogs, the status and resolution rate of investigations—particularly drug-war cases—and whether CHR had sufficient personnel and resources to discharge its mandates. It also asked what additional data, staffing, and reports CHR would provide and what targets it could commit to meet.

topics.topic: Drug-war killings and extrajudicial-killing investigations
topics.summary: The deputy minority leader and Leila de Lima asked CHR about its continuing investigations into drug-war killings and its coordination with the DOJ AO 35 mechanism. CHR reported 493 cases for reinvestigation and said the task force had investigated or concluded a spoken figure rendered as 289 in one exchange, with 120 cases for disposition and 140 cases for resolution. CHR said most resolved cases had been dismissed for lack of evidence, citing hostile conditions, noncooperation, and missing PNP documents. It said its investigations would determine the presence or absence of human rights violations and could result in referrals for criminal accountability. Antonio Tinio pressed CHR on the remaining cases, the timeframe, and the broader backlog. CHR committed to prioritize the 140 cases within the year and to submit a written update before plenary; it also reported resolving 95.8 percent of a backlog described as about 28,000 cases, or 27,307 cases.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status of CHR investigations into drug-war-related killings, including the number of cases reinvestigated, investigated, and ready for resolution or disposition. Members also asked about CHR's role in the DOJ AO 35 mechanism, the prospects for criminal accountability, the remaining case backlog, and when CHR would submit updates.

topics.topic: Jail visitation and monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty
topics.summary: CHR Richard Palpalato reported that the commission visited 960 facilities in 2024, 985 in 2025, and 617 during the first semester of 2026, but could reach only about one third of 2,920 detention facilities with existing resources. He said DBM had provided 16,000,000 and 19,000 for the expanded visitation program, although the context of the 19,000 figure was unclear, and requested 108,223,700 under Tier 2 for visitation and torture prevention. Representative Reneko supported restoring the budget and pressed for more frequent jail visits, rapid-response legal teams for red-tagging, and digital-forensics capabilities. The CHR gave 323,278,000 as the total protection-program allotment but did not provide a separate jail-visitation or red-tagging amount. Leila de Lima asked which mandate faced the greatest resource gap, and the CHR identified prevention because it shared funding with protection and lacked a dedicated allocation. The CHR agreed to submit rapid-response guidelines, while funding restoration and digital evidence resources remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had sufficient funding and personnel to conduct regular visitation and preventive monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty. Members also asked how the CHR's prevention mandate was funded, including jail visitation, torture prevention, rapid response to red-tagging, and related investigative capabilities.

topics.topic: Digital privacy, cyber threats, and digital evidence capacity
topics.summary: A committee member asked whether the CHR had a dedicated program for digital privacy, online harassment, cyberbullying, misinformation, and artificial-intelligence risks. CHR chairperson Richard Palpalato said the Commission had focal officials, research, policy monitoring, and protection activities concerning emerging technology and human rights. Representative Reneko later connected red-tagging to online campaigns, doxing, and deepfakes and asked about rapid-response protocols and funding for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, and secure databases. The CHR cited a broader protection-program allotment of 323,278,000 but did not identify a separate digital-evidence allocation. The CHR agreed to submit guidelines or related materials, while the specific digital-capacity funding question was left unanswered.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had programs, funding, protocols, and operational capacity to address digital privacy violations, online harassment, cyberbullying, misinformation, artificial intelligence risks, and digitally enabled red-tagging. It also asked whether the CHR had digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, secure databases, and systems to preserve digital evidence.

topics.topic: NTF-ELCAC and barangay development-program monitoring
topics.summary: Rep. Reneko supported restoring the CHR budget and sought funding for jail visitation, rapid-response legal teams, and digital evidence capabilities in response to red-tagging. The CHR said its total protection-program allotment was 323,278,000 but did not identify a separate red-tagging allocation, and it agreed to submit relevant recommendations and guidelines. Rep. Leila de Lima asked about resource gaps, case backlogs, drug-war investigations, ICC membership, and NTF-ELCAC oversight; the CHR reported that 95.8 percent of about 28,000 backlog cases had been resolved, with around 1,200 pending, and identified 493 drug-war cases for reinvestigation. The CHR supported rejoining the ICC but said it had no formal oversight over NTF-ELCAC, limiting its role to monitoring compliance and investigating violations. An NGO caucus then asked about the roughly 740 million Support to the Barangay Development Program and the safeguards and resources needed in vulnerable communities. CHR Richard Palpalato said additional demands would involve more field monitoring, investigations, protection, documentation, and human-rights education, and reiterated the agency's tier-two resource proposal.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHR had sufficient resources and authority to monitor, investigate, and respond to human-rights risks associated with NTF-ELCAC and the Support to the Barangay Development Program. It also examined CHR's response to red-tagging, its position on ICC membership, relevant case backlogs, and safeguards or additional resources needed in vulnerable communities.

topics.topic: ICC reengagement and human-rights implications
topics.summary: The deputy minority leader asked whether the CHR would lead advocacy for the Philippines’ reengagement with the ICC. The CHR said it supported rejoining the ICC and the Rome Statute and had issued statements, policy recommendations, public-information materials, and an EJK report concerning ICC-related developments. The member urged the CHR to speak more visibly for victims and against false narratives surrounding the ICC proceedings involving former president Rodrigo Duterte. Leila de Lima later asked about the status of drug-war investigations and the CHR’s ICC position. The CHR reported 493 cases for reinvestigation and described the task force as having concluded “208 289” cases, an unclear figure, while citing lack of evidence, hostile conditions, noncooperation, and unavailable police documents as obstacles. The CHR unequivocally maintained that rejoining the ICC and Rome Statute would provide an additional assurance of accountability for human-rights violations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the CHR’s position and actions regarding the Philippines’ possible reengagement with the ICC and return to the Rome Statute. Members also asked how the CHR was investigating drug-war killings and communicating its human-rights position in relation to the ICC proceedings.

topics.topic: Gender-ombud functions and women’s human-rights programs
topics.summary: Assistant Minority Leader Aris Montes asked the CHR to define its gender-ombud functions, including complaint intake, investigation, and monitoring of government compliance with RA 9710. The CHR said it monitored treaty and statutory compliance, investigated gender-based violations, accepted complaints through multiple channels, and coordinated with the Philippine Commission on Women. The discussion cited 178 cases involving women and persons of diversity as of June 2026, although an earlier 2025 figure was garbled. Montes warned about continuing agency noncompliance and called for restoration of the original proposed CHR budget after the chair said additional dedicated resources would help. Representative Sarah Elago raised more than 800 gender-based-violence cases, the backlog described as more than 20,000 or almost 30,000 cases, and around 2,942 current cases. The CHR described a three-pillar protection mechanism for human-rights defenders and committed to submit reports on its gender-and-development mandate and labor-related human-rights violations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the CHR’s functions as gender ombud under the Magna Carta of Women, including complaint handling, investigation, and monitoring government compliance with RA 9710. It also examined whether the proposed budget would affect gender-based-violence data collection, case disposition, protection of human-rights defenders, and related reporting.

topics.topic: Protection of human-rights defenders and rapid-response legal deployment
topics.summary: The deputy minority leader questioned whether the CHR had adequate funding for job-order personnel and capital outlay, and said a motion would be made to restore capital outlay. The member also pressed the CHR to be more vocal on victims' rights and the ICC proceedings; the CHR cited its public statements, monitoring role, victim assistance, and the reopening of 493 cases, with 140 for disposition. Representative Reneko sought additional funding for jail visitation and cited a priority grant of 108,000,000, while the CHR said limited resources had restricted visit frequency and reported a total protection-program allotment of 323,278,000. Reneko asked for the direct allocation and protocols for rapid-response legal teams addressing red-tagging, as well as funding for digital forensic and secure-database capabilities; the exact allocations were not provided, but the CHR agreed to submit guidelines. Sarah Elago raised more than 800 gender-based-violence cases, the CHR's backlog of more than 20,000 or almost 30,000 cases from 1987 to 2025, and around 2,942 current cases. The CHR described a three-pillar national protection mechanism for human-rights defenders involving early warning, protection services, and monitoring, but funding and implementation details remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had sufficient resources and operational capacity to protect human-rights defenders, victims, and persons deprived of liberty, including through jail visitation, legal assistance, rapid response, and digital evidence preservation. Members also asked how the CHR was addressing red-tagging, gender-based violence, case backlogs, and the proposed national protection mechanism.

topics.topic: Community monitoring, dialogues, and human-rights education
topics.summary: A committee member asked CHR to explain its grassroots monitoring, local-government coordination, community-based dialogues, and mechanisms for referring cases to the DOJ. CHR cited barangay human rights action centers, regional coordination, complaints channels, legal clinic caravans, sectoral validation, DOJ engagement under Administrative Order Number 35, and a DOJ referral agreement. When asked for case outputs and status, CHR said it would provide the data, and the member said the committee would await it. The discussion also covered CHR activities on emerging technology, artificial intelligence, digital harms, and disinformation. Sarah Elago asked about community dialogues and human-rights education; CHR reported 34 dialogues in 2025, 122,950 participants in promotion activities, and 51,716 participants as of June 2026, although one intervening figure was transcribed as "20 in five." The agency cited partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher-education institutions, and the Philippine Association of Law Schools. A committee member also indicated support for increasing the CHR budget, whose stated total was about 1.27 billion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHR had sufficient mechanisms and resources for grassroots human-rights monitoring, community-based dialogues, local partnerships, and human-rights education. It also asked how CHR coordinated with the DOJ on referrals and prosecutions, tracked case outcomes, and addressed emerging digital and artificial-intelligence-related human-rights issues.

topics.topic: DOJ referrals and prosecution follow-through
topics.summary: A committee member asked CHR how it coordinated with the Department of Justice to ensure that investigation findings led to prosecution. CHR chairperson Richard Palpalato cited regular DOJ engagement, CHR participation as an observer in the interagency committee under Administrative Order number 35, and a memorandum of agreement for referring cases involving possible criminal liability. The member then asked for outputs and the status of referred investigations and cases. CHR said it could provide the data, and the member confirmed that the committee would wait for its submission. No referral or prosecution totals were presented during the exchange.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what mechanisms CHR used to coordinate with the Department of Justice so that CHR investigation findings involving possible criminal liability led to prosecution. It also asked for output or case-status data showing the results of those referrals.

topics.topic: Martial-law reparation trust-fund interest and release status
topics.summary: Rep. Leila de Lima asked whether about 597.7 million in martial-law reparation trust-fund interest had been released in fiscal year 2026 and sought the status of the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund. CHR Executive Director Lorette Salazar answered that the trust fund remained intact with the Bureau of the Treasury and that no amount had been released because the commission had not made a request. She said a request to the DBM would be necessary before any release. Salazar identified the fund as sourced from the 10,000,000,000 reparations fund, said distribution of reparations was complete, and described 592,000,000 as intended for memorialization. The exchange did not resolve the discrepancy between the reported interest amount and the agency's stated trust-fund amount.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether 597,742,802.78 in martial-law reparation trust-fund interest had been released during fiscal year 2026, why the corresponding provision was absent from the proposed 2027 budget, and the current status of the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund.

topics.topic: CHR program allocations for personal services, MOOE, and Arleap
topics.summary: Sarah Elago and the committee reviewed the CHR's proposed allocations for personal services, MOOE, Arleap, and its protection, promotion, policy, and jail-visitation programs. The agency reported a stated total of about 1.27 billion, along with program allocations and participation figures for community dialogues and promotion activities. Elago asked whether activities represented expansions and how human-rights education could be institutionalized; the agency cited regional dialogues and partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher educational institutions, and law schools. An NGO and civil-society representative then asked for the CHR's total proposal, the NEP recommendation, the shortfall, the reasons for reductions, affected expenditures, operational consequences, and requested augmentation. Richard Palpalato cited a proposal of about 2.75 billion, an NEP amount of about 1.27 billion, a stated 53% reduction, a capital-outlay figure of "ND152 million," and an MOOE reduction of 34,000,000. The excerpt ended without a complete answer on the DBM rationale, all operational effects, or the requested augmentation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the CHR's proposed FY 2027 budget was distributed among personal services, MOOE, Arleap, and core programs, and how those allocations supported community dialogues and human-rights education. It also asked what budget the CHR proposed to the DBM, what the NEP recommended, the resulting shortfall, and the operational effects of reductions or exclusions.

topics.topic: Public Transport Modernization Program funding and continuity
topics.summary: Members led by Rep. Carl Legaspi, Rep. Renee Co, Rep. Lim, Rep. Chan, Rep. Rodge Gutierrez, and Rep. Bonispares questioned the sharp reduction in PTMP funding and its effect on operators, commuters, vehicle supply, and program continuity. DOTr said the reduced 2027 amount would support only limited operations, ground preparation, route rationalization, industry consolidation, stakeholder support, and monitoring, while seeking congressional help for subsidies and service contracting. The agency reported a 1,500,000,000 unobligated amount in one update, and explained that the 2026 1,500,000,000 budget had only recently received its cash allotment. Members also challenged inconsistent consolidation figures, including the agency's correction from 86.23% to 83.64%, and requested updated franchise and unit data. The Secretary committed to written explanations within the following week, while other questions on utilization, passenger demand, GPS transmission, reporting baselines, and passenger infrastructure were not fully answered. The issue therefore landed with agency submissions and congressional efforts to restore funding still pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the sharply reduced FY 2027 funding would allow the Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP) to continue, including subsidies, route rationalization, consolidation, service contracting, and support for operators and commuters. Members also sought explanations for prior unobligated funds, current utilization, vehicle and consolidation data, and the department's plans to address financing distress and passenger needs.

topics.topic: Active transport, bike lanes, and Safe Pathways funding
topics.summary: Members Renee Co, Rep. Lim, Rep. Chan, Rep. Rodge Gutierrez, the Ways and Means Committee chairman, and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the sharp reduction in active-transport, bike-lane, and Safe Pathways funding. The proposed amount was cited variously as 33,900,000 or 33,000,000, compared with about 105 million in the prior year, while another presentation described a reduction from 1,100,000,000 to 33,000,000 or 34,000,000. DOTr said the proposed amount would support only about six kilometers in one exchange and 33 kilometers of Class One bike lanes in another, while DBM cited 2.66% utilization of the 60,000,000 2025 allocation and limited absorptive capacity. DOTr attributed delays to LGU partnerships and tranche-based downloading, and said it would complete procurement for a sidewalk project funded at more than 60 million and use the remaining 34,000,000 with an LGU. Members sought restoration, convergence with DPWH, clearer congressional oversight, and a report on 3,800,000,000 appropriated from 2022 to 2026. The issue remained unresolved as to the final 2027 appropriation, but the agency made implementation and reporting commitments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why active-transport, bike-lane, and Safe Pathways funding had been sharply reduced, whether the proposed amount could deliver meaningful infrastructure, and whether low utilization justified the reduction. Members also asked how projects were being implemented with LGUs, what oversight and monitoring would apply, and whether funding should be restored or amended.

topics.topic: EDSA Busway zero FY2027 allocation and operating support
topics.summary: Rep. Carl Legaspi first raised concern that the EDSA Busway had a proposed budget of about 1.79 billion but received zero allocation, alongside a sharp reduction in public-transport modernization funding. Rep. Claudine Botisdalim and Rep. Lim then asked what the zero line item would mean for busway operations, maintenance, safety, accessibility, and station rehabilitation. DOTr officials said maintenance, security, accessibility equipment, and station improvements remained necessary, and Senior Undersecretary Pastor identified a FY2027 request of about 1.7 billion to rehabilitate 12 more stations and facilities. Pastor also cited ridership rising from 90,000 to 190,000 passengers per month at one renovated station. Rep. Lim appealed for the full request, while Rep. Rodge Gutierrez later supported restoring transport programs and examining convergence arrangements. The hearing did not record a committee decision restoring the allocation, leaving the issue unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the EDSA Busway had no FY2027 line-item allocation and whether the absence of funding would disrupt its operations, maintenance, safety, accessibility, and rehabilitation. Members also sought clarification on the amount needed to sustain and improve the busway.

topics.topic: PTMP consolidation, franchise data, and route capacity
topics.summary: Congresswoman Renee Co raised conflicting fleet data and argued that modernization may have removed about 171,000 PUJ units and roughly 34,000,000 in daily passenger capacity, while the agency attributed the decline mainly to route rationalization and authorized-unit limits. She also questioned nearly 9 billion in PTMP funding and cited 1.6 billion in unobligated 2022 funds; the Secretary committed to submit written explanations and a budget report within the next week. Congressman Bonispares challenged the reported 86.23% franchise-consolidation rate, and the agency corrected it to 83.64% while promising more detailed franchise and provisional-authority data. He also questioned how a 176 million FY 2027 request could sustain a program previously associated with amounts including 1,500,000,000, 2,500,000,000, and 1,000,000,000; the Secretary maintained that the program would continue but acknowledged implementation problems. Civil-society questions sought route-demand testing, GPS compliance, modernization baselines, staffing data, and passenger infrastructure, but several received no precise answer. The issue therefore landed with documentary commitments but material data and accountability questions unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the actual number of public transport units and franchises before and after modernization, whether consolidation reduced passenger-carrying capacity, and how route rationalization affected authorized units. It also examined PTMP funding utilization, the basis for the proposed FY 2027 allocation, and whether the program would continue with adequate data, monitoring, and passenger infrastructure.

topics.topic: Unobligated and underutilized transport-modernization funds
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co questioned the loss of transport capacity and cited unobligated PTMP amounts, including nearly 9 billion and 1.6 billion in 2022; DOTr attributed lower vehicle counts to route rationalization and acknowledged that earlier funding required further explanation. The secretary committed to submit a written PTMP report from 2018 through 2025 within the following week. Other members challenged reductions in PTMP, fuel subsidy, service contracting, EDSA Busway, and active-transport funding; DOTr said limited fiscal space, delayed releases, and weak absorptive capacity contributed to the reductions and sought congressional help to restore funds. The agency described the proposed PTMP budget as about 177 million, including financing, route rationalization, consolidation, stakeholder support, and monitoring activities, and said a 1 billion NCA would fund subsidy support. DBM cited 2.66% active-transport utilization for 2025, while DOTr attributed low utilization partly to tranche-based LGU releases and committed to accelerate procurement and submit progress data. Civil-society questions on passenger-demand testing, GPS validity, modernization baselines, passenger infrastructure, and staffing were read into the record, but several answers, especially the GPS percentage and staffing figures, remained incomplete.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why transport-modernization and related public-transport appropriations were unobligated or underutilized, and whether reduced FY2027 funding would impair PTMP continuity, fuel subsidy, service contracting, active transport, and passenger infrastructure. Members also sought updated consolidation, utilization, and monitoring data and asked whether the agency would provide documents or seek restoration of funds.

topics.topic: Fuel subsidy and public-transport service contracting
topics.summary: Rep. Lim questioned the effects of reduced or zero funding for the EDSA Busway, fuel subsidy, active transport, and public-transport modernization. DOTr said the 2025 fuel-subsidy allocation of about 2.5 billion had been downloaded to the LTFRB and fully disbursed, while the agency's stated 2027 fuel figure was garbled and unclear. The agency said about 176.83 million for modernization would support only limited operations, including financing, route rationalization, LPTRP, industry consolidation, stakeholder support, and personnel. Rep. Chan and Rep. Rodge Gutierrez separately pressed for restoration of fuel subsidy and service contracting and highlighted steep reductions in active transport and modernization. DOTr attributed the reductions to limited fiscal space and said it would seek congressional help. The committee members manifested support, but no restoration or appropriation was finally adopted in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 budget would affect the EDSA Busway, fuel subsidy, active transport, public-transport modernization, and service contracting. Members also asked whether DOTr intended to restore zeroed-out support for transport operators and drivers, particularly amid an oil crisis and financial pressure on modernized jeepney cooperatives.

topics.topic: North-South Commuter Railway funding, utilization, and completion
topics.summary: Committee members first sought the status of relocation for 637 affected families and were told that none had yet been relocated, although site construction and inspection were ongoing. The DOTr right-of-way official gave April 2027 as the target for completion and was asked to submit detailed relocation and turnover data. Chairman Franz Pumaren questioned whether inadequate funding could affect NSCR utilization. Representative Bong Son Dai then examined the NSCR allocation of about 123.8 billion, foreign-assisted project utilization, right-of-way acquisition, and the financing gap; the DOTr reported an NSCR funding total of about 67 billion, an obligation rate of 89.89%, and a disbursement rate of 47.94% as of June 2026. The Department said the first phase was targeted for December 2027, the Clark demonstration run for June 2028, and revenue operations toward Clark for the last quarter of 2028. The financing gap and a firm full-project completion date remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) had adequate and usable funding, including foreign-loan and GOP counterpart financing, and whether obligations and disbursements were keeping pace. Members also asked about right-of-way constraints, relocation, utilization, and the realistic dates for partial and full operations.

The Secretary of Transportation referred the response to the agency's right-of-way official, who said construction and site inspection were ongoing and indicated that none of the 637 families had yet been relocated. It identified a San Pedro, Laguna relocation site for 38 families and referred to an on-site relocation arrangement. The chair requested a detailed submission covering demolition, relocation, affected families, site construction, and turnover units, leaving the issue committed for further documentation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the relocation status of the 637 families affected by the South Commuter Railway, including the relocation-site construction status, the resettlement timeline, and the number of families covered by specific relocation sites. It also sought a consolidated submission on demolition, relocation, affected families, site construction, and turnover of units.

topics.topic: Metro Manila Subway and other railway completion targets
topics.summary: Rep. Bong Son Dai questioned the scale and utilization of railway appropriations, emphasizing that the North-South Railway and Metro Manila Subway together represented about 191.3 billion and roughly 76% of the DOTr-OSEC expenditure program. DOTr officials reported an 82 obligation rate as of July 2026, 33 billion in June and July disbursements for foreign-assisted NSCR and subway projects, and 89.89% obligations against 47.94% disbursements for NSCR as of June. They said about 90% of NSCR and subway right of way had been acquired, while funding remained incomplete, including only 26 billion of a 47 billion GOP counterpart requirement. The agency targeted December 2027 for initial NSCR partial operations, June 2028 for a demonstration run, late 2028 for revenue operations, and around 2031 for Metro Manila Subway operations. Rep. France separately questioned whether the PNR South Long Haul investment was justified, and a PNR official cited current ridership of about 1,600 daily and projected ridership of 20 to 25,000 under the original alignment. PNR committed to submit written data and justification before plenary consideration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 railway allocations were being utilized effectively, whether right-of-way and counterpart-funding constraints could be managed, and when the North-South Commuter Railway and Metro Manila Subway would reach operations. It also asked whether the proposed PNR South Long Haul investment was financially justified and requested supporting ridership and investment data.

topics.topic: LRT-2 capacity and improvement funding
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co raised LRT-2's record ridership of 250,578 passengers and cited 197,000,000,000 in proposed rail transport funding for improvement. The LRTA or rail administrator said LRT-2 had begun with 18 train sets, that the trains were more than twenty-two years old, and that aging equipment constrained peak-hour capacity. The agency said the Gen Four train sets were financed through an ODA loan and described LRMC revenues, including about 31 billion in total revenues, about 14 billion for rehabilitation, and about 6 billion in 2015 operating expenses. Rep. Renee Co also questioned LRMC's responsibility for leaks, flooding, cleanliness, and other service failures; the administrator cited 121,000,000 in outstanding penalties. The agency undertook to submit NNIC revenue and passenger-service-charge data, while Rep. Renee Co said she would submit a formal written request. The capacity and debt issues were not fully resolved in the hearing segment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed rail transport investment would address LRT-2's rising ridership and limited train capacity. It also examined the financing and use of rail revenues, responsibility for LRT-1 service deficiencies, and whether additional revenue and passenger-service data would be submitted.

topics.topic: PNR South Long Haul Express investment
topics.summary: Rep. France questioned whether the PNR South Long Haul Express remained worth pursuing after the China loan was expected to expire and referred to 6,000,000,000 in associated funding. The agency said it was continuing rehabilitation of the typhoon-damaged line using the 2026 budget and needed additional capital funding to complete the 422 kilometer route. It reported current ridership of about 1,600 daily passengers, projected 5,000 to 6,000 with improvements, and estimated 20 to 25,000 daily under the original alignment. Rep. France required the agency to provide written data and justification before the project was brought to plenary. The agency committed to submit the materials in coordination with the Secretary, leaving the investment decision pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether continuing the PNR South Long Haul Express was justified after the China loan was expected to expire, including the project's cost, ridership potential, and expected return on investment. Rep. France also asked the agency to provide the supporting data and justification in writing before plenary consideration.

topics.topic: General Santos Airport repairs and passenger boarding bridges
topics.summary: Dennis Hernandez raised the status of repairs at General Santos Airport and sought a firm completion timetable. The DOTr said ongoing repair and rehabilitation works were targeted for November, with the latest date extending to the first week of December. Hernandez recalled that the agency had accepted a 200,000,000 repair budget and argued that it should also cover redesign and passenger boarding bridges. He warned that boarding-gate congestion would worsen once the airport became fully operational and handled more flights. The agency referred to aircraft separation requirements for Airbus three thirty operations, but did not fully explain the technical plan for resolving congestion. The matter landed with a timetable commitment, while the detailed boarding-bridge and expansion plan remained incompletely answered.
topics.question: The committee sought the status and completion timetable for repairs at General Santos Airport, including the second-floor works and passenger boarding bridges. It also sought assurance that the 200,000,000 repair budget would address boarding-gate congestion as airport operations and flights expanded.

topics.topic: Naga Airport runway and right-of-way funding
topics.summary: Rep. Nelson Legacion raised the Naga Airport's prolonged delay, attributing it to property acquisition and right-of-way problems dating back to the project's decision in 2014. He asked whether the 2027 allocation of about 900 million would complete the 2.1-kilometer runway earthworks and also start the concrete runway. The Secretary of Transportation and agency project officials said the allocation would complete the 2,100 embankment activities and commence initial pavement or concreting simultaneously. The agency said Phase One was expected by January and Phase Two by the first quarter of 2027, while acknowledging a six-month delay and contractor price-escalation concerns. The Secretary also committed to closer implementation and a catch-up plan if needed. The issue landed with agency commitments, although some dates and the cited accomplishment figure remained unclear in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the Naga Airport project had been delayed, whether the 2027 allocation would complete the runway earthworks, and how much of that allocation could be used to begin concrete runway construction. It also sought the agency's timetable for completing Phases One and Two.

topics.topic: Calbayog Airport upgrading and runway completion
topics.summary: Representative Stephen James Tan raised the need to complete the Calbayog Airport upgrade and restore a direct Manila flight. He cited 2026 funding of about 62 million for strip grade correction and 100 million for perimeter fencing and asphalt overlay, and identified requirements of about 117 million for road transfer, 100 million for right of way, and 350,000,000 for runway completion. Secretary Giovanni Lopez cited general right-of-way funding of about 2.7 billion and said DOTr would coordinate with CAAP. A CAAP official said procurement was ongoing and that the works were being targeted for completion by 2027, subject to the contract of award and coordination with DOTr. CAAP also said the matter would be elevated to top management, but did not expressly confirm the requested 350,000,000 2027 allocation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the remaining requirements for upgrading Calbayog Airport—including the road transfer, right-of-way, and runway completion—would be funded in the 2027 program. The member also asked whether CAAP would commit to the 350,000,000 runway-completion requirement for 2027.

topics.topic: Tuguegarao Airport infrastructure and multiyear funding
topics.summary: Joseph Lara raised the importance of Tuguegarao Airport as the Region 2 gateway and questioned whether earlier and multiyear appropriations would be implemented. He cited a previous amount spoken as 150,000,020.24 and sought 100% assurance on the multiyear funding. Secretary Banoy identified 150,000,000 and a corporate operating budget multiyear allocation of 477,000,000, while saying the corporate operating budget would be used. On runway and safety issues, Banoy referred to an unclear amount and the DOTr general right-of-way fund. Lara also requested tower and equipment improvements, all-weather capability, and a night rating. Banoy gave a qualified assurance that the night-rating program would proceed if it met organizational priorities, leaving the implementation details open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether prior and proposed multiyear funding would deliver the Tuguegarao Airport infrastructure required for the Region 2 gateway, including runway, tower, equipment, all-weather capability, and night operations. It also asked how the funding would be implemented and whether additional right-of-way and safety needs were covered.

topics.topic: Laguindingan Airport international operations and access
topics.summary: Deputy Speaker Bobby Mano raised the need to honor Laguindingan and Misamis Oriental in the airport’s name or gateway branding. The agency indicated that recognition could be arranged and said the proponent would be advised accordingly. Mano then asked when the airport would be converted to international operations after its transfer and privatization. The implementing-unit official answered that the infrastructure was ready, but the concessionaire still had to secure airlines for international flights and discussions were ongoing. The agency committed to provide a more concrete timeline after consulting the relevant concessionaire or group. Mano said he was satisfied with that commitment, although no definite operational date was given.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether Laguindingan Airport could be renamed or otherwise identified in a way that honors Misamis Oriental, and when the airport would begin international operations. Deputy Speaker Bobby Mano also sought a concrete timeline that he could report to constituents in Northern Mindanao.

topics.topic: Ozamis City Airport modernization funding
topics.summary: Representative Inviu Aminal raised Ozamis City Airport modernization as a regional and presidential priority targeted for completion by 2028. DOTr officials confirmed that the project had received no DOTr funding from 2023 onward and cited limited fiscal space and low obligation or utilization rates as possible reasons. The secretary mentioned about 300 million in connection with the proposal, while the implementing authority confirmed a ballpark modernization requirement of about 2.1 billion. The agency also cited 169 million for site acquisition, a transcribed phase-one amount of 303,300,000,000, and 891,000,000 for the FY2027 phase-two asphalt overlay. The secretary declined to commit to a specific final FY2027 amount without board consultation and undertook to get back to the committee, leaving completion funding unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Department of Transportation had recognized Ozamis City Airport modernization as a priority and whether the FY2027 proposal contained funding for it. Representative Inviu Aminal also asked what funding could be provided through the end of the President’s term to complete the project by 2028.

topics.topic: Palawan port and airport development
topics.summary: Rep. Carl Legaspi requested updates on Palawan’s ports and airports, including Port San Fernando, Buliluyan Port, Taytay-Sandoval Airport, and Busuanga Airport. PPA said San Fernando and Borac ports were being prepared for turnover to the provincial government, after which the province would handle further development, including a passenger terminal at San Fernando. It reported ongoing Buliluyan expansion and commitments for further RoRo and Cagayancillo facilities. DOTr officials said Busuanga had an allocation of about 573 million, an ongoing 2,100-meter runway, and a 2027 allocation of about 950 million for landside development. They also said procurement for the Taytay-Sandoval feasibility study would proceed within the month, with a hoped-for award by November. The matter landed with agency implementation commitments rather than a new committee funding action.

It also sought to establish the Department's budget participation in the airport initiatives and the availability of funding for ongoing facilities.

topics.topic: MARINA cybersecurity, seafarer systems, and processing charges
topics.summary: Chairman Franz Pumaren asked MARINA to confirm the cyber incident, identify system accountability, and explain the effect on seafarer-document processing. MARINA clarified that the incident occurred on August 13 and said the affected system was about seven years old, with a technology refresh and disaster-recovery system included in its Tier 2 proposal. The agency said it had used a temporary system, preserved data, and resumed operations in a controlled environment. The chairman then raised reports that the usual 1,000 charge had become 10,000 to 20,000 for fast-track processing. MARINA agreed to investigate the alleged charges and possible middlemen, while the chairman requested a report. The issue therefore landed as committed rather than resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether MARINA's IT system had suffered a cyberattack, who was accountable for the system and its recovery, and whether the agency had adequate funding for a technology refresh and disaster-recovery system. It also sought an explanation for reports that seafarers were being charged substantially higher amounts for fast-track processing.

topics.topic: NLEX flooding mitigation and alternative transport routes
topics.summary: Rep. Anna York Bondoc raised the severe NLEX flooding and traffic disruption, reporting delays of about ten to twelve hours over roughly 10 kilometers. Vince Dizon cited short-term measures including raising the pavement by about point six meters northbound and point five meters southbound, flood walls, dredging, floodgates, sheet piles, and heavy-duty pumps. He also said TRB had issued NLEX a notice to explain, was studying possible reimbursement, and had sought toll-free passage and proactive advisories. Bondoc pressed for alternative expressways or viaducts, unfinished bridges and bypass roads, and public transport options because McArthur Highway and railway access were flooded. Dizon said the agency would coordinate with other officials and ask its planning office to study additional rail infrastructure, while identifying elevated public transport as a long-term solution. Bondoc also requested full Coast Guard support and cited the clearing of 15,000 items or material, although the transcript's description of that figure was unclear. The issue landed with agency commitments and further coordination, but without a complete resolution of the alternative-route and public transport gaps.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DOTr and other agencies would address recurring NLEX flooding and severe traffic disruptions, including immediate flood-control measures, alternative roads and bridges, public transport options, and longer-term elevated or rail infrastructure. It also sought clarification on the status of related PPP infrastructure and support for emergency responders.

topics.summary: Rep. France questioned MARINA about Orient classification society's continued preventive suspension and whether it was being favored or treated differently from other societies. topics.question: The committee sought to establish why Orient classification society remained under preventive suspension without being blacklisted, how MARINA regulated and accredited classification societies for domestic vessels, and whether passengers were adequately insured before vessels were authorized to operate. It also asked what had happened to prior committee recommendations on passenger insurance.

topics.topic: Land acquisition and distribution balances and the 2027 target
topics.summary: Secretary Estrella reported accelerating land-title distribution, including 410,179 titles covering 556,088 hectares under the Marcos administration as of 08/12/2026. Members questioned whether the 2027 target of about 20,000 to 22,000 hectares was adequate, and DAR acknowledged that the target was constrained by the DBM budget ceiling and was not enough. The civil society representative highlighted conflicting LAAD balances of 147,493 hectares, about 700,000 hectares, and 563,076 hectares; Secretary Estrella said 750,000 hectares was the more accurate figure and suggested DAR might reduce it to 500 or a little less during the year. DAR said much of the larger balance related to partializing collective CLOAs rather than entirely new acquisitions. The agency also described its balance-cleansing process under MC 4 series of 2014 and said it was reviewing the policy to impose stricter, Secretary-level controls. DAR committed to provide official LAAD figures and Agrarian Reform Fund utilization data, but the committee did not resolve which balance should govern the 2027 budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish DAR's actual land-acquisition and distribution balance, the figure underlying the President's 2027 title-distribution directive, and whether the proposed funding and targets were sufficient. It also examined how DAR cleanses the LAAD balance, reports accomplishments, and addresses land titles affected by legal or documentation problems.

topics.topic: LAAD funding, land deletions, and the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance
topics.summary: A civil society representative questioned DAR's conflicting LAAD balances, which ranged from 147,493 hectares and 563,076 hectares to about 700,000 hectares and a response referring to 750,000 hectares. The representative challenged DAR's 20,000-hectare target, the deletion of land from the balance, and the agency's ability to preserve the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance. DAR said it was following MC 4 series of 2014 but was reviewing and seeking to amend the deletion process, including possible centralization under the Secretary. On funding, DAR attributed its proposal to the DBM ceiling and cited about 7 billion in landowners' compensation, including 2.2 billion in cash, while the representative presented substantially larger amounts for completing the balance. DAR agreed to publish official LAAD figures and requested one or two days to submit missing ARF utilization data. It also reported 135,884 validated collective CLOA-equivalents, 1,481,491 hectares, 1,075,672 beneficiaries, and 330,497 e-Titles, but the central balance and funding questions remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which LAAD balance DAR was using for budgeting, the legal and procedural basis for deleting land from that balance, and how DAR could meet the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance. It also sought official accomplishment, funding, and utilization data supporting DAR's reported figures.

topics.topic: SPLIT project, World Bank loan, collective CLOAs, and e-titles
topics.summary: Rep. Leila de Lima asked whether SPLIT remained a DAR priority, whether its World Bank loan was exhausted, and whether the project could be completed before its 12/31/2027 expiration. Secretary Conrad Estrella III said SPLIT was proceeding at full speed, remained a priority, and had an unexhausted loan, while explaining that it was needed to parcelize collective CLOAs. DAR officials said the DBM ceiling supported about 20,000 hectares annually, or roughly 20,000 to 22,000 hectares in 2027, at an estimated 10,000 per hectare, which they acknowledged was insufficient. De Lima requested regional 2025–2026 output data and the loan's disbursement status, but those figures were not supplied in the transcript. DAR also reported about 703,000 debt-condonation certificates distributed, cumulative distribution of 4,800,000 hectares from the start of CARP, ongoing regional shapefile work, and digitalization estimated at 80 to 90%. The matter landed with DAR commitments to validate excluded beneficiaries and complete shapefile work, while requested SPLIT performance and disbursement details remained outstanding.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the SPLIT project remained a DAR priority, whether its World Bank loan had been exhausted, and whether the project could be completed before the loan expired. Members also asked for 2025–2026 regional output data, 2027 funding adequacy, the status of collective CLOA parcelization, shapefiles, and digital titles.

topics.topic: Landowners’ compensation backlog and the 500,000,000 2026 cash allocation
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DAR about the landowners’ compensation budget, the 2026 allocation of about 500 million, and the proposed 2027 amount of about 100 million. DAR said the outstanding balance was about 7.2 billion, with about 2.2 billion required in cash. The agency explained that 70% could be paid through government bonds and 30% in cash, with Land Bank issuing the bonds and handling valuation. DAR said the 2026 allocation had zero utilization because OP approval for its release was still pending, and that payments followed a first-in, first-out process. The agency committed to provide a supporting list of pending landowners’ compensation payments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the size and composition of DAR’s landowners’ compensation backlog, the status and utilization of the 2026 cash allocation, and the payment mechanism for the proposed 2027 funding. It also asked how payments were prioritized and whether DAR could provide a list supporting the pending compensation claims.

topics.topic: PBBM Bridges foreign-assisted project and FY2027 loan treatment
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio asked whether the PBBM Bridges project was financed by a Republic of Korea loan and how its proposed funding of about 1.4 billion would be reflected in the FY 2027 budget ceiling. The foreign-assisted-projects undersecretary answered that the total loan package was 22 billion and said the loan contract was scheduled for final signing on Monday. Rep. Marlo Bancoro asked whether at least six bridges in his district could be implemented, while DAR said it was trying to implement projects that year and conservatively expected one third of the list to proceed. Rep. Tim Cayton asked about selection criteria and a Nueva Vizcaya crossing; DAR cited validation, farmer beneficiaries, food security, and economic internal rate of return, after reviewing 1,200 locations and approving "three fifty" sites as transcribed. The financing reconciliation and definitive 2027 schedule were not resolved, but DAR made implementation and follow-up commitments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the PBBM Bridges project was financed by a Republic of Korea loan or ODA, how loan proceeds and the GOP counterpart would be reflected in the FY 2027 budget ceiling, and whether proposed bridges could be implemented in 2027. Members also asked how bridge sites were selected and whether a specific Nueva Vizcaya crossing could be considered.

topics.topic: Agrarian debt condonation and land-tenure security
topics.summary: Secretary Conrad Estrella III presented debt condonation as a central DAR and presidential priority under Republic Act No. 11,953 and said the statutory 06/30/2026 completion deadline had been met. DAR reported about 703,000 certificates distributed, covering about 901,246 hectares, while the identified statutory scope involved approximately 57,760,000,000 in agrarian debt; some debt figures in the transcript were inconsistent or unclear. Representative Leila De Lima asked whether SPLIT and its World Bank loan remained priorities, and Estrella answered that SPLIT was proceeding at full speed, the loan was not exhausted, and the project would expire on 12/31/2027. DAR officials said the DBM ceiling supported only about 20,000 to 22,000 hectares annually and that 10,000 per hectare was insufficient. The chair questioned why some beneficiaries had not received certificates, and DAR cited the BARM distribution as the remaining verified gap while undertaking to validate other alleged exclusions and submit a detailed explanation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status and completion of DAR’s agrarian debt-condonation program, including the number of beneficiaries and obligations covered, any exclusions, and the remaining distribution of certificates. It also examined whether the SPLIT project and World Bank financing remained priorities for FY 2027 and whether the proposed land-tenure-security funding was sufficient.

topics.topic: Protection of CLOA holders and ARBs in land disputes
topics.summary: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella raised the Wanderlust title overlap and asked DAR to identify the affected land, titles, ARBs, and barangays. DAR reported around 745 hectares affected, 63 collective titles covering about 677 hectares, 276 affected ARBs, and around four ARBs directly affected by fencing, while confirming the initial 438.5-hectare projection. DAR's legal undersecretary said conflicting titles required cancellation of one title and that eligible and disposable portions covered by CLOAs should remain free from Wanderlust claims. DAR said it was coordinating with the OSG and DNR, investigating the missing survey plan, and collating areas for possible reversion action, but gave no timetable. Fuentebella requested certified lists and technical survey materials within the week, and the chair committed to pursuing the concern. Rep. Elijah San Fernando separately questioned 2027 land-distribution backlogs, which DAR attributed primarily to insufficient funding and DBM budget ceilings, and raised the unresolved Saraya case and protection of CLOA holders.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of the Wanderlust title overlap, the number of affected hectares, titles, and ARBs, and DAR's legal position and timetable for protecting CLOA holders. It also sought explanations for DAR's 2027 land-distribution targets, funding constraints, and the status of the Saraya case and related protection of farmers.

topics.topic: Climate Resilience Productivity Support Program and farm inputs
topics.summary: Rep. Leo Rodriguez raised the Climate Resilience Productivity Support Program for disaster-prone provinces and asked whether the farm-livelihood intervention would be prioritized in 2027. DAR referred the matter to Undersecretary Jal Martinez, who said the program would include targeted farm-input support and farm machinery and equipment. Martinez cited "seven thirty four" for the input-support target and again for the machinery and equipment component, but the amount or unit was unclear, and he said around 26,980 people were expected to be served. He also discussed community-shared-expense tractors, including fuel and maintenance considerations, and referred to convergence involving regional and provincial DAR offices and local officials. The hearing did not establish a clear peso allocation, detailed project list, or documented commitment for the convergence plans, leaving the issue unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DAR would prioritize and fund the Climate Resilience Productivity Support Program for 2027 in disaster-prone provinces, including farm-input assistance, machinery and equipment, and inter-agency convergence. It also sought clarification on the program's targets and regional and provincial implementation plans.

topics.topic: Agricultural land-use conversion, inactivity penalties, and renewable-energy projects
topics.summary: A committee member first asked how DAR monitored and enforced reported illegal agricultural land conversions. Secretary Conrad Estrella said local government units were responsible for many conversions, while DAR called them out, directed parties to the proper procedure, and reported that many had complied. Rep. Sarah Elago then raised a study showing a decline in agricultural land from 50.19% to the transcript's unclear 47.64333.3%, alongside solar-farm expansion, and questioned a proposed PacSilica project involving 4,000 acres or an unclear hectare figure. Estrella said DAR would contest PacSilica's or BCDA's eminent-domain exercise, and a DAR undersecretary reported distribution of about 13,775 hectares while offering updated data. Elago requested reports covering conversion applications, approvals, converted lands, and related implementation for specified years. Rep. Salvador Plato separately asked whether the penalty for agricultural inactivity and premature conversion under the cited statutory provision was strictly enforced, and DAR answered yes. The enforcement position was stated, but detailed conversion data remained subject to submission.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DAR was adequately monitoring and enforcing agricultural land-use rules, including illegal conversion, renewable-energy projects, agricultural inactivity, and premature conversion. Members also asked for data on land conversion, ARB land status, and DAR's implementation of related programs and mandates.

topics.topic: ARB revalidation and inclusion in the RSBSA database
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago asked DAR when it had last revalidated ARB status and whether phased revalidation was ongoing, saying the initial response had not answered her questions. A DAR official gave an incomplete response in the transcript, while a DAR undersecretary later reported that about 13,775 hectares had been distributed, with data segregated from 2021 to 2026 by year and ARB classification. The undersecretary undertook to provide updated copies of the data to the committee and the member's office. Rep. Salvador Plato separately invoked the statutory requirement for mandatory ARB inclusion in the RSBSA and asked about DAR's coordination with the Department of Agriculture. Undersecretary Jal Martinez said DAR was collaborating with the DA and working to bring the ARB database on board, but acknowledged challenges in including all beneficiaries. The revalidation question remained without a clear answer, while the data submissions and interagency coordination were left as agency commitments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish when DAR last revalidated the status of agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs), whether revalidation was ongoing, and how DAR was coordinating with the Department of Agriculture to include ARBs in the RSBSA database. It also sought updated beneficiary and land-distribution data supporting these processes.

topics.topic: Shapefiles, collective-parcel splitting, and digitalization of titles
topics.summary: Rep. Jay Vergara raised questions about the legal and administrative basis of agrarian-reform land distribution and asked about shapefiles, collective parcels, and digitalized titles. A DAR official said the agency had distributed 4,800,000 hectares to about 2,900 ARBs since the start of the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program. The official said shapefile implementation was under way and was being completed region by region, with hoped-for completion by the end of the year. In response to questions about titles after collective parcels were split, an agency official estimated the digitalization or title-processing work at 80 to 90%. The exact scope of that estimate and several follow-up references, including 2022 and December 2025, were not clear, but DAR committed to continuing the shapefile work.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish the status of DAR's agrarian-reform land distribution records, including the completion of shapefiles, the splitting of collective parcels, and the digitalization of titles. It also sought the extent of title processing and the expected timeline for completing the work.

topics.topic: FY2027 DAR budget, utilization, and support-services allocation
topics.summary: The committee reviewed DAR’s FY2027 proposed allocation and its utilization of prior appropriations. The chair cited a proposed net budget of about 14.691 billion and identified allocations for land tenure security, agrarian justice, and beneficiary development and support. Secretary Conrad Estrella III reported support-services accomplishments and utilization rates, including a 47% obligation rate and 70% disbursement rate for FY2026 as of June. He presented the FY2027 net as 16,935,000,000, with about 7.066 billion for personnel services and 8,610,000,000 for maintenance and other operating expenses, although some transcript figures were unclear or internally inconsistent. DAR committed to complete remaining debt-condonation work, improve implementation and utilization, and continue land, justice, and support-service programs. Representative Sheen Gonzales moved to terminate the briefing, and the chair approved the motion without objection.
topics.question: The committee was establishing DAR’s FY2027 proposed budget, how it had used prior appropriations, and whether the requested resources were aligned with land tenure, agrarian justice, debt condonation, and support-services priorities. It also sought to determine what DAR committed to deliver with the proposed allocation.

topics.topic: DOH FY2027 budget reduction and priority-item restoration
topics.summary: The committee chair highlighted a proposed DOH budget of about 354 billion and described a reduction of roughly 95 billion, or 21.2%, against the FY2026 enacted level. Secretary Mercado said the DOH had requested 837,000,000,000 but received approval for 353,000,000,000, and identified the indirect-member PhilHealth gap, HFEP, and hospital operations as priority restoration items. PhilHealth officials described an indirect-member benefit requirement of about 2.44 or R244 billion dollars against an allocation of 74, with an additional 170 identified as necessary to reach breakeven. Mercado cited PHP19 billion requested for HFEP against PHP14.5 billion provided and about 12,000,000,000 for hospital operations. Rodriguez supported the DOH and PhilHealth budgets and said he would seek the requested increases. The committee also requested rare-disease lists and earmarked-revenue information, but the exact 2027 sin-tax and rare-disease funding figures were not established.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 DOH budget was sufficient to sustain the Department's five pillars, universal health-care commitments, hospitals, facilities, and PhilHealth-related benefits. It also sought to identify the priority items and amounts that should be restored, and to clarify the funding gap for indirect-member premium subsidies and earmarked revenues.

topics.topic: Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) cuts, utilization, and reverted funds
topics.summary: Members questioned the reduction of HFEP funding from the DOH request of about 19 billion to an allocation of about 14.5 billion, although the Secretary also gave an inconsistent stated shortfall of PHP15.1 billion. Representative Suntay cited an audit showing only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities operational, or roughly 33 percent, and challenged facility planning and political allocation. The Secretary said site conditions, catchment planning, facility standards, and a rules-based referral network would guide future projects, and undertook to improve compliance and oversight. Representative Garin raised low HFEP obligation and disbursement figures and called for projects to have complete designs, programs of work, budgets, and procurement arrangements before inclusion. Representative Nava said completed super health centers remained unequipped and asked for primary-care standards and the amount of funds reverted to the National Treasury. The Secretary said active construction would be completed before new projects were started, and the Chair directed the DOH to submit reverted-funds data before plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the HFEP allocation was reduced, how effectively HFEP-funded facilities and projects were being used, and whether projects were being prioritized according to health-network needs rather than political requests. Members also asked what funds had been reverted to the National Treasury and whether those funds could be restored or repurposed for health facilities.
