topics.topic: Delayed or canceled transport projects and congressional insertions
topics.summary: A committee member asked DOTr to account for foreign-assisted projects, delays, penalties, and commitment fees, and DOTr estimated that there were about seven such projects. DOTr confirmed that commitment fees were part of loan contracts, while Congresswoman Mula cited about three hundred eight million pesos for 2024, 3,400,000,000 pesos in DOF-cited fees for DPWH and DOTr from 2022 to the present, and about one point six billion at the DPWH hearing. DOTr said DOF actually paid the fees and undertook to coordinate with it and report back, while the member requested complete project, timeline, and financial data. Congresswoman Mula also asked about the terminated Zamboanga Port passenger-terminal contract, and PPA reported about 52% accomplishment, with rebidding or reimplementation discussed but no clear roadmap supplied. The chair later cited a foreign-assisted-project budget of 232,000,000,000 and questioned the funding basis for congressional insertions. The agency confirmed that loan agreements were perfected, but the detailed appropriation and insertion issues remained subject to clarification and document submission.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which DOTr foreign-assisted projects had been delayed, canceled, or placed under unprogrammed appropriations; the commitment fees paid or incurred for them; and whether congressional insertions had funding and valid loan support. It also sought an update on the terminated Zamboanga Port passenger-terminal contract.

topics.topic: Zamboanga Port passenger-terminal contract termination and rebidding
topics.summary: Congresswoman Mula raised the termination of the PPA contract with Mac Builders, Inc. for the Zamboanga Port Passenger Terminal Building because of prolonged delays. The PPA general manager said the contract was terminated after assessment and reported project accomplishment at about 52%, while an agency interjection cited 18% without clarification. Mula then asked for an update because Zamboanga was a busy port and requested the rebidding plan, timeline, and roadmap. The PPA began an answer concerning the award and reimplementation of the project, but the recorded response was incomplete and unclear. No rebidding schedule, completion date, or related future funding requirement was established.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the Philippine Ports Authority terminated the Mac Builders, Inc. contract for the Zamboanga Port Passenger Terminal Building and what would happen next. Congresswoman Mula specifically asked for an update on rebidding, the project timeline, and a roadmap for completion.

topics.topic: MARINA vessel-safety inspection personnel and capacity
topics.summary: Congresswoman Mula asked MARINA about its 2027 plan to address nationwide vessel-safety inspection staffing and capacity gaps. MARINA said its MOOE was so far sufficient but that it needed additional personnel and continuing technical capacity building for highly technical maritime-safety work. The agency said it had submitted a comprehensive manpower proposal under the Government Optimization Plan, which would be evaluated by DBM and used to strengthen regional offices. It also appealed for consideration of another tier-two proposal for 2027. Congresswoman Mula called for continued monitoring of reforms, budget utilization, inspection compliance with international conventions, and maritime-industry oversight. The request remained subject to evaluation and committee consideration, with no final funding decision recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish MARINA’s 2027 plan for addressing gaps in vessel-safety inspection personnel and capacity nationwide. It also sought clarification on the budgetary support requested for additional personnel and continuing technical training.

topics.topic: Active-transport funding for bike lanes and sidewalks
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Cendaña asked whether the active-transport allocation was adequate and equitable for expanding and maintaining bike lanes and sidewalks. The agency said the program was commuter-centered, involved civil-society partnerships, and was being implemented nationwide, while urging Congress to provide sufficient and proper funding. An agency official cited an initial proposal of about 1.13 billion and an objective of at least 2,400 kilometers of bike lanes and expanded sidewalks, with another figure of 1,030 kilometers mentioned. The proposal was also described as 1.1 billion for expanding bike lanes and sidewalks. Cendaña cited 34 million as a commuter allocation for active transport, but its precise status was unclear. No adjustment, document submission, or other action was recorded, and the adequacy question remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed active-transport allocation was adequate and equitable for expanding and maintaining walking and cycling infrastructure, in light of the stated commuter access figures and targets.

topics.topic: DOTr absorptive capacity and regional allocation
topics.summary: DOTr presented 2025 and July 2026 obligation and disbursement rates and said it was confident its performance would improve. Rep. Romeo Momo questioned the proposed increase from about 158 billion to about 301 billion and the agency's ability to absorb a capital-outlay-heavy budget. DOTr answered that its whole-agency 2025 rates were about 89.35% for obligations and 56.94% for disbursements, while July 2026 rates were 74.1% and 56.18%, respectively, and attributed differences to foreign-assisted projects using cash availment authority. Momo also questioned the regional distribution, citing about 0.1% for his region versus Davao's roughly 15.3 billion or 5.1%. The committee pressed for completion of Tandag Airport and improved facilities in Surigao del Sur. DOTr targeted Tandag completion by year-end, said it would reevaluate the project, and committed to prepare a 2027 program for Surigao del Sur.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DOTr could absorb and disburse its substantially increased FY 2027 budget, particularly its capital-outlay allocation. It also questioned whether the proposed allocation adequately covered regions such as Surigao del Sur and whether specific airport and transport projects would be completed.

topics.topic: Tandag Airport completion and Surigao del Sur transport facilities
topics.summary: A committee member criticized the area's reported allocation of only about 1% of the DOTr budget and pressed the agency on Tandag Airport's completion. The member said the airport appeared to be roughly 97% to 98% complete and sought turnover so airlines could be engaged. The DOTr said the project was almost substantially complete, identified the seven-story control tower, apron, grade corrections, and perimeter fence, and targeted completion of the vertical structures by year-end. The member pushed for completion within the month and cited 7% disbursement absorptive capacity, while the agency undertook to revisit the accomplishment. The member also sought improvements to Surigao del Sur's port and Kagwa Airport facilities, and the agency committed to immediately prepare a program for 2027.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the DOTr's regional budget allocation and the completion status and operational readiness of Tandag Airport. It also sought action on transport facilities serving Surigao del Sur, including the port and Kagwa Airport.

topics.topic: NLEX disruption response, toll reimbursement, and traffic management
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Cendaña raised the NLEX disruption, asking about traffic management, toll treatment, and short-, medium-, and long-term mitigation. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said the TRB would examine possible reimbursement within three days, while emphasizing proactive warnings through SMS, RFID-holder notices, variable message signs, and other public-information channels. Cendaña noted that toll-fee collection had continued for more than twenty four hours, and Lopez said toll suspension was governed by the toll-operations agreement and that more reimbursement was needed. Lopez also said the TRB had issued NLEX a notice to explain regarding the toll holiday and liability. Rep. Adore Plato separately questioned the response to severe-weather stranding and the implementation of early-warning protocols. NLEX representative Robin Ignacio said advisories had begun on August 28, but no final reimbursement or protocol determination was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOTr and the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) responded to the NLEX disruption, including traffic management, toll collection or reimbursement, and communication with motorists. It also examined whether NLEX and the TRB had adequate early-warning protocols for severe-weather events.

topics.topic: LTFRB Region 3 hearing-officer requirements and discipline
topics.summary: Eli San Fernando raised an allegation that LTFRB Region 3 hearing officer Attorney Jennifer Rodriguez arbitrarily required additional documents and 40,000 on the same day they were submitted. He also questioned why the hearing officer was operating from a private law office in the LTFRB office and asked who had disciplinary authority, citing possible collusion or conflict of interest and a memorandum dated 02/19/2026. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said it was his first time hearing of the matter and stated that disciplinary authority over appointed officials belonged to the appointing authority. An LTFRB board member identified as Greg said a notice to explain had been issued, a complaint was pending before the LTFRB disciplinary board, and Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office. The board member also said the regional director had begun hearing the complaint and that the LTFRB had filed its comment with the CSC. The immediate allegations and the broader oversight concerns remained open, although the agency reported ongoing disciplinary action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether an LTFRB Region 3 hearing officer had improperly imposed additional requirements and a 40,000 payment on the same day, and whether the regional director or another authority had disciplinary jurisdiction. It also sought the status of the disciplinary case and corrective action, including whether similar conflicts could occur in other regions.

topics.topic: DA FY2027 budget restoration and agency funding priorities
topics.summary: Christopherson Yap supported the DA budget and possible increases, highlighting soil laboratories, irrigation reforms, and local food security planning. The chair later asked DA officials for their top three priorities for possible restoration or additional funding and said the remaining requests could be submitted in writing. DA administrator Paul presented a written-request wishlist that included about 8.7 billion for fertilizer assistance, as much as 10 billion for Rice for All, roughly 9.2 billion for farm-to-market bridges, and about 20 billion for NMIS operating-budget restoration and DA realignment funds. He also cited requests for solar irrigation, laboratories, coconut planting, sugarcane, Ube, dairy, and agricultural food hubs. The committee did not approve a specific restoration during the recorded exchange, but the agency's requests were placed on the record for continuing budget-amendment deliberations.
topics.question: The committee sought to determine which DA programs and projects should be considered for budget restoration or additional funding during institutional amendments. The chair specifically asked the DA leadership to identify its top three priorities and provide the remaining requests in writing.

topics.topic: NIA FY2027 budget restoration and irrigation project flexibility
topics.summary: Sheen Gonzales sought DA intervention and rehabilitation planning for irrigation facilities in Dolores, Eastern Samar, and Secretary Kiko Laurel committed to inspect the area in October for possible 2027 action. Carl Cari asked what rapid funding mechanisms NIA had for typhoon-damaged irrigation facilities; an NIA official cited a request of about 2.8 billion and a proposal of 66,000,000, with repairs requested through OCD. NIA Administrator Ed Gillian said NIA had requested about 233 billion for FY2027, but only 46 billion was included, compared with nearly 64 billion in FY2026. He warned that the reduction could delay ongoing irrigation projects and asked that the budget be restored to a program-based presentation. The chair distinguished that request from the special provision on project modifications and required safeguards, validation, and accountability. NIA agreed to submit proposed special-provision language and a prioritized list of items for the budget amendment subcommittee.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what support was available for irrigation rehabilitation and emergency repairs, and whether NIA’s FY2027 funding was sufficient to complete ongoing projects. It also examined whether NIA should receive greater flexibility to modify project line items while retaining congressional safeguards and accountability.

topics.topic: Solar irrigation program and emergency irrigation repairs
topics.summary: Carl Cari asked NIA how its FY 2027 budget would enable rapid repairs to typhoon-damaged irrigation facilities, and an NIA official cited a garbled district request of 2.8, billion and a proposal of 66,000,000. The DA administrator later listed solar power irrigation as a requested item of about 1 billion. NIA administrator Ed Gillian said NIA had requested about 233 billion but that only about 46 billion was included, compared with nearly 64 billion in FY 2026, and sought restoration to a program-based presentation. The chair also questioned NIA about modifying project line items and required safeguards for accountability. NIA agreed to submit a letter and prioritized list of specific requests, including special provisions, while the committee said it would examine NIA's separate solar irrigation program. No final restoration or emergency-repair appropriation was decided in the excerpts.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what funding was available for solar-powered irrigation and how quickly NIA could repair irrigation facilities damaged by typhoons. It also examined whether the FY 2027 DA and NIA budgets should be restored or amended to support these needs.

topics.topic: El Niño, drought, and climate-resilient farmer assistance
topics.summary: Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA how the 2027 budget would help farmers and Palawan fisherfolk withstand climate-related losses and access inputs, insurance, equipment, and markets. The DA cited solar irrigation, solar pumps, solar-powered aerators, drought- and heat-resistant seeds, fertilizer support, crop insurance, recovery loans, and soil laboratories, as well as Palawan port and ice facilities. Carl Cari later asked about direct assistance during a prolonged El Niño and drought, and the DA answered that it would coordinate with DSWD and provide alternative seeds, fertilizer, and land-preparation support. NIA cited a request of about 2.8 billion and a proposal of 66,000,000 for repair-related needs, but did not clearly explain a rapid-release mechanism. The Chair then asked for El Niño contingency funding, and the DA cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and an increase in the fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar aerators and solar pumps. The DA committed to submit detailed, separately prioritized information, while the final adequacy of contingency and emergency-repair funding remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what the 2027 budget would provide for farmers and fisherfolk facing climate-related crop and fisheries losses, especially prolonged El Niño, drought, and water shortages. It also examined whether contingency funds, irrigation repairs, insurance, inputs, equipment, and recovery assistance would be available and quickly released.

topics.topic: African swine fever response, farmer payouts, and vaccine validation
topics.summary: An Iloilo member questioned the DA's claim that its ASF vaccine was safe and effective, citing the contrary positions of two FDA veterinary experts and the US Department of Agriculture. The DA reported that it had distributed about half a million doses and observed efficacy of about 85% to 90%, then committed to send the supporting clinical-trial documents. Representative Carl Cari asked about 2027 funding for community pig-raising facilities, faster indemnification, and low-cost biosecurity training, citing 4,900,000 in prior indemnification aid in Southern Leyte. The DA mentioned 1,000,000,000 for ASF or AI vaccines in case of an outbreak and described coordination with a state university and ATI under the Inspire 600 program, with a transcript-unclear figure of 12.5 or 13,500,000 per setup. The vaccine documentation and training coordination were committed, but the broader budget and facility-grant questions remained without a complete answer.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DA had conclusive evidence that its ASF vaccine was safe and effective, and whether the agency would submit that evidence. It also asked what 2027 resources would support ASF vaccine deployment, farmer indemnification, biosecurity training, and community pig-raising or recovery facilities.

topics.topic: Rice procurement, floor-price implementation, and Rice for All
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago asked how EO 100's rice floor price applied and sought clarification on NFA procurement, Rice for All funding, storage, and EO 101 implementation. The agency said NFA was buying at 21 and cited dry-rice prices of 25 to 27 pesos per kilo, while reporting 9,000,000,000 for NFA and 10,000,000,000 for Rice for All. An agency official said NFA warehouse capacity had risen from 500,000 tons to 800,000 tons, with procurement discussed at 20,000 to eventually 40,000 tons a month. The chair then questioned reports that LGU suppliers were selling imported rice instead of local rice and called for validation and investigation. The agency committed to providing details, and reported that the Sagibsaka desk had about 2,000,000, stated as exactly 1,950,000 for ICT equipment, with an additional 95,000,000 figure that was unclear in context.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how Executive Order 100's rice floor-price policy was being implemented, including whether it applied to private-sector buyers, and how NFA procurement, Rice for All funding, and storage capacity supported the policy. It also sought clarification on supplier validation, the implementation of Executive Orders 100 and 101, and funding for the Sagibsaka desk.

topics.topic: Rice storage capacity and delayed Iloilo processing facility
topics.summary: The Iloilo member pressed the DA over a rice processing facility that had remained unimplemented despite a commitment made about three years earlier. PhilMech described a warehouse of about 1,200 square meters, a 12-ton dryer, and a processing system with a stated capacity of three tons per hour, while DBM clearance for hauling trucks remained pending. The DA committed the rice processing system for June 2027 and scheduled tractors and combined harvesters for distribution from October through December. Sarah Elago then asked about EO 100, temporary storage, and NFA use of private warehouses. The agency cited Rice-for-All funding of about 10 billion, NFA funding of about 9 billion, and a stated total of 19,000,000,020.26, while reporting NFA internal storage capacity of 800,000 tons and procurement of 20,000 to eventually 40,000 tons a month. The discussion ended with commitments and agency assurances, but unresolved clearance and storage-arrangement details.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the Iloilo rice processing facility had not been implemented despite earlier commitments, what equipment and delivery dates were covered, and whether storage capacity was sufficient for rice procurement and the Rice-for-All program. It also asked how Executive Order No. 100's floor-price policy applied and what funding and warehouse capacity were available.

topics.topic: Fish ports, deepwater ports, and fisheries infrastructure
topics.summary: Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA about fisheries livelihood and production support in Palawan, and the agency cited a 15 hectare Puerto Princesa-area port with ice, cold-storage, and blast-freezer facilities, along with solar-powered ice plants with five to 10 tons per day capacity. Rep. Howard Guintu questioned PFDA’s fish-port funding, which was stated as 3,800,000,003.08 and then 3,800,000,000, while another response cited 8,000,000,000 for old and new ports after an unclear initial figure of 88,000,000,000. He also raised the effect of US restrictions on blue swimming crab, noting that 90% of the market was in the United States; the fisheries undersecretary answered that the issue involved fishing gear and Irrawaddy dolphin interactions and cited a reduction of the gill-net limit to 500 meters. The chair asked about deepwater-port implementation and fisherfolk contingency assistance, and the DA said Mindoro construction would be bid out, cited 8,700,000,000 for El Niño fertilizers, and reported an increase in the BFAR fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000. The chair requested that fisherfolk needs be separately prioritized, and the DA committed to submit the requested details.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much funding was proposed for fish ports and deepwater ports in 2027, how existing and new projects would be financed and implemented, and what support would improve fisheries communities’ access to ice, cold storage, markets, and fishing gear. Members also asked how the agency would protect fisheries market access, particularly for blue swimming crab, and whether contingency support would be available for fisherfolk affected by climate and fuel-related disruptions.

topics.topic: Fisherfolk assistance during fishing bans and market restrictions
topics.summary: Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA what assistance would be available to Palawan fisherfolk, including fuel, ice, gear, insurance, and market support. The DA cited a port facility near Puerto Princesa, solar-powered ice plants, seaweed and livestock programs, and proposed ice-plant capacities of about five to 10 tons per day. Rep. Howard Guintu questioned PFDA fish-port funding and raised the US restrictions affecting blue swimming crab exports; BFAR explained the Marine Mammal Protection Act issue, the Irrawaddy dolphin risk, the 500-meter gill-net limit, and its assistance and reporting commitments. The committee also sought support for fisherfolk affected by fishing bans and military exercises, but the duration and precise assistance remained unclear. The Chair later pressed the DA on deepwater-port implementation, the depleted Presidential Assistance program, and El Niño contingency funding; the DA cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and a BFAR budget increase from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar equipment. The DA agreed to submit detailed, separately identified fisherfolk priorities.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what livelihood, production, market-access, and emergency assistance would be available to fisherfolk affected by fishing restrictions, export-market barriers, and national-security-related fishing bans. It also examined the funding and implementation of fish ports, fisherfolk programs, and contingency support in the FY 2027 budget.

topics.topic: RSSI sugarcane infestation control and the 35,000,000 LGU allocation
topics.summary: Sarah Elago raised concerns about the cost and environmental effects of chemical pesticides and asked whether lower-cost biological controls could reach all RSSI-affected sugarcane farms. The DA reported 134,000 hectares affected and 67,443 hectares verified, while the administrator said chemicals had covered about 35,000 hectares. The DA said it had provided 209,000,000, including 23,000,000 for chemical pesticides, had an additional 10,000,000 for chemicals, and estimated about 120,000,000 more for the initial response. It identified slow fungal production and limited laboratory capacity as the principal constraints, while citing an earmarked 300,000,000 for laboratories. The DA committed 35,000,000 directly to LGUs, based on verified affected areas, for Negros Island, with further quick response funding as needed. Expansion of biocontrol production was committed, but the complete transition away from chemical control was not fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of RSSI infestation in sugarcane farms, the cost and coverage of chemical pesticide assistance, and whether lower-cost biological or nature-based controls could replace or complement chemical measures. It also asked what immediate assistance could be provided before the FY 2027 budget, including how the 35,000,000 LGU allocation would be distributed.

topics.topic: Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund delivery
topics.summary: Carl Cari asked how the PCA and DA would use the 2027 Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund resources to reduce paperwork and ensure timely delivery of free fertilizer and planting materials. An agency official said the PCA budget was mostly for replanting, with a target of 100,000,000 trees and an expected 40,000,000 trees planted by the end of the year. The official also said coco levy funds needed to be unlocked through the new bill and referred to value-adding facilities, scholarships, and education for coconut farmers. No specific process for reducing paperwork or accelerating input delivery was provided. Cari later supported the DA and NIA budgets, but the Trust Fund delivery question remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the PCA and DA would use the 2027 Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund resources to reduce paperwork and delivery bottlenecks. It specifically asked how free fertilizer and planting materials would reach coconut-farming communities on time.

topics.topic: Food logistics chain, mega food hubs, and public markets
topics.summary: A committee member raised consultation with public-market vendors, price monitoring, and local-government responsibilities for public markets. The member then asked for details of the food logistics chain plan. The agency said food hubs were being implemented in 2026 in Clark, Isabella, and an unclear location, citing 22,000,000,000 for Clark, 125,000,000 for Isabella, and other amounts including 500,000,000. For 20.27, it cited 500,000,000, 250,000,000 for San Pablo Lagoon, another 250,000,000, and a stated total of 1,000,000,000 for food hubs. It described a network integrating livestock, laboratories, cold storage, traders, farmers, consumers, LGUs, local cooperatives, and 800 Cadiwa sites, with a target of 10 to 12 mega food hubs. The matter remained informational, with several spoken allocations and references unclear and no further commitment recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how public markets would be coordinated with the Department of Agriculture's price monitoring and logistics functions, and how the proposed mega food hub network would be designed and funded. It also sought details on the food logistics chain, links to local government units, and the planned Cadiwa sites.

topics.topic: FY2027 OVP budget overview, program delivery, and utilization
topics.summary: The chair limited the briefing to the OVP budget and then recognized the agency to present its FY 2027 proposal. The OVP presented a proposed budget of about 785 million, with over 70% for operating expenses and about 193.1 million for goods and grants under socioeconomic program delivery. It described delivery through 10 satellite offices and one extension office, with a target of about 1.4 million beneficiaries. The agency reported that it served about 1.396 million individuals and groups in 2025, obligated about 851.8 million, and disbursed about 687.8 million. For the first half of 2026, it reported about 773,858 beneficiaries served, 43% obligation of the available allotment, and a 62% disbursement rate, although the spoken disbursement amount was unclear. The presentation ended without a recorded challenge, request, or commitment.
topics.question: What was the OVP's proposed FY 2027 budget, how would it be distributed across personnel, operating expenses, capital outlay, and direct program delivery, and what did the OVP report about program reach and budget utilization? The committee also sought to establish the implementation structure supporting nationwide delivery.

topics.topic: OVP personnel-services proposal of about 220.232 million pesos
topics.summary: A committee member asked how many personnel the OVP's FY2027 personnel-services proposal would support and requested a comparison of plantilla, permanent, contractual, and actual staffing. The OVP reported 248 authorized plantilla positions, including permanent and coterminous positions, with 182 actual employees. It also reported 69 casual and contractual positions beyond the plantilla. The agency stated that the total personnel-services budget was 220,000,000 pesos excluding Arlev, after correcting its initial statement. The requested breakdown of salaries, allowances, other compensation, and the services rendered remained unanswered in the excerpt.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how many personnel the OVP's FY2027 personnel-services proposal would support, how the plantilla compared with permanent and contractual staffing, and how much was spent on salaries, allowances, and other compensation relative to services rendered.

topics.topic: OVP travel budget of about 51 million pesos
topics.summary: A committee member questioned the proposed travel allocation of about 51 million pesos for 2027 and asked about 2025 and 2026-to-date spending. The OVP reported a 2025 travel budget of PHP56 million, but the amounts spent on foreign and local travel were each transcribed only as "million" and were therefore unclear. The OVP said the budget covered OVP and some security personnel, official engagements, and program implementation, including travel to last-mile schools and Jida areas. The exchange ended without a clear 2026-to-date figure or a follow-up commitment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the proposed OVP travel allocation for 2027 and the amounts actually spent in 2025 and 2026 to date. It also sought to determine what the travel expenses covered and whether they were necessary for OVP programs.

topics.topic: OVP enterprise and civil-society grants and post-grant outcomes
topics.summary: Sarah Elago asked the OVP to identify measurable outcomes from its enterprise and civil-society grants, including how many beneficiaries had grown or sustained their enterprises. OVP director Norman Baloro said CSO grants were around 150,000 pesos, individual grants were PHP 15,000 each, and groups generally had 20 to 25 members or clients. He said the OVP conducted post-grant monitoring after ninety days and described monthly meetings, mentoring, and other support activities. Elago pressed for 2023 outcome numbers and an activities report. Baloro committed to provide lists of individual and group beneficiaries, while the requested evidence of enterprise sustainability remained outstanding.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the eligibility requirements and grant amounts for OVP enterprise and civil-society beneficiaries. It also sought measurable evidence that beneficiaries had grown or sustained their enterprises, including post-grant monitoring data and beneficiary lists.

topics.topic: You Can Be VP grant of 550,000 per learner
topics.summary: A committee member questioned the You Can Be VP program's reported grant of 550,000 per learner and asked about its beneficiary count and cost basis. The member cited a proposed target of 1,100,000 beneficiaries and a separate reference to 500,000 plus, although the transcript did not clearly connect those figures to the program. OVP operations director Norman Baloro said the program covered local or international engagements, junior leadership, mentoring, and skills development. He said five recipients had already been identified, while two learners were described as a target for eligibility. Baloro clarified that 500,000 was to support activities under the program rather than necessarily being paid directly to each learner. The hearing did not reconcile the 550,000 figure raised by the member with the agency's 500,000 explanation or the different beneficiary counts.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the number of You Can Be VP beneficiaries and the basis for the reported grant of 550,000 per learner. It also asked whether the amount was paid directly to each learner or used for broader program activities.

topics.topic: Libreng Sakay routes, contracting, and passenger capacity
topics.summary: A committee member asked how the 22,000,000 Libreng Sakay allocation related to the reported 1,400,000 beneficiaries, of whom 1,200,000 were attributed to the program. The OVP said the service operated nine buses nationwide, with routes planned in partnership with the LTFRB, MMDA, and another agency rendered as "OTR," and with private operators including Jackliner, Rural Transit Mindanao Incorporated, Oyinco City Tours, and Kudos Trucking Corporation. The agency said two buses had been purchased by the OVP and that each bus had capacity for around 46 passengers. It described peak-hour operations from 5AM to 9AM and 5PM to 9PM, but the passenger examples of 442 and 422 were unclear and did not fully establish the reported reach. The OVP also projected reaching 4,000,000 passengers around mid-November. The committee requested a list of providers, leaving the capacity and allocation calculations partly unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the OVP's Libreng Sakay allocation translated into routes, contracted operators, bus ownership, operating costs, and passenger reach. It also asked how the reported beneficiary figures were calculated and what capacity the program could actually deliver.

topics.topic: Beneficiary selection and duplication controls
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Ko asked how the OVP selected beneficiaries for bags, wheelchairs, and Aljanaza kits and how it avoided duplication with LGUs and other agencies. OVP Director for Operations Norman Baloro said the Department of Education and people's organizations identified recipients, with priority for GIDA and last-mile schools, while wheelchairs could be provided upon requests from organizations, LGUs, or walk-in clients. He cited dashboard monitoring and a Department of Education-verified master list as safeguards against duplication. The discussion also covered the proposed OVP charter, House Bill Number 4 2 1 5, which the OVP said would establish a dedicated policy-research function; current policy work was handled by the Strategic Management Office. Rep. Ko asked for the OVP or Vice President's position on “Paxilica,” but the agency official declined to comment, said the question would be noted, and the Chair requested any response in writing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the OVP selected beneficiaries for bags, wheelchairs, and Aljanaza kits, and how it prevented duplication with assistance from LGUs, people's organizations, and other agencies. Rep. Renee Ko also asked who handled OVP policy research and whether the office had a policy position on the issue referred to in the transcript as “Paxilica.”

topics.topic: Funding and targeting of wheelchair and Aljanaza kits
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Ko asked how the OVP selected beneficiaries for wheelchair and Aljanaza kits and how it controlled duplication with other assistance providers. She referenced one fifty thousand learners and 600 clients associated with the programs. The OVP said wheelchair assistance could be requested by organizations, local government units, or walk-in clients, while Aljanaza kits were made available through the OVP's assistance network and were intended to be provided within twenty four hours after a Muslim death. The OVP said the Department of Education and people's organizations identified school recipients, with priority given to GIDA areas and last-mile schools. It also cited a dashboard and a Department of Education-verified master list as duplication-monitoring measures. The hearing received the explanation, but did not establish a detailed cross-agency duplication-control process.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the OVP selected beneficiaries for wheelchair and Aljanaza kits, whether distributions were walk-in or partnership-based, and how the OVP prevented duplication with other agencies, local government units, and people's organizations.

topics.topic: OVP maintenance and other operating expenses and program manuals
topics.summary: A committee member questioned whether OVP programs had publicly accessible manuals and requirements because the OVP directly implemented its programs. The OVP said all nine core programs had regularly updated manuals, although the You Can Be VP procedure was not in the citizens charter. OVP officials explained that the You Can Be VP allocation included program activities and reported five recipients against a target of two learners. The member also questioned Libreng Sakay's cited beneficiary totals and 22,000,000 budget; the OVP described nine buses, private and government partnerships, two buses being purchased, and POL costs charged to the OVP. The OVP cited 46 passengers per bus and a daily figure recorded inconsistently as 442 and 422, with operations during morning and afternoon peak hours. The exchange ended with a request for a list of providers and related You Can Be VP information, while the beneficiary calculations remained unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the OVP's discretionary programs had publicly accessible operating guidelines and whether the proposed amounts and beneficiary targets for programs such as You Can Be VP and Libreng Sakay were justified. It also asked how Libreng Sakay was implemented, funded, and supported by private bus operators.

topics.topic: OVP policy research capacity and charter-related functions
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co asked how the OVP selected beneficiaries for learner bags, wheelchairs, and Aljanaza kits, citing one fifty thousand learners and 600 clients. OVP operations director Norman Baloro said DepEd, regional offices, and people's organizations identified recipients, with priority for GDA areas, last-mile schools, and Madrasa schools. He said the OVP used a DepEd-verified dashboard and master list to control duplication, while wheelchair requests could come from organizations, local government units, or walk-in clients. On policy capacity, the OVP said House Bill number 4 2 1 5 proposed a charter with a dedicated policy-research office, but the Strategic Management Office currently performed that function. The agency declined to state Vice President Sara Duterte's position on Paxilica, and the Chair required any response to be submitted in writing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the OVP selected beneficiaries for bags, wheelchairs, and Aljanaza kits; how it prevented duplication with other agencies; and whether the OVP had a defined policy research and advisory function. It also asked who currently handled policy positions while the proposed OVP charter remained pending.

topics.topic: JO/COS absorption, plantilla vacancies, and professionalization funding
topics.summary: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. led the inquiry into 919,868 JO and COS workers, vacant plantilla positions, and the absence of measurable absorption and vacancy-reduction targets. CSC described preferential rating, qualification requirements, Prime ESG, agency optimization, and a target covering 40 agencies, but said it could not establish a direct correlation between the programs and JO/COS absorption. The agency distinguished regular and necessary functions that should be staffed permanently from temporary or episodic work, and proposed reviews of LGU personnel-service caps and DBM's scrap-and-build policy. Representative Elijah San Fernando and Representative Kaloy Bulilla raised worker precarity, political accommodation, public-sector unionism, and a DSWD worker's case, while CSC discussed joint work with DBM and COA and possible benefits coverage. Representative Democrito Mendoza questioned 224999 vacancies, examination pass rates, and proposed equivalency legislation; CSC said the principal problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete vacancies, staffing constraints, and merit-and-fitness concerns. The issue remained unresolved, with several administrative and legislative follow-ups contemplated.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how CSC would reduce plantilla vacancies and government-wide reliance on job-order (JO) and contract-of-service (COS) workers, including whether qualified long-serving workers could be absorbed into permanent positions. Members also asked what measurable results would come from the proposed professionalization and modernization allocations and whether CSC would support legislative and monitoring mechanisms.

topics.topic: Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and digital transformation
topics.summary: CSC presented the PCSMP as a central part of its digital transformation, covering Prime ESG, HRMIS plus payroll, a national learning platform, electronic administrative justice, and a civil-service data management system. The agency cited a proposed PCSMP allocation of about 1.34 billion in the budget breakdown, while the opening presentation separately cited 453 million for implementation. Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. pressed for measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and JO/COS dependence, but CSC acknowledged that it had no indicators establishing those correlations and could not guarantee absorption into the civil service. A committee member confirmed that the contact center used written referrals and that CSC's electronic case system could track cases nationwide. Representative Ryan questioned cybersecurity, online oath-taking authentication, SALN rules, and the failed data-center bidding; CSC undertook to submit a cybersecurity cost breakdown and defended the failed bidding as a privacy safeguard. Representative Elijah San Fernando raised delayed administrative cases, and CSC said CLASS would be implemented in 2027 to enable online filing and digital transmission of case records.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and related digital-transformation spending would produce measurable improvements in recruitment, appointment processing, HR records, payroll, case resolution, cybersecurity, and service delivery. Members also asked whether CSC had concrete targets for reducing vacancies and dependence on job-order and contract-of-service workers, and whether safeguards would protect sensitive personnel and SALN data.

topics.topic: CSC administrative justice, case backlog, and electronic adjudication
topics.summary: CSC reported that it had disposed of about 10,052 cases in 2024, 9,148 in 2025, and 4,897 in 2026, while aging-case resolution remained an active priority. A committee member asked whether Contact Center 888 provided complainants with status information, and CSC said reports were referred, monitored, and answered in writing. Rep. Solomon Chungalao submitted a pending regional-office complaint involving state-university students, which CSC agreed to check. Rep. Eli San Fernando questioned why a Land Bank employees’ complaint filed in 2019 took six years to resolve and cited 100,000 pesos in removed benefits and incentives. CSC described procedural reforms and said CLASS would permit online filing and digital transmission of case records, with implementation targeted for 2027. CSC did not state the requested CLASS budget figure, leaving the funding impact and specific complaints open while committing to follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CSC’s administrative-justice reforms and proposed digital systems would reduce the backlog, shorten the time for resolving complaints, and give complainants reliable case-status information. Members also asked how the 2027 budget would support electronic adjudication and followed up on specific pending complaints.

topics.topic: Cybersecurity, online oath-taking, and the 212,000,000 data center
topics.summary: Rep. Ryan asked the CSC to identify its cybersecurity allocation, noting a modernization figure of about 1.4 billion, and requested a breakdown because cybersecurity was integrated across digital programs. The CSC said it was drafting a data privacy and cybersecurity manual and committed to submit a disaggregated budget breakdown. Ryan questioned whether online oath-taking relied only on Zoom and warned about AI-enabled impersonation; the CSC said oath administrators had to verify identity, ask questions, and accept liability for inadequate precautions. The CSC said it had a continuing ICT partnership with DICT and would raise the authentication concerns there. On SALN filing, the CSC explained that personal properties could be grouped under "others," while cash and registered properties had separate treatment under rules issued in 2025. Ryan also raised the roughly 212 million pesos data-center project, and the CSC said the sole bidder failed confidentiality requirements, leading to a declared failure of bidding and rebidding. Ryan endorsed that decision, but the cybersecurity breakdown and rebidding outcome were not yet resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the CSC's modernization budget was specifically devoted to cybersecurity, how online oath-taking and SALN filing would be authenticated and protected, and why the central-office data-center procurement failed. It also sought assurances that the rebidding would preserve data confidentiality and that the failed bidding would not prejudice the CSC's budget.

topics.topic: Civil-service examinations, eligibility, and equivalency pathways
topics.summary: Representative Nassal pressed the CSC for a government-wide plan, measurable targets, and concrete results from proposed programs addressing vacancies and dependence on about 919,868 JO and COS workers. The CSC described preferential rating, including the 70% grade score, 10% avenue, and experience-based treatment, but said it could not guarantee appointments or establish a direct correlation with absorption. Representative Ismula raised possible preferential eligibility for IPMRs, and the CSC said it could work toward extending coverage after consultations and subject to legal requirements. Representative Mendoza later urged support for House Bill 93, which would create an equivalency pathway after at least three years of satisfactory service, but the CSC warned that this could encourage agencies to retain unqualified hires and undermine merit and fitness. The CSC said it was producing more than 160 thousand eligibles annually and that the central problems were vacancies, obsolete positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates rather than a shortage of eligibles. The hearing ended without a clear CSC commitment to support House Bill 93 or deliver numerical vacancy and absorption targets, although the agency undertook related work on IPMR preferential rating, modernization guidance, and JO/COS regulation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the CSC would help qualified JO and COS workers obtain eligibility, fill vacant plantilla positions, and reduce reliance on contractual arrangements. Members also examined preferential-rating and equivalency pathways, civil-service examination standards and pass rates, and the CSC's position on related legislation.

topics.topic: Public-sector unionism and labor-management representation
topics.summary: Rep. Eli San Fernando asked about the public-sector unionism subprogram's allocation, outputs, and targets and raised the precarious status of job order and contract of service workers. The stated allocation was 30,000 pesos to 88,000 pesos per regional office, and a CSC official said organizations were to be credited and recognized within seven days. The committee did not receive a complete account of the 2026 and 2027 output indicators, and Rep. San Fernando said he would return to the JO/COS issue in the second round. Rep. Democrito Mendoza then questioned the quality of civil-service examinees and sought CSC support for an equivalency or pathway-to-permanency bill based on three years of service. A CSC commissioner said that position was personal and warned that the proposal could undermine merit and fitness. Mendoza also sought support for a labor-representation bill, and a CSC official expressed openness while describing the existing PSLMC selection mechanism. The issues therefore remained partly open, with further consideration implied rather than fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the allocation, output indicators, and targets for CSC's public-sector unionism subprogram, including the registration and recognition of public-sector employee organizations. Members also sought CSC's position on the precarious status of job order and contract of service workers and on proposed bills concerning civil-service eligibility and labor-management representation.

topics.topic: CSC facilities, field offices, and Region VI rehabilitation
topics.summary: The CSC chairperson identified regional and field-office infrastructure, vehicle replacement, and green-energy systems as implementation-ready priorities. The agency cited facility renovations, records storage, dormitories, parking, waterworks, mobility vehicles, and solar-panel and generator systems, with vehicles averaging seven to nine years old. A committee member asked whether the building and field-office requirements should receive budget priority and indicated that additional funding might be sought. Near adjournment, the committee chairperson expressed support for the rehabilitation request for the Region VI office and referred to a transcript-rendered figure of 1.6, whose unit and context were unclear. No specific funding approval or agency commitment for Region VI rehabilitation was recorded before the hearing was terminated.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CSC's regional and field-office facilities, vehicles, and backup energy systems should be treated as budget priorities. It also sought clarification on the status and support for the rehabilitation of the CSC Region VI office.

topics.topic: Employee compensation, PERA, and salary-related reforms
topics.summary: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula asked whether the CSC supported increasing PERA, including a reference to 2,000 pesos and House Bill Number 3874. The CSC said it supported higher PERA and other benefits for government personnel. Ismula also sought recommendations for compensation reforms that would be sustainable and equitable, and the CSC said it could continue discussions with the DBM on position classification and qualification standards while leaving resource allocation to the government. The Chair later asked whether salary adjustments for agriculturist one positions could be enforced in national agencies, SUCs, and local government units. The CSC pointed to draft agriculturist qualification standards expected to be considered in September, and the Chair requested copies for review. No specific salary-adjustment amount or final funding decision was provided.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CSC supported increasing PERA and advancing broader compensation reforms, and whether such reforms could be made sustainable and equitable. It also sought clarification on whether salary adjustments could be enforced for agriculturist positions after updated qualification standards were issued.

topics.topic: Anti-sexual-harassment compliance and workplace wellness leave
topics.summary: Congresswoman Ilago asked whether agencies were complying with the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act and maintaining functional committees on decorum and investigation. The CSC said the mechanisms were legally required, regional offices conducted regular inspections, and the agency could handle certain cases involving officials and employees of other agencies. It said sexual-harassment and Safe Spaces Act provisions had been integrated into the RACs and related CSC rules, but it did not provide a clear timeline for new Convention 190 guidelines. The CSC cited a special emergency leave policy issued in 2013 that provided five days annually to calamity victims who could show proof. The chair directed the CSC to submit data and a status report, including on wellness leave, leaving those requested materials and the separate wellness-leave issue pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether agencies had functional mechanisms for preventing and investigating sexual harassment, how the Civil Service Commission (CSC) enforced compliance, and whether the CSC had issued or planned guidelines implementing ILO Convention 190. It also sought the status of workplace wellness leave and related employee protections.

topics.topic: Solo-parent leave and benefits for JO/COS workers
topics.summary: Minority member Roberto Nazal Jr. raised whether qualified JO and COS solo parents were entitled to the seven-day solo-parent leave under Republic 11/1961 and the 2025 joint circular. CSC answered that it interpreted section 11.2 as covering benefits granted under existing laws and said it had recognized seven-day solo-parent leave since 2004. Nassal warned that departments remained hesitant because of audit concerns. CSC undertook to reiterate the provision to departments and said it was coordinating with DSWD, the primary implementing agency, while DBM's position was still needed. Representative Kaloy Bulilla later supported the CSC budget and raised the plight of a DSWD JO worker. CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta reaffirmed coverage of JO and COS workers and committed to work with DBM and COA on a mechanism for implementation and grievances.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether qualified solo-parent job order (JO) and contract of service (COS) workers were entitled to the seven-day solo-parent leave under Republic Act 11/1961 and the applicable joint memorandum circular. It also sought to determine whether CSC had communicated and would enforce that interpretation across departments despite audit and implementation concerns.

topics.topic: Hospital and agriculturist qualification standards for appointments
topics.summary: Rep. Romeo Momo requested that Adela Siorati Memorial Hospital be allowed to use the higher qualification standards in DOH Administrative Order 2016-003 after its upgrade from a second-level to a third-level hospital. CSC said the hospital had to submit supporting documents, including the DOH circular, and undertook to review the request and act immediately. The Chair then raised a civil-society question citing Republic Act 12215, section 31, and the law's stated effect on agriculturist appointments in national and local government. CSC said draft qualification standards for agriculturists were under Commission consideration and could possibly be finalized after a scheduled September meeting, although the scheduling reference was unclear. The committee requested copies of the relevant materials, but the transcript did not resolve the status of the final circular, nonregistered appointments, or salary adjustments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CSC would approve higher qualification standards for appointments at Adela Siorati Memorial Hospital and how it was addressing the statutory qualification requirements for agriculturist positions. It also sought clarification on pending CSC guidelines, appointments of nonregistered agriculturists, and related salary adjustments.

topics.topic: CSC compliance and enforcement of personnel rules
topics.summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula questioned how the CSC enforced its expanded gambling ban and whether it covered online gambling. The CSC said complaints could be filed anonymously through contact centers and complaints desks in regional and field offices, and Assistant Commissioner Ariel Ronquillo said the prohibition covered both on-site and online gambling. Ismula also asked about preferential civil-service eligibility for IPMRs; the CSC said it would consult Indigenous Peoples communities and could develop a preferential-rating system, potentially crediting one to three years of representative service toward a five-year experience requirement, subject to law. The member raised a 2,000 pesos compensation reform and House Bill Number 3874, and the CSC expressed support for increased benefits and continued discussions with DBM. Rep. Isabel Segabaria then challenged the CSC's authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule. The CSC acknowledged the need for legal basis but defended the rule under the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly, leaving the scope of the agency's authority unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the CSC monitored and enforced its expanded gambling prohibition, whether it could provide preferential civil-service eligibility treatment for indigenous peoples mandatory representatives (IPMRs), and what reforms it supported for government compensation. It also sought to clarify whether the CSC had statutory authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule.

topics.topic: 2028 election-preparation funding and proposed COMELEC budget cuts
topics.summary: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia presented a proposed FY2027 budget of about 29.5 billion, including roughly 23.92 billion for 2028 election preparations, and warned that a reduction of about 9 billion could compromise the election. Rep. Mercy Sindania characterized the NEP level as a recipe for disaster and asked what would happen if the reduction remained; Garcia said COMELEC could sacrifice features such as voter verification but could not compromise core preparation for a presidential and vice-presidential election. Rep. Edgar Erice questioned the 23 billion machine request and suggested that a lower requirement could save about 6 billion, while Garcia defended the need for about 124,000 machines because of voter growth and inflation. Other members supported restoring COMELEC's broader request to about 44 billion. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez moved to approve the budget and sought a special provision allowing about 11 billion in unused Barangay and SK election funds to continue for critical 2028 preparations. Garcia agreed to submit the proposed language, and also committed to provide updates on overseas voting and address vacant positions, but the final funding level and machine allocation remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 funding would give COMELEC sufficient resources to prepare for credible 2028 national and local elections. Members also examined the effect of reduced machine, infrastructure, staffing, overseas-voting, and election-preparation funds, and whether unused Barangay and SK election appropriations could be made available for 2028 preparations.

topics.topic: Automated election-machine procurement, leasing, and readiness
topics.summary: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia warned that the proposed reduction in election-preparation funding could compromise 2028 readiness and said about 74 million voters would require roughly 124,000 machines, including contingency units. He explained that the 2025 lease cost 17,990,000,000 or about 18 billion in the discussion, and covered warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement, while the proposed 2028 lease was discussed at 23,000,000,000. Rep. Edgar Erice challenged that figure and argued that purchase, reuse, or upgrading could reduce the cost to about 17.8 billion and save about 6 billion. A member separately asked about cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting, and COMELEC cited 337,000,000 for ICT equipment, continuous monitoring, enrollment controls, and a projected 55 to 60% overseas turnout. Erice also requested the COMELEC Advisory Council's terms of reference, meeting minutes, and resolution, and Chairman Garcia committed to submit them before plenary debates. The lease-versus-purchase issue remained open, subject to the documents and further congressional budget action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC should lease, purchase, or upgrade automated counting machines for the 2028 elections, and whether the proposed funding would provide enough machines and related readiness measures. Members also asked about machine standards, cybersecurity, overseas Internet voting, and the documents supporting COMELEC's procurement position.

topics.topic: Barangay and SK election postponement, term fixing, and unused funds
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co questioned whether the BSKE elections would proceed and asked about COMELEC’s pending procurement and overtime obligations. COMELEC said it had obligated about 8 billion for election materials and reported PHP 1,200,000,000 in six months of overtime, while supporting periodic, regular, and definite elections but deferring the policy decision on postponement or term fixing to Congress and the courts. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported fixing the barangay officials’ terms and sought authority to retain unused BSKE funds, with figures discussed ranging from about 9 billion to 11 billion and an estimated unutilized balance of about 10.9 billion. COMELEC proposed that unused BSKE appropriations become continuing appropriations for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes. DBM raised no objection to the concept or proposed wording, but the committee deferred final action and requested a formal submission for consideration by the budget amendments review subcommittee. The Senior Deputy Speaker also confirmed that COMELEC would implement Congress’s term-fixing decision and remain bound by procurement contracts already covered by notices to proceed.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the barangay and SK elections would proceed as scheduled or be postponed or reset through term fixing, and what that would mean for COMELEC’s procurement, overtime, and election appropriations. Members also sought to determine whether unutilized BSKE funds could remain available for the 2028 national and local elections through a special provision.

topics.topic: Proposed special provision for unused barangay and SK election funds
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez raised the possibility that resetting the barangay and SK elections would leave substantial funds unused and sought a special provision to preserve those funds for COMELEC's future needs. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said the continuing appropriation could make about 11 billion available, later estimating an unutilized BSKE balance of about 10,900,000,000 and proposing its use for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes. Rodriguez moved to approve the COMELEC budget and provision, but the motion was deferred because the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee had to address the wording. The Senior Deputy Speaker later asked DBM whether a 2027 provision could govern funds appropriated in the 2026 GAA, and DBM said it had no objection because COMELEC's constitutionally autonomous funds remain valid until fully spent. The committee requested a formal letter and left final language and approval to the subcommittee process.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the appropriations for the barangay and SK elections could remain available if those elections were reset or not held, and what special-provision wording would authorize COMELEC to use the funds for other lawful purposes. It also sought DBM's technical position on including in the FY 2027 budget a provision concerning funds appropriated in the FY 2026 GAA.

topics.topic: Machine funding requirement of 23,000,000,000 versus DBM funding
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice raised the gap between COMELEC's 23,000,000,000 machine requirement and DBM's 21,000,000,000 funding, while COMELEC described the shortfall as 1,500,000,000. Chairman Garcia justified the requirement by citing inflation, projected voter growth to about 74 million, and a need for 124,000 machines. Erice argued that the machines could cost about 17.8 billion, potentially producing savings of 6 billion, and another member questioned whether purchasing or upgrading would be cheaper than leasing. COMELEC maintained that a one-time lease was appropriate for the critical 2028 presidential election and cited warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement costs. The agency also described cybersecurity measures and its planned overseas Internet-voting enrollment and authentication process. The chairman undertook to consider the lower-cost proposal, but the final funding and procurement approach remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why COMELEC projected a machine requirement of 23,000,000,000 for the 2028 elections when DBM funding was stated at 21,000,000,000, and whether leasing, purchasing, or upgrading machines would provide the most economical and reliable option. Members also examined machine readiness, cybersecurity, and the implementation of overseas Internet voting.

topics.topic: Ballot and voter-information printing cut from 3,280,000,000 to 348,000,000
topics.summary: Rep. John Tracy Cagas raised the reduction in the printing allocation from 3,280,000,000 to 348,000,000, a stated cut of 2,930,000,000. COMELEC Chair George Irwin M. Garcia said the reduction was critical and would affect ballot printing, mandatory voter-information sheets, pre-printing activities, and possible reprinting. He identified 2,940,000,000 pesos for the 2028 budget and said procurement and printing should begin in January 2028. Garcia also said that 74 million ballots might have to be printed and that reprinting related to national candidates could cost 20 million. A member connected the issue to deployment and logistics, while Garcia discussed compromised deployment activities, increased machines from 107,000 to 124,000, and other supplies and specifications. No restoration of funds or other concrete action was recorded, so the adequacy of the reduced allocation remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the effect of reducing the proposed allocation for ballot forms and voter-information sheets, and whether the remaining amount could cover printing, reprinting, deployment, and related election supplies. It also examined the timing and budget needed for the 2028 election.

topics.topic: BSK election budget, obligations, and remaining balances
topics.summary: Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores questioned why the BSK budget had increased despite reported high absorptive capacity and pressed COMELEC on the large ICT reduction and case-disposition backlog. COMELEC attributed the higher requirement to increased precincts, voters, teachers, honoraria, training, cybersecurity, and procurement, and said case disposition would continue regardless of a budget reduction. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos then examined spending and obligations, citing about 8 billion spent from an approximately 19 billion BSK budget and a possible additional requirement of roughly 2.5 to 3.5 billion; Garcia cited 4 billion earmarked and about 3.9 to 4 billion obligated, although the reconciliation remained unclear. The discussion also covered a Cavite special-election budget of about 200 million, including 128 million in COMELEC funding and a 50 million LGU advance subject to reimbursement. Rep. Renee Co asked about pending deliveries, overtime, and postponement; Garcia cited 8,003,000,000 pesos obligated, six months of overtime totaling PHP 1,200,000,000, and pending delivery of election materials. COMELEC committed to submit case information and updates, but the precise remaining balance and the effect of any postponement were not fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the actual cost, obligations, expenditures, deliveries, and remaining balances for the BSK election, including whether funds could be reused if the election were postponed. It also examined special-election advances, pending procurement, overtime, and the implications of any further postponement.

topics.topic: ICT, cybersecurity, and election-system security after proposed reductions
topics.summary: Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores questioned COMELEC's ability to protect election data after almost 87.4% of its proposed ICT funding was removed. Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia cited 24-hour monitoring, 32,000,000 Internet attempts before an election, 3,000,000 attempts per month, and 337,000,000 for ICT-related requirements, while saying additional cybersecurity personnel and system improvements were needed. A committee member also questioned the approximately 17,990,000,000 lease for 110,000 ACMs and the readiness and integrity of machines for 2028. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned overseas Internet voting, registration funding, and regulation of social media and artificial intelligence; COMELEC said it supported regulation but acknowledged constitutional and legislative limits. Vice Chair Zia Alonto Adiong asked about security and election-related violence before the BARMM barangay election, and COMELEC reported preparations involving 3,393,000 voters, 5,212 voting centers, and 5,212 machines. COMELEC committed to submit case lists and updates, but the budget restoration and several security and regulatory issues were not finally settled.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC could maintain secure election systems, protect voter and election data, and prepare for the 2028 and BARMM elections despite proposed ICT and other budget reductions. Members also asked how cybersecurity, Internet voting, overseas registration, social-media regulation, and election-related security would be handled.

topics.topic: Election-teacher and poll-worker honoraria
topics.summary: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised the BSK election budget and asked how much had been spent or obligated, particularly for poll-worker training. COMELEC said it would train about 1 million teachers, electoral-board members, and support staff, and cited 4 billion as earmarked and roughly 3.9 4,000,000,000 as obligated, although the reported total was garbled. A member also commended 2 million in savings. Rep. Antonio Tinio then raised election-teacher honoraria, and the COMELEC chairperson cited rates ranging from 10,000 to 15,000, including 15,000 per teacher and 15,000 for the chairman. Tinio sought to increase the appropriation from 2,000,000,000 to 2,500,000,000. COMELEC undertook to support the proposal before the relevant committees and DBM, while Tinio requested formal data and a position paper.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the BSK election budget had been spent or obligated, particularly for poll-worker training and related preparations, and whether additional funding would be needed. It also examined the honoraria rates for election teachers and whether the appropriation should be increased.

topics.topic: Overseas voting, Internet voting, and continuing registration
topics.summary: Committee members, led by Rep. Sarah Elago and a minority member, questioned whether overseas registration and Internet voting would close persistent participation gaps. COMELEC said the DFA supervised overseas voting under the law while COMELEC coordinated, and described registration, identity verification, one-time PINs, and enrollment lasting three to five minutes. Garcia cited 1,200,000 overseas voters, a hoped-for increase to 2,000,000, and turnout targets ranging from at least 50% to 55 to 60%; Elago cited a 67,000,000 proposal for overseas voting and continuing registration. Members also pressed for accessible registration, voter education, and social-media accountability, while Garcia cited 3,000,000 deactivated voters and promised to activate them for 2028. The agency committed to update the committee on reforms and turnout, and a member manifested support for restoring COMELEC's proposed 2027 budget cut, but the funding question remained unsettled.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC's overseas registration and Internet-voting arrangements would improve participation, accessibility, and security, particularly for overseas voters. Members also asked how continuing registration, funding, social-media regulation, and staffing would support the 2028 elections.

topics.topic: Voter registration, education, and inclusion of vulnerable voters
topics.summary: Rep. John Tracy Cagas questioned the reduction in printing funds from about 3.28 billion to about 348 million, warning that it could affect ballot and voter-information-sheet production. COMELEC Chair George Irwin M. Garcia said the reduction would affect 2028 procurement and could force the printing of about 74 million ballots without adequate preparation, while also citing 124,000 registration machines compared with 107,000 in 2025. Rep. Sarah Elago asked about overseas voting, Internet voting, continuing registration, and a revised proposal of about 67 million, and pressed COMELEC on social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation. Garcia said COMELEC coordinated with the DFA, was preparing for secure Internet voting, had limited authority to punish conduct without a law, and could request takedowns of discriminatory material. The discussion also covered roughly 3 million deactivated voters, Indigenous peoples, elderly voters, and registration in geographically isolated areas. COMELEC committed to inclusive registration and manifested support for restoring its 2027 budget cut, but the transcript did not record a committee decision on restoration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether proposed reductions in printing, registration, overseas voting, and voter-education resources would impair the 2028 elections, particularly for overseas voters, deactivated voters, and people in geographically isolated or vulnerable communities. It also examined COMELEC's plans for Internet voting, social-media regulation, and inclusive registration.

topics.topic: Election-cycle costs, QRF, and possible longer election intervals
topics.summary: Representative Jobo Yagino asked about the QRF and whether holding elections every five years could produce savings compared with the existing three-year cycle. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said an automated national and local election required about 26 billion for preparation and 20 billion for the election year, or almost 46 billion, while the BSKE figure was stated as 19.57 and 20 billion, with the combined three-year figure rendered unclearly as 6,066,000,000,000. Garcia said changing the election term might be a solution but would require a constitutional amendment or revision because the Constitution provides three-year terms for specified positions. Yagino asked that the issue be placed on the record and potentially referred to House lawyers. He expressed full support for COMELEC's budget, preferred an increase, and moved for approval, but the excerpt contained no ruling on the motion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much COMELEC's election-related costs could be reduced by lengthening the election interval and whether such a change would affect the proposed budget. It also considered whether the issue required legal or constitutional action and whether COMELEC's budget should be approved.

topics.topic: Election-case disposition and political-finance enforcement
topics.summary: Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores asked whether budget reductions would delay disposition of about 14,000 election cases and clarified which COMELEC offices handled them. Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia said cases dated as far back as 2000, involved the Law Department and the Contest and Adjudication Department, and required due process because some were criminal in nature. Garcia assured the committee that disposition would proceed despite budget reductions and said the Political Finance and Affairs Department initiated cases involving overspending. He cited 7,000 SK-related cases involving candidates over 24 years of age and said the prescriptive period was five years. Flores supported restoring COMELEC's budget but urged faster action, while Garcia committed to submit the relevant case list and updates to the committees.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC's budget reductions would affect the disposition of roughly 14,000 election cases, including cases involving political-finance violations and overspending. It also asked whether COMELEC was initiating cases on its own and whether older cases could become time-barred.

topics.topic: Election procurement contracts and financial consequences of postponement
topics.summary: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos and Rep. Renee Co questioned COMELEC about the roughly 19 billion BSK budget, the amounts already spent or obligated, pending deliveries, and overtime costs if the election were postponed. COMELEC cited about 8,000,000,000 in obligations or earmarks, 70,000 ballot boxes, and PHP 1,200,000,000 in six months of overtime, although several obligation figures were unclear in the transcript. Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said notices to proceed could create perfected sales or contracts, leaving COMELEC bound to suppliers and responsible for delivery, warranty, and warehousing. He also said postponement was a policy and political-question issue, while elections should remain periodic, regular, and definite. The Senior Deputy Speaker connected the issue to proposed term fixing and asked whether fiscal autonomy could produce savings if contracts were not yet awarded. COMELEC did not provide a clear savings estimate or definitive treatment of all pending contracts, and the hearing was moved for termination.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much COMELEC had already spent, earmarked, or obligated for the barangay and SK elections; what procurement contracts and deliveries would remain binding if the elections were postponed or canceled; and whether fiscal autonomy could permit savings or budget reallocation. It also examined how term fixing would affect COMELEC’s preparations and liabilities.
