topics.topic: Social-media, artificial-intelligence, and political-ad regulation
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago asked COMELEC about guidelines for social-media, artificial-intelligence, and Internet technology use in fair, nondiscriminatory campaigning. A COMELEC official said the agency would strengthen measures to protect individual rights and regarded the 2028 election as crucial, with his term ending by 2029. He cautioned that regulation could intrude on freedom of expression and speech and said COMELEC could not punish conduct or define crimes without legal authority. He supported policy addressing foreign intervention and interference but questioned how platforms could be sanctioned. Elago then raised social-media accountability, cited a July 2026 investigative report on rebranded Facebook pages and political ads, and asked about a dedicated task force. COMELEC referred to same-day takedown requests, but the record did not resolve the task-force proposal or the agency's broader enforcement authority.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how COMELEC would regulate social-media political advertising, artificial-intelligence-enabled campaigning, discrimination, and possible foreign intervention while respecting freedom of expression and the limits of its legal authority. It also asked whether COMELEC had a dedicated mechanism to hold platforms and political actors accountable.

topics.topic: COMELEC vacant positions and staffing capacity
topics.summary: A minority member asked about COMELEC's vacant positions, particularly entry-level election-officer posts. George Irwin M. Garcia said COMELEC had 800 vacant positions and hoped to fill half of them before the end of the year. He later cited 831 unfilled positions, 627 job-order personnel, 343 main and field contract-of-service personnel, 37 contractual personnel, and 867 casual personnel. He also gave several NCR-related figures—21, 24, 25, 18, and 21—but their categories were unclear in the transcript. The issue landed with COMELEC's staffing commitment, while the precise relationship among the figures remained unresolved.

topics.topic: BARMM barangay-election preparation and polling-place security
topics.summary: Rep. Eli San Fernando asked COMELEC to explain the cancellation of a candidate’s candidacy and whether the decision affected the Bangsamoro peace process. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said the basis was failure to establish domicile, while the candidate’s name would remain pending the September 14 decision and possible Supreme Court relief. Vice Chair Zia Alonto Adiong then asked for an update on the BARMM barangay election and whether an ambush involving the interim chief minister was politically motivated or likely to threaten the polls. Garcia cited 3,393,000, 5,212, and an unclear reference to “eighteen sixteen” polling places or voting centers, and later said 5,212 machines would undergo final testing and sealing. He also mentioned voter education, September 11 command conferences, proclamation and results transmission, and expressed hope that there would be no failure of election. The security-motive question remained unanswered in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how COMELEC was addressing the BARMM barangay election, including the legal and peace-process context of a candidate’s cancellation, election preparations, equipment and polling-place requirements, and security risks. It also asked whether a recent ambush was politically motivated and what measures would support an orderly and peaceful election.

topics.topic: FY 2027 DA budget reduction and available fiscal space
topics.summary: The chair and Undersecretary Nora Olivares presented substantial reductions in the agriculture-sector and DA budgets, including a reported agriculture-sector decrease of about 35.3 billion and a DA decrease of about 17.2 billion, or 8%. The presentation also showed the farm-to-market road allocation falling from 33 billion in 2025 to 16 billion in 2027. A minority representative and the chair questioned whether fiscal space constrained priority programs and whether irrigation projects were being selected transparently. DA and NIA officials cited fiscal ceilings, economic viability, project readiness, statutory requirements, geographic disadvantage, drought, and irrigation-development levels as selection criteria. The chair raised 46,000,000 in fiscal space and concerns about anomalous infrastructure insertions, while NIA described technical validation, costing, procurement, audit, engineering, and reporting controls. The agency committed to submit documentation on irrigation projects under Agrarian Reform Fund guidelines, leaving broader restoration and transparency questions open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the FY 2027 DA and agriculture-sector budgets were reduced, how much fiscal space remained for restoration or priority programs, and how DA and NIA would prioritize projects within that constraint. It also sought the basis for NIA irrigation-project selection and documentation to guard against irregular infrastructure insertions.

topics.topic: Farm-to-market-road funding, unit costs, releases, and transparency
topics.summary: Members questioned the proposed 16,000,000,000 FY 2027 FMR budget against an estimated 55,000-kilometer network and a reduction from 33,000,000,000 in 2026. DA said project selection considered farmers, production, poverty, connectivity, road condition, climate, traffic, and new production areas, and identified about 60 billion annually as a bare-minimum ideal that could build about 4,000 kilometers. The minority also challenged unit costs ranging from 9,400,000 to 15,900,000 per kilometer, large Benguet projects, and incomplete or questionable project coordinates. DA attributed the higher 15,000,000 cost to fuel and construction-price increases and promised to check the coordinates and present reports. Members further asked about releases, with the transcript citing 10,700,000,000 as the corrected 2025 release and 5.7 as a current release figure whose meaning was unclear. DA's infrastructure official requested an additional 30,000,000,000 for 2,000 kilometers, and Rufus Rodriguez endorsed tripling the allocation, but no final funding decision was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 farm-to-market-road allocation was sufficient, how projects and unit costs were selected, and whether DA could implement the program transparently and within available capacity. Members also asked about releases, road standards, project coordinates, regional allocations, and the effect of budget restrictions on implementation.

topics.topic: NIA irrigation budget, project prioritization, and district allocations
topics.summary: The chair and NIA administrator presented a FY 2027 irrigation proposal of about 233.85 billion, against an NEP amount of about 47.43 billion, and NIA sought House support for an increase. NIA said the reduced fiscal space required priority for ongoing, validated, high-impact, and implementation-ready projects, while members questioned district allocations, Region 8 funding, Bukidnon support, and the adequacy of maintenance and development funding. The agency described prioritization criteria that included irrigable potential, fiscal and economic viability, project readiness, statutory requirements, geographic disadvantage, and drought exposure. Members Allan Ty and Robert Nazal Jr. pressed NIA on whether program-based appropriations or rigid itemized listings better protected accountability and implementation; NIA preferred program-based appropriations supported by separately submitted project lists. NIA committed to submit allocation and project documents, modification lists, and its request to restore program-based budgeting. The requested budget increase and disputed district allocations remained open for subsequent committee action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether NIA's FY 2027 funding was sufficient to expand, rehabilitate, restore, and climate-proof irrigation systems, and how the agency prioritized projects and district allocations under fiscal constraints. Members also asked whether NIA should retain program-based appropriations or return to rigid, itemized project listings, and what documents and safeguards would preserve congressional oversight.

topics.topic: Rice production support and fertilizer assistance
topics.summary: Members raised agricultural damage, rice production support, fertilizer procurement, irrigation, mechanization, and high-value-crops funding. The DA cited National Rice Program support of about 26.4 billion, projected 2026 rice production of about 19 million tons, and possible imports of up to 5 million tons because of El Niño. The agency said inorganic fertilizer assistance for 2027 would primarily use a QR-code voucher system and requested 8.73 billion for fertilizer. Officials also sought higher funding for farm-to-market roads, post-harvest facilities, and high-value crops, while the committee manifested support for tripling the road request and confirmed a 20% Mindanao share. The DA committed to provide equipment and seed-program details, review the seed proposal for funding, and complete geofencing by year-end.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 budget would adequately support rice production, fertilizer access, irrigation, mechanization, post-harvest capacity, and high-value crops. Members also pressed the DA on projected rice imports and the measures intended to reduce import dependence.

topics.topic: Agricultural damage, calamity assistance, and farmer indemnification
topics.summary: Vice Chair Anna York identified flood recovery, farmer welfare, and food security as central budget concerns. Agency officials said DSWD and DOLE would cover immediate relief and rehabilitation, while the DA would use its quick response fund for replanting and pursue indemnification and production assistance. They cited 2,500,000,000 pesos in agricultural damage, P1.14 billion in 2024 damage and losses, 6,700,000,000 for El Niño preparation, and a 2027 assistance package of about 10 billion. A member also questioned the agricultural impact of the PacSilica initiative, and the agency estimated about 1,600 directly affected farmers while acknowledging that the full impact was unclear. Rufus Rodriguez raised hog-raiser indemnification, for which the agency cited 391,000,000 pending DBM approval and considered feed assistance or a supplemental 2027 budget. The agency committed to submit information, try to complete geofencing by year-end, and provide further plans, while related concerns were scheduled for the September 3 consultation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the scale of agricultural damage and the funding available for immediate disaster assistance, replanting, and farmer indemnification in 2027. It also examined whether unresolved hog-raiser claims required supplemental funding and what measures would support affected agricultural sectors.

topics.topic: Climate resilience, flood mitigation, and post-harvest loss reduction
topics.summary: Vice Chair Anna York and other members framed flooding, climate risk, food security, and post-harvest losses as central budget concerns. The DA said climate shocks had caused around 114 billion in agricultural damage and losses between 2024 and 2026, while irrigation coverage remained incomplete and post-harvest infrastructure and cold storage had significant gaps. Officials cited 6.7 billion for El Niño-related fuel and transport subsidies, about 10 billion for the 2027 assistance package, and an additional 10 billion being considered for climate-resilient DA facilities. NIA explained that irrigation projects were prioritized using weighted technical, economic, fiscal, regulatory, geographic, and drought-related criteria. Members also sought action on flood mitigation, sedimentation, dam capacity, the Ifugao rice terraces, and rubber-gate replacement. The agencies committed to submit documents and complete geofencing by year-end, but several project-specific issues remained unresolved or unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DA and NIA would use the FY 2027 budget to protect agriculture from flooding, climate shocks, irrigation shortfalls, and post-harvest losses. Members also asked whether the agencies had sufficient fiscal space, how irrigation and flood-control projects were prioritized, and what measures would be taken to preserve vulnerable production areas and facilities.

topics.topic: Agricultural mechanization and equipment procurement quality
topics.summary: Rep. Kaka Bag-ao sought the total 2027 irrigation budget, including solar-powered irrigation, and asked how the agency would address the remaining 30% of irrigation needs and the reported 70% rehabilitation share. An agency official cited 1,600,000,000 for solar-powered irrigation but did not provide the requested complete breakdown, and later said the data would be checked. Rep. Arnan Panaligan challenged lowest-bid procurement of PhilMech machinery, reporting that combine harvesters were prone to breakdowns and lacked spare parts. Secretary Laurel agreed that better-quality equipment was needed and committed to having PhilMech obtain the details. Panaligan also raised solar-irrigation projects pending since October 2025. NIA officials discussed around 100 megawatts of solar-powered pumps, estimated pilot income of 600,000,000, and a rate of 4 pesos per kilowatt hour, but the broader implementation and land-use questions remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether agricultural mechanization and solar-powered irrigation procurements were producing durable, effective equipment and timely implementation. Members also sought the budget allocations, implementation breakdowns, and corrective actions for irrigation and machinery programs, particularly where procurement quality or delays were reported.

topics.topic: Animal-industry competitiveness, ASF, vaccines, and pork imports
topics.summary: Allan Ty asked how the DA would use the animal competitiveness allocation and whether it would comply with RA 12308 and use livestock tariff collections as the revenue source. The DA said full use of 20,000,000,000 would effectively begin in 2028, while a 2027 framework would support herd buildup, repopulation, dairy, and related programs; it undertook to submit an amendment. DA officials cited current livestock tariff collections of about 22 billion annually, including 11,100,000,000 certified collections, and said a tariff classification change could yield 4,000,000,000, peso in additional revenue. Members also sought anti-rabies data, an animal-industry intervention breakdown, and responses to ASF and low hog prices. Secretary Laurel attributed farm-gate pressure to ASF, cited declining pork imports in some categories, opposed continuous importation subject to WTO constraints, and supported ASF vaccine deployment and livestock repopulation. Nicanor Briones requested vaccine funding, border biosecurity facilities, and reference-value import valuation, with the DA undertaking to coordinate with DBM and implement the valuation request.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DA would use the animal competitiveness allocation, finance animal-health and production interventions, address ASF and low hog prices, and manage pork imports and biosecurity. Members also asked whether the DA would provide vaccines, strengthen border inspection, and revise import valuation and tariff practices.

topics.topic: Sugarcane RSSI response, SRA utilization, and biological control
topics.summary: Rep. Raymond Mendoza asked the DA to disclose the RSSI expenditure breakdown and cited 25,000,000 in RSSI spending plus 10,000,000 for application and chemical usage; the Secretary later corrected the next-year pest-intervention figure from 250,000,000 to 300,000,000. Minority member Siberi questioned why the SRA had utilized only about 1,000,000,000 from a 2,000,000,000 budget and was told that procurement rules had delayed utilization and cut CEDA implementation by 50%. The SRA reported industry assistance of 420 something million and almost 100,000,000 in releases, but could not immediately state Bukidnon's share and promised to provide it. The DA Region 10 director described capacity growth from five hectares per day to 30 hectares per day, with a target of 100 hectares per day, and identified a proposed 150,000,000 laboratory quick response plan. Siberi supported increasing both DA and SRA funding, while the SRA committed to address procurement delays and the DA committed to submit requested information.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much had been appropriated and utilized for sugar-sector interventions, including the response to red striped soft scale insect (RSSI), and whether the DA and SRA had sufficient laboratory, biological-control, and procurement capacity. Members also asked what programs were affected by SRA underspending and how quickly agencies could expand their response.

topics.topic: Fishery, coconut, and coastal livelihood assistance
topics.summary: Rep. Ian Amatong asked DA officials for concrete Region 9 interventions for fishing and coconut livelihoods, farm-to-market roads, and port infrastructure, including an on-site assessment. The Secretary cited coconut levy facilities, a proposed deepwater port and food hub, and a DA mega hatchery, while an agency official committed to scheduling a regional visit. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez reported that the PCA had delivered 60,000 coconut seedlings after a request for 30,000 and sought another 30,000. He also pressed for fish-port integration at Makabalan, delivery of reinforced fiberglass boats, and 100 sets of fishing equipment, with the agency agreeing to delivery before plenary and by the first week of September. Rodriguez challenged agencies over undelivered livestock commitments involving 100 cattle, goats, and 400 carabaos; officials promised delivery subject to farmer qualification, breeding schedules, and beneficiary lists. He also reported irrigation figures of 125,000,000, 575,000,000, 15,000,000 each, and 200,000,000, with an official confirming the reported approval.
topics.question: What concrete interventions and delivery commitments would DA and its attached agencies provide for Region 9 and Cagayan de Oro, particularly for coconut seedlings, fish ports, fishing equipment, livestock, and irrigation? The committee also sought firm delivery dates and assurances for previously promised assistance.

topics.topic: Post-harvest facilities, food hubs, ice plants, and cold storage
topics.summary: The DA described a network of food hubs, processing centers, and mega cold storage facilities, including projects associated with Benguet State University and Clark. A minority member questioned large Benguet farm-to-market-road allocations and requested coordinates and project reports to verify that the roads were needed and not duplicative. DA officials said annual post-harvest losses were 250 billion and identified around 6.5 billion for 2027 post-harvest funding, while the High Value Crops Development Program requested an 8 billion increase from its current 1.7 billion budget. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported larger infrastructure funding, and an agency official requested a 50% increase in post-harvest support. Rep. Romeo Momo Sr. sought support for a 739 million Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor in Marihatag, including 47 million for 2027, and confirmed that a proposed Lianga facility was an ice plant and cold storage. The DA undertook to check coordinates, provide reports, and endeavor to advance the Marihatag project, but no final funding approval was recorded.
topics.question: What funding, projects, and implementation details did the DA and attached agencies have for post-harvest facilities, food hubs, ice plants, and cold storage? The committee also sought to establish whether proposed facilities and supporting roads were adequately funded, properly located, and integrated with production and marketing areas.

topics.topic: Mindanao and regional equity in DA and NIA allocations
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed the DA to raise Mindanao's share to 20%, citing Mindanao's contribution to food production, while DA officials sought additional FMR, post-harvest, fertilizer, and high-value-crops funding. The FMR infrastructure request included about 30 billion for an additional 2,000 kilometers, while post-harvest funding was cited at about 6.5 billion, fertilizer at about 8.73 billion, and the requested high-value-crops increase at about 8 billion over a current 1.7 billion budget. Rep. Reynolds Michael Tan questioned unreleased FMR funds, road standards, and declining Region 8 NIA allocations, and requested province- and project-level breakdowns. Rep. Nelson Legacion challenged FMR reductions and sought proportionate irrigation funding and hatchery support; the DA said its regional director would act on the hatchery concerns. A minority member requested a regional seed-system breakdown, and Secretary Laurel said the DA would review it and commit to funding it. Minority member Soberi linked Bukidnon's output of about 36.09 billion to the need for NIA support, but the apparent district allocation discrepancy remained unresolved while NIA undertook to update the figures.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DA and NIA allocations for Mindanao, regions, provinces, and congressional districts were proportionate to agricultural output, irrigable land, validated projects, and implementation needs. Members also asked whether FMR, irrigation, post-harvest, fertilizer, high-value-crops, seed-system, and hatchery funding should be increased or reallocated.

topics.topic: Land-use conversion, geofencing, and agricultural-land protection
topics.summary: Members raised concerns about the PacSilica development, industrial projects, marshland conversion, and solar installations on irrigable or rice land. The DA cited about 1,600 directly affected farmers in the Clark area but said the full agricultural impact had not yet been established. The DA supported geofencing of key crop lands, with 3 million hectares of rice land identified as needed and an 8% slope threshold discussed for land-use decisions. The secretary committed to complete geofencing by the end of this year and to undertake studies on industrial impacts and marshlands, with possible marshland implementation in mid-2027 subject to World Bank support. The DA also said solar-powered pumps could involve 100 megawatts, potential income of 600,000,000, and a proposed rate of 4 pesos per kilowatt hour, but said the agricultural effects of solar use on flat rice land still required research. A minority member additionally requested a breakdown of the 34,000,000 seed system program budget, which the secretary agreed to review.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DA would protect agricultural and irrigable land from conversion, industrial development, and solar projects, including through geofencing and impact studies. Members also asked what studies, implementation timelines, and program-level interventions would be provided for 2027.

topics.topic: National irrigation systems, maintenance, and infrastructure rehabilitation
topics.summary: DA Undersecretary Asis Perez reported that about 2.2 million hectares of an estimated 3.13 million irrigable hectares had been served, while the DA had added about 21,400 hectares and restored about 3,600 hectares through small-scale irrigation and canal works. Representative Juju Cesar Bergara sought action on an irrigation siphon, for which an agency official cited a request for 45,000,000 and a 194.5-meter length. Representative Marlo Bancoro pressed for multi-year irrigation and solar-irrigation implementation; the agency cited a 2027 proposal of about 1.12 billion but only 29,000,000 for the relevant item because of fiscal limits. Members also urged marshland studies, preservation of the Ifugao rice terraces through irrigation, and investigation of stalled solar projects. NIA reported a dam capacity of 54,000,000 cubic meters and discussed rubber-gate lifespans ranging from 15 to 45 years, but the replacement schedule was unclear. Representative Romeo Momo argued that the 5,000,000 NIA maintenance allocation for his district was inadequate, and NIA committed to provide a list of budget modifications or savings.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether irrigation systems, canals, dams, siphons, gates, and solar-irrigation facilities were adequately funded and maintained for 2027. Members also sought to determine which rehabilitation and expansion projects would be prioritized, and whether the agencies would provide studies, revised allocations, or implementation timelines.

topics.topic: Local dairy production and school milk-feeding funding
topics.summary: Krisel Lagman asked the National Dairy Authority and the Philippine Carabao Center about local milk production, import dependence, and the capacity of the school milk-feeding program to create demand for local dairy. The agency reported production of about 29 million liters in 2024 and 43,000,043 liters in 2025, while national milk sufficiency rose from 1% to 2.2% and imported dairy remained at 98 percent. The discussion cited a 2026 target of 44,500,000 and an NDA allocation of about 3 billion for DepEd's program, excluding DSWD's program, while another agency figure was stated as 2,163,000,000,000. Lagman also warned that fermented and flavored milk supplied nine to 21 grams of sugar, or two point two to five teaspoons, per serving. The agency's explanation of its production strategy and future targets was incomplete, and an agency official committed to provide requested sugar and industry data to her office.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the level of local milk production, the extent of reliance on imported dairy, and whether the proposed milk-feeding funding and agricultural support would expand domestic dairy capacity. It also examined the health and sugar implications of serving fermented and flavored milk beverages in schools.

topics.topic: Organic agriculture, agricultural credit, and high-value crops
topics.summary: Rep. Marlo Bancoro raised organic agriculture as a national concern and obtained a commitment from DA officials to meet and discuss the program's structure and regional direction. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed the DA on Mindanao's share, citing its contribution to corn, pineapple, banana, and overall food requirements; the Secretary ultimately confirmed a 20% share after an initial unclear response. The high-value-crops official requested an additional 8,000,000,000 over the existing 1,700,000,000 budget, citing targets for annual industry growth, higher farmer income, diversification, value addition, and post-harvest-loss reduction. ACPC requested no additional funding, but asked that credit be integrated into DA programs; it reported annual funding of 2,750,000,000 and lending of 3,250,000,000. The organic-agriculture budget issue was not resolved because the agency said its main concern was program structure and should be handled under another agenda.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DA would support organic agriculture, integrate agricultural credit into commodity programs, and expand assistance for high-value crops. It also examined Mindanao's funding share and the additional resources requested for diversification, value addition, and post-harvest needs.

topics.topic: Palm oil, banana, abaca, and coffee industry development
topics.summary: Rep. Raymond Mendoza sought DA support for urgent certification of the palm-oil and banana bills, stronger palm-oil funding, and a breakdown of pest-control spending. The DA supported the bills, cited a palm-oil roadmap targeting 300,000 hectares, and described funding of 500,000,000 in the first year and 1,000,000,000 in succeeding years, while committing to make an official recommendation and provide the pest-control breakdown. A minority representative requested marshland studies and a timetable for implementation, and the DA said the study would be completed by year-end with implementation potentially beginning in mid 2027. The same member raised coffee development, and the DA cited nurseries, high-yielding varieties, and processing equipment as planned measures. Rep. Romeo Momo Sr. presented the Marihatag Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor, citing 4,140 metric tons of 2025 production, a total project cost of 739,000,000, and a proposed 47,000,000 2027 allocation. The corridor funding was identified as Tier 2 and was not finally resolved during the exchange.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Department of Agriculture would support legislation and provide funding for palm oil, banana, pest-control, coffee, and abaca development. It also examined implementation timelines and funding arrangements for marshland studies and the proposed Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor in Marihatag.

topics.topic: Animal vaccination and the national anti-rabies program
topics.summary: Minority member Reniko asked how the national anti-rabies program would meet its stated elimination targets and what annual vaccination capacity and budget would be required. The DA Undersecretary for Livestock said that twenty twenty five one hundred fifty million had been distributed, although the transcript did not clarify what the figure measured. He said the agency planned to produce its own rabies vaccine and cited around 30 million dogs and cats, with roughly twenty to thirty percent requiring vaccination and a stated need for 27 million vaccinations. Reniko requested population-growth, vaccination-rate, budget, TNR, and impounding data, including information on free-roaming cats and dogs after impounding. The excerpt ended without the requested data being submitted or a firm agency commitment to provide it.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the national anti-rabies program would meet the country's targets for eliminating rabies, including the annual vaccination requirement, available vaccine supply, and the budget needed to vaccinate dogs and cats. The minority member also sought data on population growth, vaccination rates, and the implementation of the TNR and impounding policies for free-roaming animals.

topics.topic: NIA appropriation structure and congressional oversight
topics.summary: Allan Ty questioned the NIA administrator on whether irrigation appropriations should be program-based or rigidly itemized, and whether program-based budgeting still subjected projects to DBM validation, procurement laws, auditing, engineering standards, and congressional oversight. NIA answered that it preferred program-based appropriations supported by a separately submitted and validated project list, because itemization in 2026 had limited its ability to respond to cost changes, rights-of-way problems, calamities, and implementation delays. Robert Nazal Jr. separately questioned the DA's farm-to-market road funding, noting a 55,050-kilometer deficit, a reduction from about 33 billion in 2026 to about 16 billion in 2027, and a stated 51.5% cut. Secretary Laurel said roughly 60 billion annually could build about 4,000 kilometers, with the minimum effort taking ten to twelve years, and said DA had allocated 30% of its 33 billion budget based on absorptive capacity and manpower. Nassal also asked whether special provision number eight had constrained NIA utilization and requested a written proposal before plenary. The issue landed with NIA's requested program-based structure still subject to committee consideration, supported by document submissions, while the answer on whether cuts would leave projects functionally incomplete remained unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether NIA's irrigation appropriations should remain program-based or be itemized by project, and whether either structure preserved DBM validation, procurement and audit compliance, implementation flexibility, and congressional oversight. It also examined whether budget restrictions affected NIA's utilization and whether DA had the capacity to implement the proposed farm-to-market road funding.

topics.topic: OP FY2027 budget and proposed budget reduction
topics.summary: The chair presented the Office of the President's proposed FY2027 allocation as 10,156,000,000, while Executive Secretary Ralph Recto stated a proposal of MXN 10,150,000,000. Recto said the proposal was about 0.14% of the proposed national budget and was 64% lower than the previous year's level because of reduced operational requirements and the completion of ASEAN Summit activities. He said the amount would support the Office of the President's 49 delivery units and core presidential operations. The minority and majority moved to extend institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminate the committee deliberations. A minority member objected and raised transparency, flood-control, and confidential and intelligence fund questions, including 550,000,000 in such funds. The motion passed with 37 votes in favor and five against, while the chair recorded that outstanding questions would be answered on or before plenary.
topics.question: What was the Office of the President's proposed FY2027 allocation, and why was it reportedly lower than the previous year's level? The committee also sought to determine whether questions on flood control and confidential and intelligence funds would receive answers despite terminating the committee-level deliberations.

topics.topic: Confidential and intelligence funds and spending transparency
topics.summary: Members objected to ending the Office of the President budget discussion without scrutiny of confidential and intelligence funds and related accountability issues. One member cited 550,000,000 in confidential and intelligence funds, while other members raised transparency, flood-control, and possible political-patronage concerns. The Office of the President did not give a substantive answer in these stretches, although Executive Secretary Ralph Recto stated that the office respected Congress's authority and was ready to answer questions. Rep. Edgar Erice supported the budget and said confidential funds were necessary, while Rep. Iris Marie Montes said her negative vote defended Congress's duty to scrutinize every peso of public funds. The chair carried the motion to terminate deliberations by a vote of 37 to five and committed the outstanding answers to the plenary stage.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether the Office of the President's confidential and intelligence funds, and related budgetary issues, would receive meaningful congressional scrutiny and transparent accountability before approval. It also sought to determine when the Office of the President would answer the questions deferred by the committee's grant of institutional and interbranch courtesy.

topics.topic: Flood-control projects and reported anomalies
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice raised flood-control anomalies while discussing the President's budget, fiscal space, and developmental spending. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported the Office of the President budget and said the flood-control projects in the 2nd District of Cagayan de Oro were completed, compliant, and cleared by COA, NBI, DPWH, and NEDA. He also said persons responsible for irregularities should face justice through the Ombudsman. A separate member said plenary answers remained due and raised questions about flood control, possible kickbacks, and the transparency of confidential and intelligence funds. The member cited 550 million in confidential and intelligence funds, while other budget figures raised during the related discussion included about 58 billion in presidential pork and about 1.1 trillion for developmental projects. The excerpt ended without an agency response, leaving the questions parked for plenary.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish how flood-control anomalies and alleged irregularities related to the Office of the President budget and executive oversight. Members also sought clarification on alleged kickbacks, the role of executive officials, and the reported use of confidential and intelligence funds.

topics.topic: Barangay Development Program and NTF-ELCAC funding
topics.summary: Member Tonchi objected to terminating deliberations without direct answers and called for transparency concerning the Office of the President. Renee Co later explained her vote and specifically raised the Barangay Development Program and NTF-ELCAC, questioning their transparency, implementation, and audit support and referring to possible pork barrel or political patronage. She cited 1.95 billion, 258.0 billion, and 269.74 billion in figures rendered in the transcript as 1,950,000,000.20, 258,000,000,020, and 269,740,000,000, although their precise labels were unclear. No agency official answered these questions in the recorded stretch. The committee nevertheless approved termination by 37 votes to five, while the chair said the concerns would be noted before plenary.
topics.question: The committee was considering whether institutional and interbranch courtesy should end further deliberation of the Office of the President’s proposed FY 2027 budget despite transparency questions. A member specifically sought clarification on the Barangay Development Program and NTF-ELCAC, including their funding, implementation, and audit support.

topics.topic: Developmental projects and available fiscal space
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice expressed support for the President's proposed budget while discussing austerity, economic deceleration, and the fiscal space available for developmental projects. He cited capital-outlay or developmental-project shares of about 25% in 2023, 21% in 2024, and 19% in both 2025 and 2026. He also mentioned presidential-pork figures of 58,000,000,000 and 8,000,000,000, scholarship funding of 100,000, and developmental projects of 1,100,000,000,000. Rep. Erice referenced 1,600,000,000 trillion and 1,600,000,000,000, with the first expression unclear, and raised absorptive capacity as a concern. No agency official answered, no document or funding commitment was made, and the chair treated the remarks as a significant manifestation before moving on.
topics.question: The committee was considering whether the proposed FY 2027 budget preserved sufficient fiscal space for developmental projects and capital outlays. The discussion also raised the allocation of resources between government operations and development spending, including absorptive capacity.

topics.topic: Assistance for farmers and fisherfolk
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez raised the President's assistance to farmers and fisherfolk while manifesting full support for the Office of the President's budget. He said the President had distributed 10,000 to farmers and fisherfolk in Region 10. He also cited congressional access to DSWD, DOLE, TESDA, and the Department of Health as related support. No agency official answered or contested the statement, and the chair accepted Rep. Rodriguez's manifestation.
topics.question: The committee was considering whether the cited assistance for farmers and fisherfolk supported the member's position in favor of the Office of the President's proposed budget. The record also identified the amount and beneficiaries of the assistance mentioned.

topics.topic: ASEAN Summit funding and preparations
topics.summary: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto raised the ASEAN Summit in presenting the OP's proposed FY 2027 budget. He said the proposed budget was 64% lower than the previous year's level, partly because activities related to the Philippines' hosting of the Summit had been completed. He stated that no additional funding would be required for the Summit in FY 2027. The agency treated the existing proposal as sufficient and did not identify a continuing Summit-related funding need. No member questioned the statement or requested supporting documents in the provided excerpt.
topics.question: The committee was being informed how the completion of activities related to the Philippines' hosting of the ASEAN Summit affected the Office of the President's proposed FY 2027 budget. The presentation also established whether the OP expected to seek additional ASEAN Summit funding in FY 2027.

topics.topic: Commission on Audit opinion and budget accountability
topics.summary: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto raised fiscal discipline and accountability as central principles in the Office of the President's operations. He reported that COA had issued the OP an unmodified opinion for fiscal year 2025, described as the highest audit opinion an agency may receive. He said it was the OP's third consecutive unmodified opinion since 2022 and meant that its financial statements were fairly presented and compliant with applicable public sector accounting standards. Recto characterized the opinion as a badge of good housekeeping and evidence that public funds were accounted for. He also stated that the proposed budget followed DBM parameters and sought no special treatment. The issue remained informational, with no recorded committee follow-up or unresolved challenge.
topics.question: The committee was assessing whether the Office of the President had maintained proper financial management and accountability for public funds. The presentation focused on the significance of the Commission on Audit opinion and its relevance to the proposed budget.

topics.topic: PCO and attached-agency budget reductions and restoration request
topics.summary: Secretary Dave M. Gomez presented a PCO and attached-agency FY 2027 proposal of about 2.62 billion, 6.6% below the 2026 level, while the net department allocation was about 2.48 billion. Robert Nazal Jr. questioned the reductions and the PIA increase, and Gomez attributed the PCO reduction primarily to the end of ASEAN-hosting requirements while saying the PIA increase would fund retrofitting of its 44-year-old building. Gomez said IBC 13 received no subsidy because it was being prepared for privatization, while IBC officials described arbitration and operating pressures. Representative Zia Alonto Adiong pressed whether PCO could meet rising digital and anti-disinformation demands with a reduced budget; Gomez said it could remain effective but would perform much better with additional resources, including the 128,000,000 pesos requested for Bagong Filipinas Studios. Adiong formally sought restoration of the original PCO and attached-agency requests, and Representative Brian Yamsuan supported increasing and restoring the budget. The committee left restoration for a later review and required PCO to submit its original request, identify the cuts, and justify restoration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the PCO and most attached agencies received reduced FY 2027 allocations, whether the reductions would impair government communications and digital-information services, and whether the original budget requests should be restored. Members also asked what justified the Philippine Information Agency increase, how IBC 13's privatization affected its funding, and what resources were needed for Bagong Filipinas Studios.

topics.topic: IBC 13 zero budget, privatization, and transitional funding
topics.summary: Representatives Roberto Nazal Jr., Maria Victoria Copilar, Brian Yamsuan, and Antonino Roman III challenged the proposed zero allocation for IBC 13 and questioned the timing and consequences of privatization. The agency said the zero budget was tied to the planned sale, but warned that privatization might not be completed by the end of the year and requested restoration of funding for salaries, station upkeep, programming, and legal obligations. IBC 13 described government-information programming, Congress TV, multiple stations and programs, and employee and arbitration-related needs, including a request cited as 479,000,000 and an arbitration amount generally described as about 50,000,000. Copilar sought a transitional budget, while Secretary Gomez assured the committee that employee welfare would be protected and that Congress TV would move to PTV 4 if needed. DBM said IBC 13's ongoing privatization status explained the zero allocation, but acknowledged that it had not received documentation of the arbitration award. The committee indicated that the matter would be included in a new budget quotation, but the funding amount and final disposition remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why IBC 13 had a zero proposed allocation for FY 2027 despite its continuing operations and government-information programming, and whether transitional funding was needed pending privatization. It also sought clarity on the fate of IBC 13 programs, employees, operating obligations, and the arbitration award.

topics.topic: IBC 13 legal obligations, arbitration award, and employee compensation
topics.summary: Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong asked whether IBC 13 had to honor a court or mediation order involving former employees who had been waiting since 1998. An IBC official said the National Mediation Board had ordered payment of 50,000,000 for 26 employees, reduced from more than a 100,000,000, and said it was a legal obligation. Antonino Roman III later questioned IBC 13's defunding and raised 58,000,000, while the agency referred to a 50,000,000 request and DBM cited a separate arbitration award of 15,000,000. DBM said IBC's zero FY 2027 budget resulted from ongoing privatization and that it had received no record or request for the award. Roman pressed whether a budget amendment was required, but DBM said Congress would decide. Secretary Dave asked that IBC 13's funding be restored, and the Chair indicated that a new submission or budget quotation should be made.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the amount and legal status of IBC 13's obligations to former employees, including the arbitration award, and whether FY 2027 funding or a budget amendment was needed. Members also sought to determine why IBC 13 had been given zero funding and how its compensation obligations would be met during the proposed privatization.

topics.topic: PTV 4 budget, reach, equipment investment, and operating support
topics.summary: Representative Nazzal asked whether PTV 4's budget, reach, equipment, and staffing were adequate for its state-broadcasting mandate. The PTV 4 general manager said the station had about 136,000,000, also referring to 138,000,000, and requested 1,700,000,000; he said a competitive budget could require roughly five to seven billion. He reported current household reach of about 30%, projected reach of about 42% or more after equipment repairs, and reach above 50% with three additional towers. The general manager also said the current budget could not support a network and that international and regional state broadcasters spent billions in pesos. Members Lemanzeras and Yamsuan supported stronger government-media funding, while the PCO secretary said communications resources were inadequate and committed to pushing the request after a formal submission. The issue was not finally resolved in the hearing and was referred for subsequent committee and BARC discussion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PTV 4's proposed funding, transmission reach, equipment, and staffing were sufficient for it to fulfill its state-broadcasting and developmental-communication mandate. Members also examined the broader adequacy of PCO and government communications funding and whether additional support should be requested.

topics.topic: PIA capital outlay, office rent, and building rehabilitation
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked why PIA's budget had increased, and Secretary Dave M. Gomez said the principal reason was capital outlay for retrofitting its 44-year-old building. Brian Yamsuan then raised PIA's omitted request for 20,000,000 pesos in temporary rent, which Secretary Gomez confirmed was needed while construction proceeded. Members questioned whether retrofitting the deteriorated building was preferable to constructing a new one and requested photographs and videos of its condition. Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong supported maintaining adequate facilities for PCO and its attached agencies. Deputy Speaker Bambi Emano raised the proposed no-cost land donation for a Region 10 PIA office in El Salvador City and sought capital-outlay funding. PIA committed to the infrastructure project if funding was made available, while members committed to work for budget reinstatement or augmentation; no final appropriation was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PIA's budget increased, whether the increase would fund rehabilitation of its 44-year-old building, and why the separate request for temporary office rent was omitted. Members also sought support for capital outlay for PIA and attached-agency facilities, including a proposed Region 10 office in El Salvador City.

topics.topic: Bagong Filipinas Studios multiyear funding
topics.summary: Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong asked what would happen to PCO's Bagong Filipinas Studios multiyear program after the budget reduction. Secretary Dave M. Gomez said the program was a Tier 2 request and had received no funding for the following year. He said PCO requested 128,000,000 to develop three to five additional studios by using existing PIA and other attached-agency facilities. The studios were intended to support local news production teams, including Radyo Pilipinas and the Philippine News Agency, while also being available to private content creators and influencers. Adiong said the project could help mainstream and official media modernize, compete with social media, regain public trust, and combat misinformation. The issue ended without a recorded funding action or agency commitment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Bagong Filipinas Studios multiyear program would be affected by the reduced FY 2027 budget, including how much continuation funding PCO requested and who would benefit from the studios.

topics.topic: PCO digital information services and misinformation response
topics.summary: Secretary Gomez presented a proposed PCO budget of about 2.62 billion, a 6.6% reduction from the 2026 level, while describing expanded digital, media-literacy, and misinformation-response programs. Representative Adiong questioned whether the reduction would impair the PCO's ability to digitalize information services and provide accurate, timely information amid social-media misinformation. Gomez said the PCO could remain effective through organizational agility and streamlined operations, but acknowledged that it could be much better with additional resources. Adiong then asked about the unfunded continuation of Bagong Filipinas Studios, and Gomez identified a request of 128,000,000 for three to five additional studios. Adiong supported the studios as a means of modernizing state media and rebuilding public trust. Representative Yamsuan also supported increased resources and asked the PCO to submit a formal request for committee consideration; the proposed increase therefore remained subject to later action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed reduction in the PCO budget would impair digital information services, media and information literacy, and the government's response to misinformation and disinformation. It also examined whether funding for Bagong Filipinas Studios would continue and whether additional resources were needed.

topics.topic: PCO communications personnel and vacant critical positions
topics.summary: Secretary Dave M. Gomez reported that PCO proper had 577 available positions but only 469 active personnel, or about 81%, leaving 93 plantilla positions and 15 contractual items unfilled. He also said the proposed personal-services budget covered 185 unfilled positions and 17 non-permanent positions. Representative Nazzal asked why the Director for Communication Service position remained vacant and what prevented other critical positions from being filled. Gomez answered that nominations for some positions were being processed and that others were covered by an optimization plan submitted to the DBM. Nazzal and the PTV 4 general manager also discussed PTV 4’s limited budget, with the manager describing the allocation as 136,000,000 and elsewhere 138,000,000, against a request for 1,700,000,000 and an estimated competitive requirement of five to seven billion. Representative Brian Yamsuan supported increasing the PCO budget and asked PCO to submit a formal request for committee consideration. The vacancy process was ongoing, while the funding request remained subject to later budget deliberations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how PCO’s staffing complement and critical vacancies, particularly the Director for Communication Service position, affected its communications and government-media operations. Members also examined whether PTV 4 had sufficient resources and personnel to fulfill its mandate.

topics.topic: Government communications ecosystem and developmental communication funding
topics.summary: Brian Yamsuan asked the PTV 4 general manager whether the broadcaster could fulfill its new mandate with its existing funding. The general manager said PTV 4 could probably buy or collaborate on only one show with its budget and could not build a network with about 138 million, while neighboring state broadcasters spent billions in pesos. PCO Secretary Dave Gomez said developmental communication required viewing the communications ecosystem as a whole and corrected the PCO figure to zero point zero three percent, against a government budget of about 7.2 trillion. He also said social-media distribution was cheaper but production was significantly more expensive, and cited 5,000,000,000 in an example involving 10% of potential energy-sector losses. Rep. Brian Yamsuan supported higher PCO funding and the restoration of 1,700,000,000 for PTV and IBC. The matter was left with a request for a formal submission and commitments to pursue the issue in the BARC and committee deliberations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PTV 4, PCO, and other government communication outlets had sufficient resources to carry out developmental communication and compete across broadcast and social-media platforms. Members also sought the agencies' funding needs and any formal request that could support budget deliberations.

topics.topic: IBC 13 and attached-agency operating reductions
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned the lower proposed funding for PCO attached agencies and the increase for PIA, while also examining IBC 13's operating needs and planned sale. Secretary Dave M. Gomez attributed the PCO reduction to the one-time higher budget for ASEAN hosting and said PIA's increase would largely fund retrofitting of its 44-year-old building. Gomez asked that at least the agencies' original net plan be restored and said PCO was completing the steps needed to privatize IBC 13. IBC president Jimmy Policarpo cited an arbitration amount of 50,000,000, government-information programming comprising 80% of output, and income of 5,000,000 a month, while saying income covered roughly half of operating needs. Nazal questioned further investment in an entity already slated for sale, and stated that IBC's responsibilities and mandate would transfer to PTV if sold. The issue was left with commitments to advance the privatization process, while budget restoration and the final operating arrangement remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the PCO and several attached agencies faced reductions in the FY 2027 proposed budget while the Philippine Information Agency received an increase. It also questioned the operating needs, subsidy dependence, and planned privatization of IBC 13.

topics.topic: Local Government Support Fund rationale, allocation, and monitoring
topics.summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DILG's authority, monitoring role, transparency, and treatment of unused LGSF balances. DILG said DBM released and validated the assistance while DILG monitored distribution, implementation, and reports, and Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to submit utilization reports covering 2025 and 2026. The agency defended the proposed LGSF of about 58 billion as supplemental funding because the national tax allotment was spread across many provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays. DILG described engineers, project evaluation officers, local monitoring committees, CSO and NGO participation, and the Subay Bayan portal as safeguards. A civil-society-backed line of questioning sought justification after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, evidence against duplication, open-data disclosure, participatory budgeting, and human-rights safeguards. DILG answered these questions in part, but the broader policy and accountability concerns remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why a separate Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) remained necessary after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling increased LGUs' national tax allotment, what programs and fiscal gaps it addressed, and how funds were allocated, validated, implemented, monitored, and disclosed. Members also asked whether DILG or DBM controlled distribution and whether community participation and human-rights safeguards were adequate.

topics.topic: Barangay Development Program and SBDP per-barangay allocations
topics.summary: Jose Teves Jr. pressed for a higher SBDP allocation, arguing that 5,000,000 per barangay was insufficient for classrooms, health centers, water, electrification, and other needs. DILG said it had requested 10,000,000 per barangay and would welcome a congressional increase to 7,000,000 or more. Members then sought delivery rates, audits, beneficiary verification, and third-party monitoring, while DILG reported delivery rates ranging from 29% to 100% across the cited years and said 700 monitoring personnel were deployed. Rep. Caroline Agyao obtained clarifications on EL CAC coverage and annual allocations, including 2,500,000 in 2025, 10,000,000 in 2026, and 5,000,000 proposed for 2027. DILG said municipalities implemented the projects, DILG monitored them, and coordination was intended to prevent duplication. A CSO representative questioned the rationale and accountability of the LGSF and SBDP, and DILG described three-tier monitoring, DBM vetting, grassroots consultations, and the SubayBayan portal. The hearing ended with document requests and commitments, while the adequacy of the 2027 allocation and the broader evidence supporting it remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the appropriate per-barangay allocation for the Barangay Development Program/SBDP, the basis for changes in the proposed budget, and whether projects were properly selected, implemented, audited, monitored, and protected against duplication. Members and CSOs also asked what role DILG played in the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), what safeguards existed, and what documents and performance data would be submitted.

topics.topic: BFP fire-truck procurement, repair, stations, and emergency capacity
topics.summary: Members repeatedly questioned DILG and the BFP about fire-truck shortages, station gaps, procurement corruption, repair and replacement, and emergency-response capacity. The agency said it was pursuing a government-to-government procurement with South Korea for about 1,500 trucks, with a maintenance contract and a stated cost advantage over prior purchases and Japan. Officials said BFP fire-code collections were remitted to the national treasury, while DBM released only about 1 billion annually, leaving the BFP with limited access to funds despite collections and earmarks totaling several billion pesos. Members cited municipalities without stations or trucks and shortages in protective equipment, while the BFP requested search-and-rescue trucks, ambulances, Unified 911 operating funds, and additional recruitment. The committee noted or supported possible trust-fund and appropriations action, and Rodriguez manifested an intent to seek approval of the requested increases. The Korea procurement remained under negotiation, with technical specifications and a written status update requested, so the issue landed as a supported but not fully resolved commitment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the BFP would finance, procure, maintain, and distribute fire trucks, rescue vehicles, ambulances, stations, and related equipment; how much it collected and actually received from fire-code fees; and whether the proposed government-to-government procurement with Korea would address national shortages. Members also asked about procurement safeguards, repair and replacement needs, station gaps, and emergency-response capacity.

topics.topic: PNP additional funding, mobility, staffing, and regional equipment
topics.summary: The chair presented the DILG's proposed budget of about 32.5 billion, including about 142.5 billion for the PNP, and linked public-safety funding to school security and law-enforcement capability. Mark Huanko supported the DILG budget but pressed for implementation of the Lingayen road project, recovery of disputed PNP property, and replacement of aging vehicles; the PNP committed to act, investigate, coordinate, and report back. The agency said 95% of the Mahindra vehicles acquired in 2010 and 2011 were beyond economic repair, and Huanko requested 231 vehicles for the district's 231 barangays. Mica Gonzales asked about recruitment into violence and permanent police presence near schools, and the agency said sensitive details could be discussed in executive session while school police presence was already policy. Rufus Rodriguez cited Region 10 mobility deliveries and supported additional PNP funding; the PNP chief confirmed an additional request of 2,025,000,000 after initially stating conflicting figures. A majority member also raised DILG field-office staffing shortages, and the agency said a government optimization plan was being prepared.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DILG and PNP had sufficient funding, vehicles, personnel, and regional equipment to meet public-safety needs. Members also asked about the implementation of a Lingayen police-road project, recovery of disputed PNP property, school-area police deployment, and proposed staffing increases for DILG field offices.

topics.topic: School-violence prevention, active-shooter drills, and school police presence
topics.summary: The Chair and several members raised concerns about school violence, online recruitment into violence, firearms used by minors, and the need for faster police response. DILG and PNP officials said police were already present during school entry and dismissal and that barangay tanods would be allowed inside schools under a joint memorandum circular. Officials reported 50 school-related incidents involving minors, a 97% five-minute 911 response compliance rate, and a PNP operations increase of about 15 billion. The agencies proposed nationwide active-attack drills with DepEd, a youth ambassadors program, coordination with DICT and NTC on malicious online sites, and expanded Unified 911 vehicles. The Secretary also proposed stricter firearm-safekeeping inspections and penalties, while members questioned the emphasis on video games and stressed broader social and mental-health factors. The agencies committed to refine and submit drill guidelines, but the hearing left the definite schedule, dedicated budget line, and firearm-enforcement data unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what DILG, the PNP, DepEd, LGUs, and attached agencies were budgeting and implementing to prevent school violence, monitor online recruitment into violence, secure firearms, conduct active-attack drills, and ensure rapid police response. Members also asked whether police presence near schools could be made permanent or assigned to individual schools.

topics.topic: Firearms control, safekeeping, and police use of firearms
topics.summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula, Rep. Rolando Valeriano, Rep. Edgar Erice, Renee Co, Rep. Robert Raymond Estrella, and Anna York Bondoc questioned the DILG and PNP about firearm safekeeping, loose firearms, mobilization protocols, and school safety. The agency said 800,000 uniformed personnel were covered by firearm-responsibility rules, but acknowledged that firearms in the Tacloban and Zamboanga incidents had not been properly secured. Officials proposed advance-notice PNP inspections of lawful firearm owners' homes, stronger penalties for irresponsible safekeeping, and repeal of the Robin Padilla law; they repeatedly cited 98% as the share of firearm violence or firearm-related cases involving loose or unlicensed firearms. The PNP said it had only 2,000 body cameras for 320,000 personnel and was procuring another 10 or 20,000, while acknowledging that firearms carried during mobilizations may have reflected a mistake. For school security, officials cited barangay tanods, police coordination, active-attack drills, online-platform coordination, and community participation, but said assigning police to each of about 56,000 schools was impractical. The committee requested reports on the mobilizations, the Zamboanga mistaken-identity case, and the DILG's firearm-regulation recommendations; data on license suspensions and related cases was not supplied.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DILG and PNP were preventing firearms from being misused, particularly firearms issued to uniformed personnel or legally owned by civilians. Members also asked about controls during police mobilizations, penalties for irresponsible safekeeping, school security, and whether additional enforcement, inspection, identification, and accountability measures were needed.

topics.topic: PCW budget cut and gender-based violence services
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago questioned the PCW and ECCD Council budget reductions, regionalization plans, gender-and-development compliance, and the adequacy of local gender-based violence services. The PCW said the cut would mainly affect expansion to Mindanao, sought another 30,000,000 for that purpose, and reported 488 agencies in its gender mainstream system with about 77.46% compliance. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said DBM had cut the submitted budget and that restoration could make it more effective, while the ECCD Council reported a gap affecting 3,743 centers. DILG and PNP officials said local governments should address many frontline services within their budgets and committed to corrective or enforcement action on personnel-related violence and insensitive materials. The NCMF later reported inadequate Hajj medical funding, citing 95 pesos per pilgrim from a spoken allocation of 600 16,000 pesos, and requested support for three priority programs. The committee directed the NCMF to submit its request, and members expressed support, but the funding issues were not finally resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the reduced PCW and ECCD Council allocations would affect regionalization, gender-and-development compliance, child development centers, and frontline services for survivors of gender-based violence. It also examined whether NCMF's reduced medical allocation for Hajj and its priority programs required additional funding.

topics.topic: ECCD Council budget cut and child development centers
topics.summary: A committee member raised the scale of the child development center and day-care network and asked how the early childhood system would be supported. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said day-care centers were primarily funded through barangays and other LGUs, with additional infrastructure potentially involving DPWH and the provinces, because 96% of the DILG budget covered operating expenses or salaries. He cited an allocation of about 124 million for early-childhood feeding and capacity building. Representative Sarah Elago then questioned the 2027 ECCD Council figure of 232,000,000 pesos and asked how the cut would affect the council's mandate. The secretary said DBM had reduced DILG's submitted budget and that restoration could be requested, while the ECCD Council warned that the cut would limit center rehabilitation and the procurement of learning materials, furniture, fixtures, and other contents. Elago said she would propose a special line item for child development centers, but no restoration or final funding action was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the ECCD Council's reduced 2027 allocation would affect its mandate, regional services, and child development center infrastructure. It also examined which government level or agency was responsible for funding additional day-care centers and their contents.

topics.topic: BFP recruitment integrity, manpower, and personnel needs
topics.summary: Perci Cendaña raised alleged BFP recruitment slot-selling and sought clarification on the agency's controls. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said prior slot prices ranged from 200,000 to 800,000 per slot and referred the matter to the BFP chief, who described the online e-hiring system and confirmed a recent Region Three entrapment operation involving recruitment anomalies. The BFP said future recruitment would be fair, transparent, and based on merit and fitness. The chief reported that DBM provided about 2,000 recruits annually against a stated ideal manpower requirement of about 78,000; the transcript also gave an authorized strength of 43, with the unit unclear. He said the current rate would require twenty years and sought an additional 2,000 recruits per year. The Chair welcomed the agency action, but no approval of the additional recruitment request was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether BFP recruitment slots had been sold, whether the agency had detected and acted on recruitment-related corruption, and what controls were in place to prevent a recurrence. It also examined whether BFP's manpower level was adequate and whether additional annual recruitment authority was needed.

topics.topic: BJMP jail congestion and facility construction
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez asked BJMP about its budget request and the funding needed to address severe jail congestion. BJMP identified an additional request of 229,157,000 for jail-facility construction and cited further requirements involving Cagayan de Oro and Region 10, including 100,000,000 for Region 10 and a combined figure summarized as 800. The committee also raised problems caused by separate records systems among municipal and provincial jails, BJMP, and BuCor, while Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla advocated combining the agencies and creating common computerized records. Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned BJMP's restriction of visits primarily to direct family, lawyers, and doctors, especially for PDLs needing support from others. BJMP explained that most facilities were locked visitation spaces but agreed to submit its standard operating procedure and study possible changes. Funding support was expressed, but the construction figures and agency-consolidation proposal were not finally resolved in the recorded exchanges.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how BJMP would address jail congestion, including the additional funding needed for jail-facility construction and projects in Region 10. It also examined how detainee records could be consolidated across jail systems and whether BJMP visitation rules improperly excluded non-direct-family visitors.

topics.topic: Youth programs, NYC budget, and ICT modernization
topics.summary: A committee member questioned the NYC's proposed budget reduction of about 19,000,000 and the omission of requests for Muslim and creative youth summits and ICT modernization. The NYC explained the summit proposals and identified an ICT request of 24,000,948, while acknowledging that only two people handled procurement and that additional personnel-services funding was needed to absorb more funds. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula and Jambaranda pressed the NYC on programs, data, and curriculum for out-of-school youth; the NYC cited a 2,500,000 youth entrepreneurship allocation, support for a Magna Carta, and interagency coordination, but said available data was incomplete. Jambaronda also sought broader SK training and compliance, leading DILG to commit to revisiting modules and issuing further guidance. Members additionally requested active-shooter-drill guidelines and information on political-dynasty recommendations, with agencies undertaking to submit or obtain the requested materials. The budget increase itself remained unapproved in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the National Youth Commission's reduced 2027 budget could support its expanding youth mandate, including Muslim and creative youth summits, ICT modernization, youth mental-health and entrepreneurship programs, SK training, and services for out-of-school youth. Members also sought specific agency commitments, data, and interagency coordination on youth safety and political-dynasty concerns.

topics.topic: SK training, compliance, elections, and local youth governance
topics.summary: Rep. Jambaranda raised concerns about SK training, annual development plans, fiscal compliance, regular federation meetings, and the possible postponement of SK elections. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to an immediate memorandum circular on annual development plans and said noncompliant local governments could be excluded from the SGLG; he also took note of the request to regulate barangay travel. Rep. Bambi Mano asked whether DILG could hear and correct an appeal from an SK chair's dismissal, and the DILG undersecretary answered that it could under section 67 of the Local Government Code and the SK-related laws, subject to a written follow-up. The NYC described continuing SK training, auditing guidance, trainer-of-trainers arrangements, and an MOU with local government accountants, while DILG committed to revisit the one-day orientation modules. The NYC reported a training estimate of roughly 70 plus million, with the transcript also recording 72,000,000,000, and said a survey of 120 federation presidents was examining support for an extension or special elections. The agencies agreed to issue further guidance and submit information, but election timing, removal data, and out-of-school youth data remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether SK and barangay officials were receiving adequate training, complying with planning and fiscal requirements, and subject to effective oversight and removal procedures. It also sought clarification on DILG's appellate authority over SK dismissals, the timing of SK elections or special elections, and the reliability of out-of-school youth data.

topics.topic: Disaster preparedness, LGU capacity, and flood rescue
topics.summary: The chair and members linked disaster resilience and LGU capacity to the DILG budget, citing 50,441 evacuation centers and more than 126,000 deployed uniformed personnel. Teves questioned BFP capital outlay and rescue capacity, while Remulla attributed the earlier reduction to procurement reforms and pointed to planned acquisitions, including 1,500 trucks through a government-to-government transaction. Erice pressed for an integrated Metro Manila flood-control and garbage-management structure, and Remulla said aging drainage systems and fragmented LGU responsibilities required structural reform. Rodriguez sought additional BFP resources from collected fire-code fees, and the chair noted the proposal. York asked about institutional disaster preparation, class-suspension deadlines, and water rescue in flood-prone Pampanga; DILG described operational protocols, Pagasa coordination, monitoring, and continued LGU training. BFP said watercraft and life vests would be distributed geographically and committed to capacity building and future equipment acquisition, while the broader funding and governance issues remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DILG and LGUs were being capacitated for recurring disasters, flooding, and emergency rescue, including the availability and deployment of fire stations, fire trucks, boats, ambulances, personnel, and operating protocols. Members also sought clearer timelines and guidelines for disaster response and class suspensions, and asked whether funding and institutional responsibilities were sufficient.

topics.topic: Anti-illegal-drug operations and community-based health approach
topics.summary: Rep. Richard Gomez asked the DILG to strengthen anti-drug and peace-and-order support in his district and requested checks on police and CIDG records. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the department was committed and undertook to provide additional police vehicles, ambulances, and two fire trucks, while Gomez expressed full support for the proposed 2027 DILG budget. A PNP representative said anti-illegal-drug operations continued through supply and demand reduction, community engagement, intelligence gathering, and police operations. Minority members questioned barangay drug-watch lists and sought a community-based, health-centered and rehabilitation-oriented approach, but the record did not establish a definitive policy change. NAPOLCOM said it had zero case backlog and committed to submit a 2025–2026 disciplinary-action status report on Tuesday.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the anti-illegal-drug campaign would be sustained and coordinated with peace-and-order programs, including supply and demand reduction. It also questioned the continued use and verification of barangay-level drug-watch lists, rehabilitation-oriented alternatives, safeguards in police operations, and disciplinary action for flawed operations.
