topics.topic: Seal of Good Local Governance validation and compliance
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice challenged whether the SGLG measured actual governance outcomes or merely documentary compliance. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the DILG had moved to a whole-of-term assessment, reducing the former 10 indicators and as many as 14 categories to resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation; he cited 5,000,000 man hours previously spent annually and an estimated 5,000,000,000 cost for full third-party validation. Erice proposed using an appropriations provision to fund third-party validation, which the secretary welcomed. Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked that electric-bill compliance be added to fiscal-management criteria, and the secretary committed to include it in the next evaluation. In response to Rep. Jambaranda, the secretary committed to an immediate memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and excluding noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG. The request to regulate barangay travel orders was noted but not resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) measured actual improvements in local services and governance, rather than merely documentary compliance. Members also asked whether third-party validation and additional fiscal-management criteria could be incorporated into the SGLG.

topics.topic: LGU revenue sharing and local fiscal management
topics.summary: Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked DILG to enforce the local-tax exemption for the 121 electric cooperatives and to include electric-bill compliance in fiscal-management awards. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla assured him of support, and committed to include the criterion in the next evaluation round. Rep. Jambaranda raised SK, barangay development-plan, social-protection, and travel-regulation concerns; the Secretary said DILG could issue a memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and exclude noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG, while taking note of the travel request. Rep. Antonino Roman III asked for the status and timetable of Local Government Code amendments. DILG said consultations were under way, committed to submit available materials by next week, and supported reviewing the LGU share of national tax allocation from 40% to a higher level. The agency also discussed replacing the 25% equal-sharing component with equity sharing, but the allocation changes remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DILG would enforce local-tax exemptions for electric cooperatives, strengthen local planning and fiscal-management requirements, and regulate barangay travel. It also examined the status of proposed Local Government Code amendments, including possible changes to national tax allocation and equalization criteria.

topics.topic: Solid-waste management and LGU contract oversight
topics.summary: Jose Teves Jr. asked who was responsible for overseeing LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the Local Government Code assigned waste disposal to municipalities and cities, producing fragmented and potentially inefficient systems, and proposed a regional approach. Rep. Edgar Erice later tied the issue to Metro Manila's 14,000,000 residents and 12,000 metric tons of daily garbage, asking whether DILG could use its general-supervision authority to review LGU contracts. Remulla said DILG had no supervisory power over those contracts and identified COWA as the responsible body as rendered in the transcript. He maintained that the Local Government Code should be revisited because regionalized collection would be more effective than detailed supervision of 40,000 LGUs. The issue remained unresolved, with no specific legal change or oversight mechanism adopted.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which level or agency was responsible for ensuring LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003 and whether DILG could exercise supervisory authority over LGU garbage-collection contracts. Members also examined whether the current LGU-by-LGU system was adequate for the scale of waste and flooding problems, particularly in Metro Manila.

topics.topic: PNP accountability, body cameras, and public-assembly operations
topics.summary: Jose Teves Jr. raised PNP oversight and anti-hazing accountability, while DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla reported that NAPOCOM had cleared a backlog of about 15,000 cases and had no remaining backlog. Renee Co questioned arrests during mobilizations, police firearms, and the reported more than 700,000 Safer Cities apprehensions. The secretary defended the arrests and initiative but acknowledged that the PNP had only 2,000 body-worn cameras for 320,000 personnel, with another 10 or 20,000 being procured, and said crime reductions ranged from about 30% to 60% depending on the category. The member also challenged the agency’s explanation of school violence and raised arbitrary barangay-level drug-watch listings; officials cited intelligence procedures, supply-and-demand reduction, and operational safeguards. The agency agreed to provide operation reports, incident logs, updated statistics, and a disciplinary report, with the latter committed for submission on Tuesday. The broader questions about firearms, arrests, and enforcement safeguards remained contested.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PNP arrests and public-assembly operations complied with human-rights and public-assembly rules, including restrictions on firearms and requirements for body-worn cameras. Members also sought the factual basis and safeguards for the Safer Cities Initiative, the agency’s approach to school violence and drug-watch listings, and the status of police-accountability cases and reports.

topics.topic: LGSF and local-project implementation safeguards
topics.summary: Rep. Miro Quimbo raised recurring building-permit delays that had stranded local projects, especially schools and health facilities, and DILG agreed to examine specific cases after receiving data. A member then asked DILG and the PNP to distinguish excavation from quarrying and clarify heavy-equipment impoundment; DILG said local governments generally lacked that authority, while the PNP said it enforced violations in coordination with the DENR and LGUs. A CSO representative questioned the rationale for retaining LGSF despite an estimated national tax allocation of about 1.32 to 1.4 billion trillion pesos, and DILG defended the roughly 58 billion fund as additional support for local basic services. DILG said DBM handled proposal vetting while DILG monitored implementation through technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. Members also sought safeguards against duplicate projects, weak participation, red-tagging, and ineffective implementation, while DILG and NAPOLCOM described existing monitoring and complaint mechanisms. DILG said the proposed SBDP allocation of about 9.74 billion actually reduced the per-barangay amount to 5,000,000 because coverage expanded to 1,904 barangays, leaving several requests for supporting evidence and public accountability information unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DILG would use its supervisory and monitoring powers to address delayed building permits, stranded local projects, and questionable local enforcement actions. It also examined the policy rationale, safeguards, monitoring responsibilities, and proposed funding levels for the Local Government Support Fund and related programs.

topics.topic: NCMF Hajj medical expenses and priority programs
topics.summary: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula raised the adequacy of the NCMF's Hajj operations and medical budget for 2027. The NCMF said its medical allocation was only 600 16,000 pesos, or 95 pesos per projected pilgrim for 6,000 pilgrims, and sought an increase to 6,100,000. The agency also identified three priority programs: Madaris at 87,500,000, the Halal and Muslim community economic empowerment program at the unclear figure "89.04 94,000,000," and Hajj operation modernization at 6,100,000; it stated a total of 24,000,537. A committee member asked for the written request and said the request would be supported and advocated. Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula separately manifested full support for the NCMF budget, but the transcript did not establish final approval of any additional amount.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the NCMF's proposed 2027 budget adequately covered Hajj operations and medical needs for the projected pilgrims. It also asked which NCMF priority programs required additional consideration or funding.

topics.topic: Free higher education deficiency payments to SUCs
topics.summary: Members questioned CHED about unpaid free-higher-education deficiencies, SUC budget reductions, and whether continuing and incoming scholarship beneficiaries would be funded. CHED said 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing deficiency, while 667,000,000 remained associated with unpaid 2025 free higher education for 137,000 beneficiaries. The agency attributed future deficiencies partly to SUCs enrolling beyond capacity and to the unrealistic one-is-to-25 faculty-student assumption, and said it was developing a one-is-to-40 formula. Members also highlighted an 11,000,000,000 scholarship funding gap affecting roughly 1,000,000 students and a reported 29,200,000,000 deficit under UACTE alone. The chair required CHED to submit updated enrollment simulations, a prioritized funding request, and aligned beneficiary figures with DSWD before plenary. CHED committed to settle the existing deficiency by the third week of September, but the full 2027 funding requirement remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether free higher education deficiency payments to SUCs had been released, what deficiencies remained for 2025–2027, and whether proposed scholarship and SUC funding would cover continuing and incoming beneficiaries. Members also examined the enrollment-capacity and faculty-ratio assumptions behind the deficiency calculations and requested measures to prevent future shortfalls.

topics.topic: Tertiary scholarships, TES and TDP funding gaps
topics.summary: CHED presented a proposed 70,200,000,000 budget against a 35,430,000,000 NEP amount and identified a gap of roughly 34.8 billion, including scholarship, TES, TDP, and free-higher-education deficiencies. It said the TES proposal of about 35.5 billion was reduced to about 17.1 billion, potentially affecting roughly 833,780 beneficiaries, while TDP faced a shortfall that could affect 93,000 students. Members questioned delayed releases, unused funds, access for 4Ps and solo-parent beneficiaries, and the accuracy of CHED's overlapping beneficiary categories. CHED attributed prior delays to liquidation and validation requirements, reported that about 721,000 to 722,000 students had LandBank accounts, and committed to faster direct releases and reconciliation with DSWD. Members also challenged the scholarship reduction of 697,000,000 and requested detailed allocation and program breakdowns. The committee accepted CHED's explanations provisionally but left the funding and beneficiary totals for further reconciliation and plenary consideration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED's proposed funding for tertiary scholarships, TES, TDP, free higher education, and related student assistance would cover continuing and incoming beneficiaries. Members also examined delayed or unused funds, the accuracy of beneficiary counts, distribution mechanisms, and what CHED would submit or do to address funding gaps and possible reductions.

topics.topic: CHED FY 2027 funding gap and restoration request
topics.summary: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis presented a proposed budget of about 70.2 billion against an NEP allocation of about 35.43 billion, leaving a gap of roughly 34.8 billion. She identified major unfunded priorities including scholarships, free higher education, digital transformation, and monitoring and evaluation, and said the full request was data-driven. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported restoring the entire gap, while Brian Poe focused on the scholarship reduction and asked about AI funding; CHED reported 5,000,000 for AI initiatives. Chair Mikaswan Singh questioned the release of about 9.7 billion in SUC deficiency payments and sought assurance that remaining deficiencies would be settled by the third week of September. Singh also required CHED to reconcile scholarship and 4Ps beneficiary counts with DSWD and submit enrollment-capacity data and a prioritized formal request. The issue remained subject to validation and budget amendments review rather than being resolved at the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the size and composition of CHED's FY 2027 funding gap, which priorities were unfunded, and whether the agency's beneficiary and deficiency estimates were accurate. Members also sought commitments for detailed breakdowns, coordination with DSWD and DBM, and settlement of SUC deficiencies.

topics.topic: Scholarship and education-assistance utilization and validation
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno and Rep. Robert Nassal questioned unobligated CHED allotments, access to TES, solo-parent scholarship implementation, and billions in unused or lapsed education-assistance funds. CHED attributed the delays to school-year timing, reliance on DSWD lists, validation requirements, and processing constraints, while reporting improved utilization and committing to submit beneficiary lists and address rejected cases. Rep. Mauricio Domogan challenged the centralized processing system and the 7,500 assistance amount, while CHED explained that regional offices validated applications before central processing and agreed to verify Baguio's submissions. Rep. Brian Poe highlighted the LandBank system, through which CHED reported about 722,000 students had received accounts, and reviewed the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship's 20,000 slots and more than 39,000 applicants. Chair Mikaswan Singh focused on SUC deficiencies, citing a 12,000,000,000 initial requirement, a 9,700,000,000 release or processing amount, and a possible 29,200,000,000 UACTE deficit. CHED committed to settle deficiencies by the third week of September, reconcile 4Ps beneficiary categories with DSWD, update its enrollment-capacity simulations, and submit a prioritized funding request.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why CHED had unobligated or delayed scholarship and education-assistance funds, how beneficiaries were identified and validated, and whether the reported beneficiary gaps reflected funding, processing, or data problems. Members also sought assurances on the settlement of SUC deficiencies and requested beneficiary and utilization data before budget deliberations.

topics.topic: 4Ps beneficiary alignment and access to student assistance
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno raised the low participation of poor and 4Ps-linked students in TES and cited a 5.54% rate against a 40% government target. CHED said it was using DSWD data, targeting 50% of 423,000 identified 4Ps beneficiaries, and validating a larger applicant pool. Rep. Mauricio Domogan argued that the 7,500 assistance amount was inadequate against tuition of about 50,000 and suggested 15,500, while CHED said the amount was set by the UniFAST Board to broaden coverage and could be reviewed. Rep. Edgar Erice requested CHED's 2026 allocation data and 2027 plan before plenary. Chair Mikaswan Singh later questioned an 11,370,000,000 4Ps deficiency, possible double-counting, and a 29,200,000,000 UACTE deficit. CHED and the House undertook to reconcile the categories with DSWD and submit prioritized and updated data, leaving the final funding decision unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether TES and other student-assistance programs were reaching the poorest students, particularly 4Ps beneficiaries, and whether CHED's beneficiary counts and allocations were aligned with DSWD data. Members also sought to determine whether assistance amounts and program categories were sufficient, accurately counted, and free from duplication.

topics.topic: SUC enrollment capacity, faculty plantilla items and staffing
topics.summary: Jude Acidre, Antonio Tinio, Cheeno Almario, and Chair Mikaswan Singh raised concerns about enrollment growth, overcrowded SUCs, faculty shortages, free higher education deficiencies, and regular plantilla positions. CHED reported that 68% of surveyed SUCs exceeded estimated capacity and supported a one-is-to-40 faculty-student ratio, with additional classrooms, faculty items, and nonteaching positions needed. Tinio cited 20,964 faculty plantilla items and asked CHED to address job-order staffing and the salary grade 12 entry level for instructors requiring a master's degree. CHED undertook to provide validated staffing data, consult the Civil Service Commission, and submit a position paper. On deficiencies, CHED reported a release of about 9.7 billion against a prior total of about 12 billion, while Singh cited a broader UACTE deficit of about 29.2 billion and requested reconciliation of the figures. The committee and CHED set a third-week-of-September target for deficiency settlement and requested updated capacity simulations and a prioritized funding letter, but the final staffing and funding requirements remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether SUCs had sufficient enrollment capacity, classrooms, regular faculty plantilla items, and nonteaching staff to support free higher education. It also examined the faculty-student ratio used for funding and enrollment projections, the treatment of job-order and contract-of-service faculty, and the salary grade and qualification of entry-level instructors.

topics.topic: Student housing and PPP dormitory facilities
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno and Ian Amatong raised student housing as an infrastructure need affecting disadvantaged students' access and graduation. CHED said more than 100 SUCs could avail of Pag-IBIG financing and proposed one dormitory per SUC, with a possible government-funded second unit through a multiyear allocation. The agency cited financing at 3% rather than 8% per annum, a 10-year period, and an initial indicative cost of about 100 to 120 million per unit. CHED said small facilities would have 20 to 30 rooms, medium facilities 50 to 80 rooms, and large facilities would be three to five stories, depending on the SUC's land and capacity. Rep. Amatong requested the design and costing, and CHED agreed to provide them and arrange further consultations. Final design, capacity, and funding commitments remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how CHED proposed to address student housing shortages affecting access and graduation, including the scale, financing, design, cost, and capacity of dormitory facilities. Members also asked whether CHED could provide the dormitory design and costing and consult more regularly with legislators and universities.

topics.topic: Legal Education Board program funding
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez asked CHED to identify its full unfunded requirement and supported restoration of the entire 34,800,000,000 gap, including LEB funding. CHED Chairperson Shirley A. Agrupis confirmed the total and said detailed smaller requirements would be submitted to the appropriations committee. LEB Commissioner Justin Kalnapala reported that CLEP, LEAP, and LEADS each received 0 pesos in the proposed budget. An agency official presented LEB requests including 216,000,000 for CLEP, 57,000,000 for LEADS, 83,000,000 for LEAP, 24,000,000 for an unclear additional program, and 51,000,000 for LERP augmentation. Rep. Sarah Elago demanded restoration of the affected programs, including safe-spaces, faculty-development, and scholarship funding. Rep. Cheeno Almario later manifested support for increasing the Clinical Legal Education Program budget. The matter was deferred, with detailed submissions and committee review still pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the amount of CHED's unfunded requirements and whether Legal Education Board (LEB) programs, including clinical legal education, scholarships, faculty development, and related support, required restoration. It also considered whether the committee should support an increase or restoration of the requested funding.

topics.topic: Inclusive education and equity-group funding
topics.summary: Rep. Percy raised inclusive education priorities, including resource centers, health professionals, and learners with disabilities, and called for restoration of the budget during a learning crisis. CHED Chairperson Shirley A. Agrupis said CHED had completed research identifying equity groups and had incorporated them into policy and scholarship priorities. She cited programs in special needs education, speech pathology, occupational therapy, clinical psychology, and certification. CHED had proposed 418,000,000, or about 418 million, under the equity-group proposal. The exchange ended with Rep. Percy describing the funding situation as depriving programs of resources, without a recorded commitment to restore the budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how CHED was funding inclusive education, inclusive learning resource centers, and health-professional programs for learners with disabilities and other equity groups. The member also pressed whether the proposed budget cuts should be restored in light of the learning crisis.

topics.topic: Higher-education research, development and artificial intelligence
topics.summary: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agropis presented a proposed budget of about 70.2 billion against an NEP allocation of about 35 billion, identifying a roughly 34.8 billion gap that included scholarship, digital-system, and monitoring shortfalls. Rep. Brian Poe asked which items had been reduced, clarified the 697,000,000 scholarship gap, and requested its breakdown. He also asked about CHED's AI road map and research-and-development funding. CHED said it had adopted a national AI in higher education policy, allocated 5,000,000 for several AI applications, and was building faculty capacity. For research, CHED said faculty-researcher capacity building was in its proposal while project funding was placed under HEDF, including about 1.4 billion for pillar-funded projects. CHED undertook to submit the scholarship breakdown, research initiatives, and scholar-distribution data, while Rep. Poe expressed support for additional or restored CHED funding.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which higher-education priorities were reduced or excluded from CHED's FY 2027 budget, particularly digital transformation, artificial intelligence, research and development, and scholarships. It also asked how CHED was funding AI and research initiatives and which scholars would be affected by the reported reductions.

topics.topic: Medical scholarships and state university Colleges of Medicine
topics.summary: Jose Aquino II asked CHED about MSRS slots for state universities and colleges with Colleges of Medicine and raised the status of Caraga State University's commitments. CHED said allocations followed a regional formula based on medical-doctor availability and cited 1,786 new slots, 3,101 ongoing slots, and separately 3,300 ongoing slots, with the discrepancy left unclear. The discussion identified 102 active scholars and an allotment of 45, while Aquino referred to a prior commitment of about 25 and negotiations involving 10 slots with Caraga LGUs. CHED also cited facility funding of 40,000,000, while Aquino raised a possible 10 or 15,000,000 road requirement and the need for lighting. Rep. Sheen Gonzales separately expressed support for CHED and the Eastern Samar State University College of Medicine. No definitive increase in Caraga scholarship slots or additional infrastructure funding was committed.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how many MSRS scholarship slots were allocated to state universities and colleges with Colleges of Medicine, including the status of commitments and releases for Caraga State University. It also considered support for medical education infrastructure and state university medical programs.

topics.topic: Higher-education safety, Safe Spaces compliance and mental health
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno raised reports of restrictions on speech and assembly, red-tagging, online harassment, and potentially harmful active-attack drills, and CHED committed to policy review, student dialogue, and mental-health and campus-safety measures. Minority member Sara Elago focused on Safe Spaces Law enforcement, routine inspection, and CODI functionality. CHED said it was surveying about 2,347 higher-education institutions, including 561 SUCs and campuses, and reported that 66% had functional CODIs for informal anti-sexual-harassment investigations. CHED cited 697,000,000 for scholarship and faculty development and 258,000,000 for monitoring and evaluation, including Safe Spaces monitoring, but promised to submit the precise allocation for Safe Spaces compliance monitoring. Jay Vergara received CHED's account of a student safety portal covering about 5.8 million students and identifying online threats, bullying, violence, and dormitory safety among reported concerns. The agency's commitments were recorded, but the full compliance picture and exact Safe Spaces funding remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED was monitoring and enforcing Safe Spaces compliance and whether its policies and programs adequately protected academic freedom, student dialogue, campus safety, and mental health. Members also asked whether CHED had sufficient monitoring, complaint, and intervention mechanisms for violence, online threats, and psychological risks.

topics.topic: Private higher-education regulation and tuition-fee sharing
topics.summary: Eli San Fernando questioned CHED's delayed labor-education rules and enforcement of the 70% tuition-fee-sharing requirement in private HEIs. CHED said labor education would be integrated into NSTP and other courses, and it undertook to investigate faculty and staff complaints, coordinate with DOLE, and revise the private-higher-education regulatory manual. Rep. Solomon Chungalao asked about open universities, diploma mills, student complaints, and a campus building; CHED said about 31 of 113 universities were authorized for limited open-university programs, that violations could lead to closure, and that it would receive his documents. Rep. Renee Co raised unresolved free-higher-education deficiencies and student-welfare protections, while CHED acknowledged continuing deficiencies and said it was moving toward a one-to-forty faculty-student ratio and ongoing guideline deployment. Rep. Cheeno Almario cited severe faculty shortages and requested higher TDP funding and possible private-institution partnerships, with the chair taking the budget manifestation into consideration. Rep. Antonio Tinio raised constitutional concerns over legislative intervention in scholarship implementation, and Rep. Jude Acidre urged stronger attention to private HEIs because more than half of college students were enrolled there.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED was enforcing labor-education and tuition-fee-sharing requirements in private higher-education institutions, regulating open universities and diploma mills, and protecting faculty, staff, and student rights. Members also asked how CHED was addressing free-higher-education deficiencies, overcrowding and faculty shortages, the role of private institutions, and regulatory gaps affecting local and private institutions.

topics.topic: HEDF portfolio management and travel-tax funding
topics.summary: CHED chairperson Shirley Agropis reported that HEDF had released about 7.8 billion to address free higher-education deficiencies, with Congress adding about 4 billion plus and bringing the cited total to about 12 billion. She also reported remittances of about 12.54 billion and said CHED had submitted about 11.3 billion, while describing the average HEDF release rate as 54%. Nassal asked which government financial institution was the HEDF portfolio manager under Republic Act 7722, and Agropis said the Bureau of the Treasury was involved while CHED had approached Land Bank and other institutions. Nassal challenged that arrangement as a violation of the law and demanded transfer to a qualified government financial institution or an amendatory law. The chair said the issue would be taken up with partner agencies. Brian Yamsoo An later raised the 40% travel-tax collection, and CHED said it did not object provided its HEDF utilization was presented, while warning that it lacked capacity to finance existing programs without another funding source.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) was being managed, whether CHED had appointed the government financial institution required by Section 11 of Republic Act 7722, and how much of requested HEDF funding was actually released. It also asked about the proposed 40% travel-tax collection and whether CHED could finance its existing higher-education programs without that funding window.

topics.topic: Scholarship program administration and constitutional authority
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Poe examined CHED's LandBank partnership and sought assurance that the agency could manage a larger scholarship budget. CHED said the system expedited direct distribution, and reported that about 80% of the backlog had been addressed, including 722,000 students with bank accounts. Poe also questioned the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship, for which CHED described eligibility based on grades, household income, first-generation status, priority programs, and regional allocation; the program had 20,000 slots and more than 39,000 applicants, with support figures including 80,000, 90,000, and 45,000 as spoken. Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez then challenged the reduction from roughly 35.5 billion to roughly 17.1 billion, identifying an 11,000,000,000 gap and warning that about 1,000,000 students could be affected. He urged restoration and coordination of barangay scholarship funds with CHED. Rep. Antonio Tinio separately argued that legislative intervention in implementation could violate the PDAF ruling and executive authority, but the chair only noted the manifestation. CHED committed to provide regional distribution data and more accurate figures, leaving the funding and constitutional issues open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED could efficiently administer an expanded scholarship budget, how the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship selected beneficiaries, and why tertiary scholarship funding was being reduced. Members also questioned whether legislative involvement in scholarship implementation raised constitutional concerns under the PDAF ruling.

topics.topic: CHED regional access, monitoring and administrative capacity
topics.summary: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agropis said the commission lacked sufficient personnel, regional-office support, monitoring resources, and digital infrastructure to oversee about 39,000 academic programs across 2,365 higher education institutions. She cited 258,252,500 for monitoring and evaluation, regional-office requirements of 35,600,000 for CAR, 16,640,000 for Caraga, and 12,860,000 for Region 2, as well as an unfunded 331,300,000 ISSP request. Ian Amatong asked for assurances that TES would be released within the semester, requested dormitory design and costing, and sought better access to consultations. CHED said it was targeting full direct delivery by the end of September, agreed to provide the dormitory documents, and accepted a consultation arrangement. Rep. Rommel T. Angara proposed a CHED annex or sub-office in Aurora because travel to Pampanga took about four to six hours; the chair accepted the proposal, committed to interim outreach there, and directed preparation of complete staff work. The issue therefore landed with agency commitments, while the funding and final institutional approval remained open.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish whether CHED had sufficient personnel, regional offices, monitoring resources, digital systems, and consultation capacity to oversee higher education programs nationwide. Members also asked whether CHED could improve access for geographically distant areas, including Aurora, and provide timely assistance and requested documents.

topics.topic: OWA's additional 2,000,000,000 request and Emergency Repatriation Fund
topics.summary: Minority member Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether OWA's additional 2,000,000,000 request was the minimum needed for life-and-safety and crisis-response obligations. OWA cited emergency repatriation expenses and geopolitical uncertainty, while Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac expressly endorsed the full request and said utilization alone was not a safe basis for reducing the ERF. Nazal raised the need for contingency planning for nearly 200,000 Filipinos potentially affected by a Taiwan Strait conflict and asked for information on OFWs in China and Hong Kong; DMW said it lacked data on overstayers and secondary employment but had crisis manuals and interagency preparations. DMW reported extensive Action Fund assistance, including 44,445 financial-assistance beneficiaries and 606,921 total assistance and beneficiaries over the longer period reported. Majority member Johanne Monich Bautista supported an additional 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund and restoration of the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000. The chair later sought DBM clarification because the apparent NEP gap depended on how programs and net levels were presented, leaving the final funding decision open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether OWA's requested additional 2,000,000,000 was the irreducible minimum for statutory life-and-safety services, emergency repatriation, and other crisis-response needs. It also examined the adequacy of the Emergency Repatriation Fund (ERF), the basis for its proposed reduction, and whether contingency plans for Taiwan, China, and Hong Kong were costed and funded.

topics.topic: Restoration of 2,000,000,000 in DMW funding
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez questioned the reduction of DMW's proposed budget and asked for a documented restoration request. Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said DMW was seeking about 2 billion, including about 1 billion for the Action Fund, 60 million for Servicio caravans, 60 million for international labor affairs, 180 million for general administration, and amounts for NMP, the OFW Hospital, migrant protection, and migrant workers' offices. OWWA separately defended an additional 2 billion for MOOE, operations, emergency repatriation, capital outlay, facilities, upskilling, and scholarships. Rodriguez moved to approve both increases, but the chair deferred action because the proceeding was only a budget briefing. Rep. Niko Raul Daza also supported the increases and established that NMP's free maritime training could continue under the proposed budget, while NMP sought 92 million for additional facilities and information systems. The issue therefore remained subject to later committee consideration, with document submissions and facility assessments still expected.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DMW's proposed budget had been reduced, whether DMW and OWWA needed additional funding, and how the requested amounts would be itemized and justified. Members also examined whether the proposed funding would sustain expanded OFW services, including the Action Fund, free maritime training, facilities, and anti-illegal-recruitment programs.

topics.topic: Action Fund disbursement, assistance, and crisis-response funding
topics.summary: Members questioned how the Action Fund had been used for financial, legal, medical, welfare, and repatriation assistance, particularly during the Middle East crisis. DMW reported 80,000 financial-assistance cases, 14,000 legal cases, around 5,000 medical cases, and January-to-July 2026 assistance figures including 44,445 financial beneficiaries, 2,610 legal beneficiaries, 7,329 repatriation beneficiaries, and 9,891 welfare-case beneficiaries. The agency cited general rates of 50,000 for distressed cases, seventy five thousand for medical situations, and one hundred thousand for an OFW, with quick-action assistance ranging from 5,000 to 30,000 and a 30,000 pesos rate for certain trafficking and scam-hub victims. It said the Action Fund covered documented and undocumented OFWs, had no ceiling for certain hospital bills, and could assist in medical disputes and abused dependents. DMW undertook to review and amend the disbursement guidelines, while Johanne Monich Bautista manifested support for an additional 1,000,000,000 for the fund. The funding request and some garbled utilization figures were not finally resolved in the excerpt.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Action Fund was being disbursed, what standards governed legal, medical, financial, and repatriation assistance, and whether its funding was sufficient for ordinary cases and geopolitical crises. Members also asked whether the fund covered medical disputes and abused dependents, and requested utilization and beneficiary records.

topics.topic: Emergency repatriation and evacuation preparedness amid global conflicts
topics.summary: Members questioned whether DMW and OWWA could sustain OFW repatriation, financial assistance, and evacuation during the Middle East conflict and future geopolitical crises. DMW described activated crisis manuals, DFA coordination, prepositioned personnel, and the repatriation of about 12,000 people, while reporting Action Fund amounts of about 2 billion and a presidential supplemental allocation of 3 billion peso. Members, particularly Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. and Rep. Johanne Monich Bautista, argued that emergency funding should not be reduced solely because of historical utilization and supported restoring the ERF to at least 1.2 billion and increasing the Action Fund by about 1 billion. OWWA reported that the ERF had served 139,688 clients by July 31 and forecast serving roughly 240,000 to 250,000 clients. The agency also addressed Cambodia scam-hub victims, Strait of Hormuz seafarer evacuations, and medical-repatriation procedures. The issue landed with agency commitments to endorse and justify the requested increases and submit supporting records, but final congressional funding levels remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DMW and OWWA had sufficient funds, personnel, systems, and contingency plans to protect and repatriate OFWs during the Middle East conflict and other geopolitical emergencies. Members also asked how Action Fund and emergency repatriation resources were being disbursed, whether proposed increases were justified, and whether specific evacuation and medical-repatriation procedures were ready.

topics.topic: OFW Hospital procurement, staffing, access, and specialty care
topics.summary: Rep. Mica Gonzales asked about OFW Hospital procurement and staffing, and the agency said medical-supplies procurement had largely been resolved while equipment procurement continued. DMW reported that 77% of procurement items had been acted upon, around 198 regular positions had been filled, and an additional 110 plantilla positions had been provided. Rep. Tina Pancho asked about access, eligibility, referrals, and zero billing; the agency said eligible current or former OFWs and immediate dependents could directly access the hospital and receive fully paid services, with level-three cases referred to JBL and other hospitals. Rep. Florabel Yatco raised the proposed budget, patient volume, cancer-care center, and dialysis services; the agency cited a budget of 423,590,000, sought an additional 100,000,000, reported close to 60,000 patients in 2025, and said the 2027 budget was around 400,000,000. Vice Chair Bella Suansing asked whether abused OFW dependents were covered by the Action Fund, and the agency answered yes while outlining a proposed interagency aftercare and mental-health framework. The agency made commitments on equipment delivery, staffing, cancer care, dialysis, mental-health services, and submission of budget breakdowns, but the funding and level-three upgrade were not finally settled.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status of OFW Hospital procurement, staffing, access, eligibility, referrals, and zero-billing services. Members also asked about the hospital's proposed 2027 funding, patient volume, cancer-care and dialysis services, and mental-health support for OFW dependents.

topics.topic: NMP budget reduction and free seafarer training
topics.summary: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac and NMP Executive Director Vic Del Rosario presented NMP's modernization projects and explained that the apparent reduction in its budget was mainly due to lower capital outlay after a large current-year infrastructure allocation. Representative Niko Raul Daza asked whether free maritime training, begun on August 3 under DMW Memorandum Order 360, could be sustained despite the cited 210,000,000 or 52% reduction between the 2026 GAA and 2027 NEP. Del Rosario said operating funds were sufficient, with NMP expecting to serve about 30,000 seafarers in 2027 after training about 28,000 in the current year. He said NMP needed restoration of 92,000,000, including 67,000,000 for a training building and 16,000,000 for information systems, to add 15 training rooms and address increased enrollment. Daza manifested support for the requested increase, while NMP said feasibility studies for separate Cavite and Davao centers could support a budget proposal for fiscal year 2028. No final restoration or committee action was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the National Maritime Polytechnic could sustain its free maritime training program despite the reported reduction in its 2027 budget. Members also asked what funding and facilities were needed to accommodate increased enrollment and whether requested infrastructure funds would be restored.

topics.topic: OFW reintegration, livelihood assistance, and outcome measurement
topics.summary: Rep. Mica Gonzales asked how Middle East returnees were being reintegrated and whether they could return to overseas employment or pursue local options. DMW reported that about 12,000 people had returned, including roughly 9,000 OFWs and 3,000 dependents, and said it was profiling skills and matching job orders while offering livelihood and training assistance. DMW and OWWA later reported about 6,000 welfare interventions, nearly 5,000 training interventions, projected beneficiaries of about 51,000, and funding figures including 300,000,000 and 321,000,000. Rep. Johanne Monich Bautista said she supported the requested 300,000,000 increase for reintegration and additional funding for the action plan and ERF. Rep. Jude Acidre pressed for impact data rather than beneficiary counts and urged proactive pathways before OFWs returned. OWWA reported that over 60% had an employment or livelihood pathway after twelve months and supplied pathway percentages from interviews, but acknowledged continuing needs for monitoring, digitalization, and resources for a broader rollout.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how returning OFWs, particularly those affected by Middle East conflicts, were being profiled and assisted toward overseas reemployment, local employment, livelihood, or skills training. It also sought the funding, beneficiary basis, and measurable outcomes of the reintegration programs, including whether beneficiaries had obtained jobs or sustained businesses.

topics.topic: OFW medical, mental-health, and dependent-support services
topics.summary: Rep. Bryan Revilla raised OFW health-care coverage and urged the government to provide extra assistance to OFWs. DMW said PhilHealth coverage was mandatory, most OFWs had host-country insurance, and the Action Fund could assist with hospital bills without a set ceiling, citing a case costing more than 1,000,000. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned regional cooperation, medical retainerships, mental-health care, gender-sensitive services, and the use of verification fees; DMW identified 130,000,000 for medical and legal retainers and said each verified contract carried a 10 US dollar fee. DMW reported verification-fee collections of about 5.85 billion and earmarks ranging from about 163 million to about 700 million across the cited years. Vice Chair Bella Suansing asked whether abused OFW dependents were covered, and DMW answered yes while proposing an interagency aftercare system for children left behind. The OFW Hospital reported having a psychologist but needing a psychiatrist, leaving expansion of regional mental-health capacity as an ongoing commitment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DMW and partner agencies covered OFWs' medical and mental-health needs, including insurance, hospital assistance, medical retainership, and gender-responsive care. It also examined whether assistance extended to abused OFW dependents and children left behind, and how contract-verification fees supported these services.

topics.topic: US500 minimum wage for migrant domestic workers
topics.summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula asked how DMW would enforce the increase in the minimum wage for migrant domestic workers from 400 US dollar to 500 US dollar. DMW said the policy, issued through Department Order 25 in August 2025, was initially voluntary because of its effect on existing contracts, and reported 17,375 processed job orders at the 500 US dollar salary. The agency cited video interviews, employer screening, skills training, and livelihood options as safeguards and said it would continue implementation until the rate became acceptable enough for mandatory imposition. The exchange also covered Action Fund disbursement, including a 2,000,000,000 fund, a 3,000,000,000 peso allocation, and assistance rates ranging from 2,000 to 100,000. DMW committed to provide release documentation, cover pending claims by the early fourth quarter, and review and amend the disbursement guidelines. The wage issue was therefore committed for continued implementation but was not shown to have been fully enforced across all destination countries and agencies.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DMW would ensure implementation and compliance with the increased minimum wage for migrant domestic workers, including whether the standard would eventually become mandatory. The member also asked about Action Fund disbursement and the adequacy and timing of assistance for distressed workers.

topics.topic: Contract verification fees and use of Treasury collections
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago raised the issue of verification fees and asked about the reported increases. The DMW Secretary said each verified contract carried a 10 US dollar fee and that collections partially reverted to DMW operations. The DMW undersecretary reported about 5.85 billion in collections for fiscal year 2023 to 2026, present, meaning January to July, deposited in the Bureau of Treasury. The agency reported GAA earmarks of about 163 million for 2024, 580 million for 2025, 580 million for 2026, and about 700 million for 2027. In response to the follow-up, the agency said the fee had not increased and remained 10 US dollars.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the verification fee charged for each contract, whether the fee had increased, how much had been collected and deposited with the Bureau of the Treasury, and what portions had been earmarked in the General Appropriations Act.

topics.topic: Illegal recruitment and human-trafficking enforcement outside Metro Manila
topics.summary: Rep. Jude Acidre raised the case of 23 families of 23 OFWs imprisoned in Cambodia and asked about DMW's broader response to scam-hub trafficking. DMW said it was providing welfare assistance, repatriation, financial assistance, legal support, and coordination with the DFA and DOJ, while expanding migrant workers offices in Cambodia and Thailand and working toward a presence in Myanmar. The secretary also described bilateral and ASEAN efforts on fair and ethical recruitment, while a medical arrangement in Dubai served about 700,000 Filipino workers. Rep. Niko Raul Daza questioned whether NMP could sustain free maritime training after a 52% budget reduction; NMP said its national-government subsidy could support training about 30,000 seafarers in 2027 but requested 92,000,000 for facilities and information systems. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez then asked how DMW would make anti-illegal-recruitment and anti-trafficking services accessible outside Metro Manila after applicants were reportedly charged 350,000 by an unauthorized recruiter. DMW answered that it had expanded regional staffing, operated 16 regional offices, and used surveillance, verification, closure operations, and LGU and law-enforcement partnerships. The funding restoration and broader budget increases were not resolved in the excerpt.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DMW was responding to Filipinos trapped in overseas scam hubs and how it was coordinating with other countries to prevent trafficking and illegal recruitment. It also examined whether DMW and NMP had sufficient regional personnel, facilities, medical arrangements, and funding to provide protection and services outside Metro Manila.

topics.topic: OFW database consolidation, e-registration, and cybersecurity
topics.summary: Rep. Plato asked how DMW was consolidating OFW records, addressing registration glitches, and protecting sensitive data. DMW said it was coordinating with DICT on e-government, database registration, cybersecurity, and technical assistance, and reported that about 1.5 million OFW Passes had been issued. The Secretary said DMW monitored attacks 24/7, had thwarted daily attacks, and had not seen the database breached, although some email accounts had been affected. The budget official cited 290,000,000, later clarified 53,000,000 and an additional requested 11,000,000 for 2027; the transcript also contains an unclear initial reference to 309. Rep. Plato urged stronger cybersecurity operations, third-party penetration testing, and Data Privacy Act compliance, while manifesting support for DMW's 2027 budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DMW was consolidating OFW records, addressing registration mismatches and e-registration glitches, and protecting sensitive OFW data. Rep. Plato also sought information on the budget for DMW's IT infrastructure and cybersecurity program.

topics.topic: DMW staffing, headquarters, and regional facilities
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed DMW to explain the reduction from its proposed budget and supported restoration of about 2 billion. Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said DMW sought the restoration for the action fund, overseas service activities, administration, facilities, NMP, the OFW Hospital, and additional migrant workers' offices, and said the agency had authority to build its main headquarters at Agham Road. OWWA separately requested about 2 billion for MOOE, operations, capital outlay, seafarer welfare and regional facilities, global centers, and scholarships; its administrator cited serious seismic-safety deficiencies in an existing building. Rep. Nico Raul Daza then questioned whether NMP could sustain newly free maritime training despite a budget reduction, and NMP answered that personnel and operating funds were adequate but requested 92 million for additional training capacity and information systems. NMP said it could train about 30,000 seafarers in 2027 and would study future centers in Cavite and Davao for a possible 2028 budget proposal. The committee requested supporting documents and manifested support, but the funding increases were not finally resolved in the excerpt.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DMW and its attached agencies had sufficient personnel, operating funds, capital outlay, headquarters, regional offices, and training facilities to deliver services to overseas Filipino workers and seafarers. Members also asked what additional funding and facilities were required and whether the requested expansions were sustainable.

topics.topic: OFW scholarships and migrant-worker education support
topics.summary: An agency official first described the Congressional Migrant Workers Scholarship Program under the 1995 law, citing support of 60,000 per year, 50,000,000 in congressional funding, and 20,000 scholars. During Rufus Rodriguez's questioning of OWA's additional funding needs, the OWA administrator said the program had initially received 150,000,000 from PCSO and 50,000,000 from the former CDF. The administrator said the program supported OFWs and their dependents up to 60,000 a year for four years, while OWA's regular scholarship program used a private trust fund. OWA requested an additional 50,000,000 for the congressional scholarship program as part of a total additional request of 2,000,000,000. The committee received the explanation, but no final ruling on the scholarship funding was recorded.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish the scope and funding needs of OFW and migrant-worker scholarship programs, including the Congressional Migrant Workers Scholarship Program and OWA's regular scholarship support. It also sought to determine what additional funding the agency requested for these programs and whether the request was supported by documentation.

topics.topic: Saudi residence permits and OFW legal assistance
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez raised a constituent's case involving the non-issuance of a Saudi residence permit and asked why the permit was not being issued and who was responsible for assisting affected OFWs. An agency official answered that residence-permit problems could involve overstaying or perceived violations and said legal assistance was available through the action fund, the Tebian Law Office, retained counsel, and in-house lawyers. The official said the Saudi law firm had 30 lawyers and that the agency shouldered hospital or immigration-related penalties. Rodriguez then moved to increase the DMW and OA budgets by 2,000,000,000 each. The chair said the motion would be considered at the proper time because the proceeding was only a budget briefing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why some OFWs in Saudi Arabia were not receiving residence permits and which office or mechanism was responsible for addressing their cases. It also sought clarification on whether legal assistance and related penalties were covered.

topics.topic: DENR FY2027 budget reduction and institutional amendments
topics.summary: The DENR presented a requested FY 2027 budget of about 28.04 billion and later disclosed that it had proposed about 55.04 billion to the DBM, including tier two. Members questioned the substantial reduction and identified priority augmentations for land management, patent registration, foreshore mapping, the Land Management Bureau building, and water-resource programs. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez moved an additional 556,617,000 pesos, and the committee approved it subject to consolidation and available fiscal space. The DENR also committed to follow up on Nagat Island monitoring, Eastern Samar mining rehabilitation, and stewardship-approval thresholds. Rep. Rodriguez separately sought 400,000,000 for rehabilitation of previously planted areas, but the chair required a new written request. The Appropriations chair directed the DENR to submit a formal and prioritized list for budget amendments review before plenary deliberations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the DENR's FY 2027 request, the extent and reasons for the reduction from the amount proposed to the DBM, and which additional programs or institutional amendments should receive funding. It also examined whether the proposed augmentation was approved or remained subject to available fiscal space and further review.

topics.topic: Mining monitoring, enforcement, and illegal-mining operations
topics.summary: Members questioned whether the roughly 53.6 million national MGB monitoring budget and the 12.829 million Caraga regional budget were adequate for illegal-mining enforcement, particularly in Dinagat Island. DENR committed to visit Dinagat, review mining claims, issue a proper public statement, and consider closure where warranted, but no final closure decision was recorded. Rep. Alexander Pimentel pressed DENR to release 10 seized conveyances in a Surigao del Sur case, and the secretary assured him that release would occur the following day. Members also sought action on Chinese nationals in illegal mining, small-scale mining applications, white-clay extraction and stockpiles, and quarry permits; the agency committed to reports, inspections, operator lists, and coordination. The agency stated that small-scale mining was capped at 50,000 metric tons per annum and cited 3.1 billion pesos for EMB and 1.89 billion for MGB. The hearing ended with several actions committed but with the Dinagat closure, white-clay seizure order, and mangrove earth-balling suspension unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DENR and the Mines and Geosciences Bureau had sufficient budget, personnel, and authority to monitor mining and quarrying, stop illegal operations, and act on confiscation, closure, and permit-compliance issues. Members also sought specific follow-through on Dinagat Island, small-scale mining, white-clay stockpiles, quarry permits, and mining claims.

topics.topic: Mining permits, FTAAs, MPSAs, and small-scale mining regulation
topics.summary: Members questioned DENR on illegal mining involving Chinese nationals, FTAA renewals, dredging permits, MPSA assignments and operating agreements, small-scale mining applications, and contested exploration permits in Nueva Vizcaya. DENR reported six approved FTAAs, said renewal extensions could apply in force-majeure cases, and described public consultation at the project-feasibility and ECC stages. It said small-scale mining was limited to 50,000 metric tons per annum and committed to a one-stop shop in Davao de Oro, inspections, and submission of operator lists. MGB said one operator per MPSA had been prohibited by policy in 2021 or 2022 and committed to investigate the Mount Sinai and Eastern Samar arrangements. On critical minerals, DENR cited about 9,000,000 hectares of potentially mineralized land, current exploration funding of 157,000,000, a proposed MGB budget of 1,577,000,000, and only 2% of the potential area explored. The discussion landed on multiple agency commitments, while the allocation of mining proceeds for exploration and the suspension of mangrove earth-balling remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status and regulatory basis of mining permits, FTAAs, MPSAs, operating agreements, and small-scale mining applications. It also examined whether DENR had adequate guidelines, enforcement capacity, consultation procedures, rehabilitation requirements, and funding for mineral exploration and critical-mineral development.

topics.topic: Land management, surveys, patents, foreshore tenure, and reversion
topics.summary: DENR presented land titling as a priority, with a target of up to 43,000 patents, while its Land Management Bureau acknowledged that survey-dispute funding was insufficient and that regional offices handled the work. Rep. Rodriguez secured committee approval of an additional 556,617,000 pesos for land management, foreshore mapping, patent issuance, the Land Management Bureau building, and water resources, subject to fiscal space. A member raised the 1,014.92-hectare Wanderlust Corporation claim in Siroma, and the Secretary said DENR was completing a survey and targeting a reversion filing in the second week of October limited to forest lands. Members also sought funding and action for Cordillera forest reserves, solid-waste disposal sites, a proposed marine protected area, and development options for built-up forest land. MGB committed to investigate contested Nueva Vizcaya exploration activities, while the Secretary committed to a biophysical assessment for possible reclassification. The chair required DENR to submit a formal, prioritized request for additional funding before further budget deliberation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DENR would fund and administer land surveys, dispute resolution, patents, foreshore tenure, land classification, and reversion proceedings. Members also asked whether specific forest, protected-area, and land-management concerns would receive funding or agency action.

topics.topic: Solid-waste management, LGU compliance, and waste-facility funding
topics.summary: Members questioned DENR's role in LGU waste-contract oversight, RA 9003 enforcement, source segregation, flooding, and the availability of waste facilities. DENR said LGUs were primarily responsible, while DENR provided technical assistance for MRFs and solid-waste plans, conducted education campaigns, and monitored sanitary landfills for ECC compliance. Rep. Teves cited 92% LGU compliance, a 95% 2027 target, and only six of 17 Metro Manila LGUs compliant with source segregation; he also cited 2,230,000,000 in 2025 annual DENR appropriations as a possible source of assistance. The commission representative disclosed a very limited budget, described the status of ten-year LGU plans, and reported a resolution recommending activation of barangay solid-waste committees. Rep. Rise linked roughly 12,000 tons a day of Metro Manila garbage and an estimated 30% left in waterways to flooding, while proposing a regional-government approach. Rep. Domogan requested identification or reservation of suitable disposal sites, and DENR committed to coordinate regionally; other requests and enforcement concerns remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DENR, the National Solid Waste Management Commission, and LGUs had adequate authority, funding, facilities, and enforcement mechanisms to comply with RA 9003 and address flooding caused by improper waste disposal. Members also sought commitments on technical assistance, environmental education, waste-facility siting, and requests for additional funding.

topics.topic: Flood management, watershed rehabilitation, and nature-based mitigation
topics.summary: Members asked DENR to define its responsibility for waterways, flood prevention, watershed rehabilitation, and coordination with DPWH. DENR said its mandate included environmental impact assessment, wastewater regulation, water-quality management, watershed and river-basin programs, and nature-based solutions complementary to DPWH infrastructure. It cited about 28 million for nature-based solutions, 78 million for integrated water-resource management, 21 million for river-basin operations, and 33 billion for forest development, protection, soil conservation, and related rehabilitation, although the watershed-by-watershed allocation was not provided. DENR said the national and Central Luzon flood frameworks and a unified water database were still being finalized or developed, while the Pampanga initiative remained at the risk-assessment stage. Members pressed for greater mangrove and greening support, and the chair said an additional 30 million would be pursued. DENR also committed to examine the Bulacan Airport’s environmental effects, submit Manila Bay enforcement and rehabilitation information, and continue work on ECC thresholds for flood-control projects.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish DENR’s responsibility for flood prevention, watershed and waterway management, and nature-based mitigation; its coordination with DPWH; and the funding, monitoring, and environmental-clearance requirements for related projects. Members also asked what specific programs and databases would support flood-risk reduction in Central Luzon and Manila Bay.

topics.topic: Protected-area funding, staffing, and forest protection
topics.summary: DENR presented protected-area management and forest landscape restoration as strategic priorities within its proposed budget of about 28 billion, covering 121 legislated protected areas and 15.8 million hectares of classified forest lands. Members questioned the 1,300,000,000 protected-area management budget and learned that allocations generally arose from regional fiscal space, equity considerations, and protected-area management-board proposals rather than a single needs-based formula. Rep. Mario cited Mount Hamiguitan's 16,923 hectares of protected land and 9,000-plus hectare buffer zone and requested a more concrete funding formula, while also criticizing ranger coverage ratios involving as much as 3,000 hectares per ranger. DENR reported National Greening Program targets of 18,000 hectares for planting, 30,375 hectares for enhancement, and 30,000 hectares with a stated budget of 408,000,000, while Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought an additional 400,000,000 for rehabilitation. Members also raised Cordillera forest-reserve funding, Catanduanes' lack of permanent plantilla positions, and a proposed marine protected area, and DENR described requests to DBM ranging from 1,000 to 1,706 positions. The issues remained dependent on written submissions, DBM approvals, and possible budget augmentation, with DENR undertaking follow-up coordination and documents.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DENR's proposed funding and staffing were sufficient to manage protected areas, protect forests, support National Greening Program priorities, and respond to local conservation and rehabilitation needs. Members also sought a needs-based protected-area funding formula, permanent plantilla positions for rangers, and clearer options for managing forest lands and reserves.

topics.topic: Environmental impact assessments and ECCs for major projects
topics.summary: Members raised concerns about mining-related tree cutting, quarry and exploration permits, tree-cutting requirements for ADB bridges, New Clark City data centers, the Bulacan Airport ECC, and ECC coverage for flood-control and pumping-station projects. DENR said specific projects required clear descriptions and, where applicable, EIA, ECC processing, consultation, public hearings, and cumulative-impact assessment; it also said the New Clark City master-plan ECC covered about 9,400 hectares while projects within a 1,600-hectare area would require project-specific review. The committee cited an EIA budget of about 251 million, DENR budget figures including a 2027 request of about 28.05 billion, mangrove allocations of 13,900,000 for 2026 and 15,000,015 million for 2027, and a proposed additional 30,000,000 for water-related work. DENR returned the ADB bridge application covering 17 trees, reduced from 21, pending consultation and other requirements, and stated replacement ratios of 100 for naturally growing trees and 50 for planted trees. For Bulacan Airport, DENR undertook to develop terms of reference for an environmental review addressing Pampanga impacts. The hearing ended with commitments for reports, investigations, interagency coordination, and an administrative order clarifying which flood-control projects require ECCs.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DENR evaluates environmental impacts, processes ECC applications, conducts consultations, and enforces mitigation requirements for major infrastructure, energy, industrial, airport, mining, quarrying, and flood-control projects. Members also asked what funding, reviews, and interagency mechanisms were available to support those functions.

topics.topic: Water resources governance, river basins, and water-district support
topics.summary: DENR presented direct assistance of PHP 124,000,000 for local water districts and described funding for aquifer recharge and digital water governance. Rep. Rodriguez secured approval of an additional 556,617,000 pesos for the DENR budget, including water-resource priorities. Members raised delays involving the Butuan City Water District, insufficient LWUA funding, and the need for a technical review of La Mesa Dam; officials undertook follow-up actions, but the transcript did not show final resolution of those matters. DENR said its flood-management framework remained subject to final review and interagency consultation, while its 2027 water-related allocations included about 78,000,000 for integrated water-resource management, PHP21 million for river-basin organizations, and 28,000,000 for nature-based solutions. Members also pressed for a unified water database and stronger watershed rehabilitation, with DENR identifying 131 critical watersheds and 16 priority landscapes. The hearing left the framework, database, water-district financing needs, and dam review as committed or continuing actions rather than fully resolved outcomes.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DENR and its attached agencies would finance and coordinate water-resource management, river-basin planning, watershed rehabilitation, flood mitigation, and support for water districts. Members also asked whether agencies had adequate authority, data systems, and technical capacity to address water-district delays, dam safety, and disputes involving joint-venture operators.

topics.topic: Forest restoration, National Greening Program, and mine rehabilitation
topics.summary: The DENR Secretary presented the National Greening Program as a landscape-restoration program and described progressive rehabilitation as a mining safeguard. A member challenged DENR over alleged tree cutting, FPIC failures, and inadequate rehabilitation, prompting commitments for central-office enforcement review. Rep. Brian requested guidelines under Executive Order 122, and DENR described progressive rehabilitation and a forthcoming critical-minerals list. Rep. Mica Gonzales raised Eastern Samar MPSA assignments and operating agreements; DENR said it would inspect the tenement, address rehabilitation and compliance concerns, and respond by October. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez questioned replanting funds and proposed an additional 400,000,000, while DENR identified a 1,600,000,000 NGP request and 408,000,000 for a 30,000-hectare target. Members also sought needs-based protected-area funding, more forest rangers, and detailed watershed funding; DENR committed to several submissions, but the allocation formulas and some figures remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DENR would fund and implement forest restoration, the National Greening Program, watershed rehabilitation, protected-area management, and mine rehabilitation. Members also asked whether DENR had adequate enforcement, staffing, allocation formulas, and safeguards against abusive mining and deforestation.

topics.topic: Mangrove rehabilitation and earth-balling policy
topics.summary: Leila de Lima questioned whether DENR had a mangrove rehabilitation budget and challenged the October 2025 memorandum allowing mangrove earth-balling for infrastructure projects. DENR said cutting mangroves was prohibited, earth-balling was allowed under a mitigation hierarchy, and a survival-rate study involving its research and biodiversity bureaus and civil-society groups was still underway. The agency projected completion of the study by December and a new policy in early 2027, but Delima and the Chair questioned the memorandum's scientific basis and the claimed survival results. Delima requested suspension of earth-balling, and the Secretary said DENR would evaluate the suggestion. A separate congresswoman pressed for mangrove planting as natural flood control; DENR cited 13,900,000 for 2026, a 200-hectare target, and a stated 2027 allocation of 15,000,015 million, while the Chair undertook to seek an additional 30,000,000.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DENR had adequate funding for mangrove rehabilitation and planting, and what natural flood-control measures it was implementing. It also sought to determine the scientific, legal, and consultative basis for allowing mangrove earth-balling and whether the interim memorandum had effectively become a permanent policy.

topics.topic: Critical-mineral exploration and mineral-reservation program
topics.summary: Rep. Brian asked DENR to clarify the guidelines and safeguards required under EO 122, and DENR cited progressive rehabilitation and a planned critical-minerals list. Rep. Reniko then asked DENR and MGB to implement a national exploration and mineral-reservation program and requested the United States-Philippines MOU. MGB said exploration was continuing for minerals including gold, copper, and nickel, while DENR said domestic processing and value-adding were policy objectives. The secretary cited current exploration funding of about 157 million, and MGB cited a proposal of about 1.577 billion while saying more resources were needed. Members proposed using a percentage of mineral-related proceeds for exploration and development, and MGB identified only 2% of the prospective area as explored and 17 highly prospective areas for prioritization. The matter remained unresolved pending policy documents, the MOU, and possible legislative action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DENR and MGB would implement EO 122, identify and reserve critical-mineral deposits, and determine whether the Philippines had sufficient reserves for feasible domestic processing. Members also asked what exploration funding was needed and whether mineral-related proceeds could be reused for exploration and resource development.

topics.topic: Geohazard, liquefaction, and elevation mapping for land-use decisions
topics.summary: A member asked DENR and MGB to integrate liquefaction data into geohazard maps used for building permits, zoning, CLUPs, and infrastructure decisions, citing a magnitude 7.8 event and a reported 38% liquefaction figure. MGB said Administrative Order 2000-28 already required engineering geological and geohazard assessments before infrastructure projects and that hazard maps could be integrated for local land-use planning. Jay Vergara raised additional concerns involving elevation references, permitting, agency coordination, and gravel-tax collections of about 400,935 in 2022 and 1,034,880 in 2,023. The Secretary and MGB Central committed to establish a technical working group with DPWH and other agencies and to study and report on the matter. Congressman Clayton separately sought review of exploration permits in Nueva Vizcaya, citing protests, alleged lack of consultation, and possible overlap with forest reserves, ancestral domains, and watersheds. MGB said operations were suspended and an investigation would be conducted, while DENR committed to a biophysical assessment supporting possible land reclassification.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether liquefaction and other geohazard data were being integrated into maps used for building permits, zoning, CLUPs, and infrastructure planning. It also sought clarification on elevation references, interagency coordination, mining-permit reviews in Nueva Vizcaya, and the classification of occupied forest or public land.

topics.topic: Manila Bay rehabilitation, pollution enforcement, and relocation
topics.summary: Congresswoman York asked what the DENR was doing on natural flood control in the Manila Bay area and pressed for more mangrove funding. The DENR cited mangrove planting, Estero Rangers, a 200-hectare 2026 target, 13,900,000 for 2026, and a 2027 figure transcribed as 15,000,015 million. The chair committed to fighting for an additional 30,000,000, while the member advocated 30,000,000 a year for ten years. York also sought Pampanga's inclusion in the Bulacan Airport environmental assessment and ECC mitigation measures; the DENR committed to coordinate with the region and formulate terms of reference. Sarah Elago asked about the Manila Bay strategy through 2031, relocation and resettlement, funding, enforcement collections, and a status report. The DENR described five key result areas and reported inspections of 67,535 establishments, 16,722 notices of violation, 350 cease-and-desist orders, and 191 ex parte orders, while committing to submit collection and rehabilitation-status data.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what natural flood-control and mangrove measures the DENR was implementing in the Manila Bay area, and whether funding was adequate. It also asked about the Bulacan Airport's environmental impacts on Pampanga, Manila Bay rehabilitation planning and funding through 2031, pollution-enforcement results, collections, and relocation requirements.

topics.topic: E-waste, solar-panel, and lithium-battery waste management
topics.summary: A member questioned whether DENR was ready to manage end-of-life rooftop solar panels and lithium batteries, noting that batteries could be discarded after about 10 years and that disposal could become imminent within two or three years. DENR and the EMB said TSD facilities existed and were being accredited and registered, but the EMB acknowledged the scale concern; no specific nationwide personnel or capacity plan was given. Rep. Remeco then raised 234 e-waste shipments through March 2026, plus additional intercepted shipments, and asked whether they could be returned to their countries of origin. The EMB said it was monitoring recyclers, coordinating with Customs, retaining subsequent shipments onboard, and generally pursuing return of shipments or segregated materials. Rep. Remeco also sought an update on Basel Ban Amendment ratification; DENR said PEZA and DTI had not yet issued certificates of concurrence. The matter therefore landed with agency monitoring and return-related commitments, while ratification and long-term waste capacity remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DENR had the facilities, personnel, and nationwide enforcement capacity to manage end-of-life solar panels and lithium batteries. It also sought clarification on DENR's handling of imported e-waste shipments and the status of the Basel Ban Amendment ratification.
