topics.topic: Flood-control master plans and integrated Metro Manila drainage planning
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno established that DPWH did not have a consolidated national flood-control and drainage plan, although the agency maintained master plans for all 18 major river basins and was updating 14 of them. DPWH said the updates were targeted for the first half of 2027 and supported a national legislative framework while favoring river-basin and locality-level implementation. Rep. Edgar Erice pressed for an integrated Metro Manila plan, and DPWH said an NCR-wide master-plan update would be completed by the end of the year or early the following year, with coordination among local-government plans. Rep. Renee Co cited the 2016 audit concerns and asked about delayed planning and projects that might worsen flooding; DPWH said audits and investigations were ongoing. An Iloilo member sought priority for floodway and drainage studies, and DPWH confirmed 102,000,000 for the feasibility-study update, although the stated combined total of 150,000,000 or 152,000,000 was not resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had a national flood-control and drainage plan, how river-basin and urban plans were being coordinated, and when outdated plans would be completed. Members also asked whether Metro Manila had an integrated, NCR-wide plan and whether specific local studies and floodway projects would be funded and prioritized.

topics.topic: Ghost, substandard, and ineffective flood-control projects
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno questioned the absence of a consolidated national flood-control plan, and Secretary Vince Dizon defended the river-basin and urban-center approach while committing to update the plans by 2027. Members also pressed DPWH on lifestyle checks, contractor disclosures, convergence-program reforms, and nature-based solutions; the agency cited a one-strike policy, 12 blacklisted contractors, and proposed stronger disclosure rules. Rep. Antonio Tinio examined project vetting and central-office allocations, including the 50,000,000 threshold for central implementation, while DPWH cited certificates of implementability, geotagged photographs, and other documentation. Rep. Renee Co raised delayed master plans and projects that may have worsened flooding, and DPWH said audits with investigative agencies were ongoing. Rep. Stephen James Tan asked for the number of ghost projects; DPWH identified two areas, while the member characterized the situation as roughly 10 projects across two districts and about 183 engineering districts. DPWH reported 76% of contracts advertised, 32% awarded, and an 80% target by the end of September, but the ghost-project inventory and the status of flood-aggravating projects remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate nationwide or river-basin flood-control plans, and whether its systems could prevent ghost, double-funded, substandard, or ineffective projects. Members also asked how projects were vetted and audited, how contractors and personnel were disciplined, how appropriations were distributed and implemented, and what reforms or reports DPWH would provide.

topics.topic: Distribution of DPWH projects between districts, regions, and central office
topics.summary: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales raised concerns about weak engineering studies, consultant accountability, district project implementation, and earthquake rehabilitation. Secretary Vince Dizon said proper studies ideally required 5% to 6% of capital outlay—roughly about 30 billion based on 460,000,000,000—but only 6,000,000,000 was budgeted for those activities, and he committed to report on project and rehabilitation concerns. Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned project traceability, leadership and district allocables, and the concentration of funds in the central office; Dizon cited certificates of implementability, geotagging, LGU coordination, and the 50,000,000 implementation threshold. A minority member questioned unusually uniform evacuation-center and social-facility allocations and wide district disparities, but the agency's explanation of five-year planning and interagency site identification did not fully resolve the basis for all allocations. Tinio also questioned why projects were distributed among only some of the 1,099 district engineering offices and warned that amendments and insertions could contribute to delays. Dizon committed to submit reports, justify changes, and move toward stricter, more consolidated and multiyear flood-control programming.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH projects were properly vetted, traceable, and allocated on a needs-based basis among district engineering offices, regional offices, and the central office. Members also questioned whether fragmented project allocations and congressional changes contributed to duplication, weak accountability, and delays, particularly in flood control and post-earthquake rehabilitation.

topics.topic: Fragmented flood-control projects versus concentrated flagship investments
topics.summary: Minority members questioned the basis for district and regional allocations and argued that flood-control funding should respond to need, hazard exposure, and project readiness rather than political or district distribution. They cited annual district allocations ranging from about 36,000,000 to 18 billion, as well as a 2022–2025 allocation of about 8.1 billion for Quezon City's 4th District. A member also criticized flood-control projects below 50,000,000 as fragmented and proposed concentrating resources in a flagship program for priority areas. Secretary Vince Dizon said centralized management was ideal, acknowledged that the current arrangement was not yet ideal, and pointed to stricter controls. He committed DPWH to environmental-impact studies for flood-mitigation projects affecting waterways and agreed that multiyear appropriations were the best solution, leaving the specific allocation formula unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether flood-control funding should be allocated through fragmented district-level projects or concentrated in priority areas under a flagship, needs-based program. It also examined whether environmental-impact and project-preparation requirements should govern flood-control allocations.

topics.topic: Flood-control facilities, pumping stations, detention basins, and water diversion
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno established that DPWH did not have a single consolidated national flood-control plan, although all 18 major river basins had plans and 14 were being updated, with completion targeted for 2027. Secretary Vince Dizon defended a river-basin and locality-based approach, while supporting detention basins, nature-based measures such as gabions, and upstream interventions. Rep. Roy Gonzales sought a Silang-Santa Rosa diversion or spillway solution, and DPWH cited 82,000,000 for a related feasibility study and undertook to pursue the study next year. Members raised Metro Manila detention sites, Pampanga pumping stations and bridges, Iloilo floodway studies, and dredging; DPWH committed to maintain or complete facilities, confirmed 102,000,000 for the Iloilo study update, and described dredging as a regular maintenance need. The hearing produced several agency commitments, but detention-facility performance targets and the final funding and sequencing of some projects remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had a coherent national and river-basin flood-control plan, how proposed detention, diversion, pumping, dredging, and nature-based facilities would be prioritized and maintained, and whether specific local projects would receive funding or completion commitments. Members also asked for technical studies, measurable flood-mitigation targets, and updates on unfinished facilities and bridges.

topics.topic: Right-of-way acquisition and landowner compensation funding
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago sought updates and records concerning right-of-way payments and compensation for affected households and small businesses in the ADB Metro Manila Bridges Project. DPWH cited right-of-way obligations close to 90,000,000,009.00 and later described an accumulated obligation of 90,000,000,000. Rep. Mark Cojuangco urged stronger nationwide right-of-way acquisition funding, while Secretary Vince Dizon expressed support. Rep. Howard asked how funds were allocated and was told that payments were prioritized by project, voucher readiness, court order, or negotiated settlement; expropriation cases required a 15% deposit. The Secretary stated an FY 2027 allocation of 15,000,000,020.27, while the exchange also referred to 5,000,000,000 and 5,000,000,020.26 for the current year. Howard requested additional funding because right-of-way payment delays were delaying projects, and Dizon said additional funding would be welcome but made no specific appropriation commitment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH allocated and prioritized funds for right-of-way acquisition and landowner compensation, including the FY 2027 amount. Members also asked whether additional funding was needed to prevent project delays and requested records on affected households, businesses, and major projects.

topics.topic: FY2025 SAROs, discontinued projects, savings, and fund realignment
topics.summary: Rep. Robert Massal asked Secretary Vince Dizon about FY 2025 projects whose SAROs had been issued but whose SARs were not, including the disposition of their allotments. Dizon cited a total of 90,000,000,000, alternatively stated as 90,300,000,000, with more than 30,000,000,000 attributed to flood control projects, and said projects with incomplete documents were returned to DBM after additional vetting. He agreed to provide the committee with the relevant letters and a list of discontinued projects. Dizon said the funds were effectively declared savings and that much of the budget cover was used for the uplift program, relying on the GAA general provisions and describing the projects as unimplementable or abandoned. Erice then cited DBM records dated 11/27/2025 showing augmentation sourced from declared DPWH savings and sought clarification on whether the affected projects were included. DPWH did not resolve that specific question during the hearing and committed to comply with documentary requirements.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what happened to FY 2025 projects whose SAROs had been issued but whose corresponding SARs were not issued, including the status of their allotments. It also questioned whether the funds were declared savings, how they were used or realigned, and what legal authority supported those actions.

topics.topic: MVUC and the discontinued stand-alone Special Road Fund
topics.summary: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam questioned why the stand-alone Special Road Fund had disappeared from the FY 2027 PAP schedule and been placed under Asset Preservation. He cited the prior amount of 14,833,952,000 and the FY 2027 amount of 15,000,000,000, arguing that the new presentation made the earmarked fund less visible and could narrow its use because bridges were in a separate PAP. DPWH Undersecretary Nick Conti answered that Republic Act 11239 limited MVUC to roads, bridges, and road drainage and that qualifying projects under Asset Preservation Organizational Outcome No. 1 were attributed to MVUC. The agency said the 15,000,000,000 amount had been specified by DBM and offered to submit the detailed project list. Ongwam also raised constitutional, Supreme Court, and prior veto-message concerns, but those issues were not directly resolved. The immediate result was an agency commitment to provide supporting project documentation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 presentation of MVUC collections under the DPWH Asset Preservation Program improperly obscured or narrowed the statutory Special Road Fund. Rep. Sidhu Ongwam also asked whether DPWH requested this treatment or whether it was imposed by DBM.

topics.topic: Project vetting, feasibility studies, and detailed engineering capacity
topics.summary: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales questioned DPWH's allocation for detailed engineering and geotechnical studies, consultant accountability, and the basis for earthquake rehabilitation projects. Secretary Vince Dizon said the ideal allocation was about 5% to 6% of capital outlay—roughly about 30 billion based on the cited 2026 capital outlay—but only 6 billion was budgeted for the studies. He also acknowledged that DPWH lacked the personnel and specialized equipment needed to conduct studies for all 11,000 proposed 2027 projects. Rep. Antonio Tinio examined project traceability, certificates of implementability, geotagged documentation, and the central-office implementation of projects above the 50 million threshold. A congresswoman secured commitments for lists of feasibility-study and tourism-road projects and was told that projects costing 1 billion and above required a feasibility study. DPWH said tourism-road identification would be led by the concerned department, with joint technical validation with DPWH, while foreign-assisted and convergence projects would continue under documented implementation arrangements.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had sufficient funding, personnel, systems, and accountability mechanisms for feasibility studies, detailed engineering, geotechnical investigations, and project validation. Members also asked how projects were assigned, technically validated, and implemented, including convergence and foreign-assisted projects.

topics.topic: Major bridges, inter-island connectivity, and multiyear completion funding
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought support for Cagayan de Oro bypass roads and bridges, citing about 34 billion for the Coastal Bypass Road, about 7 billion for the Eastern Interior Road, and additional funding for local bridges and walkways. He also highlighted feasibility-study funding for the Mindanao-Visayas connection, including 350 million for the Surigao-to-Southern Leyte bridge study. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned the status of 944 TCAS projects and the ADB Metro Manila Bridges Project, citing more than 3 billion pesos in disbursements and requesting detailed records, traffic studies, blueprints, and compensation information. Secretary Dizon said DPWH would verify the project information and submit the requested reports, except that the MRT 7 blueprint would be referred to DOTR. Rep. Salvador Pleyto and Rep. Timothy Titan pressed for complete multiyear bridge funding, earthquake assessment, anti-overloading enforcement, and safety improvements. Rep. Anna York Bondoc raised unfinished Pampanga pumping stations and bridges, including the 95%-complete Delta Bridge; Secretary Dizon committed to fund and finish the facilities and said the Delta Bridge would be completed by early the following year.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which major bridge, bypass-road, flood-control, and inter-island connectivity projects required funding; whether projects would be completed rather than left in phases; and what schedules, feasibility studies, project records, and implementation responsibilities applied.

topics.topic: Earthquake rehabilitation, bridge safety, and seismic retrofitting
topics.summary: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales questioned DPWH's allocation and capacity for geotechnical and detailed engineering studies, citing earthquake-related structural damage and soil-liquefaction risks. Secretary Vince Dizon said the department ideally needed 5% to 6% of capital outlay for such work—roughly about 30 billion based on 460 billion—but had only 6 billion in 2026. He acknowledged that DPWH lacked the personnel and equipment to conduct studies for all 11,000 proposed 2027 projects and committed to seek additional funds and report on consultant accountability and procurement requirements. Lugrales also raised her district's reduction from about 1.7 billion to more or less 500 million after a 7.8 earthquake, and Dizon committed to having regional and district officials address rehabilitation of yellow- and red-tagged facilities. Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores raised a dangerous critical bridge whose delays cost around 147 million per day, and Dizon cited retrofit and replacement amounts, including 150,000,000 and unclear figures spoken as 150.20 26 and 600,000,020.27. Rep. Salvador Pleyto requested plans for retrofitting critical infrastructure and inspecting buildings for the West Valley Fault risk, and Dizon committed to submit the ongoing World Bank-funded NCR assessment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate resources, technical capacity, and accountability mechanisms for geotechnical studies and the rehabilitation or retrofitting of earthquake-damaged and critical bridges. It also sought commitments on completing bridge projects, assessing critical infrastructure, and reporting measurable resilience and rehabilitation plans.

topics.topic: National-road maintenance and post-construction asset preservation
topics.summary: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam questioned why the MVUC special road fund was no longer displayed as a standalone FY 2027 program and argued that embedding it in Asset Preservation reduced legislative visibility. DPWH Undersecretary Nick Conti and Secretary Vince Dizon said the amount was attributed to itemized Asset Preservation projects pursuant to the statutory limits on MVUC use and identified the 2027 amount as about 15 billion. DPWH undertook to furnish the committee with the relevant project lists, but the record did not resolve Ongwam's concerns about bridges, post-enactment disaggregation, or the legality of the presentation. Rep. Michael Pan raised right-of-way and routine and post-construction maintenance problems affecting national highways, particularly in Samar. The secretary committed to address post-construction maintenance and said national roads remained DPWH's primary mandate, while local-road concerns involving remote and island municipalities were left for continuing coordination with regional and district offices.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the motor vehicle users charge (MVUC) collections were properly and visibly appropriated for their statutory purposes, including roads, bridges, and drainage. Members also sought assurance that DPWH would adequately fund routine and post-construction maintenance of national highways while addressing right-of-way and local-road concerns in remote areas.

topics.topic: Transparency, contractor accountability, and anti-corruption controls
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked Secretary Vince Dizon to make DPWH project information, procurement records, financial data, monitoring results, contractor ratings, and complaints publicly accessible. Dizon said the Transparency Portal already covered completed and ongoing projects, bidding livestreams, satellite-based monitoring, and supporting documents for PLN 11,000 plus projects, and committed to quarterly reports. Rep. Chel Diokno pressed DPWH on the absence of a consolidated national flood-control plan, lifestyle checks, contractor disclosures, convergence-program reforms, and nature-based solutions; Dizon cited plans for all 18 major river basins, with 14 being updated, and a target of 2027 for completion. Rep. Renee Co asked about blacklisting, delayed master plans, and audits, and DPWH reported 12 blacklisted contractors and ongoing investigations. Eli San Fernando questioned Redicon and R2 Builders, including figures of 9,000,000,000 and 2,700,000,000 pesos, and raised an alleged worker-wage shortfall involving 60 pesos over an 85 pesos rate. The agency's response on that allegation was garbled, leaving that issue unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had effective transparency, disclosure, monitoring, auditing, and contractor-accountability mechanisms to protect public funds. Members also asked what information would be published, how anti-corruption controls were being implemented, and whether DPWH would act on questionable contracts, project quality, and worker-wage compliance.

topics.topic: Classroom construction, evacuation centers, and social-facility appropriations
topics.summary: A minority member questioned the specificity and allocation basis of regional appropriations for evacuation centers, PWD facilities, and senior-citizen facilities, citing 180,000,000, 5,000,000, and 20,000,000. The agency said evacuation-center sites and amounts were governed by a five-year plan and required coordination, validation, and implementability checks, while the Chair requested a district-by-district breakdown. Congressman Joseph Tan discussed project convergence, foreign-assisted projects, and a total DPWH amount of about 200 plus billion pesos, but the exchange did not produce a detailed accounting. Another member said only 30% of the FY2026 budget had been awarded and warned that the delay threatened the 6,000-classroom target. Secretary Vince Dizon corrected the reported classroom data and cited a 20,000,000,000 DPWH budget for 6,000 classrooms, while explaining that construction commonly began in the third quarter after validation and bidding. The Chair agreed to bring forward a proposal for clearer GAA line items and closer coordination or grouping of classroom funds with DepEd, leaving the broader accountability questions unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether FY2027 appropriations for evacuation centers, facilities for persons with disabilities and senior citizens, and classrooms were sufficiently specific, needs-based, and implementable. Members also questioned whether project-award delays and broad GAA line items were undermining accountability and the target to complete 6,000 classrooms.

topics.topic: Pedestrian, bicycle, sidewalk, and PWD infrastructure
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co pressed DPWH to prioritize pedestrians and cyclists, separate pedestrian projects from general rehabilitation, and provide wider sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and improved PWD facilities. DPWH cited a pedestrian-walkway expansion cost of about 6 billion, an original EDSA project cost of about 17 billion, EDSA pedestrian widths ranging from a minimum of 2.8 meters to as much as five meters, and a minimum bike-lane width of 1.5 meters. Co also cited a total DPWH budget of roughly 644 billion and a 510 million allocation for PWD, elderly, senior, and gender-responsive facilities, while the secretary said the PWD budget would increase three times from 170 million. Rep. Timothy Titan then asked for stronger anti-overloading enforcement, additional weighing facilities, multiyear bridge funding, and two more pedestrian overpasses along the Maharlika Highway. Secretary Vince Dizon committed to doing his best to enforce anti-overloading rules and suggested multiyear bridge appropriations from 2027 onward, but no definitive action on the overpass request was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's FY2027 program adequately funded pedestrianization, protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and facilities for persons with disabilities, and whether the agency would address unsafe bridges, overloaded trucks, and requested pedestrian overpasses. Members also pressed DPWH on applicable standards, enforcement, and multiyear infrastructure planning.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted, convergence, tourism-road, and special infrastructure projects
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno and another congresswoman pressed DPWH on convergence-program reforms, feasibility-study funding, and responsibility for tourism roads. DPWH said sector departments would identify and prioritize their own projects, while DPWH would participate in joint technical validation and implementation; it also said projects costing 1,000,000,000 and above required a feasibility study. The agency cited 130,000,000 in counterpart funding and 350,000,000 for the Southern Gate to Surigao feasibility study, while Rep. Tan referred to a total DPWH amount of 200 plus billion pesos. Rep. Tan also raised approval documents, foreign-assisted projects, project clustering, and figures that were partly garbled in the transcript. A Pampanga member separately urged progress on the Korea-assisted flood-control project's second part, while DPWH described dredging as a critical and regular maintenance activity. DPWH undertook to submit lists of major feasibility-study projects and ongoing Trip C projects, but the status of several foreign-assisted and Korea-assisted items remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH was restructuring convergence and special infrastructure programs, including which agencies would identify, validate, and implement sector-specific projects. Members also asked about feasibility-study requirements, foreign-assisted projects, project clustering, the total DPWH allocation, and the status of a Korea-assisted flood-control project.

topics.topic: Flood mitigation, drainage, and river-basin master-plan alignment
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented flood mitigation as a 2027 priority and said DPWH would shift toward basin-wide flood management, using major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans. He cited 83.84 billion in locally funded 2027 flood-mitigation projects and described ongoing dredging and desilting needs after more than twelve years without dredging major rivers. Representative Tobit Janko pressed for full publication of projects and allocations by legislative district, while Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula requested complete master-plan data and tables showing whether 2025–2027 projects aligned with those plans. DPWH's flood-mitigation director said the agency was updating plans for all 18 major river basins with catchment areas of 1,400 square kilometer and up, with climate-change updating every three years. Bivensio Dizon undertook to provide the requested alignment information and said a dredging and desilting plan was being prepared. A majority member also identified nationwide lump-sum items of 369,000,000 for dredging and waterway cleaning and 500,000,000 for drainage and flood-mitigation repairs, which DPWH said would be implemented based on need.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's flood-mitigation, drainage, dredging, and desilting projects were guided by current river-basin and local drainage master plans. It also sought the plans' status, the projects aligned with them, and how nationwide flood-mitigation lump-sum items would be allocated.

topics.topic: DPWH FY2027 budget and major program allocations
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented the proposed DPWH FY 2027 budget at 643,950,000,000, roughly about 20% higher than the prior budget. He identified roughly 200 billion for national roads and bridges and roughly about 118 billion for foreign-assisted projects. Flood mitigation figures included eighty three point eighty four billion for locally funded projects, 117 billion for foreign-assisted ongoing projects, and 19 billion for other foreign-assisted projects. The basic infrastructure components included about 105 billion for access roads and bridges, about 41 billion for multipurpose buildings, and smaller allocations for coastal roads and local ports. He also cited allocations for PWD and elderly infrastructure, disaster response, water supply, right-of-way, and general administration. A member requested presentation copies, and Dizon said detailed information would be provided through the committee materials and the National Expenditure Program.
topics.question: What was DPWH's proposed FY 2027 budget, and how was it allocated among national roads and bridges, foreign-assisted projects, flood mitigation, basic infrastructure, and support operations? The committee also sought access to the presentation materials so members could properly examine the proposed allocations.

topics.topic: Project rationalization and DPWH absorptive capacity
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon said DPWH had reduced project numbers by eliminating duplicate and overlapping projects, removing projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program, and focusing on larger projects that implementing offices could absorb. He said DPWH had previously reached about 25,000 projects, compared with a typical average of 20,000, and that some offices had carried two to four times their ideal workload. The agency also reported that its 2026 capital outlay involved about 460 billion, with 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded as of 08/23/2026, and targeted 80% awards by the end of September. Representative Mike Tan asked whether DPWH had conservatively estimated implementing-office capacity and requested rough capacity figures. Yusick Ador answered that the ideal was seven projects per PE and requested congressional support for additional engineers. Tan also sought support for ongoing convergence projects, but Dizon deferred the matter to Congress while citing executive policies.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether DPWH had rationalized its project portfolio to match the capacity of its implementing offices and whether the 2027 budget should prioritize projects that could realistically be delivered. It also examined the effect of delayed releases, early procurement, ongoing-project funding, and convergence-program reforms on DPWH’s implementation capacity.

topics.topic: District-level project and congressional-allocation transparency
topics.summary: Rep. Tobit Janko raised the need for full, nonselective transparency in DPWH infrastructure allocations and requested publication by region, legislative district, party-list representative, and line item. DPWH said its portal already carried roughly ten years of project records and supporting documents, but acknowledged that its existing summary followed district engineering offices rather than legislative districts. Bivensio Dizon committed to submit and publish the legislative-district NEP and supporting information, initially requested before the end of the meeting and later set by the chair for before 01:00. Rep. Janko also cited a flood-control example involving 900 million, 1 billion, and 100 million to show why phased project amounts should be disclosed. Dizon described multiyear appropriations as the policy direction for ongoing projects and agreed to follow the process for identifying congressional amendments or insertions. The chair clarified that the submission had to cover all legislative districts nationwide, but the transcript did not establish that delivery or publication had already occurred.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's proposed 2027 projects and allocations could be published by region and by legislative district, including party-list districts and project-level amounts. It also examined whether multiyear treatment and disclosure of congressional amendments would improve transparency and manage expectations for phased projects.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted projects, delays, and commitment fees
topics.summary: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula asked DPWH for the exact pipeline of foreign-assisted projects and for confirmation of commitment fees paid by taxpayers. Bivensio Dizon reported 50 priority ODA projects, of which seven were completed and 26 were under construction, with the remainder in feasibility study or detailed engineering. A committee member cited about 3,400,000,000 pesos in commitment fees reportedly paid in 2022 and requested data from 2022 to the present on delayed projects, unprogrammed appropriations and lender charges. The committee also asked whether penalties and other fees had resulted from delays. Dizon said most, if not all, of the projects were delayed, agreed that avoidable commitment fees should be avoided, and undertook to submit the requested data and project table. The matter remained pending the agency's submissions.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the exact pipeline of DPWH foreign-assisted or ODA projects, including their completion and implementation status. It also sought data on commitment fees, possible penalties and other charges arising from delays, including the reportedly paid 3,400,000,000 pesos in 2022.

topics.topic: Unfinished, ongoing, and delayed DPWH projects
topics.summary: The DPWH presenter attributed slow 2026 procurement to the late release of roughly 460 billion in capital-outlay projects and reported 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded out of 17,764 projects. DPWH targeted 80% awards by the end of September 2026. Ian Amatong pressed for stronger project-engineer oversight, rapid completion of a hospital, and a policy prioritizing unfinished roads and other ongoing works; Bivensio Dizon agreed but said staffing and DBM rules constrained DPWH. Dizon said the department would seek additional engineer items and a possible exemption for continuing projects, and would provide an update on the Quezon Bridge. Dadah Kiram Ismula requested data on 50 ODA projects, commitment fees, and possible penalties, citing around 3,400,000,000 pesos in fees; DPWH undertook to submit the information. Mike Tan then questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH reiterated the need for additional engineers and agreed to help identify unfinished projects. The issue landed with commitments for follow-up, while key policy and funding questions remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DPWH projects remained unfinished, delayed, or slow to be awarded and whether the department had sufficient implementation and supervisory capacity. Members also asked DPWH to prioritize ongoing works, complete hospitals and other unfinished projects, and account for delay-related commitment fees and other charges.

topics.topic: Road widening and national road-system priorities
topics.summary: Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan raised the proposed national road system, and Bivensio Dizon said DPWH was rationalizing widening toward the most dilapidated and priority sections. Libanan then pressed for a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, for which Dizon cited allocations of 120,000,000 and later 130,000,000, although the year-by-year breakdown was unclear. Dizon described the bridge as roughly 20 kilometers long, cited economic returns of 33% and 42%, and estimated six years for construction; he also committed to consider tourism in the evaluation. Representative Ian Amatong raised inadequate project-engineer coverage, citing an actual workload of one engineer for 30 projects against an ideal one-to-seven or one-to-10 ratio, and Dizon sought committee help for more DBM items. Amatong also sought faster hospital completion and prioritization of unfinished approach works, while Dizon agreed in principle and said DPWH would pursue a DBM exemption and prioritize ongoing projects. The chair additionally called for stronger preconstruction coordination, and Dizon agreed that such activities were critical.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH was prioritizing road widening within the proposed national road system and whether major inter-island links, particularly the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, were feasible and adequately funded. It also examined whether project oversight, hospital construction, unfinished works, and preconstruction coordination were sufficient to ensure that district infrastructure priorities were delivered.

topics.topic: Sorsogon–Northern Samar and other major bridge projects
topics.summary: Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan asked DPWH to establish the feasibility of the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, including its economic return, timetable, and financing. Bivensio Dizon said the project was a critical Luzon–Visayas link and cited 120,000,000, later correcting or supplementing the figure with 130,000,000 for the feasibility study. He described the link as roughly 20 kilometers, cited a 42% economic rate of return, identified ADB, Korea, JICA, and AIIB as possible funders, and estimated six years for construction after feasibility and approvals. The Chair required tourism benefits to be considered in the evaluation, and the Secretary agreed. Rep. Ian Amatong and Rep. Mike Tan separately raised concerns about project-engineer workloads, technical assignment, absorptive capacity, and unfinished or ongoing projects; DPWH acknowledged the constraints and sought additional engineer items and continued coordination with Congress and DBM. The bridge feasibility commitment advanced, but financing, final approvals, and implementation remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the feasibility, economic return, financing, timetable, and technical implementation arrangements for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge and other major bridge projects. Members also examined whether DPWH had enough project engineers and absorptive capacity to deliver technically demanding and ongoing bridge works.

topics.topic: School-building and basic-education facility allocations
topics.summary: A majority member asked DPWH to provide the 2025 and 2026 school-building allocations for Regions 3, 4A, and 5 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund. The member cited 595,000,000 and 261 classrooms for Region 3, 523,000,000 pesos I 48 and 297 classrooms for Region 4A, and 5 hundred seventy eight million and 280 completed classrooms for Region 5, with some accompanying figures unclear. Bivensio Dizon responded that DPWH had a 5,000-classroom catch-up target for 2026 using the 13,000,000,000 Basic Education Fund for 2025. He attributed the 2025 timing problem to an August 2025 DepEd-DPWH agreement and said classroom bidding could begin in October or November, while the 2026 process had started earlier in April and proceeded to procurement in August. He expected construction to start by September and occur in November or December. The transcript did not record a complete regional 2025-2026 breakdown or a formal follow-up submission, so the matter remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the budget intended for school-building construction in Regions 3, 4A, and 5 for 2025 and 2026 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund, which had been assigned to DPWH as implementing agency. It also sought clarification on DPWH's classroom catch-up target and the timing of the DepEd-DPWH procurement and construction process.
