topics.topic: Nationwide flood-control lump-sum items
topics.summary: A majority member raised the two nationwide flood-control lump-sum items and asked how they would be implemented. The member cited 369,000,000 for dredging and cleaning waterways and 500,000,000 for repair, rehabilitation, and maintenance of flood-mitigation structures in drainage systems. Bivensio Dizon answered that DPWH would implement the work based on need, deploy equipment, and support equipment operations. He also indicated that an undersecretary would assess conditions and prepare a dredging and desilting plan. The chair clarified that the allocation guide covered equipment operations, gasoline, crude oil, and personnel, and the secretary confirmed it. The issue landed with a commitment to develop a plan, while detailed prioritization and controls remained unspecified.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how two nationwide lump-sum flood-control appropriations would be implemented, prioritized, and controlled. It also sought clarification on whether DPWH would prepare a dredging and desilting plan and what operational costs the allocations would cover.

topics.topic: Asset preservation, road rehabilitation, and bridge maintenance
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented road-slip rehabilitation, drainage, safety barriers, aging bridges, flood mitigation, makeshift bridge replacement, and completion of unfinished buildings as asset-preservation priorities. He said many bridges were about 40 to 50 years old and that DPWH had often relied on savings because regular funding was insufficient. Rep. Ian Amatong challenged DPWH on absent project engineers and an unfinished hospital, while Dizon acknowledged workloads that could reach one engineer for 30 projects instead of the ideal one for seven. Dizon agreed that hospitals and other unfinished projects should be prioritized and said DPWH would seek DBM flexibility and additional engineering positions. Rep. Mike Tan then questioned absorptive capacity and project assignments; DPWH cited an expectation to award 80% of 2026 projects by the end of September and an ideal workload of seven projects per engineer. The exchanges ended with commitments to provide information, assist in identifying projects, and submit ongoing-project funding issues to Congress, without a final funding resolution.
topics.question: The committee was examining whether DPWH had sufficient funding, personnel, and implementation capacity to preserve existing roads and bridges, complete unfinished infrastructure, and address hospitals and other ongoing projects. Members also sought to establish whether project-engineer workloads, preconstruction coordination, and budget policies were contributing to delays or quality risks.

topics.topic: Project evaluation, geotagging, and right-of-way controls
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's stricter project-evaluation and documentation system. He said projects would require supporting documents, validated on-site geotagged photographs, and certificates covering implementability, right-of-way availability, duplicate-project checks, and specific locations. He also said DPWH would require BP two zero two compliance forms, although the transcript's wording was unclear. Dizon reported that many master plans were about ten or fifteen years old and cited rainfall assumptions associated with 2010, 2013, and 2015. He said DPWH would update outdated plans and seek development-council coordination or certificates of no objection from local government units. The segment ended with the reforms presented as transparency and project-readiness controls, without a recorded committee ruling or unresolved challenge.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish how DPWH would evaluate projects before inclusion in the budget, verify project locations and readiness, prevent duplicate funding, and address right-of-way and outdated master-plan risks. The presentation also set out what certifications and supporting documents implementing offices would be required to provide.

topics.topic: Contractor blacklisting and labor-standard compliance
topics.summary: Rep. Percy Sindania asked DPWH for an update on blacklisted contractors and suppliers and pressed whether labor violations should affect contractor eligibility. Bivensio Dizon said the preliminary figure was more than 10, clarified as between 10 to 15, and committed to provide the complete list through the committee. Sindania identified poor working conditions, occupational health and safety violations, and refusal to follow regional wage orders as labor violations that should support blacklisting. He also requested the list of projects awarded to Reddycon during the last three years. Dizon said DPWH would comply, but the final blacklist count and the formal status of labor standards as a blacklisting guideline remained unestablished.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how many contractors and suppliers had been blacklisted and whether labor-rights and labor-standard violations should be grounds for blacklisting. It also asked DPWH to submit records of projects awarded to Reddycon during the last three years.

topics.topic: Road, construction-site, and accessibility compliance
topics.summary: Rep. Percy Sindania questioned DPWH about blacklisted contractors, labor and occupational-safety violations, BP 344 compliance, PWD facilities, and road-crash prevention. Bivensio Dizon estimated that between 10 to 15 contractors or suppliers were blacklisted and committed to submit the complete list, as well as projects awarded to Reddycon in the last three years. Dizon candidly described historical accessibility compliance as poor, but said rehabilitation projects would widen sidewalks and meet accessibility standards, supported by about 100 million previously, 170 million last year, and 500 million this year. He and a DPWH safety official described stricter construction-site enforcement, project-engineer training, and an updated safety handbook. Sindania cited 13,125 road-crash deaths in 2023 and said 94% of commuters were at risk daily, while the agency undertook corrective and reporting measures. The chair was told that PWD structures had a separate funding line item, leaving implementation of the standards as the principal open issue.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH was funding and enforcing standards for road rehabilitation, bridge and construction-site safety, and accessibility under BP 344. Members also asked how many contractors had been blacklisted, whether labor violations could support blacklisting, and whether PWD facilities had dedicated funding.

topics.topic: Regional allocation equity and convergence priorities
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's effort to shift regional allocations toward a more needs-based distribution, reducing Luzon's historical share from about 56% to roughly 52%, while raising the Visayas share to 20% and placing Mindanao at about 28%. He acknowledged that the distribution was not yet fully equitable and invited Congress to consider further reallocations, particularly for high-poverty regions. Dizon also said DPWH had reduced projects from a typical average of about 20,000 and the 2024–2025 level of about 25,000 by removing duplicates, emphasizing larger projects, and eliminating projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program. Representative Mike Tan questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH answered that 80% of the 2026 program was expected to be awarded by the end of September; Yusick Ador gave an ideal capacity of seven projects per project engineer and requested help securing additional engineers. Tan later asked about ongoing convergence projects, including hospital and tourism-road works, and Dizon said their funding would be submitted to Congress subject to executive policies. The issue therefore produced agency commitments and explanations but left final reallocations and ongoing-project funding for congressional action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's regional allocations and convergence projects were distributed according to need and whether implementing offices had sufficient absorptive capacity. It also asked whether ongoing hospital, tourism-road, and related convergence projects would continue to receive funding despite the rationalization of responsibilities.

topics.topic: Hospital construction and interagency project coordination
topics.summary: Rep. Ian Amatong raised concerns about absent project engineers, a delayed hospital in his district, and the need to finish unfinished works before starting new projects. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged that engineers were handling workloads as high as one to thirty projects against an ideal one-to-seven ratio and sought additional DBM items. Dizon said hospitals often fell under DOH budgets and that DPWH would seek flexibility for continuing hospital projects, while the chair called for stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangays. Rep. Mike Tan then questioned DPWH's absorptive capacity, and Dizon projected 80% award of the 2026 program by the end of September. DPWH official Yusick Ador reiterated the ideal seven-project workload and requested more engineers. The agency agreed to help identify unfinished projects and said funding for ongoing convergence projects would be submitted to Congress, leaving DBM approvals and several project-specific matters open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate project-engineer and implementing-office capacity to supervise hospital, road, bridge, and other convergence projects. It also examined whether DPWH coordinated sufficiently with local governments and partner agencies before construction, and whether unfinished or ongoing projects should be prioritized and funded.

topics.topic: Project-engineer oversight and implementation accountability
topics.summary: Ian Amatong raised concerns about project engineers being absent during implementation and asked for stronger transparency, coordination, and accountability before project turnover. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged a structural staffing problem: about 75,000 employees supported a workload that could reach one engineer for thirty projects or more, compared with an ideal ratio of one to seven or one to ten. Amatong also pressed for completion of a hospital in his district within one year rather than four or five years; the transcript gave the hospital amount as "607,100,000,000,000 million," which was unclear. Vince said hospital funding arrangements involved DOH and DBM and offered to seek an exemption for continuing projects, while asking the committee to help persuade DBM. Amatong urged DPWH to prioritize unfinished works and requested exact information on the Quezon Bridge, with Vince undertaking to report back. The chair and secretary also supported stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials, barangay captains, and communities.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH would ensure that project engineers were present and accountable during implementation, and whether the department could improve coordination with local communities before construction. Members also pressed for faster completion and prioritization of unfinished and continuing projects.

topics.topic: AFP modernization funding, loans, and Horizon Three acquisitions
topics.summary: Secretary Teodoro said AFP modernization required an integrated package of equipment, infrastructure, logistics, secure networks, and support systems. Deputy Majority Leader Panaligan asked for the items charged to the 2026 modernization allocation of about 40 billion and the proposed 2027 allocation of about 50 billion, as well as the appropriate loan-ceiling policy; the Secretary favored retaining a cap controlled by DBM and DOF. The DND confirmed an intent to acquire additional frigates and said multirole fighters remained under consideration, but only as part of a broader force package. Members Poe and Patalbano pressed for a clearer drone-program update, and the DND said drones were funded through modernization but that detailed systems were classified and that control, connectivity, and integration were the immediate priorities. The DND cited about 40 billion for a complete Tagoloan dry dock and said U.S. support for Lumbia was still being scoped. The chair requested a prioritized formal letter identifying omitted capital-outlay and other institutional needs, and the DND committed to submit it within the week.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the AFP modernization program would be financed and implemented, including the items charged to the 2026 and 2027 modernization appropriations, the treatment of unprogrammed appropriations and loans, and the status of Horizon Three acquisitions. Members also asked how modernization funding would support drones, fighters, frigates, infrastructure, EDCA sites, and a proposed naval dry dock.

topics.topic: AFP modernization’s proposed 50,000,000,000 and prior 40,000,000,000
topics.summary: Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan asked DND to identify the items covered by about 40 billion for 2026 and the proposed 50 billion for 2027, and urged access to 50 billion in unprogrammed appropriations. The secretary's recorded response to the itemization request was unclear, and no detailed list was supplied in the exchange. Panaligan then raised his bill to revise or remove the PD 415 loan ceiling, while Secretary Gilbert Teodoro favored retaining a cap controlled by DBM and DOF. Teodoro said enacted US legislation could provide about 100 million in the following year, with a maximum of US500 million dollars per year subject to availability, and that Japan's assistance would also help. He confirmed an intent to acquire two more missile frigates but said the acquisition trigger had not been pulled, and said multirole fighters remained dependent on financing and supporting systems. The loan-ceiling question was committed to a technical working group, while the requested allocation documents and unprogrammed-funding access remained unanswered in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which AFP modernization items would be charged against the proposed 2027 allocation and the prior-year allocation, including whether unprogrammed appropriations could be accessed. It also examined whether the statutory ceiling on modernization loans should be retained, increased, or removed, and how external financing could support the program.

topics.topic: Modernization-loan ceiling and foreign defense assistance
topics.summary: Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan asked which items would be financed from the proposed PHP 50,000,000,000 2027 modernization allocation and requested the corresponding 2026 and 2027 itemization. He also proposed increasing or removing the USD 300,000,000 loan ceiling, while Secretary Gilbert Teodoro favored retaining a cap set by DBM and DOF according to fiscal capacity. Teodoro confirmed that a U.S. defense-capabilities measure had been enacted, with about 100,000,000 expected for the following year and a US500 million dollars annual maximum subject to Treasury availability. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez then asked about Lumbia, where DND reported 115,000,000 remaining for the current year, no U.S. counterpart funding yet, and no agreed U.S.-built structure because assistance was still being scoped. Teodoro estimated the proposed Tagoloan dry dock at about 40,000,000,000 including equipment, but said titling had to be completed before construction could proceed. The loan issue and modernization documents required further action, while Lumbia assistance and the construction timetable remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which AFP modernization items would be funded under the proposed 2027 allocation and whether DND preferred retaining, increasing, or removing the statutory modernization-loan ceiling. It also examined how foreign military financing and U.S. assistance would support modernization-related facilities, including Lumbia and the proposed Tagoloan dry dock.

topics.topic: AFP earmarked revenues, BCDA shares, and DND off-budget balances
topics.summary: Roberto Nazal Jr. raised whether about 10.285 billion in accumulated BCDA earmarked revenues and about 4.029 billion in DND off-budget balances were available before Congress provided additional funding. He asked whether the balances reflected insufficient AFP requests, DBM non-approval, deliberate conservation, or legal and regulatory restrictions. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro answered that the BCDA funds were matched to existing programs and contracts and were pledged for payments, while the off-budget funds were held in the BTR and were not earning interest. He identified ongoing projects, including the Lumbia Airbase runway, and said trust-receipt items had to be remitted to DBM before disbursement. He also stated that the resources and interest receipts were considered in the AFP submissions used to prepare the FY 2027 request. The committee requested lists of the pledged and ongoing projects, with the Chair directing the department to provide the information.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether AFP earmarked revenues and DND off-budget balances were genuinely available for additional programs or were already committed, legally restricted, or unused because of agency or DBM action. It also asked whether these resources had been considered in preparing the FY 2027 budget request.

topics.topic: Defense self-reliance, Government Arsenal cuts, and ammunition production
topics.summary: Eli San Fernando asked Secretary Gilbert Teodoro to define self-reliance and explain the Government Arsenal's roughly 21.8% budget reduction. The Secretary defined self-reliance as securing supply chains quickly and cost-effectively, rather than achieving complete domestic production. He said the Arsenal had produced 60 million rounds but was being redirected toward more advanced capabilities, while the member highlighted a 2026 target of 60 million rounds against actual output of 500,000. The Secretary attributed the shortfall to a worldwide shortage of nitrocellulose precursors and said the materials could come from a small number of foreign sources. San Fernando argued that industrial policy was essential for defense resilience, and the Secretary agreed. Representative Jay Vernego separately asked about reducing imported-arms dependence, local manufacturing, LBIT Systems procurement, and drone guidelines; the Secretary said there were no new LBIT contracts, local industry remained focused on small arms, and drone guidelines could be shared in non-sensitive form. The issue remained substantively unresolved on restoring Arsenal funding or closing the production gap, although the agency committed to support industrial policy and provide or report additional information.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what the Department of National Defense meant by a self-reliant defense force, whether the Government Arsenal's reduced budget and low ammunition output undermined that goal, and what role local industry and industrial policy should play. Members also asked how foreign procurement, technology transfer, local arms and drone production, and operational guidelines fit within that policy.

topics.topic: Local defense-industry procurement and technology transfer
topics.summary: Johanne Monich Bautista asked DND about uniform and fabric allocations and compliance with the Philippine Tropical Fabrics Law, including the cited 5% Philippine-fabric requirement. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro identified 162,000 for uniformed personnel but said the aggregated clothing figure and projected compliant-fabric spending were not yet available, citing safety, fireproofing, and supply-chain constraints. Bautista then asked about 2027 spending under the Self-Reliant Defense Posture Law, and Teodoro said there would be none because the law lacked equity, risk capital, research and development, and meaningful intellectual-property rights. Rep. Elijah San Fernando questioned the meaning of self-reliance, the 21.8% Government Arsenal budget reduction, and the gap between a 60,000,000 ammunition target and 500,000 actual output; DND attributed the output gap to a worldwide precursor shortage and endorsed industrial policy in principle. Rep. Vernego asked about Elbit Systems procurement, local arms production, drones, and written operational guidelines; Teodoro said only missile replenishment was planned, local industry was not yet suited to DND's priority capabilities, and drone guidelines could be disclosed subject to protecting sensitive system details. The discussion ended with information and document-related commitments, while several policy and implementation issues remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DND's uniform and defense procurement would comply with Philippine-made fabric requirements and strengthen local suppliers, manufacturing, maintenance, and technology transfer. Members also examined the meaning of self-reliance, the Government Arsenal's reduced budget and output, local arms production, and guidelines for drone procurement and use.

topics.topic: West Philippine Sea operations and maritime-security capability
topics.summary: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro framed the West Philippine Sea as the immediate focus of a broader maritime domain of about 2.4 million square kilometers and described the need for naval, Coast Guard, infrastructure, logistics, and technically trained personnel. A minority member asked about hazard pay for civilian personnel deployed in the West Philippine Sea, and Teodoro supported it while acknowledging unresolved issues concerning implementation and other benefits. The minority member also questioned alleged Chinese recruitment and influence operations; the Secretary said there were grounds for suspicion but that evidentiary determinations belonged largely to law-enforcement and financial authorities. The member manifested support for an increased West Philippine Sea budget, but no specific increase was recorded. Representative Egay Risa obtained the DND's position that EDCA and Philippine territory could be used only consistently with Philippine law, the Constitution, presidential guidance, and defensive treaty circumstances. Representative Rufus Rodriguez raised evacuation-center criteria and Eastern Seaboard surveillance and naval-basing needs; the agency undertook to provide an update on the proposed base, while the site criteria and funding questions remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DND was funding and strengthening operations in the West Philippine Sea and other maritime domains, including surveillance, patrols, Pag-asa Island services, and personnel capability. It also examined the legal and operational limits of the Mutual Defense Treaty, EDCA sites, and DND-supervised facilities in relation to China-related security concerns.

topics.topic: EDCA, U.S. facilities, and defense-cooperation infrastructure
topics.summary: Representative Egay Risa questioned Secretary Gilbert Teodoro on what would trigger the Mutual Defense Treaty and whether EDCA sites could be used in a Taiwan conflict or for offensive missile operations. Teodoro answered that treaty activation required a government call after an attack and that EDCA sites could not be used offensively unless the Philippines was under attack or threat, subject to the Constitution and Philippine law. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez asked about Lumbia's budget and U.S. counterpart funding; DND cited about 115 million for the current-year remaining amount, while the reference to 450 million for the following year was unclear, and it said no U.S. counterpart contribution had yet been agreed. DND said Lumbia development was delayed by right-of-way and informal-settlement issues and that U.S. officials were still scoping a possible warehouse. The proposed Tagoloan dry dock was estimated at about 40 billion including equipment, but titling and a construction timetable remained pending. Congressman Antonio Tinio warned that dual-use U.S. facilities and critical infrastructure could become targets and expose the Philippines to supply-chain risks, while Teodoro defended broader partnerships and resilient domestic supply chains as necessary for deterrence.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and operational limits of the Mutual Defense Treaty and EDCA, including whether U.S. forces could use Philippine territory for offensive operations. It also examined the Philippine and U.S. contributions to EDCA-related infrastructure, the status and cost of planned facilities, and the security and supply-chain risks associated with expanded defense cooperation.

topics.topic: Drones and unmanned systems for the AFP
topics.summary: Brian Poe asked whether the Philippine Air Force and Navy budgets contained specific drone-procurement line items and whether modernization planning was preparing for rapidly changing drone technology. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro answered that drones were covered by the modernization fund, while specific systems were classified, and emphasized integration, secure connectivity, and operational control rather than hardware alone. Poe cited an approximate 70 million cost for one F-16 and compared it with about 2,000 Shahed-class drones. Rep. Vernego then asked about local drone production and written operational guidelines; Teodoro said drone production was relatively easy, but payload technology and AI-related systems were the critical elements, and that current use was for surveillance. Vernego requested guideline and program updates, with Teodoro indicating that disclosable material could be provided without compromising sensitive details. Tony Patalbano separately requested a status report on the drone program, and Teodoro said the DND was building its framework and backbone and developing control systems.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether drone procurement was specifically funded in the FY 2027 DND or service budgets, how drones were treated under the AFP modernization program, and whether the AFP had the personnel, network, control systems, and guidelines needed to use them responsibly. Members also sought an update on the drone program and related reporting to the committee.

topics.topic: Veterans’ pensions, health care, and retirement support
topics.summary: Representative Erline Ayon raised concerns about whether the budget adequately protected veterans’ pensions, benefits, health care, and retirement support, especially for elderly and medically vulnerable veterans. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said pension increases should be decoupled from active-duty salaries and reported a compromise providing 5% increases for three years, or 15% by 2028. He also cited 71,000,000,000 for AFP retirees and JPY 11,000,000,000 for veterans ameliorations in the special-purpose-fund breakdown. The Department described valor clinics, preventive care, mental-health and geriatric programs, and Veterans Memorial Medical Center improvements; it said the center had treated 11,100 inpatients but could accommodate only about nine percent of veterans. Teodoro committed to pursuing a first hospice by the end of the year and assured the committee that the Department would fight for veterans’ benefits. Pension reform, including separate treatment for AFP retirees, was not settled and remained subject to further study.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget adequately protected veterans’ pensions, health care, retirement support, and related welfare programs. It also asked how Congress and the Department of National Defense could ensure that elderly and medically vulnerable veterans would not be left without benefits or care.

topics.topic: MUP pension reform and contribution-based financing
topics.summary: Antonio Tinio raised the increase in the MUP pension budget from about 68.6 billion in 2015 to about 154 billion in the proposed 2027 budget and asked about a contribution-based reform. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said the reform required decisions on when it would begin and who would be covered, with the armed forces separated from civilian agencies. He said LGUs might fairly share the pension burden for locally oriented services such as the police, but that the fiscal and actuarial effects needed study. The secretary said the department was open to requiring greater contributions and to proposals easing the national government's burden. He also said a system could be designed to mature gradually before pension drawdown. The issue landed with further study and no definitive contribution or LGU-sharing arrangement.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed MUP pension reform would shift from government-subsidized pensions toward contributions, including when the system would begin and who would be covered. It also asked whether LGUs would share responsibility for the pension burden of civilian uniformed personnel, particularly the police.

topics.topic: Disaster-response assets, OCD capacity, and evacuation centers
topics.summary: DND said disaster response required larger airlift platforms, distributed logistics centers, prepositioned supplies, and stronger OCD coordination; it cited about 46 Black Hawk helicopters but said that capacity was insufficient. Representative Poe questioned OCD's 0.96% capital-outlay reduction from a budget of 2,500,000,000, and Secretary Teodoro said the reduction affected capital outlay and that OCD needed relocation from crowded Camp Aguinaldo. Representative Rufus Rodriguez asked for 2027 Ligtas Pinoy sites and selection criteria; the response referred to DNR hazard mapping but did not clearly identify the sites, while the transcript gave inconsistent figures of 60,000,000, 34 centers, and 90,000,000 per center. Members raised delays in rescue and relief processing, the need for Navy dredgers, insufficiently detailed Negros rehabilitation plans, and climate-flooded roads in Central Luzon. Secretary Teodoro committed to national-level coordination, an OCD anticipation deliverable, a revised earthquake-impact study process, and infrastructure referrals, while Representative Salvador cited delivery of 1,200 family packs and supported the FY 2027 DND budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DND and OCD had sufficient assets, logistics, evacuation facilities, communications, and coordination systems for disaster response, including prepositioning and response to flooding and a major earthquake. Members also asked how the 2027 evacuation-center program would select sites and whether OCD's reduced capital outlay would impair operations.

topics.topic: DND-DPWH military infrastructure and unfinished projects
topics.summary: Representative Sara Hirado questioned Secretary Gilbert Teodoro about the DND-DPWH infrastructure program and projects that remained unfinished or unusable. Teodoro said DND had received 100% of released amounts but that funding was insufficient, citing 27 non-implementable and 51 implementable projects out of 78. Hirado cited an earlier report of 648 completed out of 944 projects and a figure of 15,000,000,000 pesos for uncompleted, idle, and unusable infrastructure, but the discrepancy was not clearly resolved. Teodoro also said reduced capital outlays threatened modernization support and delayed rehabilitation of the 70-year-old DND and Legacy buildings. The chair requested a formal prioritized list of omitted or reduced projects, and Teodoro committed to submit it within the week. The committee indicated that restoration would be considered during the budget amendment process.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status of the DND-DPWH military infrastructure program, particularly projects that remained unfinished or unusable, the accountability measures taken, and the funding needed to complete or rehabilitate them. It also sought to determine whether reduced capital outlays had omitted critical infrastructure support for modernization projects.

topics.topic: Naval bases, dry docks, and strategic military facilities
topics.summary: Members examined AFP modernization allocations, naval frigate plans, base logistics, and the development of Lumbia and Tagoloan facilities. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said the proposed 2027 modernization allocation was tied to fiscal capacity, confirmed an intent to acquire additional frigates, and emphasized that infrastructure was necessary to make advanced equipment useful. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez was told that Lumbia had about 115 million remaining for the current year and a 450 million amount cited for the next year, while no U.S. EDCA counterpart had yet been agreed. DND estimated the proposed complete Tagoloan dry dock at about 40 billion, including equipment, but said titling had to be completed and Sangley was becoming unusable for naval maneuvering. Anna York Bondoc requested Navy dredgers for silted ports, and the secretary agreed that dredging was needed and said one dredger was in the pipeline. Antonio Tinio's security questions about the Sangley-area Chinese-linked company were answered with references to environmental and enforcement actions, but the Navy's need for a dedicated dry dock remained.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DND and the AFP would prioritize modernization, naval-base and dry-dock development, and related logistics facilities within fiscal constraints. Members also asked whether proposed sites were legally, operationally, and securely ready, and what documents or follow-up actions the agency would provide.

topics.topic: FY 2027 DND budget restorations and institutional amendments
topics.summary: DND presented a proposed budget of about 324.6 billion and identified reduced capital outlay as the principal immediate restoration concern. The agency said the capital-outlay proposal was 239,000,000 and that reductions could delay infrastructure supporting modernization equipment and the restoration of the DND's 70-year-old legacy building. The agency also cited a 50,000,000,000 modernization fund, a 98 or 99% troop-strength fill-up rate, and 10 modernization projects, but no restoration amount was approved. The committee chair asked for a formal and prioritized list of critical programs omitted from the NEP for consideration in the H-GAP. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro committed to submit the list within the week, while the chair committed to have the requests reviewed line by line by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee. Representatives Isidro Ungab and Salvador expressed support for the DND and AFP budgets, with Ungab separately requesting a brief district-related meeting.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which DND and AFP programs or projects had been reduced or omitted from the NEP and should be restored through institutional amendments. It also sought a prioritized, formal list from the agency so the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee could evaluate the requests line by line.

topics.topic: COA FY2027 budget and omitted priority requests
topics.summary: COA presented a FY2027 NEP budget of about 16.46 billion, with no capital outlay, while identifying substantial omitted requests for technology, citizen participatory audit, furniture, vehicles, and pre-audit staffing. Members questioned whether the allocation matched the government’s anti-corruption priority, citing the proposed 107 billion flood-control budget and COA’s reported PHP158 billion in DPWH notices. COA said it had proposed 146 additional pre-audit teams at an estimated 2.5 billion and explained that DBM had excluded several Tier 2 and capital-outlay items. Members also pressed COA on using its existing authority for pre-audit, expanding citizen participatory audit, and supporting a draft bill. Rep. Dumogan moved to seek an augmentation, and the committee requested detailed capital-outlay, omitted-item, and audit-report submissions. The issue landed with possible budget amendments still pending, but with COA commitments to submit the requested documents and add pre-audit personnel funding to its wish list.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish COA’s FY2027 funding level, including which Tier 2, capital outlay, staffing, pre-audit, technology, and citizen-participatory-audit requests were omitted. It also examined whether COA could expand pre-audit and anti-corruption work under its existing authority and what documents COA would submit to support possible budget amendments.

topics.topic: COA capital outlay zeroed out in the FY2027 NEP
topics.summary: COA reported that its FY2027 capital outlay proposal had been excluded from the NEP, leaving the agency with no capital outlay despite requests for ICT, facilities, equipment, vehicles, and related investments. Members argued that the omission was inconsistent with the government's anti-corruption priority and pressed COA on pre-audit capacity, including 146 additional teams and an unclear estimate of around 2,500,000,000. COA explained that DBM set the relevant ceiling, that the omitted items were submitted as Tier Two requests, and that the ISSP had been reviewed by DICT and endorsed to DBM. COA identified a capital outlay request of R656.528 million, including PHP525.405 million for ICT and PHP125.523 million for furniture and fixtures, while other wish-list figures were also cited. Rep. Dumogan moved to seek augmentation, including for pre-audit personnel. The Committee on Operations requested detailed capital outlay and institutional-amendment documents, and COA agreed to submit them, leaving funding itself unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why COA's capital outlay request was omitted from the FY2027 NEP, what investments and capabilities were affected, and whether COA had alternative authority or budget mechanisms to implement pre-audit and other anti-corruption functions. It also sought to determine what additional funding, personnel, and supporting documents should be considered through institutional amendments.

topics.topic: Funding 146 pre-audit teams with personnel and geotagging
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Sindania and Rep. Mauricio Domogan raised the need for personnel, technology, geotagging, and funding to expand COA's pre-audit capacity. COA said it needed 146 additional pre-audit teams and gave estimates ranging from more or less around 2,500,000,000 to around 2,200,000,000, while citing DPWH notices totaling 158,000,000,000. Rep. Iris Marie Montes pressed COA on its existing constitutional and statutory authority to conduct pre-audit without waiting for legislation, and COA agreed that it could do so but said the bill would strengthen the mandate. Rep. Salvador Pleyto called for continued congressional support for COA's technical manpower and systems. Rep. Mauricio Domogan later noted that COA's listed augmentation did not include pre-audit personnel, after which COA undertook to add the requirement to its wish list and Dumogan moved for budget augmentation. The transcript recorded no final ruling or approved augmentation amount.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA had sufficient personnel, technology, and budget authority to create and operate 146 additional pre-audit teams, including geotagging or geomapping of infrastructure projects. Members also asked whether COA could use its existing authority and budget mechanisms to begin pre-audit and whether additional funding and personnel would be requested.

topics.topic: COA staffing losses and restored plantilla positions
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Sindania raised COA’s staffing losses and asked about the agency’s capacity to audit potentially anomalous infrastructure projects. COA said about 716 plantilla positions had been deducted from its original plantilla, of which 332 were restored through DBM action, leaving almost 400 positions still unfilled or unrestored; the transcript’s spoken subtraction was unclear. COA attributed auditor attrition to higher pay elsewhere, residence proximity, flexible work arrangements, transfers, resignations, and optional retirement at age 60. The agency said it needed 146 additional pre-audit teams and estimated the requirement at about 2.2 billion, while an earlier estimate was rendered as “2,500,000,000 statistics.” Rep. Mauricio Domogan supported mandatory pre-audit with geotagging and said members would support a budget motion for additional personnel. COA undertook to resubmit its estimate, but the final funding decision and requested progress report were not shown.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent and causes of COA’s staffing losses, how many plantilla positions had been restored, and whether COA had sufficient personnel and funding for expanded pre-audit and geotagging work. Members also sought the budget needed to establish 146 additional pre-audit teams and the operational value of that investment.

topics.topic: DPWH flood-control project audits and notices
topics.summary: Rep. Sindania, Rep. de Morgan, Rep. Renee Co, and the Operations chair pressed COA on DPWH flood-control audits, pre-audit capacity, geotagging, audit notices, and resources. COA reported around 50 fraud-audited transactions or projects and cited DPWH notices of suspension of about 107.8 billion and notices of disallowance or charge of roughly 51.3 billion, with totals also stated as 158 billion. COA said 146 additional pre-audit teams would cost about 2.2 billion to 2.5 billion, while members supported additional resources and pre-audit linked to geotagging. Rep. Co requested a year-specific breakdown of DPWH and flood-control notices, because the issuance year did not necessarily match the year of the underlying transaction. COA undertook to submit flood-control audit materials, a master plan and compliance records, and the requested DPWH reports. The committee also requested detailed capital-outlay and audit-report submissions after noting that COA's capital-outlay proposal had been zeroed out, so the issue remained committed for follow-up rather than finally resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish COA's audit findings and enforcement actions involving DPWH, particularly flood-control projects, and whether COA had the personnel, technology, and capital resources to conduct more effective pre-audits and geotagging. Members also sought specific records on notices of suspension, disallowance, and charge, including figures attributable to flood-control projects.

topics.topic: Safeguards against manufactured savings and withheld SAROs
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned COA on whether earmarked funds remained traceable after Treasury used cash under the one-fund concept. COA said it monitored the funds, followed the money trail after release, and would flag expenditures outside the authorized purpose; DBM had also committed to place information on its portal. Nazal then raised DPWH projects that had SAROs, bidding, and validation under NDC five ninety five but allegedly lacked SAAs, asking why they were withheld and could later become manufactured savings. COA cited missing supporting documents and prior reversions caused by implementing-office unreadiness, agreed to submit a project list, and undertook to coordinate with DPWH. Nazal warned that withholding Congress-approved projects and augmenting other items with the resulting savings could let the executive rewrite the GAA. In the second round, COA agreed with the concern and promised to confirm reportedly ready projects with the DPWH central office, but no concrete safeguard was finalized.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA tracked earmarked funds after Treasury received them and whether cash fungibility could obscure their use. It also sought to determine why DPWH withheld or reverted Congress-approved projects, and what safeguards prevented implementable projects from being converted into manufactured savings and used for augmentation.

topics.topic: Tracking earmarked and off-budget funds under cash fungibility
topics.summary: Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether COA could track earmarked and off-budget funds while Treasury treated cash as fungible. COA said it monitored earmarked funds, had a latest report as of May 2026, and would flag use outside the authorized purpose, but described Treasury and DBM cash management as executive functions. The member cited DICT’s reported budget of about 25 billion or 26 billion and questioned why government systems lacked cloud capacity. The discussion also examined DPWH projects whose funds or SAAs were withheld or reverted; DPWH’s COA representative attributed some delays to missing supporting documents and unready regional or district offices. Nazal further asked whether such delays could manufacture savings and allow the Executive to rewrite the GAA, and COA agreed with his observations. On off-budget accounts, COA said deposits in authorized government depository banks were controlled by the collecting agency, earned interest for the agency in principle, and could not legally be used for another purpose without complications. COA committed to develop a protocol for monitoring balances and movements and to coordinate with DBM and the Bureau of the Treasury.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA tracked earmarked and off-budget fund balances and the movement of related cash even when Treasury treated the cash as fungible. It also examined whether agencies could delay congressionally appropriated projects, generate savings, or use off-budget funds for purposes other than those authorized by law.

topics.topic: Citizen Participatory Audit funding and implementation
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes argued that COA could conduct pre-audits under its existing authority and should budget for that function, while COA said most of its budget was already devoted to personal services and that some Tier 2 requests had been omitted. COA described the Citizen Participatory Audit as a small-scale, voluntary program in which trained citizens, NGOs, and civil society organizations joined audit teams, distinct from ordinary complaints routed through the complaints desk. COA identified an omitted Citizen Participatory Audit request of about 734,000 in one statement and R40.734 million in another, with the discrepancy preserved in the figures. Rep. Salvador Pleyto asked how citizen reports, evidence, inspections, and feedback became part of formal audits and whether COA needed additional technical personnel. Rep. Mauricio Domogan noted that the augmentation list did not include personnel for pre-audit and moved to seek an increase in COA's budget. COA committed to include the chair's recommended pre-audit amount in its wish list, but the motion's final disposition was not shown.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how COA could use its existing authority and budget mechanisms to conduct or expand pre-audits and Citizen Participatory Audits. Members also asked how citizens could report anomalies, participate in formal audits, and whether COA had sufficient personnel and funding to support these functions.

topics.topic: Digital audit systems, records management, and technical capacity
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes pressed COA to use its existing authority for pre-audit and to seek appropriate budget mechanisms, while COA explained that DBM controlled the budget ceiling and that almost 92% of its budget was for personal services. Rep. Ramil Hernandez asked about records digitization, and COA said it was required to retain documents for ten years and faced physical-storage constraints. Rep. Salvador Pleyto asked how citizens could participate in audits, and COA described a formal, trained, voluntary program involving NGOs, CSOs, and private citizens, separate from ordinary complaints. The Committee on Operations chair then questioned why COA's capital outlay was zeroed out despite a proposal stated as 1.171180000000 and a broader request of 1,180,000,000. COA described its DICT-endorsed five-year ICT roadmap and listed proposed buildings, records storage, vehicles, electrical works, and ICT equipment. The chair requested detailed capital-outlay and omitted-item lists and previous audit reports, and COA committed to submit or resend them, but no higher budget was promised.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA was using its existing authority and budget mechanisms to strengthen pre-audit, digitize and securely retain records, and obtain the ICT, capital outlay, and technical manpower needed for modern auditing. It also sought details on COA's capital outlay proposal and audit-report submissions so Congress could assess possible budget amendments.

topics.topic: Annual audit-report delays, publication, and congressional use
topics.summary: Members Iris Marie Montes and other committee officials focused on whether COA's annual audit reports were available in time for congressional oversight. COA said reports were transmitted by June 30, agencies had sixty days to submit management actions, and publication on the website was due by October 31. COA maintained that it was on time and said it provided reports to Congress and other oversight bodies, while incomplete financial statements and publication protocols could create bottlenecks. Montes questioned whether the process was substantive transparency or merely ARTA compliance and urged earlier, more useful reports. The Committee on Operations also questioned why COA's capital-outlay proposal of 1.171180000000, including an ICT request of 1,180,000,000, had been zeroed out and requested detailed capital and audit-report submissions. COA committed to resend the requested reports and materials, including the following morning.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA's annual audit reports were being completed, transmitted, and published within the applicable deadlines, and whether Congress received them in time and in a usable form for budget oversight. Members also asked what caused publication bottlenecks and requested reports and budget details to strengthen congressional review.

topics.topic: Fraud audits, contractor monopolies, and audit referrals
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Sindania asked how COA was detecting fraud, retaining auditors, and overseeing flood-control projects, including license-renting and contractor monopolies. COA cited around 50 fraud-audited transactions, referrals to the Ombudsman and ICI, data analytics, geotagging, continuous audit, and a proposed 146 additional pre-audit teams costing around 2.5 billion. COA also reported DPWH notices of suspension of PHP107.771 billion, notices of disallowance of PHP51.27 billion, and a combined amount stated as PHP158 billion. Roman Romulo questioned COA's budget, omitted capital-outlay and technology requests, referral procedures, and position on a draft bill; COA described its audit observation, suspension, disallowance, and Ombudsman-referral process and committed to submit a supporting position paper. Rep. Renee Co requested detailed DPWH and flood-control notices and records, including a flood-control master plan and prior audits, and later requested confidential-fund records from 2015 onward. COA committed to submit or compile the requested materials, but the records and reports were not delivered in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA had sufficient audit capacity and authority to detect fraud, oversee flood-control and other DPWH projects, address license-renting and contractor monopolies, and refer cases for accountability. Members also asked what audit notices had been issued, what records COA could submit, and how COA viewed proposed changes to audit and confidential-fund rules.

topics.topic: Confidential and intelligence fund audit oversight
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co asked COA for notices of suspension, disallowance, and charge involving confidential and intelligence funds since 2015, including the related expenses and AOMs. COA said the immediately available records covered 2021 to the present and included 3,016 AOMs, with another notice-of-suspension figure stated unclearly as '92 and end is '22.' COA undertook to compile records from 2015 onward and submit the requested information through the committee. The exchange also covered the joint circular's operational exceptions and the need to review acknowledgment receipts, identity and recommendation requirements, evidence of success, procurement, audit scope, security clearances, and coordination with spending units. The matter was not fully resolved during the hearing and remained subject to COA's submissions and interagency coordination.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what notices of suspension, disallowance, and charge COA had issued against confidential and intelligence fund expenditures since 2015. It also asked whether COA's existing audit rules adequately addressed the special reporting, procurement, evidence, audit-scope, and security-clearance issues associated with these funds.

topics.topic: FY2027 DHSUD budget, funding gaps, and proposed increases
topics.summary: The committee examined a FY2027 DHSUD-and-attached-agency allocation of about 5.5 billion against an aggregate agency proposal of about 60 billion. DHSUD said the funding gap would constrain its planning, housing production, emergency assistance, and community mortgage programs, and requested additional amounts including about 280 million for DHSUD, about 47.5 million for HSAC, and substantial increases for NHA and SHFC. Members generally supported higher housing appropriations, with motions and manifestations from Representatives Co-Pilar, Gonzales, Roman Romulo, Catulpos, and Vice Chair Rodriguez. The committee also raised the use of NHA unobligated funds, submerged Bacolor settlement sites, permitting delays, and whether calamity assistance could continue under the proposed allocation. DHSUD and its agencies provided answers and undertook to submit documents or proposals, including a prioritized list of additional requests. No final budget increase was approved in the recorded proceedings; consideration was left for the budget amendments process and plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to determine whether DHSUD and its attached agencies had sufficient FY2027 funding to address housing needs, continue ongoing programs, and respond to calamities. It also examined which proposed increases should be prioritized and what administrative or interagency actions were needed to accelerate housing delivery.

topics.topic: Additional budget requests and priority items for housing backlog
topics.summary: DHSUD Secretary Jose Ramon P. Aliling presented additional requests for the department and its attached agencies to address housing-sector priorities and the backlog. The requests included about 280 million for DHSUD, roughly 47.5 million for HSAC, about 1.62 billion for NHA, 2 billion for SHFC in the initial presentation, and about 8.08 billion for NHMFC. The committee chair cited a 3,600,000 housing backlog and discussed progress involving 1,300,000, although the context was unclear. Chair Mika then asked DHSUD to rank its top priorities, and the agency identified the 280,000,000 DHSUD request first, the 47,500,000 HSAC request second, and SHFC's community mortgage program third. The chair cited SHFC figures of 4,600,000,000 and 4,660,000,000, which were both retained because the transcript states both. DHSUD agreed to submit a written ranking and a breakdown showing which components could be partially funded.
topics.question: The committee sought to determine which DHSUD and attached-agency housing priorities were unfunded or underfunded and should receive additional fiscal space. It also asked DHSUD to rank those requests and identify which items could be partially funded if the full amounts were unavailable.

topics.topic: 4PH housing delivery, production targets, and interest subsidies
topics.summary: Chair Julian Jambaronda and Representative Sarah Elago pressed DHSUD and its shelter agencies on expanded 4PH eligibility, modalities, amortization, construction, takeouts, developer participation, and interest-subsidy validation. DHSUD cited 588,757 completed direct and indirect units or assistance, 544,000 still to be undertaken, and a 1,133,000 administration target, while stating that private-sector production was needed to address the 3,700,000 backlog. Officials described rental amounts below 1,500 pesos, a 3% socialized-housing interest rate, approximately 100,000 units of inventory, 30,000 approved-loan takeouts, and almost 130,000 expanded 4PH inventory units. Ilago also cited 66,700,000 pesos in 2025 interest and non-interest subsidy payments and sought independent validation. DHSUD said it was still waiting for DBM SAROs for IDSAP and EHAP, prompting a written-explanation request and a separate request for NHA's bank and developer lists. Howard Guintu later established that NHA had requested 1,000,000,000 for EHAP and 500,000,000 million million for the quick-response fund, while Pag-IBIG expected 15,000 takeouts against coverage of 33,000 units. The issues were not fully resolved, but follow-up submissions and committee consideration of additional funding were undertaken.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the expanded 4PH program was delivering eligible, affordable, and completed housing units at the required scale, and whether its financing and interest-subsidy mechanisms were adequate. It also examined delayed shelter funds, NHA production and facilities funding, developer performance, and the documents needed to validate implementation.

topics.topic: Emergency and disaster shelter assistance, including IDSAP, EHAP, and quick-response funds
topics.summary: Sarah Elago raised delays in IDSAP and EHAP, and NHA said it was still waiting for DBM SAROs. DBM explained that the EHAP request had been submitted to the Office of the President and remained in process. Howard Guintu established that NHA had requested about 1 billion for EHAP and 500 million for the quick-response fund for FY2027. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez supported 1.6 billion for NHA integrated housing and an additional 1 billion for EHAP, while citing NHA fire assistance of 20,000 for total damage and 10,000 for partial damage. Maria Isabel Gavaria asked how indigent families with fire-damaged homes could receive assistance, and DHSUD identified IDSAP, EHAP, construction materials, repair kits, and LGU modular houses. The committee requested written and supporting documents, supported budget increases, and left the delayed releases and final funding outcome for further action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why emergency and disaster shelter assistance, including IDSAP and EHAP, had been delayed; whether NHA had requested FY2027 EHAP and quick-response funds; and whether the proposed resources were sufficient to assist disaster- and fire-damaged homes. Members also asked what procedures, funding, and interagency measures would prevent delays and sustain housing projects during calamities.

topics.topic: NHA funding, production targets, and proposed budget cut
topics.summary: Undersecretary Henry Eliap presented a FY2027 NEP allocation of about 5.5 billion against attached-agency requests of approximately 60 billion, including an NHA request of about 44.7 billion versus an allocation of about 2.27 billion. Sarah Elago questioned emergency-shelter delays and NHA production, prompting a DBM explanation request and requests for lists of banks and developers. Victoria Co-Pilar and Lani Mercado argued that the funding was inadequate and moved or supported an increase, while the chair deferred the motion to plenary. Mercado specifically questioned whether 370,000,000 could address Manila Bay relocation needs; NHA said a building cost around 70 to 90,000,000 pesos and that the amount could cover around four buildings. NHA also stated that it had requested 1,000,000,000 for EHAP and 500,000,000 million million for the quick-response fund, with the latter wording unclear in the transcript. Members raised submerged Bacolor sites, old resettlement amenities, and vacant Rizal units, leading to commitments for agency follow-up and documents rather than a final funding decision.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 funding would allow NHA and other attached agencies to meet resettlement, Manila Bay relocation, emergency shelter, and old-site amenity obligations. Members also asked whether requested funds had been sought from DBM and what additional actions or budget increases were needed.

topics.topic: Attached-agency budgets, unobligated funds, and SHFC self-financing
topics.summary: Undersecretary Henry Eliap presented a 2027 NEP allocation of about 5.5 billion against agency requests totaling roughly 60 billion, including NHA's request of about 44.7 billion and SHFC's request of about 4.7 billion. Representative Victoria Co-Pilar questioned whether SHFC and the other corporate attached agencies could rely on their own income and highlighted 64 SHFC priority projects. DBM cited projected income of about 1.745 billion and said subsidies could be provided when necessary, but SHFC said its operating costs and limited net receipts prevented it from funding all programs. DBM also identified about 2.896 billion in NHA unobligated obligations from 2011 through 2024 and said NHA needed authority to use them. Co-Pilar moved to increase the budgets of SHFC and the other attached agencies, but the chair deferred action to plenary, while NHA committed to submit the requested letter to DBM. Representative Miro Quimbo separately raised concerns about housing underspending and supported the Community Mortgage Program.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the attached agencies' corporate income, operating resources, and unobligated balances justified their proposed appropriations, particularly for SHFC priority projects and NHA resettlement programs. It also sought to determine whether the requested budget increases should be acted on immediately or referred to plenary.

topics.topic: Continuing-fund utilization and 52% disbursement rate
topics.summary: The chair questioned DHSUD's 52% disbursement rate for total continuing funds and asked how the backlog would be addressed before expiration. DHSUD attributed the low utilization to the expansion of the 4PH program from a single vertical modality to multiple modalities, including horizontal, rental, transitory, proclamation, and CMP projects. The agency also cited delays while developers awaited a revised price ceiling and said ISSP had not been implemented in the previous year. DHSUD reported a current budget of about 1.455 billion, a continuing budget spoken as 1.497, and a total disbursement rate of 74%, while its comparative 2021–2025 figures showed a 95.37 overall disbursement rate. A DHSUD official assured the committee that the remaining interest-subsidy and ISSP funds would be utilized before the end of the year.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the utilization of DHSUD's current and continuing funds, particularly the reported 52% disbursement rate for continuing appropriations. It also asked what caused the backlog and whether the remaining funds would be fully utilized before expiration.

topics.topic: Community Mortgage Program financing and coastal or informal-settler communities
topics.summary: Secretary Aliling presented CMP as a major housing-needs solution, citing 1,100,000 projected CMP-related needs. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned project coverage, beneficiary amortization, interest subsidies, and the shortfall between planned production and actual takeouts; SHFC officials cited 47 projects, 60 applications, 37 projects, about 1,600,000,000, and amortization figures including 4,000 and 4,900 per month. Rep. Leila de Lima asked how many approved CMP projects served coastal fisherfolk communities, after citing 36 projects and 6,000 potential beneficiaries. SHFC answered that 47 projects had benefited almost 9,000 families and undertook to check its records for the coastal breakdown; it also reported 60 pending pipeline applications subject to funding. Rep. Miro Quimbo endorsed CMP as a social-housing and regularization mechanism. DHSUD later identified the SHFC mortgage program as a top additional-budget priority, with the chair stating figures of 4,600,000,000 and 4,660,000,000, and Secretary Aliling committed to submit a prioritized request.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Community Mortgage Program (CMP) was being financed and implemented, including its coverage of informal-settler and fisherfolk communities. It also examined CMP production, beneficiary costs, pending applications, and DHSUD's priorities for additional funding.

topics.topic: Presidential proclamations, land allocation, surveys, and legal assistance
topics.summary: Leila de Lima raised recurring delays in presidential proclamations, land titles, certificates of land allocation, basic services, and land-acquisition funding, and requested project-level status reports and 2027 budget coverage. The secretary undertook to submit the requested information, while the agency said it had received only 3,000,000 against a request for 151,000,000 for survey-related work. DHSUD officials said they were working with the Office of the Executive Secretary and the Office of the Cabinet Secretary on a consolidated interagency proclamation process, but the hearing did not establish a legal-assistance mechanism for private land claims. The SHFC president reported 47 approved projects benefiting almost 9,000 families and 60 pending applications, and agreed to verify which projects served coastal fisherfolk. Rep. Mica Gonzales sought an agency-LGU response to submerged Bacolor settlement sites; NHA said three to four sites were fully submerged, was exploring financial assistance, and agreed to coordinate. Rep. Miro Quimbo criticized housing underspending and endorsed the CMP, but no resolution of the funding and implementation concerns was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status, funding, and completion timelines of delayed presidential proclamations and socialized housing projects, including surveys, titles, land allocation, estate management, and legal assistance. It also asked what agencies would do for submerged housing sites in Bacolor and how the Community Mortgage Program (CMP) and available housing funds were being implemented.

topics.topic: Manila Bay resettlement and the 370,000,000 NHA allocation
topics.summary: Rep. Lanny Mercado questioned whether the NHA's allocation of about 370 million was sufficient for Manila Bay resettlement, citing a backlog of more than 2,000 units in her district. An agency official estimated that one building cost about 70 to 90 million pesos and that the allocation could cover about four buildings, while saying projects were multiyear and new projects could not be accommodated at current funding levels. Mercado also raised a shortage involving 117 families due 30,000 pesos each, and an agency official said EHAP funds were expected to be released within two weeks. She separately asked SHFC to support a parking building costing about 60 to 80 million pesos; the agency agreed to revisit and study the request. Mercado seconded a motion for additional housing funding, which the chair said would be acted on at the proper time.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the NHA's 370,000,000 allocation was sufficient to relocate informal settler families affected by the Supreme Court Mandamus on Manila Bay, including the reported backlog in the member's district. It also asked whether EHAP funds and SHFC assistance for parking facilities could address related shortfalls.

topics.topic: Balanced housing compliance, escrow funds, and DOJ-COA guidance
topics.summary: Former President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo asked DHSUD about the escrow fund balance, its allocation, beneficiaries, and the construction status of about 23,000 units. DHSUD stated that the balance was "12.7 around 12,700,000,000," that around 80% of 12,000,000,000 was ongoing, and that disbursements were progressive, although other allocation figures were unclear. Arroyo also challenged the homeowners' association quorum provision, and DHSUD said the Secretary had ordered a review that included that provision. Rep. Sarah Elago raised the 2027 budget, balanced-housing compliance, and DOJ-COA guidance. DHSUD cited a proposed budget of about 44 billion, a moratorium through February 2027, and prospective implementation of the DOJ opinion, while committing to process and validate amounts and address the COA AOM. The agency also offered to submit the project list, but the transcript left the detailed computations and compliance resolution unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the balance and utilization of the escrow housing-for-balanced-development fund, the status of projects and beneficiaries, and DHSUD's treatment of balanced-housing compliance in light of DOJ guidance and a COA audit observation. Members also sought clarification on the proposed 2027 budget and support for low-income housing.

topics.topic: Socialized-housing permit streamlining and developer payment delays
topics.summary: Representative Elmer Catulpos raised concerns that socialized-housing permitting was insufficiently attractive to developers and cited a permitting example involving 86 documents, 35 documents, and sixteen days, although the comparison was unclear. DHSUD answered that an interagency memorandum had reduced subdivision requirements from 223 to 62 and condominium requirements from 162 to 71, corresponding to reductions of 72% and 56%. The agency also reported stage-level processing-time reductions of as much as 76% for subdivisions and 75% for condominiums, with a 50% target for total processing time. Catulpos asked whether socialized housing would receive comparable streamlining, and DHSUD said socialized and non-socialized projects would have more or less the same streamlined requirements, with BP 220 serving as a technical reference. He also raised reports that developer payments took six months or more and could result in penalties. DHSUD cited digitalization and coordination with the Land Bank as the response, while Catulpos manifested support for increasing DHSUD's 2027 budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DHSUD had reduced permitting requirements and processing times for socialized-housing projects, and whether delays in processing payments to developers were being addressed. It also sought clarification on whether streamlining applied equally to socialized and open-market housing.

topics.topic: Resettlement units, vacant housing, and Supreme Court Mandamus obligations
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago raised the status of 26,041 resettlement units and questioned a report listing 8,477 vacant units. The NHA said most Mandamus-related units were occupied, while about 8,000 vacant units in Rizal were affected by the provincial government's preference for Rizal beneficiaries and opposition to relocations from other areas. Elago also asked about community interventions, the proposed 2027 budget, balanced housing compliance, and DOJ-COA guidance. The agency cited training, utility coordination, financial assistance, off-site CMP, and SHFC community programs, and stated that the proposed 2027 budget was about 44 billion in readable magnitude. It said a one-year moratorium ran through February 2027 and that the DOJ-related requirement would be implemented prospectively, but the computation and the additional requested budget figure remained unclear. The matter ended without a recorded resolution or final ruling.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how many resettlement units remained vacant, why vacancies persisted, and how the units related to Supreme Court Mandamus obligations. It also examined DHSUD's proposed 2027 budget, balanced housing compliance, applicable DOJ-COA guidance, and whether resettlement and community interventions were adequately funded.

topics.topic: Fire, flood, and calamity impacts on housing projects and settlements
topics.summary: Rep. Mica Gonzales raised the flooding of Bacolor settlement sites and asked the NHA, DHSUD, and other agencies for a forward plan for displaced residents. The NHA said three to four sites were fully submerged, that it was examining financial support, and that DPWH had reportedly said it would undertake repairs and flood mitigation during the year. Gonzales requested an agency-LGU meeting and supported increasing the housing budget, while the NHA agreed to coordinate. Rep. Maria Isabel Gavaria said the Negros Island Region had only 9,400,000 and asked about assistance for indigent families whose homes were destroyed by fire; the secretary cited IDSAP and EHAB, construction materials, shelter repair kits, and LGU modular houses. The vice chair then cited 16,700 partially damaged houses and 6,550 assisted houses and asked whether projects could continue amid calamities. DHSUD answered that it needed additional funds and said assistance funds could begin within the next two weeks, with the vice chair supporting the request.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DHSUD, the NHA, and partner agencies would assist communities whose settlement sites or homes were submerged, damaged by fire, or otherwise affected by calamities. Members also asked whether the proposed funding was sufficient to continue housing projects and provide emergency assistance.
