topics.topic: FY 2027 Ombudsman budget and program allocations
topics.summary: The chair and Christopher Lim presented the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 budget, with the agency citing a recommended level of about 7 billion and allocations for personnel, operations, capital outlay, programs, ICT modernization, facilities, confidential expenses, and proposed marshals. Lim also requested restatement of special provisions on savings, income, retirement benefits, and fiscal autonomy. Iris Marie Montes questioned conviction rates, high-ranking-official cases, political safeguards, digital forensic tools, and regional reach; the agency reported improved conviction rates, said it followed its constitutional mandate without fear or favor, and said digitalization and regional offices were funded or being expanded. The agency could not immediately provide data separating motu proprio investigations or measuring regional-office efficiency and undertook to provide information. Members Rufus Rodriguez, Maisa Sagarbarria, and Girlie Veloso expressed support for the budget, including marshal positions. Committee Chair Micah Swan Singh requested a written and prioritized list of additional funding requests, and Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla committed to submit it and coordinate on the special-provision wording.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 funding requirements, program allocations, and requested special provisions, and whether the proposed resources would improve its anti-corruption, investigative, digital, and regional capabilities. Members also asked what safeguards, performance results, and prioritization would guide any additional funding.

topics.topic: Additional Ombudsman funding requests and budget amendments
topics.summary: Rep. Toby Tiangco supported the Ombudsman’s budget and urged fiscal-autonomy amendments covering the Ombudsman and other constitutional commissions, saying he had advocated the issue since 2013. Chair Rufus Rodriguez agreed in principle and said the proposed language, including savings, use of income, and retirement benefits, would be recommended to the plenary subject to committee approval. Chairperson Micah Swan Singh then asked the Ombudsman to submit and prioritize in writing its additional funding requests, including confidential funds, marshal positions, motor vehicles, and a new office building. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla committed to comply as soon as possible. The chairperson also said the committee would coordinate on the special-provision wording for the 2027 GAA, building on its inclusion in the 2026 GAA. Final prioritization and appropriations for the additional requests were left for the budget-amendments review process.
topics.question: The committee was determining whether to support the Ombudsman’s requested special provisions and related fiscal-autonomy amendments, and whether the office would submit a prioritized written list of additional funding requests for budget-amendment review.

topics.topic: Ombudsman fiscal autonomy and special provisions
topics.summary: Toby Tiangco supported the Ombudsman’s budget and urged adoption of its requested fiscal-autonomy amendments. He asked that comparable amendments apply to COMELEC, the Civil Service Commission, COA, and the Commission on Human Rights, noting that fiscal autonomy had been his advocacy since 2013. The Chair said the committee supported the Ombudsman’s special provisions but still needed the approval of all members. Tiangco specified savings, use of income, retirement benefits, and validity of appropriations as additional matters, and the Chair committed to recommending the language to the plenary.
topics.question: The committee was considering whether the Ombudsman’s requested amendments to the general and special provisions should be adopted, including provisions affecting fiscal autonomy. It also considered whether similar amendments should apply to the other constitutional commissions and whether the language should be recommended to the plenary.

topics.topic: Capital outlay for digital forensic tools
topics.summary: Director Christopher Lim reported that the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 budget included total capital outlay of about 157.1 million and an IT modernization requirement described in the transcript as 497,549,000,000, including a capital-outlay component of 250 million. Iris Marie Montes asked whether the capital-outlay increase covered digital forensic tools. An agency official answered that it did, to his understanding, as part of the administration’s digitalization initiative. During a later discussion on fact-finding, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla referred to training and digital-forensics equipment, and Chel Diokno urged that these be included in the budget proposal. The hearing did not establish an itemized amount specifically for digital forensic equipment or a procurement timetable.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Ombudsman’s proposed capital outlay included digital forensic equipment and tools needed to strengthen corruption investigations. It also examined whether the agency had personnel and equipment needs related to digital forensics.

topics.topic: Regional reach and accessibility of Ombudsman services
topics.summary: Iris Marie Montes asked how the FY 2027 budget would expand Ombudsman services and accessibility in the regions. Luigi Bonoan said the agency was looking to expand investigations into the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region and had requested support for regional offices in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, as well as satellite offices. He said the funding would ensure public accessibility and continuous presence. Montes then asked for measurable indicators of regional-office efficiency. She requested that the data be submitted if it was not available during the hearing, but no agency response to that request was captured. The issue therefore remained unresolved in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the FY 2027 proposed budget would expand the Ombudsman’s presence outside the central office and make its services accessible to complainants in the regions. It also sought measurable indicators of the effectiveness of the regional and satellite offices.

topics.topic: Ombudsman staffing and lawyer recruitment
topics.summary: Christopher Lim presented personnel-services funding of about 3.76 billion and about 1.66 billion for filling positions, while seeking support for additional staffing. Representative Salvador Pleyto questioned whether the unchanged ceiling of 2,439 authorized positions was sufficient, and Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla said it had taken more than ten and a half months to hire 60 lawyers. Chel Diokno then linked staffing and digital-forensics capacity to the Ombudsman's fact-finding workload, citing 2,051 investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases. He requested detailed filing data, including the number of flood-control cases among the 10 filed this year and 12 last year. The Ombudsman identified interagency cooperation, investigator numbers, training, and digital-forensics equipment as needs, but did not provide the requested case breakdown during the hearing. The committee therefore left the data issue for follow-up, while the Ombudsman advocated case-building standards and mandatory continuous trials to reduce delays.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Ombudsman had sufficient authorized personnel and personnel-services funding to carry out its investigation, prosecution, and public-assistance mandates. Members also asked how recruitment, investigator capacity, digital-forensics capability, and case-processing delays affected the office's workload.

topics.topic: Fact-finding capacity and corruption-case processing delays
topics.summary: Mauricio Domogan questioned the Ombudsman about pending complaints, conflict-of-interest investigations, pre-audit, and processing times. The Ombudsman said fact-finding generally took thirty to sixty days and preliminary investigation another thirty to sixty days, and reported hiring 60 lawyers with 40 more planned. Rep. Chel Diokno raised the absence of a centralized system for tracking final convictions, and the Ombudsman proposed an Ombudsman Marshal office for conviction tracking, process service, and related functions. The Ombudsman also reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks and agreed that a government-wide conviction-rate measure would be useful. Rep. Kjell Jochno cited a report involving 2,051 fact-finding investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases, then requested detailed filing and flood-control data. The hearing ended with commitments on staffing and marshals, but the requested case data and broader solutions to judicial delays remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Ombudsman conducts fact-finding and preliminary investigations, how staffing and resources affect case-processing timelines, and how many corruption cases—particularly flood-control cases—advance to prosecution and conviction. Members also asked how the government tracks final convictions, conducts lifestyle checks, and addresses delays in the justice system.

topics.topic: Flood-control corruption investigations and alleged budget insertions
topics.summary: Representative Antonio Tinio raised allegations involving flood-control corruption, a 2025 budget insertion of 100,000,000,000, an allegedly related 51,000,000,000, and alleged kickbacks totaling 8,000,000,000, including 2,000,000,000 allegedly delivered through armored cars. He asked whether the Ombudsman would investigate the allegations and determine whether appropriations corresponded to projects actually delivered, but the transcript contains no substantive agency answer. Chel Diokno questioned the Ombudsman's fact-finding performance, citing 2,051 investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases, and asked for personnel, digital-forensics, and flood-control case data. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said agency cooperation, personnel, and digital-forensics equipment were needed, but the response on the number of flood-control cases was unclear. Remulla said corruption cases should be filed only after probable cause and a reasonable certainty of conviction had been established, and advocated mandatory continuous trials to avoid extreme delays. The committee's requests for data left the flood-control investigation issue committed for follow-up rather than resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Ombudsman was investigating alleged flood-control corruption and budget insertions, including whether complaints had been acted on, how many cases had been filed, and whether its resources and procedures were adequate. Members also asked what institutional or budgetary support would improve fact-finding, digital forensics, case filing, and the eventual prosecution of corruption cases.

topics.topic: Conviction rates and tracking of graft cases
topics.summary: Representative Iris Marie Montes asked about the Ombudsman’s conviction rates, comparisons with prior years, high-ranking-official cases, and Moto Propio investigations. The agency reported a Sandigan Bayan conviction rate of sixty five point five two percent, compared with forty two percent previously, and lower-court rates of seventy seven point six percent in 2025 and sixty four point nine one percent as of June 30 of the current year. It could not immediately distinguish Moto Propio cases but committed to provide the data. Representative Chel Diokno raised a decades-old recommendation for a centralized system to track convictions and asked whether the Ombudsman had acted on it. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said the proposed Ombudsman Marshall office, for which funding was requested, would track case and sentence statuses and perform related functions; the chair supported the proposal, although disagreement over imprisonment before final judgment remained. The agency also agreed that a government-wide conviction-rate statistic would be beneficial and reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman’s conviction performance, including comparisons with prior years and between courts, and whether the agency could track cases through final judgment and service of sentence. Members also asked whether the Ombudsman had safeguards against political influence, a centralized conviction-tracking system, a government-wide conviction metric, and active lifestyle-check and marshal programs.

topics.topic: Ombudsman marshals and enforcement support
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno asked how the government could track persons finally convicted of corruption offenses, particularly during lengthy appeals, and referred to an earlier study covering 110 convictions. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said the office had requested funding for an Ombudsman Marshal to track convictions and persons charged in court, serve subpoenas, and support witness-protection functions. The Ombudsman also said 107 lifestyle checks were underway and agreed that a government-wide conviction statistic would be useful, after Diokno cited a 65% conviction rate. Chair Rodriguez supported the marshals for protection, faster processes, and enforcement of final judgments, while Rep. Sagarbarria supported the proposed Ombudsman budget. The proposal was supported in the hearing, but final funding approval and implementation details were not recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Ombudsman tracks persons convicted of corruption offenses, including those whose appeals remain pending, and whether the proposed Ombudsman marshals would provide enforcement and process-serving support. It also asked about a government-wide conviction-rate measure and the status of lifestyle checks.

topics.topic: Lifestyle checks and investigation safeguards
topics.summary: Representative Iris Marie Montes questioned the Ombudsman about conviction rates, safeguards against political influence, digital investigative tools, moto proprio investigations, and regional reach. The agency reported a Sandigan Bayan conviction rate of about 65.52 percent in 2026, compared with 42 percent previously, and cited lower-court rates of about 77.6 percent in 2025 and 64.91 percent as of June 30. It lacked immediately available data separating moto proprio cases from filed complaints but undertook to provide it, while regional performance indicators were also requested. Representative Mauricio Domogan raised conflict-of-interest complaints, mandatory pre-audit, geo-mapping, and investigation timelines; the Ombudsman said conflict-of-interest information could initiate moto proprio investigations and described fact-finding and preliminary-investigation deadlines, supported by 60 lawyers hired and 40 more planned. Representative Chel Diokno pressed for centralized conviction tracking, witness-protection capacity, and a uniform government-wide conviction-rate measure, and the Ombudsman said a proposed Marshall office would handle those functions. The Ombudsman also reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks, and the chair manifested support for creating Ombudsman marshals.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman's conviction performance, safeguards against political influence, capacity for proactive and moto proprio investigations, regional accessibility, and the status of lifestyle checks. Members also asked how convictions, complaints, witnesses, and conflict-of-interest cases were being tracked and processed.

topics.topic: Witness protection and support for corruption investigations
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno raised the absence of a witness-protection proposal in the Ombudsman's submitted budget materials. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla answered that witness protection would be one of the functions of the Ombudsman marshals the agency was creating that year. He said the agency had requested funding for the marshals and believed its own personnel would be more effective than relying on police support. The marshals would also serve subpoenas and perform related functions, following the model of the Supreme Court marshals. Chair Rufus Rodriguez manifested support for creating the marshals. The issue landed with an agency commitment, but no separate witness-protection budget amount or detailed implementation plan was provided.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Ombudsman had a proposal or mechanism for witness protection, particularly because the materials submitted for the proposed budget did not identify such a program. It also sought clarification on whether the proposed Ombudsman marshals would support witness protection and related investigative and prosecutorial functions.

topics.topic: Pre-audit and geo-mapping support for government projects
topics.summary: Rep. Mauricio Domogan asked whether mandatory pre-audit of government-project payments, combined with geo-mapping, should be pursued to address ghost projects and corruption. He said the pre-audit requirement had been removed in 2011 and that COA supported the proposal with one additional personnel. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla said the measure would be a big help but belonged to COA, which might need more staff. Domogan also asked about investigation timelines; Remulla cited fact-finding periods of about 30 to 60 days and preliminary-investigation periods of about 30 to 60 days. Remulla reported that 60 lawyers had been hired, 40 more were planned, and the total would reach 100 lawyers. The issue ended with member support but without a recorded ruling or final action on the bill.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether mandatory pre-audit of government-project payments, coupled with geo-mapping, should be pursued to detect ghost projects and corruption. It also asked how the Ombudsman handled conflict-of-interest complaints and how long investigations took.

topics.topic: Impeachment-related monitoring and confidential funds
topics.summary: Rep. Kjell Jochno asked whether the Ombudsman was monitoring impeachment-related testimonies and evidence, particularly material involving confidential funds, for possible later violations and investigations. He referred to proposed confidential funds of about N55 million. Secretary Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla answered that the matter was being monitored and that an active unit was following the impeachment proceedings. Jochno said the issue raised accountability concerns. No further details or document commitments were made before the vice-chair moved to accept a motion to terminate.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Ombudsman was monitoring testimonies and evidence presented in the impeachment proceedings, particularly material involving confidential funds, for possible subsequent investigation or prosecution. It also raised the level of confidential-fund resources in the Ombudsman's budget.

topics.topic: DOST and attached-agency budget reduction, including 12.5% cut
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio raised the DOST and attached-agency reductions, including the 12.5% cut, and was told that the main reductions were in capital outlay for completed or already funded projects. He also questioned the national AI-compute plan, which DOST described as an in-country, GPU-based capability supported initially by 100,000,000 and targeted for expansion by 26 fold by 2028. The chair then examined the proposed redistribution of about 1.25 billion in grants, while DBM explained that a new policy moved ongoing attached-agency R&D funding into agency-specific budgets. DOST argued that grants were proposal-driven and required flexibility, citing 98% utilization, and the chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards. DOST identified 800,000,000 for the Virology Institute and 309,000,000 for graduate grants, covering 5,000 grantees, and the committee requested supporting tables, project lists, AI documents, and prioritized amendments. The issue remained subject to consultations and subsequent congressional action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the DOST and attached-agency budgets were reduced, particularly where reductions reflected completed capital-outlay projects, and how DOST's grants should be structured. It also examined the funding needed for national AI-compute infrastructure, the Virology Institute, graduate grants, and priority amendments.

topics.topic: DOST grants allocation, GIA reallocation, and implementation flexibility
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio asked about DOST's GIA-supported AI infrastructure, the planned 26-fold expansion of high-performance computing, and data-sovereignty plans; DOST said initial seed funding was 100,000,000 and requested capacity and strategy documents were to be submitted. The committee chair then questioned DBM's transfer of about 1.25 billion in grants from the OSEC to agency-specific budgets. DBM said the transfer was a new policy intended to streamline implementation, while DOST said grants were proposal-driven, had achieved 98% utilization, and required flexibility for cross-agency and emergency needs. The chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards and requested post-hearing consultations between DBM and DOST. DOST also identified 800,000,000 for the virology institute and 309,000,000 for graduate grants covering 5,000 recipients, with updated monthly grant levels, and was asked to submit supporting tables and prioritized amendment requests. The issue was left for consultations and further congressional action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DOST grants were allocated under the proposed budget, why the GIA funding was transferred to agency-specific budgets, and whether that arrangement would reduce DOST's ability to respond to proposal-driven and emergency research needs. It also asked what additional funding and documentation DOST needed for national AI infrastructure, virology facilities, graduate grants, and other priority amendments.

topics.topic: National AI infrastructure, high-performance computing, and data sovereignty
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DOST about the proposed national AI center, the target of increasing high-performance computing capacity by 26 fold by 2028, and whether the expansion was funded in the budget. ASTI said the existing service had evolved from a shared supercomputer into GPU-based infrastructure, with H200 processors, five major compute servers, commercial data-center space, and planned regional expansion. It identified 100,000,000 in initial DOST grant-in-aid seed funding but did not state the total cost of the expansion. The DOST Secretary said DOST would lead research and development infrastructure, talent management, and language models, while DICT would handle connectivity and related private-sector infrastructure. DOST also described a Philippine data-sovereignty platform and a planned government-managed AI hub, while acknowledging insufficient compute power and scale. Tinio supported AI and data sovereignty and requested documents on the National AI Strategy, existing compute capacity, and expansion plans.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what national high-performance computing and data infrastructure the government was building for artificial intelligence, how large and capable it was, how much expansion would cost, and whether it was reflected in the proposed budget. It also sought to clarify which agency would lead the effort and how the government would protect Philippine data and AI sovereignty.

topics.topic: Virology Institute construction funding for phases one and two
topics.summary: The committee chair asked DOST how much was needed to complete the Virology Institute's first two building phases and allow it to operate in New Clark City. DOST answered that the requirement for next year was about 800 million. The exchange indicated that the construction was ongoing and lodged under DPWH, but did not clearly resolve whether DOST or DPWH would submit the funding request. The chair said DOST had to prioritize its requests because fiscal space was limited and asked that the institutional amendment requests be submitted as soon as possible, preferably within the week. DOST agreed to submit a prioritized list, while the chair expressed support for helping secure resources for the agency.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the indicative funding needed to complete the Virology Institute's phase one and phase two buildings so the institute could operate in New Clark City. It also asked whether the request was included in DOST's Tier One submission to DBM or should come through DPWH.

topics.topic: Project SARAI and smart-agriculture climate resilience technologies
topics.summary: Rep. Bella Suansing asked the DOST secretary to explain Project SARAI, its regional coverage, crop recommendations, and links with the Department of Agriculture. DOST said SARAI integrated satellite, GIS, weather, crop, pest, soil, water, nutrient, and mobile-application data, with deployment determined by local commodity needs. The agency said SARAI did not exclude complementary technologies, including seaweed foliar fertilizer that was reported to increase rice production by up to 30%. DOST said it was shifting from pilots toward regional implementation with agriculture agencies, local governments, cooperatives, and farmers, and cited a mobile solar irrigation trailer developed in Region 3. The discussion also covered DOST's customizable disaster platform, its SOS and AI features, and its use of evacuation-site data from the Department of the Interior and Local Government and the Office of Civil Defense. The exchange ended with information provided and a general agency commitment to promote local adoption, without a specific budgetary or documentary action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how Project SARAI operated, where it was being deployed, and whether its crop, water, and climate-smart technologies were being integrated with the Department of Agriculture, local governments, and disaster-preparedness efforts. It also asked how DOST-developed platforms and technologies could be accelerated in response to El Niño and climate change.

topics.topic: Fisheries and aquaculture development programs for Bicol and Catanduanes
topics.summary: Rep. Eulogio Rodriguez raised the weak performance of Bicol’s economy and fisheries, citing GDP growth of about 0.5% in 2025, a 2.9% contraction in the agriculture, fisheries and forestry sector, and a 10.7% decline in fishery. He asked where the bottlenecks were and what measurable results DOST, PCAARRD, and partner agencies had achieved in Catanduanes and Bicol. The PCAARRD director said several aquaculture and marine-resources projects were underway, including work involving Catanduanes State University, but identified technology transfer and coordination with local governments and other agencies as challenges. For 2027, the director said PCAARRD would explore expanding the tilapia program and other marine-resource initiatives based on pilot projects elsewhere. PCAARRD committed to reviewing and enhancing its current initiatives, but no quantified outcomes or specific budget figures were provided.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why Bicol’s fisheries and aquaculture potential had not translated into stronger economic performance, particularly in Catanduanes. It asked what DOST through PCAARRD and partner agencies had done, what measurable results had been achieved, and what programs and results were proposed for 2027.

topics.topic: FNRI Phase Four building funding and budget change
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio raised the change in FNRI’s budget from 100,000,000.06 to 34,000,000 and asked for an explanation. The chair suggested that the change might involve the building FNRI needed to finish. An agency official said the item was capital outlay and confirmed that funding had been provided for 2026 and was being considered for 2027. The official said FNRI had requested 400,000,000 for the Phase Four building in 2027. The excerpt did not establish the reason for the full budget change or record a decision on the request.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the Food and Nutrition Research Institute’s budget changed from 100,000,000.06 to 34,000,000 and whether the reduction affected its building project. It also sought the amount FNRI needed for the Phase Four building in 2027.

topics.topic: Nutrition-menu bundle costs and food-poverty-threshold basis
topics.summary: Sarah Elago asked how regional nutrition-menu bundles were designed and whether their costs were based on the food poverty threshold. The nutrition official said the menus used PDRI reference values, sought to meet at least one third of requirements, and were priced using raw-material market values and a developed formula. The official said a 2023 adolescent study used 2022 figures and cited about 30 pesos and 25 centavos per meal, also rendered in the transcript as PHP30.25. Representative Ilago compared this with figures in the 2027 budget presentation: 111 pesos for the NCR poverty threshold, around 77 pesos for the food poverty threshold, 26 pesos per meal in NCR, and 23 pesos outside NCR. The official did not provide the exact computation, and the apparent discrepancy with the cited thresholds remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the regional nutrition-menu bundles were designed, including the per-person-per-day cost, the food-poverty-threshold basis, and whether the amounts remained adequate against the 2027 budget presentation. Sarah Elago also asked when the menus were last designed and what figures were used for 2022 and 2023.

topics.topic: Technology commercialization and sexual-assault-kit procurement
topics.summary: Sarah Elago raised the need to commercialize and scale the DOST-supported sexual-assault-kit technology for use by women-and-children protection units and public hospitals. A DOST official said the agency's role was to support research and development, promote the technology, and maintain dialogue with its UP producer. The official said investors were reluctant to take commercialization risks, so DOST supported production and use cases that could demonstrate the technology to potential adopters such as the DOJ and PNP. The agency also said appropriate agencies needed to procure the kit and expressed hope that the Tatak Pinoy Act would give Filipino-produced, DOST-supported technology preferential treatment. No completed procurement or specific adoption commitment was reported.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DOST-supported sexual-assault-kit technology had moved from research and development into commercialization and procurement. It also sought to determine how the technology could be scaled for use by women-and-children protection units, public hospitals, the DOJ, and the PNP.

topics.topic: PAGASA and PNRI capital-outlay-related budget decreases
topics.summary: The committee chair asked why PAGASA and PNRI had lower capital-outlay allocations, and the agency-side response attributed the decreases to completed projects, including about 345 million for PNRI. The chair then questioned the transfer of roughly 1.25 billion in DOST grants from the Office of the Secretary to attached agencies. DBM said the distribution reflected a new policy intended to fund ongoing R&D projects directly and streamline implementation, while DOST said the proposal-driven nature of grants required flexibility and that some funds had been transferred to agencies unable to implement the relevant programs. DOST reported 98% utilization under the previous centralized arrangement. The chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards, and DBM deferred to Congress. The chair requested post-hearing DBM-DOST consultations and the drafting of any necessary special provisions.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGASA and PNRI had lower capital-outlay allocations and whether the transfer of DOST grants from the Office of the Secretary to attached agencies should be reversed. It also examined whether the new grant structure would reduce flexibility and utilization, and whether safeguards or special provisions were needed.

topics.topic: DOST Office of the Secretary grant-in-aid priorities
topics.summary: Antonio Tinio questioned DOST's budget reductions, Office of the Secretary grant-in-aid priorities, and plans to build nationally controlled AI-compute and data-sovereignty capacity. DOST said the reductions were mainly capital-outlay adjustments and described grant-in-aid support for advanced manufacturing, AI, robotics, and other emerging technologies. The AI initiative had initial seed funding of about 100 million, while the agency described a planned 26-fold expansion and regional rollout. The chair asked about 800 million for the Virology Institute and roughly 309 million for master's and PhD grants covering 5,000 recipients, with increases in monthly grant rates. The committee supported DOST but required a prioritized list of institutional amendments, construction requests, grantee data, and AI strategy documents for subsequent review.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DOST's proposed budget and certain attached-agency allocations changed, what the Office of the Secretary grant-in-aid funds would support, and how DOST would prioritize institutional amendments. It also sought details on national AI-compute and data-sovereignty plans, virology construction funding, and graduate-student grants.

topics.topic: PAGCOR FY 2026 income decline and FY 2027 revenue outlook
topics.summary: Chair Mika Suansing asked PAGCOR to explain the decline from its 2025 income and to clarify the 2027 outlook. PAGCOR attributed the decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, weaker land-based casino and licensee revenues, and economic conditions affecting its CDE customer market; it projected 2027 total revenues of about 88.33 billion. PAGCOR said first-semester 2026 income was about 43.32 billion, with about 30.16 billion going to nation-building programs, and reported 2026 gaming-operations income of about 80 billion divided roughly equally between land-based and online gaming. Members also questioned the retroactive 37,000,000,000 pesos PSC obligation and online-gaming regulation, including the policing of illegal operators, advertising, influencers, and minors. PAGCOR said it was updating its regulatory framework and disclosed projected 2026 revenues of between 9 and 10 billion for Casino Filipino, about 31.5 billion for licensed casinos, and 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038 for digital e-games. The issue landed with requests for PSC remittance records and detailed revenue data, while stronger online-gaming regulation remained an ongoing commitment rather than a resolved matter.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's 2026 income and net income had declined from the assumptions underlying its approved budget, what the 2027 revenue outlook was, and how the decline would affect government remittances and social-responsibility programs. Members also sought to determine whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory capacity to manage the growth of online gaming and illegal operators.

topics.topic: Casino Filipino privatization, proceeds, and PAGCOR’s future role
topics.summary: Members asked PAGCOR about the status of privatizing roughly 30 to 40 Casino Filipino properties, its expected proceeds, and the agency's future regulatory role. PAGCOR said the transaction remained pending the GCG recommendation and Office of the President's approval, with estimated proceeds ranging from about 20 billion to 30 billion, and later about 25 billion to 30 billion. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised safeguards for approximately 10,000 employees, while PAGCOR cited retirement and special incentive packages, buyer absorption, and extensive retraining. Rep. Iris Marie Montes and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned how privatization would affect PhilHealth's UHC earmark; PAGCOR said it remitted to the National Treasury, which was responsible for the subsequent 50% UHC remittance. PAGCOR cited about 50 billion pesos remitted in 2025, implying 25 billion for the UHC fund under the statutory formula, and estimated retirement needs of about 28 billion to 30 billion against 12 billion in current retirement funding. PAGCOR agreed to submit remittance and privatization computations within forty eight hours and to study whether any proceeds remaining after retirement costs could support a UHC stabilization fund.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status, scope, valuation, and proceeds of the proposed Casino Filipino privatization, including PAGCOR's transition from operator-regulator to primarily regulator. Members also asked how privatization would affect employees, PhilHealth's Universal Health Care remittances, PAGCOR's future revenues, and the use of sale proceeds.

topics.topic: Universal Health Care and PhilHealth remittances after privatization
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked whether PAGCOR had complied with the UHC Act and requested a complete remittance history. PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco said PAGCOR had remitted regularly to the National Treasury, while the national government was responsible for transferring 50% to PhilHealth or the UHC Fund; he cited about 50 billion remitted in 2025, implying 25 billion should have gone to the UHC Fund. Montes and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked how privatization of Casino Filipino would affect the PhilHealth earmark and sought projections for 2026, 2027, 2028, and the first full year after privatization. Tengco said privatization proceeds would first cover roughly 28 billion to 30 billion in retirement obligations, against an existing retirement fund of about 12 billion, and that any balance could potentially support a stabilization fund. The requested projections and confirmation of onward remittances were not supplied during the hearing, but PAGCOR committed to provide documents within forty eight hours and to study the stabilization-fund proposal. Rep. Jean Baronda separately sought a contingency plan for UHC and support for hospitals and children with special needs, which PAGCOR said it would consider.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR had complied with the Universal Health Care Act's remittance requirement, how much had been remitted to the National Treasury and ultimately to the Universal Health Care Fund, and how privatizing Casino Filipino would affect the PhilHealth earmark. Members also asked whether a transitional UHC stabilization fund would be needed and whether PAGCOR had a contingency plan to sustain support for Universal Health Care.

topics.topic: PSC retroactive 5% remittance ruling and PAGCOR’s PSC budget
topics.summary: Chair Mika Suansing asked PAGCOR to explain the decline in 2026 income and the effect of the Supreme Court's final PSC remittance ruling. PAGCOR attributed the income decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, and weak casino revenues, while saying gaming activity had begun to recover. PAGCOR said the ruling required 5% of gross income rather than gaming revenue alone, applied retroactively to 1993, and created an obligation of 37,000,000,000 pesos. The agency said its prior average PSC contribution was about 190,000,000 pesos per month and identified a payment of 3,300,000,000 every year for the next ten years. The chair said the PSC's proposed 2027 budget was not yet commensurate with the higher remittances and undertook to scrutinize it. PAGCOR was asked to provide its 2025 and 2026 PSC remittance records, while the payment arrangement remained under discussion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's 2026 income was projected to decline and how the Supreme Court's final ruling changed PAGCOR's remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). It also sought to determine the ruling's retroactive fiscal impact and whether the PSC's proposed budget adequately reflected the higher remittances.

topics.topic: Nation-building contributions and PAGCOR social-responsibility spending
topics.summary: PAGCOR reported that it had contributed about 67 billion to nation building in 2025 and projected about 61 billion in 2026 and 63 billion in 2027, while social-civic projects rose to about 13.99 billion in 2026. It also presented a PHP 7,500,000,000 school-building commitment, PHP 300,000,000 in recent calamity-relief spending, patient transport vehicle donations, and hospital-equipment support. The chair commended PAGCOR for preserving these commitments despite lower income, while the agency explained that the Supreme Court's retroactive PSC ruling created a 37,000,000,000 pesos obligation and could substantially affect its finances. Members pressed for stronger control of illegal online gambling, protection of vulnerable gamblers, and funding for responsible-gaming and mental-health programs; PAGCOR cited KYC requirements, a licensing moratorium, enforcement coordination, and a responsible-gaming partner. Members also sought relief and classroom assistance for General Santos and hospital support for Western Visayas and Pangasinan. The hearing ended with PAGCOR agreeing to provide documents, review requests, and explore equipment assistance, but several allocations and enforcement measures remained for follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR's nation-building and social-responsibility contributions were being maintained despite lower revenues, including its relief, hospital, school-building, and social-civic programs. Members also examined whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory and responsible-gaming measures to address illegal online gambling and protect vulnerable gamblers.

topics.topic: Nationwide school-building program and classroom allocations
topics.summary: PAGCOR presented a nationwide program to build 125 three-storey school buildings, or approximately 1,500 classrooms, from 2026 through 2027. The agency stated that the program was funded at PHP 7.5 billion, while a member cited initial funding of 1,370,000,000 pesos and another referred to almost 8 billion. PAGCOR said it had earmarked close to about 3.5 billion for the 50% down payment, with later payments tied to construction progress. Rep. Sarah Elago requested a breakdown of fund utilization, but no such breakdown was submitted during the hearing. Members also questioned whether the program displaced community wellness centers, e-libraries, and evacuation centers, and PAGCOR said it could consider balancing those priorities. PAGCOR undertook to review assistance for earthquake-damaged classrooms and a district request, while conflicting transcript figures for classroom totals remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the scope, funding, implementation period, and allocation of PAGCOR's nationwide school-building program. Members also asked how much had been earmarked or utilized, how schools and local government units were selected, and whether other proposed infrastructure projects would be displaced.

topics.topic: Online-gaming revenues, e-games decline, and regulatory strategy
topics.summary: The chair and several members questioned PAGCOR about declining gaming income, especially the effects of e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, illegal operators, and weaker land-based casino activity. PAGCOR attributed the decline to a roughly 40% fall in activity after payment-app delinking, while reporting a later increase of about 10% in July and August. Members also challenged PAGCOR on advertising approvals, influencer liability, foreign operators, KYC enforcement, minors' access, and the adequacy of responsible-gaming programs. PAGCOR cited fines, coordination with BSP, DICT, NTC, CICC, and police authorities, regular rule updates, a 1% gross-gaming-revenue allocation for responsible gaming, and a possible PAGCOR application for identifying legitimate operators. Revenue figures discussed included projected 2026 gaming operations of 80,000,000,000 pesos, digital e-games revenue of 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038, Casino Filipino revenue of between 9 and 10,000,000,000, and licensed-casino revenue of about 31 and a half billion. The committee requested remittance and revenue documents and left further regulatory strengthening and several enforcement concerns for follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's projected and reported gaming revenues were declining, particularly in online and e-games operations, and how payment restrictions, illegal operators, advertising, and market conditions affected collections. It also examined whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory, responsible-gaming, and monitoring measures to protect players and sustain revenues and remittances.

topics.topic: Illegal online-gaming operators, enforcement, and monitoring capacity
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago asked how foreign illegal operators were being addressed and how the 24/7 problem-gambling helpline and related counseling programs were funded. PAGCOR said it lacked police powers, depended on DICT, CICC, NTC, and other partners, and would continue responsible-gaming initiatives supported by 1% of online gross gaming revenue, estimated at about a billion pesos per annum. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos questioned e-wallet restrictions, unauthorized payment channels, mule accounts, and KYC enforcement; PAGCOR cited coordination with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, monitoring, fines, and suspensions. Vice Chair Brian Poe reported that 44 of 52 illegal websites had initially been taken down but that some had returned, and PAGCOR said the sites had not been licensed because of a moratorium lasting two years. PAGCOR projected 2026 gross gaming revenue at about 370 billion and estimated total wagers at about 3 trillion, while acknowledging that only legal operators were tracked. The committee requested website lists, responsible-gaming data, and equipment-procurement and revenue projections, with further enforcement discussion assigned to the DICT budget hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR and other enforcement agencies were addressing illegal online-gaming operators, reopened websites, unauthorized payment channels, mule accounts, and gaps in KYC monitoring. Members also asked what resources, programs, and interagency equipment were needed to protect consumers and recover revenue that might otherwise be lost to illegal wagering.

topics.topic: Gambling advertising, influencers, and penalties
topics.summary: Rep. Elijah San Fernando raised concerns about advertising controls and influencer promotion in light of approximately 30 million registered and 10 million active online-gaming players. PAGCOR said gambling advertisements required Ad Standards Council clearance and that a licensed operator had been fined 1,000,000 pesos, with suspension and license cancellation available for repeated violations. The agency said 50% of current online-gaming operators were illegal and that it relied on DICT, NTC, CICC, and social-media platforms for enforcement against operators and endorsers outside its jurisdiction. Rep. Sarah Elago pressed for action against foreign operators and asked about support for the 24/7 helpline; PAGCOR committed to continuing the initiative and cited 1% of online gross gaming revenue, or about a billion pesos per annum, for responsible-gaming and social civic projects. Rep. Presley de Jesus challenged whether the first-offense 1,000,000 penalty was sufficient, and PAGCOR said it had been increased from 50,000 and was not the maximum sanction. The chair committed to consolidating documentary requests and following up, leaving interagency enforcement and supporting documents pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR's controls over gambling advertisements, content creators, influencers, and foreign operators were sufficient to protect vulnerable players and deter violations. Members also examined the adequacy of the first-offense penalty, the responsible-gaming helpline and programs, and the enforcement authority available against illegal operators and endorsers.

topics.topic: Responsible-gaming, addiction treatment, and player safeguards
topics.summary: Members questioned PAGCOR about advertising clearance, influencer regulation, illegal foreign operators, and protections for vulnerable online gamblers. PAGCOR described a 24/7 helpline and responsible-gaming programs with the Seagulls Flock Foundation, supported in part by 1% of online gross gaming revenue, or about a billion pesos per annum. The agency said it used KYC and secondary screening to exclude government employees and maintained a restricted-persons list of 15,000 names, while online deposit and activity caps had not yet been set. Vice Chair Brian Poe raised the reopening of illegal sites, cited about 3,000,000,000,000 pesos in estimated annual wagers, and sought enforcement and program-funding documents. PAGCOR committed to continue the helpline and submit responsible-gaming information, while the chair directed that equipment and enforcement questions also be taken up during the ICT budget deliberation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR regulated online gambling and advertising, protected vulnerable players, and funded or operated responsible-gaming, counseling, rehabilitation, and player-exclusion programs. Members also examined enforcement against illegal operators and the safeguards available to minors, government employees, and low-income earners.

topics.topic: Casino Filipino employee transition, retirement, and incentive packages
topics.summary: Bong Thebes Jinger and Jan Attorney Jan Rurik Padiernos raised the status of Casino Filipino privatization and the safeguards for approximately 10,000 employees across about 40 properties. PAGCOR said affected employees would receive regular retirement benefits plus a special incentive package, while acquiring entities would absorb employees where feasible. PAGCOR reported 5,000 completed training initiatives, initial Civil Service-related training for about 80 to 100 people, and a target of about 10,000 training initiatives by year-end. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked whether the 50% UHC earmark would continue after PAGCOR ceased operating casinos and requested projected contributions and a possible stabilization fund. PAGCOR said it had remitted 50,000,000,000 pesos to the national treasury in 2025, implying 25,000,000,000 should have gone to the UHC Fund, but it did not control the national government's onward remittance. The chairman estimated retirement needs at about 28 billion to 30 billion, an existing retirement fund of about 12 billion, and privatization proceeds of about 25 billion to 30 billion, while prioritizing employee retirement before any UHC fund. PAGCOR committed to provide the requested computations and documents within forty eight hours, leaving absorption rules and the UHC stabilization mechanism open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how Casino Filipino privatization would protect approximately 10,000 employees through absorption, training, retirement, and special incentive packages. It also sought to determine how privatization would affect the Universal Health Care earmark and whether PAGCOR or the Executive would provide transition funding or projected remittance figures.

topics.topic: Integrated resorts, gaming service administrators, and PAGCOR’s mandate
topics.summary: Rep. Presley de Jesus asked PAGCOR to define integrated resorts and explain the consequences for other casinos as the sector developed. PAGCOR cited a minimum investment of at least 1,000,000,000 US dollars for an integrated resort, a lowest category of 100,000,000 US dollars, and a license-fee range of 25 to 30 percent; the member described the billion-dollar threshold as around 60 billion in local currency. The member also questioned whether privatization would separate PAGCOR’s operator and regulator roles, but the agency’s response was unclear. On penalties, PAGCOR said the cited first-offense penalty was not the maximum: repeat violations could lead to suspension and then cancellation, with the prior 50,000 penalty calibrated to 1 million. PAGCOR said GSAs had fallen from 74 at their peak to 48, largely because operators surrendered after losing money, and it cited a 9,000,000 pesos minimum guarantee fee effective July 1, 2026. The agency confirmed that casino and online gaming were within PAGCOR’s mandate, while horse racing was under the Philippine Racing Commission; the operator-regulator transition and some financial figures remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to clarify what qualifies as an integrated resort, how casino privatization would affect PAGCOR’s operator-regulator role, and how penalties and gaming service administrator rules would work. It also asked how many gaming service administrators remained, why some surrendered their licenses, and which games fell within PAGCOR’s mandate.

topics.topic: Online-gambling limits, KYC, and government-employee screening
topics.summary: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised concerns about e-wallet restrictions, illegal payment aggregators, declining e-games revenues, and KYC bypasses involving mule accounts and minors. PAGCOR said it was coordinating with the central bank, enforcing KYC and sanctions, and considering a PAGCOR app, while citing more than 106 billion in revenues and other public-purpose allocations. Rep. Michael Gonzalez asked about daily or weekly online-gambling caps, government-employee screening, and permanent player bans; PAGCOR said caps had not yet been set but were expected in proposed legislation, while KYC and screening had prevented close to 5 billion in winnings and covered a restricted list of 15,000 names. Rep. Sherlyn Banas-Nograles asked for stronger safeguards for minors, government employees, low-income earners, and vulnerable sectors, including people affected by micro-bets. PAGCOR identified KYC as its safeguard and said it had provided more than 100,000 relief packs and was constructing 125 school buildings equivalent to about 200 classrooms. The committee left specific General Santos classroom assistance to a written request, while the broader cap issue remained dependent on proposed legislation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR was controlling online-gambling access and risks, including e-wallet use, illegal operators, KYC compliance, wager or deposit limits, government-employee participation, and exclusion of vulnerable or prohibited players. Members also asked what safeguards and assistance programs PAGCOR maintained for affected communities.

topics.topic: Infrastructure, hospital, cancer-center, and special-needs-school assistance
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes questioned PAGCOR's UHC remittances, privatization proceeds, and infrastructure priorities, and PAGCOR undertook to submit a remittance listing within 48 hours. PAGCOR said it was current with National Treasury remittances and estimated possible privatization proceeds at about 20 billion to 30 billion, while the detailed PhilHealth treatment of those proceeds remained partly unclear. Rep. Jean Baronda sought support for cancer-center equipment and schools serving children with special needs, and PAGCOR said it would seriously consider those requests. Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles asked about General Santos relief and roughly 1,400 damaged classrooms; PAGCOR cited more than 100,000 relief packs and a program for 125 new school buildings. Rep. Marco Wangkol sought help for a Pangasinan hospital project estimated at about 1 billion, but PAGCOR advised that equipment for a completed building was more feasible than partial construction funding. The requests landed as conditional commitments requiring follow-up letters, coordination, and project completion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR was complying with its Universal Health Care remittance obligations and whether its social funds, infrastructure programs, and affiliated foundations could support hospitals, cancer-center equipment, damaged classrooms, and schools serving children with special needs. Members also sought to identify the process and conditions for obtaining such assistance, including for a Pangasinan hospital project.

topics.topic: PAGCOR data submissions and supporting budget documentation
topics.summary: Committee members sought documentary support for PAGCOR's remittances, school-building allocations, revenue mix, and the effects of Casino Filipino privatization on UHC funding. PAGCOR said its school-building agreement covered 125 buildings and roughly about 1,500 classrooms at a total cost of about 7.5 billion, with close to about 3.5 billion earmarked for down payments. It maintained that it remitted its shares to the National Treasury, while the National Treasury was responsible for transferring the relevant 50% to PhilHealth or the UHC fund. PAGCOR cited 2025 National Treasury remittances of more or less 50 billion, implying 25 billion for UHC, and estimated privatization proceeds at roughly 25 billion to 30 billion after revisions, with retirement obligations estimated at about 28 billion to 30 billion. Members also requested detailed revenue lists, including projected Casino Filipino revenue of 9 to 10 billion, licensed-casino revenue of about 31.5 billion, and digital e-games revenue stated as 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038. PAGCOR committed to provide the requested records and computations, generally within forty eight hours, but the committee ended the briefing before the submissions could be examined.
topics.question: The committee sought to obtain the records and computations needed to evaluate PAGCOR's proposed budget, including remittances, fund utilization, revenue by source, school-building allocations, and the fiscal effects of privatizing Casino Filipino. It also sought documentation on the Universal Health Care and Philippine Sports Commission remittance bases and on PAGCOR's regulatory and social-civic programs.

topics.topic: FY2027 budget reductions in health, education, social protection, and agriculture
topics.summary: DBM initially explained that lower social-sector allocations reflected continuing 2026 infrastructure allocations, spillovers, and agency implementation capacity rather than zero funding. Congressman Arnan Panaligan challenged reductions in agriculture, health, social services, and education even as the proposed budget rose from about 6.7 trillions to 7,200,000,000,000. Representative Percival Sindania focused on the health allocation, which fell from approximately PHP 458 billion to PHP 362.7 billion, and was told that the change mainly reflected Facilities Enhancement Program utilization, retained medical assistance, an additional 14,000,000,000 PhilHealth subsidy, and the one-time return of 60,000,000,000 to PhilHealth. Representative Chel Diokno challenged reductions affecting education, SUCs, TESDA, health, PhilHealth, and DSWD, while DBM cited absorptive capacity, implementation status, and one-time expenditures. Jokno also questioned the 3.99% education computation, and DBM said it included national, Bangsamoro, local-government, and SUC-generated funds and undertook to provide a detailed breakdown. The chair directed the requested health reconciliation, while Jokno's call to reprioritize frontline-sector funding remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why proposed FY2027 allocations for health, education, skills development, social protection, and agriculture were lower despite a larger overall budget, and whether the reductions reflected actual service cuts or one-time 2026 expenditures and agency absorptive capacity. Members also questioned the basis for the education-sector computation and requested reconciliations of the affected appropriations.

topics.topic: PhilHealth subsidy and universal health-care financing
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked how much of the proposed budget would expand UHC financing and services and whether PhilHealth would receive funding beyond member contributions and sin-tax shares. DBM cited about 362.73 billion for the health sector, including about 270.98 billion for DOH and about 74.45 billion for PhilHealth, and confirmed that the PhilHealth subsidy came from sin-tax collections. Rep. Percival Sindania later questioned a decline from roughly 458 billion to 362.7 billion in the functional health allocation and asked whether the decrease represented actual service cuts. DBM attributed the change to agency utilization, the Facilities Enhancement Program, medical-assistance treatment, an additional 14,000,000,000 subsidy for expanded zero-balance billing, and the one-time return of 60,000,000,000 to PhilHealth. Chel Diokno also cited substantial reductions in DOH and PhilHealth budgets and urged reprioritization of health services. The chair directed the DBCC to submit a reconciliation of health-related appropriations for 2025 to 2027, leaving the sufficiency of the overall financing unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the proposed 2027 budget would expand universal health-care financing and service capacity, particularly through PhilHealth, and whether reductions in health-sector appropriations reflected real service cuts or one-time adjustments. Members also asked how the proposed allocations would affect out-of-pocket spending and frontline health services.

topics.topic: Unprogrammed appropriations, including 111,984,000,000 in operations
topics.summary: Members questioned the inclusion and scale of unprogrammed appropriations, including the 2027 operations item of about 111.984 billion and the 50 billion AFP modernization item for 2026. DBM said releases depended on triggers such as excess revenue and that foreign-assisted projects were placed in the item because loan agreements and required approvals were not yet certain. Laila Delima challenged the constitutional basis and identified about 57 billion for PDIC restoration, 42.553 billion for foreign-assisted projects, and 3.6 billion for risk management. Alan Teague asked about the 107.23 billion PDIC transfer and was told it had been treated as excess from the unrestricted portion of the Deposit Insurance Fund. DBM reported that proposed 2027 unprogrammed appropriations were 1.56% of the expenditure program and said there was no international maximum benchmark. The executive indicated that PDIC restoration could depend on excess revenue or a Supreme Court order, while DBM committed to provide project-level information before plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and fiscal basis for including unprogrammed appropriations, the projects and triggers covered by them, and whether the proposed amounts—particularly for foreign-assisted projects and PDIC fund restoration—were justified. Members also asked how the proposed level compared with historical levels and any applicable fiscal benchmarks.

topics.topic: PDIC fund-balance transfer and restoration
topics.summary: Leila de Lima raised the constitutional and policy issue of placing PDIC restoration in unprogrammed appropriations. Rep. Alan Teague then asked Secretary Goh about the transfer, which was 107,230,000,000 pesos, its DOF origin, PDIC Board approval, and its effect on depositor protection. Secretary Goh said the amount came from an unrestricted or excess portion of the deposit insurance fund and was more than sufficient for insurance eventualities. DBM reported that FY2027 unprogrammed appropriations were 1.56% of the expenditure program and cited historical percentages from 2022 through 2026. Members questioned why the full transfer was not restored, while the executive said it had proposed 57,000,000,000 because of fiscal-space constraints and could restore the balance in two tranches or later. The Bangko Sentral governor did not finally endorse the amount and said PDIC consultation was required, leaving adequacy of the restoration unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and fiscal rationale for placing PDIC fund restoration in unprogrammed appropriations, whether the 107,230,000,000 transfer had impaired PDIC's ability to protect depositors, and whether the proposed restoration was sufficient. It also examined the scale of FY2027 unprogrammed appropriations and the timetable for restoring the transferred amount.

topics.topic: Debt service, deficit targets, revenues, and fiscal consolidation
topics.summary: Members questioned debt ratios, debt service, deficit discipline, revenue forecasts, and the credibility of the 2027 fiscal-consolidation path. Agencies reported a national-government debt-to-GDP ratio of 64.9%, debt service of about 1.1 trillion, and a 2027 deficit of about 3.304 trillion pesos, while explaining that lower growth assumptions reflected external shocks and weaker domestic conditions. DBCC officials said lower GDP assumptions would reduce revenues, and they attributed the 2026 shortfall of about 180 billion mainly to consumption taxes, including about 175 billion in VAT-related effects. The committee also challenged the 2027 revenue projection of about 5.2 trillion and the 101.5 billion privatization assumption, with DOF citing Semirara and CBK proceeds. DBM said contingencies included savings, flexible agency line items, early assistance for El Nino, and reprioritization during execution. The chair directed the DBCC to submit multiple downside scenarios and reconciliations, leaving the issue committed to further documentation rather than fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget's revenue, borrowing, debt-service, deficit, and privatization assumptions were credible and whether fiscal risks had been adequately planned for. Members also asked what spending was being displaced by debt service, how weaker growth would affect revenues and debt, and what contingencies would be available if collections fell short or external shocks occurred.

topics.topic: Industrialization, manufacturing employment, and quality-job creation
topics.summary: Minority members questioned whether the 2027 budget would create quality jobs, citing a manufacturing-job target of 336 to 396,000 for 2025 alongside declines of about 177,000 in manufacturing employment and 226,000 in industry employment. DBM officials said better-quality jobs were generally wage-and-salaried positions and argued that recovery, infrastructure, energy, connectivity, and business reforms would improve employment. Congressman Arnan Panaligan pressed for a clear industrial policy, while the DBM responded that structural constraints had to be addressed before industry could become competitive. Representative Elijah San Fernando called for greater ambition and raised energy costs, including possible electricity VAT relief; economic officials said relief required replacement revenue. DEPDev also said industrial policy was reflected in the Philippine Development Plan and could work if basic constraints were fixed. The committee did not receive a firm estimate of 2027 industry jobs, and concerns about PACSILICA's strategic, environmental, and social implications remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the 2027 budget and the government's economic program had a credible industrial policy to reverse manufacturing and industry employment declines and create better-paying, higher-quality jobs. Members also asked whether energy costs, infrastructure, coordination, and the PACSILICA initiative would support industrialization.

topics.topic: Infrastructure allocation, project selection, and absorptive capacity
topics.summary: Members questioned whether the infrastructure increase was justified by implementation readiness, absorptive capacity, economic multipliers, and regional needs. DBM said the 2027 NEP infrastructure allocation was 4.4% of GDP and that PPP projects could move the ratio closer to the 5% benchmark; it also defended the DPWH increase as funding implementation-ready projects with greater multiplier effects. Members raised traffic losses of about 3.5 billion pesos a day, delayed foreign-assisted projects, right-of-way problems, and LGU permitting and political obstacles. DBM said right-of-way would now precede project approval, agencies were being required to coordinate with LGUs earlier, and DILG intervention could be sought. Rep. Nazal challenged whether SARO releases translated into actual implementation and requested detailed Fisaro project records, while the chair stress-tested the 2027 revenue and privatization assumptions. The hearing produced several commitments for documents and coordination, but did not fully resolve project execution, regional allocation, or financing-risk concerns.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether proposed infrastructure allocations were supported by implementation readiness, absorptive and monitoring capacity, sound project-selection criteria, regional equity, and credible financing assumptions. Members also asked whether delayed releases, local-government obstacles, and weak execution were reducing economic returns and contributing to underspending.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted projects, delays, and commitment fees
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice requested a breakdown and status report for support to foreign-assisted projects, and DBM committed to submit it before plenary. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula asked about fees and penalties from delayed projects; DOF reported about 3.4 billion in commitment fees since 2022 during the Marcos administration, while clarifying that these were not technically penalties. Rep. Albert Garcia pressed for cumulative data on penalties and delay-related project costs, and DBM said delays more commonly produced cost overruns, with some projects potentially doubling in cost. The agencies identified right-of-way acquisition as a principal cause of delay and said ICC now required it before project approval. Leila de Lima challenged the placement of about 42.553 billion in foreign-assisted-project support in UA, while the executive said the amount covered loan proceeds for projects still awaiting approval or loan signing. The Supreme Court issue and comprehensive penalty and cost data remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how foreign-assisted projects were being programmed, monitored, and delayed; whether delays caused commitment fees, penalties, or cost overruns; and what documentation and corrective measures the executive agencies would provide. It also examined why support for foreign-assisted projects was placed in unprogrammed appropriations and how the executive would respond to constitutional challenges.

topics.topic: Regional equity and Mindanao's proposed budget share
topics.summary: Rep. Romeo Momo first argued that regional allocation criteria should account for infrastructure deficits, land area, and road length, not only per capita funding. Rep. Jila then questioned the gap between RDC priorities and the central budget process, while DBM and DEPDev officials described ongoing efforts to harmonize planning and budgeting. A DEPDev official said about 30% to 35% of RDC priorities were reflected in the GAA, compared with 50% in the NEP. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez challenged Mindanao's 15.1% share, citing its 22.3% population share, 18% to 19% contribution to gross national product, and seven of the country's 10 poorest provinces. DBM said Mindanao had the highest average increase outside NCR from 2026 to 2027 and that centrally managed funds might not yet be attributed to the region. Rodriguez requested an increase to at least 20%, and DEPDev confirmed receipt of the supporting RDC resolution, but no increase was agreed to.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether Mindanao's 15.1% share of the proposed regional budget was equitable given its population, economic contribution, poverty levels, and development needs. Members also examined whether regional development priorities were being incorporated into the national budget and whether the share could be increased before approval.

topics.topic: Bottom-up budgeting and regional development council priorities
topics.summary: Rep. Jila raised the need for a genuine bottom-up process linking barangay, local, provincial, and regional priorities to agency ceilings and the national budget. DBM and DepDev said they were harmonizing planning and budgeting calendars and portals, but acknowledged that only about 30% to 35% of RDC priorities appeared in the GAA, compared with 50% in the NAP. Rep. Albert Garcia connected weak regional planning and connectivity to traffic losses, migration to Metro Manila, and delayed foreign-assisted projects; DBM answered that mass transit, regional connectivity, and right-of-way reforms were priorities. Rep. Rufus pressed for proactive DBM engagement with RDCs and a 20% Mindanao budget share, while DBM cited a 10.6% increase in one Mindanao region and said the allocation issue remained a work in progress. Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia later questioned bottom-up budgeting, meritocracy, CREATE MORE, and local PPPs; officials described ongoing performance reforms, cited registered investments of about 1.9 trillion, and reported about 50 LGU PPP proposals and three awarded local PPP contracts. The hearing produced commitments on calendar and planning reforms, right-of-way sequencing, and submission of comparative PPP and delay data, but did not resolve the regional allocation gap.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether bottom-up and top-down budgeting processes adequately incorporated priorities identified by local and regional development councils into agency ceilings, the national investment program, and the General Appropriations Act. Members also examined whether regional connectivity, Mindanao's budget share, local government PPPs, and related planning and investment systems were sufficiently decentralized and demand-driven.

topics.topic: NTA distribution, LGSF releases, and additional LGU fiscal transfers
topics.summary: Roman Romulo questioned whether the NTA formula gave municipalities an inequitable share compared with cities and whether utilization, poverty, absorptive capacity, and performance should affect distribution. DBM said municipalities generally received less because the Local Government Code formula controlled the allocation, while finance officials said the formula would be studied with the World Bank. Members also questioned additional LGU transfers, including about 58.5 billion in LGSF and other funds, and DBM cited lower-income LGUs, devolved functions, and the Mandanas-Garcia framework as grounds for assistance. Rep. Rami Salamat asked about underspending and LGU obstacles; Secretary Kim reported a midyear 2026 program of 3.176 against actual disbursement of about R3.175, or about R1 billion short, and agreed to submit department-level figures. Rep. Allan Ty examined LGSF releases, including PHP57.872 billion for 2026, almost 54 billion released by July 31, and a little over 7 billion remaining. The hearing also covered savings allocations, including about 6.1 billion identified under the 2026 GAA, although one 2025 savings figure was garbled and required further verification.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the NTA and other LGU transfers were distributed equitably and released under the law, particularly in light of differences between cities and municipalities. Members also examined LGSF availability and releases, savings and unused appropriations, underspending, and obstacles created by LGUs in implementing nationally funded projects.

topics.topic: Budget execution rules under NBC 595, SAROs, SAAs, and NCAs
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether NBC 595 imposed release conditions beyond the veto message and why specific DPWH projects required SAROs or additional internal allotment documents. DBM said NBC 595 requirements were intended to establish implementation readiness, and that a SARO provided obligational authority while an NCA concerned cash disbursement. DBM deferred questions about withholding SAAs and project-level implementation to the concerned departments, while acknowledging that cash availability should not prevent procurement or obligation. Rep. Rami Salamat raised underspending and LGU permitting or political obstacles; DBM said 2026 midyear disbursement was about 1 billion below program and undertook to provide departmental figures and consult DILG. Rep. Allan Ty then examined LGSF releases, including about 54 billion released as of July 31 and a little over 7 billion remaining, and questioned savings declarations ranging from about 12.87 billion for FY 2025 to about 6.1 billion under the 2026 GAA. The committee obtained commitments for documents and verification, but the precise savings figures and whether delayed obligations became manufactured savings were left open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and administrative basis for release conditions under NBC 595, and to clarify the respective functions of SAROs, SAAs, allotment authority, and NCAs. Members also examined whether delayed project awards, LGU permitting obstacles, and declarations of savings contributed to underspending or created manufactured savings.
